title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Why this book
Macroeconomics begins with facts. How fast have living standards risen? Why are some countries so much richer than others? How do output, unemployment and inflation move when the economy turns down? We need answers from the data before we can build a model. Models are our best attempt to explain the facts, and the facts tell us which models deserve our attention.
This book follows that idea in two steps:

Find the facts with data science. You download, plot and explore real macroeconomic data, and you decide for yourself what pattern the data show.
Explain the facts with macroeconomic models. You move sliders, change parameters and edit the Python code of each model, and you check how well it accounts for the facts you found.

Each chapter is an interactive notebook. You can read it on this website or run it in Google Colab, with nothing to install.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Stylized facts: where models begin
A stylized fact is a broad pattern in the data that holds across many countries or over long periods. It is “stylized” because it leaves out details and exceptions. Not every year or every country fits it exactly, but the pattern is strong enough that a good theory should explain it.
The term comes from the economist Nicholas Kaldor. In Kaldor (1961), he argued that theory should start from a summary of the facts, not from convenient assumptions. He then listed six stylized facts of economic growth:

Output per worker grows at a roughly constant rate over long periods.
Capital per worker also grows over time.
The rate of return on capital is roughly constant.
The ratio of capital to output is roughly constant.
The shares of labor and capital in national income are roughly constant.
The growth rate of output per worker differs widely across countries.

These six facts set the agenda for growth theory. With technological progress, the Solow model (Chapters 5 and 6) reproduces the first five. The sixth raised a new question, why countries differ so much, which Chapters 3 to 6 take up.
Stylized facts are not carved in stone. They summarize the data, so new data can revise them. Take labor’s share of income, long described as “about two-thirds.” Jones (2024, Chapter 2) notes that it has drifted down since around 1970. In the Chapter 2 notebook, you check this yourself with the latest U.S. national accounts. Labor earned 0.65 of income on average from 1950 to 2025, close to two-thirds, but its share has been below 0.60 since 2022. Is the old fact still a fact? The data alone do not settle it, but they tell you exactly which question to ask.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
section: From data to facts: the data-science step
text:
From data to facts: the data-science step
Jones (2024) gives data a central role. Its chapters are full of figures of real economies, and its models are judged by how well they explain what those figures show. This book takes one more step. Instead of reading the facts from a printed figure, you derive them yourself.
Every data figure in this book is interactive. Each one is built from public data, usually updated to the latest available year. You can:

Explore the figures. Hover over any point to read its value, zoom into a period, or press play to watch countries move over time.
Change the question. Switch countries, years and variables with simple widgets or a one-line change in the code. Does the fact you see for the United States also hold for Japan, Brazil or Nigeria? Does it survive if the sample starts in 1990 instead of 1960?
Get fresh data. Appendix B shows how to download data directly from FRED, the World Bank, the IMF, the ECB, Eurostat, the OECD, the Penn World Table, the Maddison Project and Our World in Data. Your facts can be as current as the data.
Go further with AI. Colab includes Gemini, an AI assistant that can explain a line of code, fix an error or write a new plot from a plain-language request. Other assistants, such as Claude or ChatGPT, work just as well. Use them freely, but always check what they produce. An AI assistant can write code that runs and still answers the wrong question.

The aim is not to replace the facts in Jones (2024). It is to make you comfortable asking the data a question and judging the answer, which is what macroeconomists do every day.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
section: From facts to models: the modeling step
text:
From facts to models: the modeling step
Once you have a fact, you want to know why it holds. That is the job of a model. The models in this book follow those in Jones (2024):

The long run: the production model, the Solow model and the Romer model of ideas.
The short run: the IS curve, monetary policy, the Phillips curve and the AS/AD framework.
Applications: consumption, investment, government budgets, trade and exchange rates.

Here, however, you can operate every model:

On this website, each model figure has a slider. Move it to see how the outcome changes with a parameter.
In Colab, each model figure has live sliders and buttons that solve the model again as you move them.
In the code, each model is a few lines of plain Python, right next to its figure. Change a parameter, add a shock or replace an equation, and see what happens. This is where you can go beyond the textbook.

Then you close the loop by putting the model next to the data. Which facts does the model explain? Which does it miss? A model that misses an important fact is not a failure; it is the reason for the next chapter. For example, the Solow model explains much of why some countries are rich and others poor. On its own, however, it cannot explain why growth continues decade after decade. The economics of ideas in Chapter 6 fills that gap.

text:
A companion to Jones (2024), not a substitute
This book is an interactive data-science companion to Jones (2024). Its 21 chapters have the same titles and follow the same order, so you can work through the two books side by side. I recommend reading a chapter of Jones (2024) first, for the economic reasoning and the full discussion. Then open the matching notebook to work with the data and the models. The notebooks do not repeat the textbook’s explanations, and they do not replace it.
This book is independent. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or the publisher of the textbook. Every figure is an original adaptation, drawn with this book’s own code:

Data figures are inspired by figures in Jones (2024). They are rebuilt from public data, usually updated to the latest year and extended to other countries.
Model figures are adapted from its diagrams, with their own parameter values, layout and interactive controls.

A Sources note below every figure names the figure in Jones (2024) that inspired it and links to the data sources, so you can open them and explore the data yourself.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Who this book is for

Undergraduate students in intermediate macroeconomics, who want to see the ideas of the course at work in real data and learn practical Python along the way.
Master’s students in business, public policy and development programs, who need a hands-on, data-driven understanding of the macroeconomy for analysis and policy work.
Self-learners, who want a hands-on path through macroeconomics at their own pace, with no software to install.
Data-science learners, who know some Python and want meaningful economic questions to apply it to.
Macroeconomists, who know the theory and want to learn Python for data science with models they already know.

No programming experience is assumed. Appendix A is a guided tour of Colab, Python and the data-science libraries used in the book. Appendix C reviews the math, with Python code for each calculation.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
How the book is organized
Like Jones (2024), this book is built around one famous graph: U.S. GDP per person since 1870. The graph shows a long-run upward trend and short-run fluctuations around it, and it raises the question of what the future holds. The chapters follow these three themes:

Preliminaries (Chapters 1–2): what macroeconomics studies and how we measure the macroeconomy.
The long run (Chapters 3–8): economic growth, production, the Solow model, ideas, the labor market and inflation.
The short run (Chapters 9–15): economic fluctuations, the Great Recession and the Covid-19 pandemic, the IS curve, monetary policy and the Phillips curve, the AS/AD framework, financial crises and DSGE models.
Applications and microfoundations (Chapters 16–20): consumption, investment, the government, international trade and exchange rates.
Conclusion (Chapter 21): parting thoughts on what macroeconomics has learned and what remains open.
Appendices A–C: Colab and Python, live access to macroeconomic data, and a math review.

Every chapter has the same structure:

A Model overview builds the chapter’s main model step by step, from assumptions to solution and predictions, and ends with the model in code.
Thematic sections work through the chapter’s figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, …). Each figure comes with a goal, the code that draws it, and a “What to notice” summary.
Your turn tasks, with hints, ask you to change the data or the model and interpret the result.
Concluding remarks sum up what the data showed and what the models explained.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each model figure gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


The data figures of this chapter let you add other countries. On the website, a menu above each of these figures adds a group of countries (the G7, a world region, …); the next cell builds those menus.

# @title Helpers for the website's country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_traces(data, y, skip, x="year", fmt=".1f", markers=False):
    """One line per country of a long table (country, x, y), leaving out the countries in skip."""
    extra = {}
    for name, part in data.groupby("country"):
        if name not in skip:
            extra[name] = [go.Scatter(x=part[x], y=part[y], name=name, mode="lines+markers" if markers else "lines",
                                      line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=2),
                                      hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: %{{y:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>")]
    return extra


def country_menu(fig, extra, countries):
    """Add the extra countries' traces hidden, and a menu that shows one group of them (G7, a region, ...).

    The traces already in fig (the textbook's) stay as they are, and slider steps only switch those."""
    n = len(fig.data)
    owner = []
    for name, traces in extra.items():
        for trace in traces:
            trace.visible = False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(name)
    groups = {"G7": countries.country[countries.g7], "G20": countries.country[countries.g20],
              "OECD": countries.country[countries.oecd]}
    for region in sorted(countries.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = countries.country[countries.region == region]
    rest, autoscale = list(range(n, len(fig.data))), {"yaxis.autorange": True}
    buttons = [dict(label="Textbook only", method="update", args=[{"visible": [False] * len(owner)}, autoscale, rest])]
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in set(members) for o in owner]
        if any(visible):
            buttons.append(dict(label=f"+ {label} ({sum(visible)})", method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, autoscale, rest]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=0, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        for step in slider.steps:
            step.args = [{"visible": list(step.args[0]["visible"])}, step.args[1], list(range(n))]
    return fig

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Model overview
Macroeconomics asks big questions: why living standards in some countries are many times those in others, why whole economies sometimes shrink, and why prices sometimes rise quickly. To answer them, economists first collect the facts and then build a model: a simplified economy written as a few equations. We feed the model some numbers that we choose, and it tells us the outcomes we want to explain.
This first chapter has no large model yet, but it already relies on four tools that return in every later chapter, and this section derives each of them step by step. The first two are measurement tools: the rates and ratios behind the facts of Figs. 1–5, and the arithmetic of compound growth behind Figs. 1 and 7. The last two show how a model works, with the smallest model there is: supply and demand in the labor market, first on its own and then with a minimum wage (Figs. 6 and 8). At the end, ### The model in code turns the results into Python functions and checks each of them with numbers.
A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number the model builder chooses, such as \(\bar{a}\) or \(\bar{f}\). Letters without a bar are endogenous variables: the model determines them. A subscript \(t\) marks the year, as in \(y_t\). In the code we simply write a, l and f.

Measuring the facts: rates, ratios and the output gap

Definitions
Almost every number in this chapter is a rate or a ratio, not a total. Dividing by the right total makes a small country comparable with a large one, and 1960 comparable with 2025.

Inflation. Let \(P_t\) be the price level in year \(t\), for example a consumer price index. The inflation rate is the percentage change of prices over one year (Fig. 3): \[\pi_t = 100\times\frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}}.\]
Jobs. Each adult is employed (\(E\)), unemployed (\(U\): has no job but is looking for one), or out of the labor force. The labor force is \(LF = E + U\), and \(Pop\) is the adult population. Three ratios describe the labor market: \[u = \frac{U}{LF}\ \ \text{(unemployment rate, Fig. 4)}, \qquad e = \frac{E}{Pop}\ \ \text{(employment-population ratio, Fig. 2)}, \qquad p = \frac{LF}{Pop}\ \ \text{(participation rate)}.\]
Deficits. With \(Y\) for GDP, both deficits of Fig. 5 are measured as shares of GDP: \[\text{budget deficit} = \frac{\text{government spending} - \text{government revenue}}{Y}, \qquad \text{trade deficit} = \frac{\text{imports} - \text{exports}}{Y}.\] A negative deficit is a surplus.
Potential output. \(Y^{pot}_t\) is what the economy would produce if all prices could adjust freely and all workers and machines were fully used. Actual output \(Y_t\) moves around it (Fig. 7).



Deriving the key relations
Step 1: from inflation back to prices. Multiply the definition of \(\pi_t\) by \(P_{t-1}/100\), then add \(P_{t-1}\) to both sides:
\[P_t = P_{t-1}\left(1 + \frac{\pi_t}{100}\right).\]
Each year multiplies the price level by a factor \(1 + \pi_t/100\). Inflation of 3,080 percent, as in Argentina in 1989 (Fig. 3), multiplies prices by \(1 + 30.8 = 31.8\) in a single year. For prices to rise a thousandfold within one year we need \(1 + \pi/100 = 1000\), that is \(\pi = 99{,}900\) percent. Over several years the yearly factors multiply:
\[\frac{P_T}{P_0} = \left(1 + \frac{\pi_1}{100}\right)\left(1 + \frac{\pi_2}{100}\right)\cdots\left(1 + \frac{\pi_T}{100}\right).\]
Two years of 10 percent inflation raise prices by \(1.1 \times 1.1 = 1.21\), that is by 21 percent and not 20: the second year’s inflation also applies to the first year’s increase.
Step 2: employment, participation and unemployment. Start from \(E = LF - U\) and divide both sides by \(Pop\). Then take \(LF/Pop\) out as a common factor:
\[e = \frac{E}{Pop} = \frac{LF - U}{Pop} = \frac{LF}{Pop}\left(1 - \frac{U}{LF}\right),\]
so that
\[e = p\,(1 - u). \tag{1}\]
The share of adults with a job is the share in the labor force times the share of the labor force that has a job. So the employment-population ratio of Fig. 2 can fall for two different reasons: more people are unemployed, or people stop looking for work. In February 2020 about 63.3 percent of U.S. adults were in the labor force and 3.5 percent of them were unemployed, so \(e = 63.3 \times (1 - 0.035) \approx 61.1\) percent, the value in Fig. 2.
Step 3: the output gap. The gap measures how far actual output is from potential, in percent of potential:
\[\text{gap}_t = 100\times\left(\frac{Y_t}{Y^{pot}_t} - 1\right). \tag{2}\]
Multiplying out gives the gap in dollars, \(Y_t - Y^{pot}_t = (\text{gap}_t/100)\times Y^{pot}_t\). The same formula works per person: dividing both outputs by the population leaves the ratio \(Y_t/Y^{pot}_t\) unchanged, so the gap in percent is the same, and the gap in dollars per person is \((\text{gap}_t/100)\times Y^{pot}_t/Pop_t\). For small gaps, \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) (Appendix C.6) gives the log form \(\text{gap}_t \approx 100\,(\ln Y_t - \ln Y^{pot}_t)\). The short-run chapters measure fluctuations in this way.
Step 4: why divide by GDP. The growth rate of a ratio is the growth rate of its numerator minus that of its denominator (Appendix C.5). For a deficit \(D\),
\[g_{D/Y} \approx g_D - g_Y.\]
A deficit that grows as fast as GDP keeps the same weight in the economy, even though in dollars it is many times larger than in 1960. That is why Fig. 5 compares shares of GDP and not dollars.


What the numbers tell us
The two labor-market ratios. The table reads equation (1) one input at a time, at the February 2020 values \(p = 63.3\%\) and \(u = 3.5\%\):








A change of …
changes \(e = p(1-u)\) by
Why




\(+1\) point in the unemployment rate \(u\)
\(-p \approx -0.63\) points
a point of \(u\) is a point of the labor force, not of all adults


\(+1\) point in the participation rate \(p\)
\(+(1-u) \approx +0.97\) points
most new participants find a job



In logs, \(\ln e = \ln p + \ln(1-u)\) (Appendix C.4), so the percentage change of \(e\) splits exactly into a participation part and an unemployment part. By April 2020 participation had dropped to about 60.1 percent and unemployment had jumped to about 14.8 percent. The check in ### The model in code shows that roughly 70 percent of the fall in \(e\) came from higher unemployment and 30 percent from people leaving the labor force.
The output gap is negative in a recession and positive in a boom. Its log form is accurate only for small gaps: for a gap as deep as the Great Depression’s, the two versions differ by about 2 points (see the check below).



Growth rates and compound growth

Definitions
The growth rate of a variable \(y_t\), such as GDP per person, from year \(t\) to year \(t+1\) is its percentage change, written as a decimal:
\[g_t = \frac{y_{t+1} - y_t}{y_t} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad y_{t+1} = y_t\,(1 + g_t).\]
The inflation rate of the block above is the growth rate of the price level, times 100. The average annual growth rate between year 0 and year \(T\) is the one constant rate \(g\) that would carry \(y_0\) to \(y_T\) in \(T\) years.


Solving: compound growth
Step 1: growth at a constant rate. If \(y\) grows at the same rate \(g\) every year, apply the rule year after year and substitute each line into the next:
\[y_1 = y_0(1+g), \qquad y_2 = y_1(1+g) = y_0(1+g)^2, \qquad y_3 = y_2(1+g) = y_0(1+g)^3, \qquad \dots\]
After \(t\) years, therefore,
\[y_t = y_0\,(1+g)^t. \tag{3}\]
This is compound growth (Appendix C.3): each year’s growth applies to a level that already includes the growth of all the years before.
Step 2: the average growth rate. Solve equation (3) for \(g\), with \(T\) years. Divide by \(y_0\), raise both sides to the power \(1/T\) (because \(\left((1+g)^T\right)^{1/T} = 1+g\)), and subtract 1:
\[\frac{y_T}{y_0} = (1+g)^T \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left(\frac{y_T}{y_0}\right)^{1/T} = 1 + g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g = \left(\frac{y_T}{y_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1. \tag{4}\]
Fig. 7 applies this formula to U.S. GDP per person from 1870 to 2025, with \(T = 155\): the answer is about 1.9 percent a year. Read backwards, the same formula tells us the growth rate a target needs: a tenfold rise in a century needs \(g = 10^{1/100} - 1 \approx 2.3\) percent a year.
Step 3: logs and the ratio scale. Take the natural log of equation (3), using \(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\) and \(\ln(x^t) = t\ln x\) (Appendix C.4):
\[\ln y_t = \ln y_0 + t\,\ln(1+g).\]
The log of \(y\) is a straight line in time, with slope \(\ln(1+g)\). A ratio scale draws exactly this, so a series that grows at a constant rate is a straight line in Figs. 1 and 7, and a steeper line means faster growth. Every doubling covers the same vertical distance, because \(\ln(2y) - \ln y = \ln 2\) whatever the level of \(y\). For small \(g\), \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\) (Appendix C.6), which gives a second way to compute an average growth rate: \(g \approx (\ln y_T - \ln y_0)/T\).
Step 4: the rule of 70. How many years does it take for \(y\) to double? Put \(y_T/y_0 = 2\) into equation (3) and take logs: \(T\ln(1+g) = \ln 2\), so \(T = \ln 2/\ln(1+g)\). Now use \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\) and \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\):
\[T_{\text{double}} \approx \frac{0.70}{g} = \frac{70}{100\,g}. \tag{5}\]
In words: divide 70 by the growth rate in percent. At 1.9 percent a year, U.S. income per person doubles about every \(70/1.9 \approx 37\) years, a little over four doublings between 1870 and 2025.


What the model predicts
Small differences in growth rates add up. Write equation (3) for two countries and divide one by the other. Relative income changes by the factor \(\left((1+g_1)/(1+g_2)\right)^t\), and in logs
\[\ln\frac{y_{1,t}}{y_{2,t}} = \ln\frac{y_{1,0}}{y_{2,0}} + t\left[\ln(1+g_1) - \ln(1+g_2)\right] \approx \ln\frac{y_{1,0}}{y_{2,0}} + t\,(g_1 - g_2).\]
A gap of only half a percentage point, kept up for 150 years, changes relative income by \(0.005 \times 150 = 0.75\) in logs, a factor of \(e^{0.75} \approx 2.1\). That is about what happened between the United States and Argentina (Fig. 7).
How the growth rate moves the outcomes. The log form gives the effect of the growth rate on the level after \(T\) years: \(d\ln y_T/dg = T/(1+g) \approx T\). One extra point of growth for 100 years adds about \(100 \times 0.01 = 1\) to \(\ln y_{100}\), which multiplies the final level by about \(e \approx 2.7\). The table shows the same effect exactly, from equations (3) and (5):

How a model works: the labor market

Assumptions
Every model in this book has the same structure. The model builder chooses the inputs, and the model’s equations determine the outcomes:

parameters are inputs that stay fixed, unless the model builder changes them in an experiment;
exogenous variables are inputs that may change over time, along a path the model builder sets in advance (for example a population that grows by 1 percent a year);
endogenous variables are the outcomes, the unknowns that the equations solve for.

The smallest example is a single market for hours of work, with a single wage \(w\). Three equations describe it:
\[L^s = \bar{a}\,w + \bar{\ell} \quad\text{(labor supply)}, \qquad L^d = \bar{f} - w \quad\text{(labor demand)}, \qquad L^s = L^d \quad\text{(the market clears)}.\]








Symbol
Role
Meaning




\(\bar{a} > 0\)
parameter
the slope of labor supply: extra hours offered when the wage rises by one dollar


\(\bar{\ell}\)
parameter (or an exogenous variable)
hours people offer even at a zero wage; it would grow with the population


\(\bar{f}\)
parameter
hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, a measure of its capacity


\(w\), \(L^s\), \(L^d\)
endogenous variables
the wage, the hours supplied and the hours demanded



Labor supply slopes up: a higher wage draws out more hours. Labor demand slopes down: each extra dollar of wage makes one hour less worth hiring. The model has three equations and three unknowns. Once the market clears, \(L^s\) and \(L^d\) are the same number, employment \(L\), so the outcomes are just \(w\) and \(L\). We assume \(\bar{f} > \bar{\ell}\): otherwise workers would offer more hours at a zero wage than the firm wants, and the wage could not be positive.


Solving the model
Step 1: one equation in one unknown. Put the supply and demand equations into the market-clearing condition. Only the wage is left:
\[\bar{a}\,w + \bar{\ell} = \bar{f} - w.\]
Step 2: solve for the wage. Add \(w\) to both sides and subtract \(\bar{\ell}\), so that all the terms with \(w\) are on the left: \(\bar{a}w + w = \bar{f} - \bar{\ell}\), or \((1+\bar{a})\,w = \bar{f} - \bar{\ell}\). Dividing by \(1+\bar{a}\):
\[w^* = \frac{\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}}{1 + \bar{a}}. \tag{6}\]
Step 3: solve for employment. Put \(w^*\) into the demand equation and write everything over the common denominator \(1+\bar{a}\):
\[L^* = \bar{f} - w^* = \frac{(1+\bar{a})\bar{f} - (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})}{1+\bar{a}},\]
so that
\[L^* = \frac{\bar{a}\bar{f} + \bar{\ell}}{1 + \bar{a}}. \tag{7}\]
The supply equation gives the same answer: \(\bar{a}w^* + \bar{\ell} = \left(\bar{a}\bar{f} - \bar{a}\bar{\ell} + \bar{\ell} + \bar{a}\bar{\ell}\right)/(1+\bar{a}) = (\bar{a}\bar{f} + \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\). At \(w^*\) the hours offered equal the hours wanted.
Intuition. The wage is high when firms want many hours (\(\bar{f}\) large) compared with the hours people offer anyway (\(\bar{\ell}\) small). Employment is a weighted average of the two, \(L^* = \frac{\bar{a}}{1+\bar{a}}\bar{f} + \frac{1}{1+\bar{a}}\bar{\ell}\): the more strongly workers respond to the wage, the closer employment gets to what firms would like to hire.
Every slider of Figs. 6 and 8 starts from the values of the textbook’s worked exercise, \(\bar{a} = 2\), \(\bar{\ell} = 30\) and \(\bar{f} = 60\). Then \(w^* = (60 - 30)/3 = 10\) and \(L^* = (2\times60 + 30)/3 = 50\).


What the model predicts
The fourth step of the method is to run experiments: change one input and compare the new outcomes with the old ones. Equations (6) and (7) are straight lines in \(\bar{f}\) and \(\bar{\ell}\), so their coefficients are the effects. For \(\bar{a}\) we differentiate (Appendix C.7): \(w^* = (\bar{f}-\bar{\ell})(1+\bar{a})^{-1}\) gives \(dw^*/d\bar{a} = -(\bar{f}-\bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})^2 = -w^*/(1+\bar{a})\), and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\) moves by the same amount in the opposite direction.

changes \(L^*\) by

\(+\dfrac{w^*}{1+\bar{a}}\)

supply pivots around its zero-wage point



Intuition. A shift of demand is shared between the wage and employment. The wage takes the share \(1/(1+\bar{a})\) and employment the rest: the more responsive workers are, the more a rise in demand shows up as extra hours and the less as higher pay. A shift of supply moves the wage and employment in opposite directions.
Elasticities. Taking logs of equations (6) and (7), \(\ln w^* = \ln(\bar{f}-\bar{\ell}) - \ln(1+\bar{a})\) and \(\ln L^* = \ln(\bar{a}\bar{f}+\bar{\ell}) - \ln(1+\bar{a})\), gives the percentage effects:

Because the model is made of straight lines rather than powers, these elasticities change with the starting point. The model is far simpler than any real labor market, with one wage and no schooling, training or distance, but it already shows the logic of every later model: write the equations, solve them for the endogenous variables, and read off how each input moves each outcome.



Extension: a minimum wage

Assumptions
The textbook’s example of a parameter is a minimum wage set by law, \(\bar{w}_{\min}\). Keep the three equations above, but forbid any wage below the floor. When the floor is above \(w^*\), the wage equals the floor, and nobody can make the firm hire more hours than it wants at that wage. Employment is then read off the demand curve, and the extra hours that workers offer are unemployment:
\[w = \max(w^*, \bar{w}_{\min}), \qquad L = L^d(w) = \bar{f} - w, \qquad U = L^s(w) - L^d(w).\]


Solving the model
Case 1: the floor does not bind, \(\bar{w}_{\min} \le w^*\). Nothing changes: \(w = w^*\), \(L = L^*\) and \(U = 0\).
Case 2: the floor binds, \(\bar{w}_{\min} > w^*\). Then \(w = \bar{w}_{\min}\). Subtract demand from supply at that wage:
\[U = (\bar{a}\,\bar{w}_{\min} + \bar{\ell}) - (\bar{f} - \bar{w}_{\min}) = (1+\bar{a})\,\bar{w}_{\min} - (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}).\]
Equation (6) says that \(\bar{f} - \bar{\ell} = (1+\bar{a})\,w^*\). Substituting it:
\[U = (1+\bar{a})\,(\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*). \tag{8}\]
Employment is \(L = \bar{f} - \bar{w}_{\min} = L^* - (\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*)\).
Intuition. Each dollar of the floor above \(w^*\) does two things at once: the firm hires one hour less, and workers offer \(\bar{a}\) hours more. The gap between them therefore grows by \(1 + \bar{a}\) hours per dollar. With the baseline values, a floor of 12 is 2 dollars above \(w^* = 10\), so employment falls to \(50 - 2 = 48\) and unemployment is \(3 \times 2 = 6\) hours, the numbers Fig. 6 shows.

No curve moves: the floor is a horizontal line in the diagram, and the market slides up the demand curve. Above \(w^*\), each extra dollar of the floor cuts employment by 1 hour and raises unemployment by \(1+\bar{a} = 3\) hours. A floor below the market wage has no effect at all.



The model in code
We now turn the results into Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes. The cells after them check the algebra above with numbers. Every later section of the notebook reuses labor_supply, labor_demand and equilibrium.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing a=2.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. A function can return two results at once, separated by a comma. ** means “to the power of”, and np.log is the natural logarithm.


def labor_supply(w, a=2.0, l=30.0):
    """Hours of work offered at the wage w: L^s = a w + l."""
    return a * w + l


def labor_demand(w, f=60.0):
    """Hours of work the firm wants to hire at the wage w: L^d = f - w."""
    return f - w


def equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """The wage and employment at which supply equals demand: equations (6) and (7)."""
    w_star = (f - l) / (1 + a)
    L_star = labor_demand(w_star, f)
    return w_star, L_star


def average_growth(start, end, years):
    """The constant yearly growth rate that turns `start` into `end` in `years` years: equation (4)."""
    return (end / start) ** (1 / years) - 1


def doubling_time(g):
    """Exact number of years it takes to double at the growth rate g: ln 2 / ln(1 + g)."""
    return np.log(2) / np.log(1 + g)

Let us check the functions against the baseline answer. The wage from equation (6), put into either curve, must give the employment of equation (7).

Python note. w_star, L_star = equilibrium() stores the two results of the function in two variables. An f-string such as f"w* = {w_star:.1f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.1f means “show one decimal”.


w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
print(f"Equilibrium wage       w* = {w_star:.1f}")
print(f"Equilibrium employment L* = {L_star:.1f}   (equation 7: {(2 * 60 + 30) / (1 + 2):.1f})")
print(f"At w*, supply = {labor_supply(w_star):.1f} and demand = {labor_demand(w_star):.1f}: the market clears")

Equilibrium wage       w* = 10.0
Equilibrium employment L* = 50.0   (equation 7: 50.0)
At w*, supply = 50.0 and demand = 50.0: the market clears


Check 1: the elasticities. Raise each parameter by 1 percent and see by what percentage \(w^*\) and \(L^*\) change. The table above predicts \(+2\%\) and \(+0.8\%\) for \(\bar{f}\), \(-1\%\) and \(+0.2\%\) for \(\bar{\ell}\), and \(-0.67\%\) and \(+0.13\%\) for \(\bar{a}\).

w0, L0 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0)
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0 * 1.01)
print(f"1% higher f: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0 * 1.01, f=60.0)
print(f"1% higher l: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0 * 1.01, l=30.0, f=60.0)
print(f"1% higher a: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")

1% higher f: w* +2.00%,  L* +0.80%
1% higher l: w* -1.00%,  L* +0.20%
1% higher a: w* -0.66%,  L* +0.13%


The answers for \(\bar{f}\) and \(\bar{\ell}\) are exact, because \(w^*\) and \(L^*\) are straight lines in those two parameters. For \(\bar{a}\) they are close but not exact, because an elasticity describes very small changes.
Check 2: the minimum wage. For several floors, we compute unemployment directly, as hours supplied minus hours demanded at the wage that holds, and compare the result with equation (8).

Python note. for w_min in (8, 11, 12, 14): runs the indented lines once for each number in the brackets. max(a, b) is the larger of two numbers, so max(w_star, w_min) is the wage that holds, and max(..., 0) turns a negative formula value into zero when the floor does not bind.


w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
for w_min in (8, 11, 12, 14):
    w = max(w_star, w_min)                                   # the wage that holds
    direct = labor_supply(w) - labor_demand(w)               # hours offered minus hours hired
    formula = max((1 + 2.0) * (w_min - w_star), 0)           # equation (8), zero if the floor does not bind
    print(f"floor {w_min:2d}: wage {w:4.1f}, employment {labor_demand(w):4.1f}, "
          f"unemployment {direct:4.1f} (direct) and {formula:4.1f} (equation 8)")

floor  8: wage 10.0, employment 50.0, unemployment  0.0 (direct) and  0.0 (equation 8)
floor 11: wage 11.0, employment 49.0, unemployment  3.0 (direct) and  3.0 (equation 8)
floor 12: wage 12.0, employment 48.0, unemployment  6.0 (direct) and  6.0 (equation 8)
floor 14: wage 14.0, employment 46.0, unemployment 12.0 (direct) and 12.0 (equation 8)


Check 3: compound growth. We let GDP per person grow by 1.9 percent a year for 155 years, one year at a time, and compare the result with equation (3). Then equation (4) must recover the growth rate, and the log formula must come close.

Python note. range(155) counts 0, 1, …, 154, so the for loop runs its indented line 155 times. level = level * (1 + 0.019) replaces the old value by the new one. The underscore _ is a name for a loop counter that we do not need.


level = 1.0
for _ in range(155):
    level = level * (1 + 0.019)                              # one year of growth
print(f"Year by year: level after 155 years = {level:.3f}")
print(f"Equation (3): (1.019)^155           = {(1 + 0.019) ** 155:.3f}")
print(f"Equation (4) recovers g             = {100 * average_growth(1.0, level, 155):.3f}%")
print(f"Log formula (ln y_T - ln y_0) / T   = {100 * (np.log(level) - np.log(1.0)) / 155:.3f}%")
print(f"Tenfold in 100 years needs g        = {100 * average_growth(1, 10, 100):.2f}%")

Year by year: level after 155 years = 18.493
Equation (3): (1.019)^155           = 18.493
Equation (4) recovers g             = 1.900%
Log formula (ln y_T - ln y_0) / T   = 1.882%
Tenfold in 100 years needs g        = 2.33%


Check 4: the rule of 70. Equation (5) against the exact doubling time, and the factor after 100 years, as in the table above.

for g in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10):
    print(f"g = {100 * g:4.1f}%: doubles in {doubling_time(g):5.1f} years (rule of 70: {70 / (100 * g):5.1f}); "
          f"factor after 100 years {(1 + g) ** 100:7.1f}")

g =  1.0%: doubles in  69.7 years (rule of 70:  70.0); factor after 100 years     2.7
g =  2.0%: doubles in  35.0 years (rule of 70:  35.0); factor after 100 years     7.2
g =  3.0%: doubles in  23.4 years (rule of 70:  23.3); factor after 100 years    19.2
g =  5.0%: doubles in  14.2 years (rule of 70:  14.0); factor after 100 years   131.5
g = 10.0%: doubles in   7.3 years (rule of 70:   7.0); factor after 100 years 13780.6


Check 5: two labor-market ratios. We plug the February and April 2020 values into both sides of equation (1). Then we split the fall of \(e\) into its two parts with logs.

Pop, LF = 100.0, 63.3                            # per 100 adults, February 2020: 63.3 in the labor force
U = 0.035 * LF                                   # 3.5 percent of the labor force is unemployed
e_feb = 100 * (LF - U) / Pop                     # left side of equation (1): E / Pop, in percent
print(f"February 2020: E/Pop = {e_feb:.2f}%,   p(1 - u) = {63.3 * (1 - 0.035):.2f}%")
e_apr = 60.1 * (1 - 0.148)                       # equation (1) for April 2020
fall = np.log(e_apr) - np.log(e_feb)
part_p = np.log(60.1) - np.log(63.3)             # participation part
part_u = np.log(1 - 0.148) - np.log(1 - 0.035)   # unemployment part
print(f"April 2020:    e = {e_apr:.1f}%, a fall of {e_feb - e_apr:.1f} points")
print(f"Share of the log fall due to participation: {part_p / fall:.0%}, to unemployment: {part_u / fall:.0%}")
print(f"The two parts add up: {part_p + part_u:.4f} = {fall:.4f}")

February 2020: E/Pop = 61.08%,   p(1 - u) = 61.08%
April 2020:    e = 51.2%, a fall of 9.9 points
Share of the log fall due to participation: 29%, to unemployment: 71%
The two parts add up: -0.1764 = -0.1764


Check 6: compounding prices and the log form of the gap. A year of 3,080 percent inflation, two years of 10 percent, and equation (2) against its log form for small and large gaps.

print(f"3,080% inflation multiplies prices by {1 + 3080 / 100:.1f}")
print(f"Two years of 10% raise prices by {100 * ((1 + 0.10) * (1 + 0.10) - 1):.0f}%")
for ratio_to_potential in (0.953, 0.83, 1.23):
    exact = 100 * (ratio_to_potential - 1)                   # equation (2)
    approx = 100 * np.log(ratio_to_potential)                # log form
    print(f"Y / Y_pot = {ratio_to_potential:.3f}: gap {exact:+6.1f}% (equation 2), {approx:+6.1f}% (log form)")

3,080% inflation multiplies prices by 31.8
Two years of 10% raise prices by 21%
Y / Y_pot = 0.953: gap   -4.7% (equation 2),   -4.8% (log form)
Y / Y_pot = 0.830: gap  -17.0% (equation 2),  -18.6% (log form)
Y / Y_pot = 1.230: gap  +23.0% (equation 2),  +20.7% (log form)


The log form is within a tenth of a point for a gap like 2009’s, but it is off by almost 2 points for the Great Depression’s 17 percent, and by more than 2 for the wartime boom of 1944.

Income over time and across countries
The first big fact of macroeconomics is how unequal incomes are, both across countries and across time. We compare GDP per person for six economies and for many more.

Fig. 1: GDP per person in six countries
Goal. Document the first big fact of macroeconomics: income differs enormously across countries and over time.
The data come from the Maddison Project, which estimates GDP per person for every country over long periods. GDP (gross domestic product) is the overall income of a country; Chapter 2 explains how it is measured. All values are in 2022 dollars, so they can be compared across years.

Python note. pd.read_csv(...) reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns. DATA_URL + "fig1-1.csv" glues the folder address and the file name together. .head() shows the first five rows.

Before we use a new file, we check that it agrees with the one we trust. For the six countries at the benchmark years, the two files should hold exactly the same numbers.

Python note. .isin(list) is True for the rows whose value is in the list. .merge(other, on=[...]) joins two tables, matching rows with the same year and country; columns with the same name get the endings _x and _y.

check = long.merge(on_benchmarks, on=["year", "country"])

Every country keeps the same color in every figure. The textbook’s countries get fixed colors of our palette, and each of the other countries one of 24 distinct colors.

Python note. for i, name in enumerate(...) hands over each name together with its position i (0, 1, 2, …). i % 24 is the remainder after dividing by 24, so the 24 colors repeat in turn. if name not in COLORS: skips the names that already have a color.

The textbook draws this figure on a ratio scale: each step up the vertical axis doubles the value (1,000, 2,000, 4,000, …). Equal distances then mean equal percentage changes, so a country growing at a steady rate draws a straight line (the log form of equation 3). Chapter 3 explains ratio scales in detail.

Python note. px.line draws one line per value of color=, and color_discrete_map=COLORS fixes each country’s color. log_y=True gives a ratio scale, and tickvals sets the numbers printed on the axis (Plotly’s own labels are hard to read on a ratio scale). On a ratio scale, the axis range is given in powers of ten: np.log10(800). The if ... else blocks run one branch or the other: here they widen the axis, in one step, when a chosen country is very poor or very rich, and x if condition else y picks x when the condition is true. set(chosen) - set(data.country) keeps the chosen names that have no data, and ", ".join(missing) writes them in one line, separated by commas.


BOOK = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Japan", "Argentina", "South Africa", "China")
TICKS = [500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000]


def gdp_per_person(scale="ratio", chosen=BOOK):
    """Fig. 1.1: GDP per person at the textbook's benchmark years, 1870-2022 (2022 dollars)."""
    data = on_benchmarks[on_benchmarks.country.isin(chosen)]
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    title = "2022: U.S. income per person 5× South Africa's; China's up 24-fold since 1950"
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", hover_name="country", markers=True,
                  log_y=(scale == "ratio"), color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  title=title, labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)", "country": "Country"})
    low = 800 if data.gdppc.min() >= 800 else 400              # a very poor country: one step lower
    high = 90000 if data.gdppc.max() <= 90000 else 250000      # a very rich country: one step higher
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=TICKS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high - 10000])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1865, 2027])
    return fig

BOOK_INFLATION = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Euro area", "Japan")


def inflation_chart(chosen=BOOK_INFLATION):
    """Fig. 1.3: CPI inflation, 1960-2025, for the chosen economies."""
    data = world_inflation[world_inflation.country.isin(chosen)]
    for top in [25, 50, 100, 250, 1000, 5000, 25000, 100000]:  # widen the axis in steps
        if data.inflation.max() <= top:
            break
    title = "Inflation peaked in the 1970s (24% in the U.K.) and surged again in 2021–22"
    if set(chosen) != set(BOOK_INFLATION) and len(data) > 0:
        row = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
        title = f"Highest inflation shown: {row.country}, {row.inflation:,.1f}% in {row.year}"
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country", title=title,
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Economy"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[min(-5, data.inflation.min() - 2), top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig

BOOK_UNEMP = ("United States", "Europe", "Japan")


def unemployment_chart(period=(2006, 2025), chosen=BOOK_UNEMP):
    """Fig. 1.4: unemployment rates, with the average Europe/U.S. ratio over a shaded period."""
    start, end = period
    chosen_years = unemp[(unemp.year >= start) & (unemp.year <= end)]
    ratio = (chosen_years["Europe"] / chosen_years["United States"]).mean()
    data = world_unemp[world_unemp.country.isin(chosen)]
    title = f"{start}–{end}: Europe's rate was {ratio:.2f} times the U.S. rate on average"
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="unrate", color="country", hover_name="country", title=title,
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "unrate": "Unemployment rate (percent)", "country": "Economy"})
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    top = 14 if data.unrate.max() <= 14 else (30 if data.unrate.max() <= 30 else 40)   # widen in steps
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1954, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig

text:
What a model does
With the facts in hand, we turn to the tool that explains them. A small live model shows how inputs go in and outcomes come out.

Fig. 6: The structure of economic models
Goal. See what a model does: it takes inputs and determines outcomes.
Every economic model has the same structure. The model builder picks the inputs:

parameters, fixed numbers such as \(\bar{a}\), \(\bar{\ell}\), \(\bar{f}\), or a minimum wage set by law;
exogenous variables, inputs that may change over time in a way the model builder decides in advance, such as the number of people in the economy.

The model, a set of equations, then determines the endogenous variables, here the wage and employment. The textbook draws this as three boxes: inputs → MODEL → outcomes. Below, the boxes are live: every slider is an input, and the right box shows the outcomes the model computes.
We add one input the textbook mentions as an example of a parameter: a minimum wage. If it is below \(w^*\), it has no effect. If it is above \(w^*\), the wage equals the minimum wage, firms hire only the hours they demand at that wage, and the hours that workers offer but cannot sell are unemployment, \(L^s - L^d\), which is equation (8) of the Model overview. (Think of \(\bar{\ell}\) as growing with the number of people in the economy: more people offer more hours at any wage.)

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="rect", ...) draws a rectangle and fig.add_annotation(...) writes text; <br> starts a new line and <b>...</b> makes text bold. An annotation with showarrow=True draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y). max(w_star, w_min) is the larger of the two numbers. The loops run once per box and once per arrow.


def structure_of_models(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0, w_min=0.0):
    """Fig. 1.6 as a live model: inputs (parameters) -> MODEL -> outcomes (endogenous variables)."""
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    w = max(w_star, w_min)                         # a minimum wage above w* sets the wage
    L = labor_demand(w, f)                         # firms hire the hours they demand at that wage
    unemployed = max(labor_supply(w, a, l) - L, 0.0)   # hours offered but not hired (zero, not -0.00, if w = w*)
    inputs = (f"<b>INPUTS</b><br><i>parameters and exogenous<br>variables</i><br><br>supply slope a = {a:.1f}"
              f"<br>hours at zero wage l = {l:.0f}<br>demand at zero wage f = {f:.0f}<br>minimum wage = {w_min:.0f}")
    model = "<b>MODEL</b><br><br>Lˢ = a·w + l<br>Lᵈ = f − w<br>Lˢ = Lᵈ, unless<br>a minimum wage<br>is above w*"
    outcomes = (f"<b>OUTCOMES</b><br><i>endogenous variables</i><br><br>wage w = {w:.2f}"
                f"<br>employment L = {L:.2f}<br>unemployment = {unemployed:.2f}")
    fig = go.Figure()
    for x0, x1, text in [[0.0, 0.33, inputs], [0.39, 0.61, model], [0.67, 1.0, outcomes]]:
        fig.add_shape(type="rect", x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=0.12, y1=0.88, fillcolor="#ecf3fa", line=dict(color=BLUE))
        fig.add_annotation(x=(x0 + x1) / 2, y=0.5, text=text, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    for x_from, x_to in [[0.33, 0.39], [0.61, 0.67]]:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x_to, y=0.5, ax=x_from, ay=0.5, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
                           text="", showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=4, arrowcolor=GREEN)
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Inputs → model → outcomes: wage w = {w:.2f}, employment L = {L:.2f}")
    return fig

Python note. data.iloc[0] is the first row and data.iloc[-1] the last, so the growth formula uses each country’s own first and last year. On a ratio-scale axis, an annotation’s height is also given in powers of ten: y=np.log10(30000).


def per_capita_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 1.7: per capita GDP on a ratio scale with its average growth rate (U.S.: also potential)."""
    if country == "United States":
        data = usgdp.rename(columns={"gdppc_actual": "Actual", "gdppc_potential": "Potential"})
        series = ["Actual", "Potential"]
    else:
        data = world[world.country == country].rename(columns={"gdppc": "Actual"})
        series = ["Actual"]
    first, last = data.iloc[0], data.iloc[-1]
    growth = (last.Actual / first.Actual) ** (1 / (last.year - first.year)) - 1
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=series, log_y=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Per capita GDP (2022 dollars, ratio scale)", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{country}: GDP per person grew {round(100 * growth, 1) + 0.0:.1f}% a year, "
                        f"{first.year:.0f}–{last.year:.0f}")       # + 0.0: no -0.0
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Potential"), line_dash="dash")
    low = 3500 if data.Actual.min() >= 3500 else (1000 if data.Actual.min() >= 1000 else 400)
    high = 100000 if data.Actual.max() <= 100000 else 250000
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000],
                     range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1865, 2030])
    fig.add_annotation(x=1870, y=np.log10(0.8 * high), showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(size=14),
                       text=f"Income in {last.year:.0f}: {last.Actual / first.Actual:.1f} times<br>its {first.year:.0f} level")
    return fig

The textbook reports $4,200 in 1870 and $76,000 in 2022, “more than a factor of 15”. Our 2022 value is close ($77,942). Our 1870 value is about 10 percent higher, because we use newer historical estimates (the Maddison Project) for the years before 1929. The rise is a factor of almost 17, and average growth is 1.9 percent a year, which the textbook rounds to 2 percent.
This series also lets us revisit the claim of Fig. 1. Here, U.S. income in 2022 is about 8.1 times its 1922 level: more than the 5.8 of the Maddison data, but still short of “more than 10 times”. The two sources disagree because estimating income a century ago is hard, and they measure prices differently. When sources disagree, report the range.


The short run: the output gap
This part stays U.S.-only: potential output comes from the CBO, which estimates it only for the United States. (The IMF and the OECD publish output-gap estimates for rich countries, but only since about 1980 and from models that differ from the CBO’s.)
The gap between actual and potential output, in percent, is \(100 \times (\text{actual} / \text{potential} - 1)\) (equation 2). It is negative in recessions. The chart below plots it for every year, and the title converts the gap of the chosen year into dollars per person and for a family of four.

Python note. usgdp["gap"] = ... adds a new column, computed row by row from two other columns. usgdp[usgdp.year == year].iloc[0] picks the one row of the chosen year. px.bar draws a bar chart, and :+,.0f in an f-string shows a sign, thousands separators and no decimals.

def output_gap_chart(year=2009):
    """Fig. 1.7, second feature: actual GDP per person relative to potential, in percent."""
    row = usgdp[usgdp.year == year].iloc[0]
    dollars = row.gdppc_actual - row.gdppc_potential
    fig = px.bar(usgdp, x="year", y="gap", color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL],
                 labels={"year": "Year", "gap": "Actual relative to potential (percent)"})
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[year], y=[row.gap], mode="markers", name=str(year),
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-20, 25])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{year}: gap {row.gap:+.1f}%, or {dollars:+,.0f} dollars per person "
                            f"({4 * dollars:+,.0f} for a family of four)")

text:
Solving a model: the labor market
Finally, we draw the labor-market model from the Model overview and use it for experiments, changing one input at a time.

Fig. 8: The labor market
Goal. Draw the supply-and-demand diagram of the labor market and see how the equilibrium moves when a parameter changes.
The diagram puts employment \(L\) on the horizontal axis and the wage \(w\) on the vertical axis. Labor supply \(L^s = \bar{a}w + \bar{\ell}\) slopes up, and labor demand \(L^d = \bar{f} - w\) slopes down. They cross at the equilibrium \((L^*, w^*)\). When you move a slider away from the textbook’s values, the textbook’s curves stay on the chart as dashed gray lines, so you can see the shift.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 30, 100) creates 100 evenly spaced wages from 0 to 30. Because the wage is on the vertical axis, we compute the hours supplied and demanded at each wage and use them as x. go.Figure() starts an empty chart, and each add_trace adds one curve or set of points. As in the textbook, the curves are named on the chart: add_annotation writes the labels Lˢ and Lᵈ at the ends of the curves, and xanchor/yanchor say which corner of the label touches that point.


def labor_market(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """Fig. 1.8: labor supply and demand, and the equilibrium (L*, w*)."""
    w = np.linspace(0, 30, 100)
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if (a, l, f) != (2.0, 30.0, 60.0):             # keep the textbook's curves for comparison
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_supply(w), y=w, name="Textbook curves (a=2, l=30, f=60)",
                                 line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_demand(w), y=w, showlegend=False, line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_supply(w, a, l), y=w, name="Lˢ", showlegend=False, line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_demand(w, f), y=w, name="Lᵈ", showlegend=False, line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    w_end = min(30, (100 - l) / a)                 # supply leaves the chart at the top or at the right edge
    fig.add_annotation(x=labor_supply(w_end, a, l), y=w_end, text="Lˢ", showarrow=False,
                       xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(size=18, color=TEAL))
    fig.add_annotation(x=labor_demand(30, f), y=30, text="Lᵈ", showarrow=False, xshift=-4,
                       xanchor="right", yanchor="top", font=dict(size=18, color=BLUE))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, L_star, L_star], y=[w_star, w_star, 0], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_star], y=[w_star], mode="markers", name="Equilibrium (L*, w*)",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=12)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Equilibrium: wage w* = {w_star:.2f}, employment L* = {L_star:.2f}", showlegend=True,
                      xaxis=dict(title="Employment, L", range=[0, 100], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Wage, w", range=[0, 30]))
    return fig

What to notice.

With the textbook’s parameters the curves cross at \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\), the answer to the textbook’s worked exercise.
A higher \(\bar{f}\) shifts labor demand to the right: the wage and employment both rise.
A higher \(\bar{\ell}\) shifts labor supply to the right: employment rises but the wage falls.
A larger \(\bar{a}\) makes supply respond more to the wage. The supply curve gets flatter in this diagram, and it pivots around the point where the wage is zero.


Key numbers: three experiments
Equations (6) and (7), \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\) and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\), show how much each parameter moves the outcomes. With \(\bar{a} = 2\), raising \(\bar{f}\) by 3 raises \(w^*\) by \(3/3 = 1\); raising \(\bar{\ell}\) by 3 lowers \(w^*\) by 1.

    print(f"{name:10}  w* = {w_new:5.2f}   L* = {L_new:5.2f}")

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Concluding remarks

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole. Its big questions start from facts like these: huge income gaps across countries, deep recessions such as 2008–09 and 2020, the inflation of the 1970s and of 2021–22, high unemployment in Europe, and large U.S. budget and trade deficits. It answers them in four steps: document the facts, build a model, compare the model with the facts, and use the model for experiments.
A model takes parameters and exogenous variables as inputs and determines the endogenous variables. In the labor-market model, equations (6) and (7) give \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1 + \bar{a})\) and \(L^* = (\bar{a}\bar{f} + \bar{\ell})/(1 + \bar{a})\). A demand shift moves both in the same direction, a supply shift moves them in opposite directions, and a binding minimum wage creates the unemployment of equation (8).
Growth compounds, equation (3). The average growth rate is equation (4), and the rule of 70, equation (5), turns a growth rate into a doubling time. U.S. GDP per person has grown at almost 2 percent a year since 1870 (the long run), doubling about every 37 years, with output gaps, equation (2), that are small except in the Great Depression and World War II (the short run).
The employment-population ratio is the participation rate times the employed share of the labor force, equation (1). Checking claims against the data matters: some textbook numbers hold exactly, others change with newer data.
The next chapter shows how GDP, the measure behind most of these figures, is defined and measured.

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Practice problems
These problems practise the chapter in three ways: conceptual problems apply its equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to its data files, and modeling problems use the labor-market model to answer policy questions. Each one is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it in the answer cell first, and only then open the Hint and the Solution. The sliders of the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website versions of Figs. 6 and 8 above.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): How much did U.S. prices rise in 2021–23? In the data of Fig. 3 (the consumer price index of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (CPIAUCNS), via FRED), U.S. inflation was 4.7 percent in 2021, 8.0 percent in 2022 and 4.1 percent in 2023.

By what percentage was the price level of 2023 higher than that of 2020?
Suppose a news report adds up the three rates and says that prices rose 16.8 percent. Why is that too low?
The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2 percent a year over the longer run. It measures inflation with a different price index, but take the target at face value: how many years of 2 percent inflation would raise prices as much as these three years did?



Hint

Step 1 of the Model overview: each year multiplies the price level by \(1 + \pi_t/100\). For (c), set \(1.02^T\) equal to your factor from (a) and take logs, as in the derivation of the rule of 70.

Your answer:


Solution


The yearly factors multiply:

\[\frac{P_{2023}}{P_{2020}} = 1.047 \times 1.080 \times 1.041 = 1.1771,\]
so the 2023 price level was 17.7 percent above that of 2020. By equation (4), that is an average of \(1.1771^{1/3} - 1 = 5.6\) percent a year.

Adding the rates ignores compounding. Multiply out the product:

\[(1 + 0.047)(1 + 0.080)(1 + 0.041) = 1 + \underbrace{0.047 + 0.080 + 0.041}_{0.168} + \underbrace{0.047 \times 0.080 + 0.047 \times 0.041 + 0.080 \times 0.041 + 0.047 \times 0.080 \times 0.041}_{0.0091}.\]
The sum, 16.8 percent, is only the first part. The cross terms, 0.9 points, are there because the 8.0 percent of 2022 applied to prices that were already 4.7 percent higher, and so on. The longer and higher the inflation, the bigger the error from adding.

Set \(1.02^T = 1.1771\) and take logs:

\[T = \frac{\ln 1.1771}{\ln 1.02} = \frac{0.1631}{0.0198} = 8.2 \text{ years}.\]
In three years, prices rose as much as they would in about eight years at the Fed’s target. Prices do not go back down when inflation falls: in 2023 the price level was 10.9 percent above the path of 2 percent inflation (\(1.1771/1.02^3 = 1.109\)).

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Spain and the United States in the Great Recession: lost jobs or lost workers? The table holds two ratios from this chapter’s data: the employment-population ratio \(e\) (ages 15 and over, ILO modelled estimates via the World Bank) and the unemployment rate \(u\) (Spain: European Commission, AMECO; United States: Bureau of Labor Statistics (UNRATE), via FRED).




\(e\), percent
\(u\), percent

8.2

Use equation (1) to compute the participation rate \(p\) of each country in both years. (The ratios come from different sources, so treat \(p\) as an approximation.)
Split the change of \(\ln e\) from 2007 to 2013 into a participation part and an unemployment part, as in Check 5 of the Model overview. What share of the fall does each part explain, in each country?
In which country did the crisis show up partly as people leaving the labor force? Suggest one reason why participation could even rise in a deep recession.



Hint

Solve equation (1) for \(p\), with \(u\) written as a decimal. Taking logs of equation (1) turns the product into a sum, so the change of \(\ln e\) is the change of \(\ln p\) plus the change of \(\ln(1-u)\).

Your answer:


Solution


Equation (1), \(e = p(1-u)\), gives \(p = e/(1-u)\):





\(p = e/(1-u)\)




Spain, 2007
\(53.5/0.918 = 58.3\)


Spain, 2013
\(43.7/0.739 = 59.1\)


United States, 2007
\(62.0/0.954 = 65.0\)


United States, 2013
\(58.1/0.926 = 62.7\)




In logs, \(\ln e = \ln p + \ln(1-u)\), so \(\Delta\ln e = \Delta\ln p + \Delta\ln(1-u)\).


Spain: \(\Delta\ln e = \ln(43.7/53.5) = -0.202\). The participation part is \(\ln(59.13/58.28) = +0.015\), and the unemployment part is \(\ln(0.739/0.918) = -0.217\). Higher unemployment explains 107 percent of the fall; participation explains \(-7\) percent, because it rose and so softened the fall.
United States: \(\Delta\ln e = \ln(58.1/62.0) = -0.065\). The participation part is \(-0.035\) (54 percent of the fall), and the unemployment part is \(-0.030\) (46 percent).


In the United States, about half of the drop in the share of adults with a job came from people who stopped looking for work. Spain lost far more jobs (its ratio fell by 9.8 points, against 3.9 in the United States), but almost all of the loss shows up in its 26 percent unemployment rate. One reason participation can rise in a slump is the added-worker effect: when one earner of a family loses a job, others start to look for work to keep up the family’s income. The lesson for reading Figs. 2 and 4 is that the same fall of \(e\) can mean very different things for \(u\), so look at both.


Problem 3 (Challenge): When could China catch up with the United States? In the Maddison data of Fig. 1 (Maddison Project Database 2023), GDP per person in 2022 was 75,459 dollars in the United States and 24,821 dollars in China, a ratio of 3.04. In these data, China’s income per person grew 7.4 percent a year from 2000 to 2010 and 5.9 percent a year from 2010 to 2022. The IMF’s World Economic Outlook of October 2026 projects that China’s real GDP growth will slow from 5.0 percent in 2025 to 3.3 percent in 2030.

Suppose both countries grow at constant rates, \(g_C\) and \(g_U\), from 2022 on. Use equation (3) to derive the number of years \(T\) until China’s income per person reaches the U.S. level. Give the approximate version for small growth rates too.
Compute \(T\) for \(g_C = 5\) percent and \(g_U = 1.5\) percent (a scenario, not a forecast).
Compute \(T\) again for \(g_C = 3.3\) percent, using the IMF’s projection for 2030 as a rough stand-in for growth per person.
What constant growth rate would China need to catch up by 2050, if U.S. income per person grows 1.5 percent a year? Why might any constant-growth answer be too optimistic for a country that is catching up?



Hint

Write equation (3) once for each country, set the two incomes equal in year \(T\), and move both growth factors to one side. Taking logs turns the powers into products. For (d), solve the same equation for \(g_C\), with \(T = 28\).

Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution


Catch-up happens when \(y_{C,0}(1+g_C)^T = y_{U,0}(1+g_U)^T\). Divide both sides by \(y_{C,0}(1+g_U)^T\):

\[\left(\frac{1+g_C}{1+g_U}\right)^T = \frac{y_{U,0}}{y_{C,0}}.\]
Take logs, using \(\ln(x^T) = T\ln x\) and \(\ln(a/b) = \ln a - \ln b\):
\[T\left[\ln(1+g_C) - \ln(1+g_U)\right] = \ln\frac{y_{U,0}}{y_{C,0}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T = \frac{\ln(y_{U,0}/y_{C,0})}{\ln(1+g_C) - \ln(1+g_U)} \approx \frac{\ln(y_{U,0}/y_{C,0})}{g_C - g_U},\]
where the last step uses \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\). China has to close a log gap of \(\ln 3.04 = 1.112\), and it closes it at a speed equal to the difference of the growth rates. This is the “small differences add up” result of the Model overview, read backwards.

\(T = 1.112/(\ln 1.05 - \ln 1.015) = 1.112/(0.0488 - 0.0149) = 1.112/0.0339 = 32.8\) years, so around 2055. The approximation gives \(1.112/0.035 = 31.8\) years.
\(T = 1.112/(\ln 1.033 - \ln 1.015) = 1.112/0.0176 = 63.3\) years, so around 2085. Growth of 3.3 instead of 5 percent cuts the speed of catch-up from 3.5 to 1.8 points a year, and so almost doubles the time.
With \(T = 28\), solve for \(g_C\): \(1 + g_C = 1.015 \times 3.04^{1/28} = 1.015 \times 1.0405 = 1.0561\), so China would need 5.6 percent a year in every year until 2050. That is faster than the 5.0 percent of 2025 and far above the projected 3.3 percent. A constant rate is optimistic because catch-up growth tends to slow down as a country gets richer: it can no longer grow fast just by building machines from a low base and copying technologies that already exist. Chapters 5 and 6 explain why.

ratio = 75459 / 24821
for g_C in (0.05, 0.033):
    T = np.log(ratio) / (np.log(1 + g_C) - np.log(1 + 0.015))
    print(f"China at {100 * g_C:.1f}%: catches up after {T:.1f} years (approximation {np.log(ratio) / (g_C - 0.015):.1f})")
print(f"Growth needed to catch up by 2050: {100 * (1.015 * ratio ** (1 / 28) - 1):.2f}% a year")



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): The misery index. Adding the inflation rate and the unemployment rate gives a rough measure of economic hardship, often called the misery index. Use the U.S. columns of fig1-3.csv (consumer prices from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (CPIAUCNS)) and fig1-4.csv (the Bureau of Labor Statistics unemployment rate (UNRATE)), both via FRED.

Compute the U.S. misery index for every year in both files.
Which five years had the highest index? What do they have in common?
Inflation reached 8.0 percent in 2022. Where does 2022 rank, and why was it a less miserable year than 1980?



Hint

.merge(other, on="year") keeps the years that are in both tables. Add the columns inflation_us and unrate_us, then use .sort_values(..., ascending=False). To find the rank of 2022, count the years with a higher index.


# Your answer here



Solution

Merge the two files on the year (1960–2025), add the two U.S. columns, and sort.
prices = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-3.csv")
jobs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-4.csv")
misery = prices.merge(jobs, on="year")
misery["misery"] = misery.inflation_us + misery.unrate_us
ranked = misery.sort_values("misery", ascending=False)
print(ranked[["year", "inflation_us", "unrate_us", "misery"]].head(5).round(1))
value_2022 = misery[misery.year == 2022].misery.iloc[0]
higher = misery[misery.misery > value_2022]
print(f"2022: index {value_2022:.1f}, rank {len(higher) + 1} of {len(misery)} years")
print("Years with a higher index:", higher.year.tolist())
The five worst years are 1980 with an index of 20.7 (inflation 13.5 percent plus unemployment 7.2 percent), then 1981 with 18.0, 1975 with 17.6, 1979 with 17.1 and 1974 with 16.7. All of them fall in the high-inflation decade of Fig. 3, and each has inflation above 9 percent. The 2022 index is 11.7, only 13th of the 66 years: every year from 1974 to 1984 was worse, and so was 2011 (low inflation, but unemployment near 9 percent). In 2022 high inflation came with very low unemployment, 3.65 percent, while in 1980 it came with a recession. The index treats a point of inflation and a point of unemployment as equally painful, which is a strong assumption, so read it as a rough summary.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Growth miracles and growth disasters since 1950. Use maddison_world.csv, GDP per person from the Maddison Project Database 2023 (Bolt and van Zanden 2024).

For every country with an estimate in both 1950 and 2022, compute the average annual growth rate of GDP per person with equation (4).
Which five countries grew fastest, and which five slowest?
How many countries were poorer in 2022 than in 1950? Which ones?
What is the median growth rate, and how often does income double at that rate (equation (5))?



Hint

Keep the rows of one year with maddison[maddison.year == 1950], and use .set_index("country").gdppc to get a column labeled by country; do the same for 2022. Dividing the two columns matches the countries, and .dropna() drops the countries that miss one of the years. The period is 72 years long.


# Your answer here



Solution

Take each country’s 1950 and 2022 values, apply equation (4) with \(T = 72\), and sort.
maddison = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
start = maddison[maddison.year == 1950].set_index("country").gdppc
end = maddison[maddison.year == 2022].set_index("country").gdppc
growth = 100 * ((end / start) ** (1 / 72) - 1)               # equation (4), in percent a year
growth = growth.dropna().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"{len(growth)} countries with estimates for 1950 and 2022")
print(growth.head(5).round(2))
print(growth.tail(5).round(2))
print("Poorer in 2022 than in 1950:", sorted(growth[growth < 0].index))
print(f"Median: {growth.median():.2f}% a year, doubling every {70 / growth.median():.0f} years")
146 countries have both estimates. The fastest growers are Oman with 5.53 percent a year, South Korea with 5.31, Taiwan with 5.12, Botswana with 5.00 and Equatorial Guinea with 4.76; China is sixth, with 4.52. At 5.3 percent a year, South Korea’s income doubled about every 13 years, so it rose about 41-fold. The slowest are Liberia (\(-1.87\) percent a year), the Central African Republic (\(-1.08\)), Mozambique (\(-0.70\)), Venezuela (\(-0.66\)) and Syria (\(-0.60\)).
Eight countries were poorer in 2022 than in 1950: the Central African Republic, DR Congo, Haiti, Liberia, Madagascar, Mozambique, Syria and Venezuela. The median country grew 2.08 percent a year, so its income doubled about every 34 years. The United States grew 1.89 percent a year in the same data (growth["United States"]), so the median country grew a little faster than the United States. Estimates for poor countries in 1950 are rough (Liberia’s 4,065 dollars is more than three times South Korea’s 1,288), so check the extremes before you build a story on them.

Problem 6 (Challenge): Output gaps and unemployment. When output falls below potential, firms need fewer workers, so the output gap of Fig. 7 and the unemployment rate of Fig. 4 should move together. Use fig1-7.csv (real GDP from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (GDPCA) and potential output from the Congressional Budget Office (GDPPOT), both via FRED) and the U.S. column of fig1-4.csv.

Compute the output gap with equation (2) and merge it with the unemployment rate. Which years do both files cover?
Compute the correlation of the gap and the unemployment rate. Then fit a straight line \(u = \alpha + \beta \times \text{gap}\). What do \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) mean?
Which two years lie furthest above the line, and which two furthest below? Suggest a reason for one of them.



Hint

.corr() gives the correlation of two columns. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits the best straight line through the points and returns its slope first and its intercept second. The distance of a year from the line is its actual unemployment rate minus the rate that the line predicts.


# Your answer here



Solution

The merged table covers 1955–2025, the years of the unemployment file. The fitted line gives each year’s predicted rate, and the “miss” is the actual rate minus the prediction.
okun = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-7.csv").merge(pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-4.csv"), on="year")
okun["gap"] = 100 * (okun.gdppc_actual / okun.gdppc_potential - 1)        # equation (2)
print(f"{len(okun)} years, {okun.year.min()}-{okun.year.max()}")
print(f"Correlation: {okun.gap.corr(okun.unrate_us):.2f}")
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(okun.gap, okun.unrate_us, 1)
print(f"Fitted line: u = {intercept:.2f} + ({slope:.2f}) x gap")
okun["miss"] = okun.unrate_us - (intercept + slope * okun.gap)
print(okun.sort_values("miss")[["year", "gap", "unrate_us", "miss"]].round(2).iloc[[0, 1, -2, -1]])

71 years, 1955–2025.
The correlation is \(-0.86\): years with output below potential are years of high unemployment. The line is \(u = 5.71 - 0.64 \times \text{gap}\). The slope \(\beta = -0.64\) says that each point of output below potential comes with about 0.64 points more unemployment. The intercept \(\alpha = 5.71\) is the unemployment rate the line predicts when output equals potential, a rough estimate of the rate that does not come from the business cycle. This relation is known as Okun’s law. Ball, Leigh and Loungani (2013) test it on U.S. data since 1948 and on twenty advanced economies, and find a strong and stable relationship in most countries. Chapter 9 returns to it.
Furthest above the line: 2010 (unemployment 9.61 percent, 1.76 points above the line) and 1966 (1.47 above). Furthest below: 2017 (1.75 below) and 2018 (1.65 below). In 2010 the gap was closing, but unemployment had not yet come down: a possible reason is that firms waited to see whether the recovery after the financial crisis would last before they hired again. In 2016–2019 unemployment fell to rates that the line would only predict for a boom: the rate that does not come from the business cycle may have fallen, or the CBO’s estimate of potential output may be too high for those years. Either way, a fitted line summarizes the average year, and the exceptions are where the interesting questions are.




Modeling problems
Problem 7 (Basic): A city council’s minimum-wage menu. The labor market of a hypothetical city is the model of Fig. 6, with the baseline values \(\bar{a} = 2\), \(\bar{\ell} = 30\) and \(\bar{f} = 60\). The council considers minimum wages of 11, 12, 13 and 14 dollars. It wants to raise the total pay of employed workers, \(w \times L\), by at least 20 percent over its value without a minimum wage, and to keep unemployment below 10 hours.

Use the slider to read employment and unemployment at each floor, and compute total pay.
Which floors meet both goals?
Under the floor you would choose, who gains and who loses?



Hint

Without a minimum wage, total pay is \(w^* L^* = 10 \times 50\). Raising it by 20 percent sets the target. Read employment and unemployment off the OUTCOMES box at each floor.


interact(structure_of_models, a=fixed(2.0), l=fixed(30.0), f=fixed(60.0),
         w_min=FloatSlider(value=10, min=10, max=20, step=1, description="minimum wage", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 6 above, adapted from Fig. 1.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution


Without a floor, total pay is \(10 \times 50 = 500\), so the target is \(1.2 \times 500 = 600\). Above \(w^* = 10\), employment is read off the demand curve, \(L = 60 - \bar{w}_{\min}\), and unemployment is equation (8), \(U = 3(\bar{w}_{\min} - 10)\):

Employment \(L\)
Unemployment \(U\)
