Compute the growth of nominal GDP, GNI and GNI* from 2014 to 2015.
Write equation (2) in changes. What fraction of the rise in GDP came from net exports?
The depreciation of relocated patents rose from €0.8 billion to €25.0 billion. Why does it count in GDP? And who receives most of the extra profit?
Government debt as a share of GDP fell from 104.5 to 76.9 percent. Compute the debt ratio with GNI* instead. Which ratio tells you more about the burden of the debt on Irish taxpayers?



Hint

A growth rate is new/old − 1. For (b), take the change of each side of equation (2). For (c), go back to the income split of value added in Step 2 of the Model overview, and ask who owns the multinationals. For (d), divide the same debt by a different measure of income.

Your answer:


Solution


Nominal GDP grew \(262.0/194.5 - 1 = 34.7\) percent, GNI \(207.2/165.9 - 1 = 24.9\) percent, and GNI* \(172.9/154.5 - 1 = 11.9\) percent. The more of the multinationals’ activity a measure removes, the slower it grows.
In changes, \(\Delta Y = \Delta C + \Delta I + \Delta G + \Delta NX\). GDP rose by \(262.0 - 194.5 = 67.5\) billion euros, and net exports by \(80 - 35 = 45\) billion, so net exports account for \(45/67.5 = 2/3\) of the rise. The reason, in the CSO’s account: products made abroad under contract for firms whose patents now sit in Ireland are counted as Irish exports, and the royalties that Irish subsidiaries used to pay abroad for the patents (imports of services) disappeared. Our World Bank data in Fig. 1 show the same jump: Ireland’s net exports went from 19.0 percent of GDP in 2014 to 29.7 percent in 2015.
GDP is gross: Step 2 of the Model overview splits it into compensation, taxes on production, the net operating surplus and depreciation. The wear and tear of patents located in Ireland is therefore part of Irish value added, even though it pays no one’s income in Ireland. The rest of the extra value added is profit (operating surplus) of firms owned abroad, and it is paid to their foreign owners: the gap between GDP and GNI widened from \(194.5 - 165.9 = 28.6\) to \(262.0 - 207.2 = 54.8\) billion euros. Employment grew only 2.3 percent, so little of the new value added was labor income. It shows in the labor share of Fig. 3: in our Penn World Table data, Ireland’s labor share fell from 0.451 in 2014 to 0.339 in 2015.
With GNI* in the denominator, the debt ratio was

\[\frac{203.3}{154.5} = 131.6\% \text{ in 2014}, \qquad \frac{201.4}{172.9} = 116.5\% \text{ in 2015}.\]
The debt itself barely changed (it fell by 1.9 billion euros). Its ratio to GDP dropped by 27.6 points only because GDP jumped, and much of that jump is not income of Irish residents: it is the depreciation of relocated patents and profits paid to foreign owners. GNI* measures the income of Irish residents better, so it gives a fairer picture of the burden; the CSO itself presents GNI* as a measure for budget and fiscal analysis.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Why chained components do not add up. A hypothetical island produces only fish, which households eat (consumption \(C\)), and boats, which fishers buy (investment \(I\)):




Year 1
Year 2




Price of fish (dollars)
2
3


Quantity of fish
100
110


Price of boats (dollars)
50
40


Quantity of boats
4
6



The island’s statistics office publishes chained real values, as the BEA does, with year 2 as the benchmark year. The BEA warns that such chained components need not add up to chained GDP (NIPA Handbook, Chapter 4).

Compute nominal GDP in both years, the Laspeyres and Paasche growth rates of real GDP, and the chain-weighted growth rate, equation (6).
Compute chained real GDP in year 1, and chained real \(C\) and \(I\) in year 1.
Show that chained \(C\) plus chained \(I\) differs from chained GDP in year 1. Then prove, for any number of goods, that the sum of the chained one-good components in year 1 equals \(\sum_i p_{i,2}\,q_{i,1}\), and that it is larger than chained GDP whenever \(g^L > g^P\).
A journalist computes the investment share of year 1 as chained investment divided by chained GDP. What does she find, what is the right number, and why?



Hint

A component with a single good grows exactly as fast as its quantity under every index, so its chained value in year 1 is its year-2 value divided by its quantity growth factor. For the proof, compare your result with the denominator of the Paasche fraction in Step 1 of the real-GDP block.

Your answer:


Solution


Nominal GDP is \(2 \times 100 + 50 \times 4 = 400\) in year 1 and \(3 \times 110 + 40 \times 6 = 570\) in year 2. At year-1 prices, year 2 is worth \(2 \times 110 + 50 \times 6 = 520\); at year-2 prices, year 1 is worth \(3 \times 100 + 40 \times 4 = 460\). So

\[1 + g^L = \frac{520}{400} = 1.300, \qquad 1 + g^P = \frac{570}{460} = 1.2391, \qquad g^{\text{chain}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(30.0\% + 23.9\%) = 27.0\%.\]

Chained GDP equals nominal GDP in the benchmark year, 570, so in year 1 it is \(570/1.26957 = 448.97\). Fish grew 10 percent and boats 50 percent, so chained \(C\) in year 1 is \(330/1.10 = 300\) and chained \(I\) is \(240/1.50 = 160\).
\(300 + 160 = 460\), which is 11.03 more than chained GDP (448.97). In general, a one-good component \(i\) has the chained value

\[X_{i,1} = \frac{p_{i,2}\,q_{i,2}}{q_{i,2}/q_{i,1}} = p_{i,2}\,q_{i,1} \qquad\text{so}\qquad \sum_i X_{i,1} = \sum_i p_{i,2}\,q_{i,1} = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,2}\,q_{i,2}}{1 + g^P},\]
where the last step is the definition of the Paasche index in Step 1. Chained GDP is instead \(X_1 = \sum_i p_{i,2}\,q_{i,2}\,/\,(1 + g^{\text{chain}})\). By equation (6), \(g^{\text{chain}} - g^P = \tfrac{1}{2}(g^L - g^P)\), so when \(g^L > g^P\) the chain-weighted growth rate is larger than the Paasche rate, its denominator is larger, and chained GDP is smaller than the sum of the components. In the benchmark year the two agree, so the gap appears only away from it; the BEA shows it as a “residual” line in its chained-dollar tables.

She finds \(160/448.97 = 35.6\) percent. The right share uses nominal values, which do add up: \(200/400 = 50.0\) percent in year 1 (and \(240/570 = 42.1\) percent in year 2). Chained year-1 values use year-2 relative prices, and boats became relatively cheaper, so chained values understate the weight of boats in year 1. That is why the Model overview says: shares from nominal values, growth rates from chained values.




Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): Has labor’s share fallen across the G7? Fig. 3 shows labor’s share of U.S. income drifting down since 1970. Is that true of all rich countries? Use the labor shares of the Penn World Table 11.0 in labor_share_world.csv, and the G7 flag of the World Bank country classifications in countries.csv. Compare 1990 and 2019 (the last year before the pandemic) for the seven G7 countries. In how many did the labor share fall? Which country had the largest fall, and which the largest rise? Is “two-thirds” a good description of the G7 in 2019?


Hint

Keep the rows of the G7 countries (countries.csv has a True/False column g7) and the two years, with .isin(...). Then .pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="labor_share") puts the two years side by side, one row per country.


# Your answer here



Solution

We keep the G7 rows for 1990 and 2019, put the two years side by side, and subtract.
pwt_shares = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "labor_share_world.csv")
groups = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
g7_names = groups[groups.g7].country
g7 = pwt_shares[pwt_shares.country.isin(g7_names) & pwt_shares.year.isin([1990, 2019])]
table = g7.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="labor_share")
table["change"] = table[2019] - table[1990]
print(table.sort_values("change").round(3))
print("G7 countries where the share fell:", (table.change < 0).sum())
print(f"G7 average in 2019: {table[2019].mean():.3f}")
The share fell in four of the seven countries: Canada (−0.052, the largest fall), Italy (−0.038), the United States (−0.023) and France (−0.001, hardly a change). It rose in Germany (+0.005), Japan (+0.010) and the United Kingdom (+0.017, the largest rise). So the decline is not universal. In 2019 the shares ranged from 0.537 in Italy to 0.659 in Canada, with a G7 average of 0.610: closer to 60 percent than to two-thirds. Remember that the Penn World Table measures the U.S. share about 0.03 below Fig. 3; in Fig. 3’s own measure, the U.S. share fell from 0.653 to 0.620 over the same years.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Prices or production? Equation (7) splits the growth of nominal GDP into inflation and real growth. Use the BEA’s national accounts in nipa_annual.csv: nominal GDP (gdp, GDPA) and real GDP in chained 2017 dollars (real_gdp, GDPCA), both via FRED.

Over the Great Depression, from 1929 to 1933, by what percentage did nominal GDP, real GDP and the price level (the deflator, nominal over real GDP) change?
In which years did nominal GDP grow while real GDP fell? What kind of years are they?
Find the three years in which the rule of thumb of equation (7) misses nominal growth by the most. What do they have in common?



Hint

Build a table with nominal GDP, real GDP and their ratio, the deflator of equation (4). .pct_change() gives every year’s growth, as in the Key numbers of Fig. 4. For (b), join two conditions with &. For (c), the miss is nominal growth minus the sum of inflation and real growth.


# Your answer here



Solution

We compute the deflator, the change over 1929–1933, every year’s growth rates, and the miss of the rule of thumb.
accounts = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "nipa_annual.csv").set_index("year")
levels = pd.DataFrame({"nominal": accounts.gdp, "real": accounts.real_gdp})
levels["prices"] = levels.nominal / levels.real            # the GDP deflator, equation (4)
print("Percent change, 1929-1933:")
print((100 * (levels.loc[1933] / levels.loc[1929] - 1)).round(1))
growth_rates = 100 * levels.pct_change()
growth_rates["miss"] = growth_rates.nominal - (growth_rates.prices + growth_rates.real)
print(growth_rates[(growth_rates.nominal > 0) & (growth_rates.real < 0)].round(2) + 0.0)   # + 0.0: no -0.00
print(growth_rates.miss.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).round(2))

From 1929 to 1933, nominal GDP fell 45.3 percent, real GDP 26.3 percent and the price level 25.8 percent. The exact split multiplies growth factors: \((1 - 0.263)(1 - 0.258) = 0.547 \approx 1 - 0.453\). About half of the collapse in spending was falling prices, and half falling production.
Nominal GDP grew while real GDP fell in nine years: 1945, 1947, 1954, 1958, 1974, 1975, 1980, 1982 and 1991. Most are recession years (1954, 1958, 1974–1975, 1980, 1982, 1991), and 1945 and 1947 are the end of World War II, when war production was wound down. In all of them prices rose faster than production fell. The clearest cases are the stagflation years 1974, 1975 and 1980, with inflation of about 9 percent and falling output: measured in dollars, the economy grew while it produced less.
The misses are largest in 1932, by 1.51 points, and in 1942 and 1946, by 1.50 points each. The miss is the cross term \(\pi\,g_{\text{real}}\), the product of the two rates, so it is large only when inflation and real growth are both large. In 1932 prices fell 11.7 percent and output 12.9 percent; in 1942, the war boom, output rose 18.9 percent and prices 7.9 percent; in 1946, after the war, output fell 11.6 percent while prices rose 12.9 percent.


Problem 6 (Challenge): Are rich countries more expensive? The Model overview argues that poor countries have low price levels, so that comparisons at exchange rates exaggerate the income gaps between countries. Test this with ppp_world.csv, a file prepared for this problem from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators: GDP at market exchange rates in billions of current dollars (gdp_usd_bn, NY.GDP.MKTP.CD), GDP at purchasing power parity in billions of international dollars (gdp_ppp_bn, NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.CD) and population in millions (population_m, SP.POP.TOTL), for about 200 economies from 1990 to 2025. An international dollar buys as much as a U.S. dollar buys in the United States.

Solve equation (8) for the relative price level. Compute it, and GDP per person at PPP, for every economy in 2024 (leave out the “Euro area” aggregate).
Compute the correlation between the log price level and log GDP per person, and the slope of a straight line through them. What does the slope mean?
Rank the economies by GDP in 2024, once at exchange rates and once at PPP. Which economy is the largest by each measure? Among the ten largest at PPP, which climb the most places, and which economies drop out of the top ten?
Find the exceptions: the economies with GDP per person above $60,000 but a price level below 0.55, and those with GDP per person below $10,000 but a price level above 0.75. What do the members of each group have in common?



Hint

In equation (8), dollar GDP is on one side and GDP at common prices on the other, so their ratio is the relative price level. Take logs with np.log. np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1] is the correlation, and np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope first, as in Fig. 3. For (c), .rank(ascending=False) gives the largest economy rank 1. For (d), join two conditions with &.


# Your answer here



Solution

Equation (8) says that GDP at common prices is dollar GDP divided by the relative price level, so the relative price level is dollar GDP divided by GDP at common prices: \(\text{price level}_i/\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}} = \text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_i \,/\, \text{real GDP}^{\text{common prices}}_i\). For the United States the two GDPs are equal, so its price level is 1.
ppp_data = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "ppp_world.csv")
y2024 = ppp_data[(ppp_data.year == 2024) & (ppp_data.country != "Euro area")].copy()
y2024["price_level"] = y2024.gdp_usd_bn / y2024.gdp_ppp_bn          # equation (8), solved
y2024["income"] = 1000 * y2024.gdp_ppp_bn / y2024.population_m      # dollars per person, PPP
log_income, log_price = np.log(y2024.income), np.log(y2024.price_level)
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(log_income, log_price, 1)
print(f"{len(y2024)} economies; correlation {np.corrcoef(log_income, log_price)[0, 1]:.2f}; slope {slope:.3f}")
y2024["rank_usd"] = y2024.gdp_usd_bn.rank(ascending=False)              # 1 = largest
y2024["rank_ppp"] = y2024.gdp_ppp_bn.rank(ascending=False)
print(y2024.nsmallest(10, "rank_ppp")[["country", "rank_usd", "rank_ppp", "price_level"]].round(2))
print(y2024[(y2024.rank_usd <= 10) & (y2024.rank_ppp > 10)][["country", "rank_usd", "rank_ppp"]])
print(y2024[(y2024.income > 60000) & (y2024.price_level < 0.55)][["country", "income", "price_level"]].round(2))
print(y2024[(y2024.income < 10000) & (y2024.price_level > 0.75)][["country", "income", "price_level"]].round(2))

Across 195 economies, the correlation of the logs is 0.53 and the slope is 0.196: the slope of a line in logs is an elasticity, so 10 percent more GDP per person goes with a price level about 1.9 percent higher (\(1.1^{0.196} = 1.019\)), and a country twice as rich is about \(2^{0.196} = 1.15\) times as expensive. The fact holds, though with a lot of spread around the line.
At exchange rates the United States is the largest economy, followed by China, Germany, Japan and India. At PPP China is the largest, followed by the United States, India, Russia and Japan: China’s price level is only 0.49 of the U.S. level, so its GDP at common prices passes U.S. GDP. Among the ten largest at PPP, Indonesia climbs the most (from 16th to 8th), then Russia (10th to 4th) and Brazil (11th to 7th), all with low price levels (0.30 to 0.46 of the U.S. level). Italy (8th) and Canada (9th) drop out of the top ten (to 12th and 16th). Moving to common prices lifts the poorer economies and lowers the richer ones, as equation (8) and part (b) predict.
The rich but cheap economies are Bahrain, Brunei, Guyana and Saudi Arabia. All four live on oil and gas: in 2021 the World Bank put their oil and gas rents at between 17 and 25 percent of GDP (oil rents, natural gas rents). Their GDP per person is high because of that revenue rather than because of high wages across the whole economy, so labor-intensive services stay cheap. The poor but expensive ones are the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu: small, remote island economies in the Pacific. A likely reason is that much of what they consume has to be shipped in over long distances, a hypothesis you could test with the World Bank’s data on imports of goods and services.




Modeling problems
Problem 7 (Basic): A target for nominal GDP. Some economists have proposed that central banks target the growth of nominal GDP instead of inflation; Hetzel (2015), at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, reviews the idea and argues that a strict target could destabilize the economy. Suppose a central bank keeps nominal GDP growing at 4 percent a year.

If real GDP grows 2 percent, what inflation does the target imply?
A recession cuts real growth to −2 percent. What inflation does the same target imply now? And if a technology boom raises real growth to 3.5 percent?
Compare with a central bank that keeps inflation at 2 percent whatever happens: what is nominal GDP growth in the three cases?



Hint

Equation (7) gives the rule of thumb. For the exact answer, solve \(1 + g_{\text{nominal}} = (1+\pi)(1+g_{\text{real}})\) for \(\pi\). For (b), move only the real-growth slider.


def nominal_target(target=4.0, real_growth=2.0):
    """Inflation implied by a nominal-GDP growth target: exact, and by the rule of thumb of equation (7)."""
    inflation = round(100 * ((1 + target / 100) / (1 + real_growth / 100) - 1), 2) + 0.0
    rule = round(target - real_growth, 2) + 0.0
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["Nominal GDP (target)", "Real GDP", "Inflation, exact", "Inflation, equation (7)"],
                           y=[target, real_growth, inflation, rule], marker_color=[BLUE, GREEN, TEAL, GRAY],
                           texttemplate="%{y:+.2f}%"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"A {target:.1f}% target with {real_growth:+.1f}% real growth implies {inflation:.2f}% inflation",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Growth rate (percent a year)", range=[-8, 14]))
    return fig


interact(nominal_target,
         target=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="nominal GDP target (%)", style=WIDE),
         real_growth=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=-4.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="real GDP growth (%)", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on equation (7) of the Model overview, adapted from the discussion of nominal GDP, real GDP and inflation in Chapter 2 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

Solving the exact relation for inflation gives \(\pi = (1 + g_{\text{nominal}})/(1 + g_{\text{real}}) - 1\), and equation (7) gives \(\pi \approx g_{\text{nominal}} - g_{\text{real}}\).

With real growth of 2 percent: \(\pi = 1.04/1.02 - 1 = 1.96\) percent, close to the rule of thumb’s 2 percent.
With −2 percent: \(\pi = 1.04/0.98 - 1 = 6.12\) percent (rule of thumb 6 percent). With 3.5 percent: \(\pi = 1.04/1.035 - 1 = 0.48\) percent (rule of thumb 0.5). With the target met, each point less real growth means about one point more inflation: the target splits a slowdown between output and prices, and lets inflation rise in a recession.
With inflation held at 2 percent, nominal GDP grows \(1.02 \times (1 + g_{\text{real}}) - 1\): 4.04 percent with 2 percent real growth, −0.04 percent with −2 percent, and 5.57 percent with 3.5 percent. Under an inflation target, nominal GDP growth swings with real growth; under a nominal-GDP target, inflation does. When output falls, a nominal-GDP target accepts higher inflation. Whether that is wise depends on what caused the fall, and is a question for the models of later chapters; the accounting only tells you how the burden is split.

for g_real in [2.0, -2.0, 3.5]:
    pi = 100 * (1.04 / (1 + g_real / 100) - 1)
    nominal = 100 * (1.02 * (1 + g_real / 100) - 1)
    print(f"real growth {g_real:+.1f}%: inflation under the target {pi:.2f}%, "
          f"nominal growth under 2% inflation {nominal:.2f}%")

Problem 8 (Intermediate): A weaker yuan and the IMF’s measure of size. The IMF gives each member a quota, which determines its voting power and its access to IMF resources (IMF factsheet). The quota formula agreed in 2008 measures each economy’s size with a blend of GDP: 60 percent at market exchange rates and 40 percent at PPP (IMF 2008, Reform of Quota and Voice). The calculator applies this blend to China and the United States, starting from the textbook’s 2019 numbers of Check 7: China’s GDP of 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar, Chinese prices at 68.4 percent of U.S. prices, and U.S. GDP of $20.6 trillion, which stays fixed. (The IMF itself works with each country’s share of world GDP.)

From 2019 to 2024 the yuan weakened from 6.91 to 7.20 per dollar (FRED AEXCHUS). With China’s yuan prices and output unchanged, how do the three measures change?
Go back to 6.91. By how much would China’s real output have to grow, with prices unchanged, for the blend to reach 100 percent of U.S. GDP? Find it with the sliders, then solve for it.
Now let China’s yuan prices rise 10 percent, with the exchange rate at 6.91 and output unchanged. What happens to each measure? Which weighting of the blend would China prefer, and why?



Hint

Dollar GDP is yuan GDP divided by \(e\). At common prices the exchange rate cancels, because China’s price level in dollars moves with \(1/e\) too (Step 4 of the PPP block). For (b), notice that all three measures are proportional to China’s output.


def china_size(e=6.91, prices=0, output=0):
    """China's GDP in percent of U.S. GDP: at the exchange rate, at common prices (equation 8) and a 60/40 blend."""
    yuan_gdp = 95.1 * (1 + prices / 100) * (1 + output / 100)       # trillions of yuan (2019: 95.1)
    relative_price = 0.684 * (6.91 / e) * (1 + prices / 100)        # China's price level / U.S. price level
    dollars = to_dollars(yuan_gdp, e)
    common = at_common_prices(dollars, relative_price)
    sizes = [100 * dollars / 20.6, 100 * common / 20.6, 100 * (0.6 * dollars + 0.4 * common) / 20.6]
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["At the exchange rate", "At common prices (PPP)", "IMF-style blend (60/40)"],
                           y=sizes, marker_color=[TEAL, GREEN, BLUE], texttemplate="%{y:.1f}"))
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dash", line_color="black")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{e:.2f} yuan per dollar; Chinese prices at {100 * relative_price:.1f}% of U.S. prices",
                      yaxis=dict(title="China's GDP (U.S. GDP = 100)", range=[0, 160]))
    return fig


interact(china_size,
         e=FloatSlider(value=6.91, min=6.0, max=8.0, step=0.01, description="yuan per dollar e", style=WIDE),
         prices=IntSlider(value=0, min=0, max=30, step=1, description="rise in yuan prices (%)", style=WIDE),
         output=IntSlider(value=0, min=0, max=40, step=1, description="rise in real output (%)", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on equation (8) and the conversion functions of the Model overview, adapted from the China–U.S. comparison in Chapter 2 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.; it starts from the textbook’s 2019 numbers.

Your answer:


Solution

At the start, China’s GDP is 66.8 percent of U.S. GDP at the exchange rate, 97.7 percent at common prices, and \(0.6 \times 66.8 + 0.4 \times 97.7 = 79.2\) percent in the blend.

At 7.20 yuan per dollar, dollar GDP falls by \(6.91/7.20 - 1 = -4.0\) percent, to 64.1 percent of U.S. GDP. GDP at common prices does not move (97.7), because China’s goods are cheaper in dollars by the same 4 percent: its relative price level falls from 68.4 to 65.6 percent. The blend falls to 77.5 percent, by 60 percent of the exchange-rate effect. A weaker currency makes a country look smaller in dollars without changing what it produces.
All three measures are proportional to China’s output, so the blend reaches 100 percent when \((1 + g) \times 0.7916 = 1\), that is \(g = 1/0.7916 - 1 = 26.3\) percent. With the slider, 26 percent gives 99.7 and 27 percent gives 100.5.
Yuan prices 10 percent higher raise dollar GDP by 10 percent, to 73.5 percent of U.S. GDP, and China’s relative price level from 68.4 to 75.2 percent. GDP at common prices is unchanged at 97.7, since only prices moved. The blend rises to 83.2 percent. China’s price level is low, so it looks much larger at PPP than at the exchange rate; the more weight the formula puts on PPP GDP, the larger China’s measured size and its quota. With a weight of 100 percent on PPP, the blend would be 97.7 instead of 79.2.

for e_rate, price_rise, output_rise in [(6.91, 0, 0), (7.20, 0, 0), (6.91, 0, 26), (6.91, 0, 27), (6.91, 10, 0)]:
    bars = china_size(e_rate, price_rise, output_rise).data[0].y
    print(f"e = {e_rate}, prices +{price_rise}%, output +{output_rise}%: "
          f"{bars[0]:.1f}, {bars[1]:.1f}, {bars[2]:.1f} percent of U.S. GDP")

Problem 9 (Challenge): How fast does a base year go out of date? Until 1996 the BEA valued real GDP at the prices of a fixed base year, which it updated about every five years; then it switched to chain weighting. In its NIPA Handbook, the BEA explains that fixed weights tend to understate growth before the base year and overstate it after. The calculator follows a hypothetical economy with two goods. In the base year, services and computers both cost $1, and the economy buys 98 units of services and 2 computers. Every year, services become 3 percent more expensive and their quantity grows 2 percent; the sliders set the yearly change of the price and the quantity of computers. The bars show real GDP growth from one year to the next, measured at base-year prices and with the indexes of equations (5) and (6).

With computer prices falling 20 percent a year and their quantity growing 30 percent, by how much do base-year prices overstate growth from the base year to the next, and 5, 10 and 20 years later?
The statistical office decides to update its base year as soon as the overstatement exceeds 1 percentage point. How often must it update?
Set the yearly change of computer prices to 0, then to +3 and +5 percent (10 years after the base year). What happens to the gap, and why?
Use the Laspeyres form of equation (5) to explain why growth at base-year prices drifts toward the growth rate of computers, while chain-weighted growth stays near 2.5 percent.



Hint

Move the first slider and read the gap in the title. For (d), growth at base-year prices is a weighted average of the goods’ growth rates, with weights \(p_{i,b}\,q_{i,t}/\sum_k p_{k,b}\,q_{k,t}\); compare how the weight of computers changes each year at base-year prices and at current prices.


def base_year_bias(years=10, computer_price=-20, computer_growth=30):
    """Real growth in one year, at base-year prices and with chain weighting (equations 5 and 6)."""
    p_base = pd.Series({"services": 1.0, "computers": 1.0})
    q_base = pd.Series({"services": 98.0, "computers": 2.0})          # computers: 2% of base-year spending
    p_step = pd.Series({"services": 1.03, "computers": 1 + computer_price / 100})
    q_step = pd.Series({"services": 1.02, "computers": 1 + computer_growth / 100})
    p_now, q_now = p_base * p_step ** years, q_base * q_step ** years
    p_next, q_next = p_now * p_step, q_now * q_step
    g_fixed = gdp_value(p_base, q_next) / gdp_value(p_base, q_now) - 1
    g_laspeyres = gdp_value(p_now, q_next) / gdp_value(p_now, q_now) - 1
    g_paasche = gdp_value(p_next, q_next) / gdp_value(p_next, q_now) - 1
    g_chain = chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche)
    gap = round(100 * (g_fixed - g_chain), 2) + 0.0
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["Base-year prices", "Laspeyres", "Paasche", "Chain-weighted"],
                           y=[100 * g_fixed, 100 * g_laspeyres, 100 * g_paasche, 100 * g_chain],
                           marker_color=[GRAY, TEAL, GREEN, BLUE], texttemplate="%{y:.2f}%"))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Year {years} to {years + 1}: base-year prices give {100 * g_fixed:.2f}%, "
                            f"chained {100 * g_chain:.2f}% (gap {gap:+.2f} points)",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Growth of real GDP (percent)", range=[0, 45]))
    return fig


interact(base_year_bias,
         years=IntSlider(value=10, min=0, max=30, step=1, description="years since the base year", style=WIDE),
         computer_price=IntSlider(value=-20, min=-30, max=5, step=1, description="computer prices (% a year)", style=WIDE),
         computer_growth=IntSlider(value=30, min=0, max=40, step=5, description="computers bought (% a year)", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on equations (5) and (6) and the functions gdp_value and chain_growth of the Model overview, adapted from the discussion of chain weighting in Chapter 2 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution


The gap between growth at base-year prices and chain-weighted growth is 0.06 points from the base year to the next, 1.32 points five years later, 4.80 points ten years later (7.25 against 2.45 percent) and 19.84 points twenty years later. Growth at base-year prices keeps rising, while chain-weighted growth stays near 2.4–2.5 percent.
The gap is 0.95 points four years after the base year and 1.32 points five years after it, so the office must update about every five years, which is roughly what the BEA used to do. Chain weighting removes the need: it updates the prices every year.
Ten years after the base year, the gap is 4.80 points when computer prices fall 20 percent a year, 1.20 points when they stay constant, 0.00 when they rise 3 percent, like services, and −0.92 points when they rise 5 percent. The gap comes from changes in relative prices. When all prices rise at the same rate, base-year and current prices give the same weights (“When do the two agree?” in the real-GDP block). When computers become relatively cheaper, base-year prices overvalue them, and because they are also the fast-growing good, growth is overstated. When they become relatively dearer, base-year prices undervalue them, and growth is understated.
Growth at base-year prices is \(g^{\text{base}}_t = \sum_i w_{i,t}\,g_i\) with \(w_{i,t} = p_{i,b}\,q_{i,t}/\sum_k p_{k,b}\,q_{k,t}\). At fixed prices, the weight of each good moves only with its quantity, so the ratio of the computers’ weight to the services’ weight grows by the factor \(1.30/1.02 = 1.27\) every year. After enough years computers carry almost all the weight, and \(g^{\text{base}}\) approaches their 30 percent growth. The chain-weighted index uses current spending shares, and computer spending grows by the factor \(0.80 \times 1.30 = 1.04\) a year, against \(1.03 \times 1.02 = 1.0506\) for services, so the computers’ share of spending drifts down slowly, from 2.0 to 1.8 percent after ten years. Chain-weighted growth therefore stays close to the share-weighted average \(0.98 \times 2\% + 0.02 \times 30\% = 2.56\) percent, the Laspeyres rate of the base year, and falls a little as the computers’ share shrinks: it is 2.50 percent from the base year to the next and 2.45 percent ten years later.

for years in [0, 4, 5, 10, 20]:
    print(years, base_year_bias(years).layout.title.text)
for computer_price in [-20, 0, 3, 5]:
    print(computer_price, base_year_bias(10, computer_price).layout.title.text)

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig




Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website versions with many countries (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_menu(fig, shown, regions, label="Textbook countries"):
    """Draw the countries in `shown` and put every other country one click away in the legend.

    `regions` maps each country to its region. With more than 40 countries, a menu above the plot
    chooses the region whose countries the legend lists. Traces that are not countries stay as they are.
    """
    countries = [trace.name for trace in fig.data if trace.name in regions]
    groups = [label] + sorted(set(regions[name] for name in countries))
    if len(countries) <= 40:
        groups = [None]                                 # a short legend lists every country at once
    buttons = []
    for group in groups:
        visible = []
        for trace in fig.data:
            if trace.name in shown:
                visible.append(True)
            elif trace.name not in regions:
                visible.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)
            elif group is None or regions[trace.name] == group:
                visible.append("legendonly")
            else:
                visible.append(False)
        buttons.append(dict(label=group, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    if len(groups) > 1:
        menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
        fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig

title: 3. An Overview of Long-Run Economic Growth
text:
Model overview
This chapter is about economic growth: the steady rise in income per person that has made people in many countries far richer than their great-grandparents. It presents facts rather than an economic model. But reading those facts takes a small toolkit: what a growth rate is, what a constant growth rate does to a number over many years, why a ratio scale turns that growth into a straight line, how long a variable takes to double, and how growth rates combine when variables are multiplied, divided or raised to a power. Every later chapter uses these tools, so this section derives each of them step by step.
There are four blocks, from the basic definition to the results built on it: growth rates and the constant growth rule; logarithms, the ratio scale and the Rule of 70; the average annual growth rate; and the rules for the growth rates of products, ratios and powers. At the end, ### The model in code turns the tools into Python functions and checks every result with numbers. The sections after it apply the tools to data: growth over two thousand years, U.S. growth on a ratio scale, growth across countries, poverty counted by people, and the growth rules in U.S. data.
A bar over a letter marks a value we hold constant and take as given, such as a constant growth rate \(\bar{g}\) for income or \(\bar{n}\) for population. A subscript is the year: \(y_t\) is the value of \(y\) in year \(t\), and \(y_0\) its value in the starting year. A growth rate without a bar, such as \(g_x\), may differ from one year to the next. In the code we simply write g and n.

Growth rates and the constant growth rule

Definitions
Let \(y_t\) be any variable that we measure once a year, such as GDP per person or the population. Its growth rate between year \(t\) and year \(t+1\) is its percentage change: the change in the variable divided by its value at the start (Appendix C.2),
\[g_t \equiv \frac{y_{t+1} - y_t}{y_t} = \frac{\Delta y_{t+1}}{y_t}.\]
A growth rate of \(0.02\) means 2 percent a year. Two features of this definition matter below. First, a growth rate has no units: GDP measured in dollars or in euros, or population counted in people or in billions, gives the same growth rate. Second, it measures change relative to the starting level. A country that adds $1,000 to an income of $10,000 grows by 10 percent; a country that adds the same $1,000 to an income of $50,000 grows by only 2 percent.


Deriving the results
Step 1: one year ahead. Suppose the growth rate takes the same value \(\bar{g}\) every year. Multiply both sides of the definition by \(y_t\), which gives \(y_{t+1} - y_t = \bar{g}\,y_t\), and then add \(y_t\) to both sides:
\[y_{t+1} = y_t + \bar{g}\,y_t = y_t\,(1+\bar{g}). \tag{1}\]
Next year’s value is this year’s value times the growth factor \(1+\bar{g}\). The 1 carries over everything that is already there, and the \(\bar{g}\) adds the new part, which is proportional to the current level. For a population \(L_t\) that grows at the rate \(\bar{n}\), equation (1) reads \(L_{t+1} = L_t(1+\bar{n})\): everyone alive this year is still counted next year, and \(\bar{n}L_t\) newcomers join them.
Step 2: one year after another. Start from \(y_0\) and apply equation (1) repeatedly, each time substituting the result of the previous year:
\[y_1 = y_0(1+\bar{g}), \qquad
y_2 = y_1(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})^2, \qquad
y_3 = y_2(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})^2(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})^3.\]
Each year contributes one more factor \((1+\bar{g})\), and a product of equal factors is a power (Appendix C.3). After \(t\) years there are \(t\) factors:
\[y_t = y_0\,(1+\bar{g})^t. \tag{2}\]
This is the constant growth rule. The pattern is not a coincidence of the first three years. If equation (2) holds in some year \(t\), then equation (1) gives \(y_{t+1} = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})^{t+1}\), so it also holds in year \(t+1\), and therefore in every year.
With the starting values of Fig. 3, a population of \(L_0 = 6\) billion that grows at \(\bar{n} = 0.02\), equation (2) gives \(L_{35} = 6 \times 1.02^{35} \approx 12.0\) billion and \(L_{70} = 6 \times 1.02^{70} \approx 24.0\) billion.
Step 3: why the yearly increase keeps getting bigger. Equation (1) says that the increase in a year is \(\Delta y_{t+1} = \bar{g}\,y_t\), a fixed percentage of a base that keeps growing. So the absolute increase is larger every year, and a chart of \(y_t\) against \(t\) bends upward. Compare this with simple growth, which adds the same amount \(\bar{g}\,y_0\) every year, so that \(y_t = y_0(1+\bar{g}t)\). Multiplying out the growth factor for two years shows where the two part ways:
\[(1+\bar{g})^2 = 1 + 2\bar{g} + \bar{g}^2.\]
The terms \(1 + 2\bar{g}\) are simple growth. The extra \(\bar{g}^2\) is growth earned in the second year on the growth of the first year. This is compounding, and over many years such extra terms pile up. At 2 percent for 35 years, simple growth multiplies the starting value by \(1 + 35 \times 0.02 = 1.7\), while compound growth doubles it: \(1.02^{35} \approx 2.0\).
Intuition. Under a constant growth rate, the growth itself grows. Each year’s increase becomes part of the base on which next year’s growth is earned.


What the results predict

Paths that bend upward. Under constant growth the level rises by a larger amount every year. That is why the population of Fig. 3 and U.S. GDP per person in Fig. 2 both curve upward on an ordinary scale, even though their growth rates hardly change.
Small differences in growth rates become large differences in levels. Take two economies that start at the same level \(y_0\). Writing equation (2) for both and dividing, \(y_0\) cancels: \(y^A_t/y^B_t = \left[(1+\bar{g}_A)/(1+\bar{g}_B)\right]^t\). Over 100 years, growth of 1 percent a year multiplies income by \(1.01^{100} \approx 2.7\), growth of 2 percent by \(1.02^{100} \approx 7.2\), and growth of 3 percent by \(1.03^{100} \approx 19.2\). Comparative statics. Taking logs of equation (2) (Appendix C.4) gives \(\ln y_t = \ln y_0 + t\ln(1+\bar{g})\). Each coefficient is an elasticity:




A change in …
changes \(y_t\) by …
reason




the starting value \(y_0\), up 1%
\(+1\%\), in every year
\(\ln y_0\) enters with coefficient 1


the growth factor \(1+\bar{g}\), up 1%
about \(+t\) percent
\(\ln(1+\bar{g})\) enters with coefficient \(t\)


the growth rate \(\bar{g}\), up 0.01 (one percentage point)
\(\ln y_t\) rises by about \(0.01\,t/(1+\bar{g})\)
the derivative of \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\) is \(1/(1+\bar{g})\) (Appendix C.7)


the horizon \(t\), longer
any gap in growth rates matters more
\(t\) multiplies \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\)



Raising growth from 2 to 3 percent for 100 years raises \(\ln y_t\) by about \(100 \times 0.01/1.02 \approx 0.98\), which multiplies the final level by about \(e^{0.98} \approx 2.7\) (exactly, \(1.03^{100}/1.02^{100} \approx 2.65\)). A change in the starting level shifts the whole path by the same percentage forever. A change in the growth rate has an effect that grows every year.



Logarithms, the ratio scale and the Rule of 70

Definitions
A ratio scale is a vertical axis whose equally spaced tick marks carry numbers with a constant ratio, such as 6, 12, 24, 48 (each twice the one before) or 1, 10, 100, 1,000 (each ten times the one before). On such an axis the height of a point is proportional to the logarithm of its value, not to the value itself. Moving up by one tick multiplies the value by the same factor, wherever on the axis you start. Plotly draws this kind of axis with log_y=True or type="log".


Deriving the results
Step 1: constant growth is a straight line in logs. Take the natural logarithm of both sides of equation (2). The log of a product is the sum of the logs, and the log of a power is the exponent times the log (Appendix C.4):
\[\ln y_t = \ln y_0 + t\,\ln(1+\bar{g}). \tag{3}\]
The right-hand side is a straight line in \(t\), with intercept \(\ln y_0\) and slope \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\). For small growth rates \(\ln(1+\bar{g}) \approx \bar{g}\) (Appendix C.6); for instance \(\ln 1.02 = 0.0198\). Between any two years \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) the slope, rise over run in logs, is
\[\frac{\ln y_{t_2} - \ln y_{t_1}}{t_2 - t_1} = \ln(1+\bar{g}) \approx \bar{g}.\]
So on a ratio scale, constant growth draws a straight line, and the slope of that line is (very nearly) the growth rate.
Step 2: the doubling time. How many years does it take until \(y_t = 2y_0\)? Put \(y_t = 2y_0\) into equation (2) and divide both sides by \(y_0\). The starting level drops out:
\[2y_0 = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2 = (1+\bar{g})^t.\]
The unknown sits in the exponent, so take logs of both sides, \(\ln 2 = t\,\ln(1+\bar{g})\), and divide by \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\):
\[t_{\text{double}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+\bar{g})}. \tag{4}\]
Step 3: the Rule of 70. Equation (4) is exact, but hard to evaluate in your head. Two approximations make it easy: \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\), and \(\ln(1+\bar{g}) \approx \bar{g}\). Write the growth rate in percent as \(g = 100\,\bar{g}\), so that \(\bar{g} = 0.02\) means \(g = 2\). Then
\[t_{\text{double}} \approx \frac{0.693}{\bar{g}} = \frac{69.3}{g} \approx \frac{70}{g}. \tag{5}\]
Why 70 and not 69.3? The log of \(1+\bar{g}\) is a little smaller than \(\bar{g}\) itself, about \(\bar{g} - \bar{g}^2/2\). Dividing by \(\bar{g}\) instead of by \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\) therefore makes the doubling time come out slightly too short, and rounding 69.3 up to 70 makes up for it at growth rates of a few percent. (It also divides evenly by 1, 2, 5, 7 and 10.) At 2 percent the exact answer is 35.0 years, \(69.3/2\) gives 34.7 and \(70/2\) gives 35.
The same steps give the time to grow by any factor \(m\): \(t = \ln m/\ln(1+\bar{g})\). And after \(k\) doubling times a variable is \(2^k\) times its starting value. At 2 percent, 70 years are two doubling times, so the variable grows by a factor of \(2^2 = 4\): the 6 billion people of Fig. 3 become 24 billion after 70 years.
Intuition. Logs turn multiplying into adding. Constant growth multiplies by the same factor every year, so in logs it adds the same amount every year, and that is a straight line.


What the results predict

The doubling time depends only on the growth rate. The starting level cancelled in step 2. A poor country and a rich country that grow at the same rate double their incomes in the same number of years.
Faster growth shortens the doubling time in proportion. By the Rule of 70 the doubling time is inversely proportional to the growth rate, an elasticity of \(-1\). Doubling the growth rate halves the doubling time; growth that is 10 percent faster, 2.2 instead of 2.0 percent a year, shortens it by about 9 percent, from 35 to about 32 years. How to read a ratio-scale chart.









On a ratio scale you see …
it means …
because …




a straight line
constant growth
equation (3) is linear in \(t\)


a steeper straight line
faster growth
the slope is \(\ln(1+\bar{g}) \approx \bar{g}\)


a line that bends upward (flattens)
growth that speeds up (slows down)
the slope changes


two parallel lines
equal growth rates and a constant ratio of levels
the vertical gap is \(\ln y^A - \ln y^B = \ln(y^A/y^B)\)


equal vertical steps
equal percentage changes
each tick is the same ratio






The average annual growth rate

Definitions
Real data rarely grow at a constant rate. Suppose we know a variable’s value \(y_0\) in a starting year and \(y_t\) in a year \(t\) years later. Its average annual growth rate \(\bar{g}\) is the constant growth rate that would take it from \(y_0\) to \(y_t\) in exactly \(t\) years.


Deriving the results
Step 1: turn the constant growth rule around. In equation (2) we knew \(y_0\) and \(\bar{g}\) and computed \(y_t\). Now \(y_0\), \(y_t\) and \(t\) are known and \(\bar{g}\) is the unknown. Divide both sides of equation (2) by \(y_0\):
\[\frac{y_t}{y_0} = (1+\bar{g})^t.\]
Step 2: undo the power. Raise both sides to the power \(1/t\). Since \(\left((1+\bar{g})^t\right)^{1/t} = (1+\bar{g})^{t/t} = 1+\bar{g}\) (Appendix C.3), we get \((y_t/y_0)^{1/t} = 1+\bar{g}\).
Step 3: subtract 1 from both sides:
\[\bar{g} = \left(\frac{y_t}{y_0}\right)^{1/t} - 1. \tag{6}\]
This is the rule for computing growth rates. For \(t = 1\) it gives \(y_1/y_0 - 1 = (y_1 - y_0)/y_0\), the definition of a growth rate we started from. Applied to the population path of Fig. 3, which goes from 6 billion to \(6 \times 1.02^{100} \approx 43.5\) billion in 100 years, it gives back \(\bar{g} = 7.245^{1/100} - 1 = 0.02\).
Step 4: the same rule in logs. Take logs of the equation in step 1 and divide by \(t\):
\[\ln(1+\bar{g}) = \frac{\ln y_t - \ln y_0}{t}.\]
The right-hand side is the slope, on a ratio scale, of the straight line that joins the first and the last point. The dashed line in Fig. 5 uses the same idea, but fits all the years at once.
Step 5: an average of growth factors. If the yearly growth rates \(g_1, g_2, \dots, g_t\) differ, applying equation (1) once for each year gives
\[y_t = y_0\,(1+g_1)(1+g_2)\cdots(1+g_t).\]
Compare this with equation (2): \((1+\bar{g})^t\) must equal the product of the yearly growth factors. So \(1+\bar{g}\) is their geometric mean, not the plain average of the growth rates. Here is why the difference matters. A variable that rises by 10 percent and then falls by 10 percent has a plain average growth rate of zero, yet it ends lower, because \(1.10 \times 0.90 = 0.99\). Equation (6) gets this right: \(0.99^{1/2} - 1 \approx -0.5\) percent a year.
Intuition. The average annual growth rate is the one steady pace that starts and ends at the same two points as the data.


What the results predict

Only the end points matter. Equation (6) uses \(y_0\), \(y_t\) and \(t\) and nothing in between. Booms and slumps inside the period count only through the level at which they leave the variable at the end. Comparative statics. From the log version, \(\ln(1+\bar{g}) = (\ln y_t - \ln y_0)/t\):








A change in …
changes \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\), close to \(\bar{g}\), by …




the final value \(y_t\), up 1%
about \(+0.01/t\)


the starting value \(y_0\), up 1%
about \(-0.01/t\)


the length \(t\), longer, with the same ratio \(y_t/y_0\)
less: the same total growth is spread over more years



Long-run growth rates are robust. Over 100 years, a 1 percent error in the final level moves the average growth rate by only about 0.01 percentage points. Over a single year, the same error moves it by a full percentage point. That is one reason why the growth rates of Fig. 5 and Fig. 7 are more reliable than any single year’s number.



Growth rates of products, ratios and powers

Definitions
Suppose two variables \(x\) and \(y\) grow at the rates \(g_x\) and \(g_y\). We want the growth rate \(g_z\) of a variable \(z\) built from them. One fact does all the work: the change in the log of a variable is approximately its growth rate. From the definition, \(v_{t+1}/v_t = 1+g_v\) for any variable \(v\), so
\[\Delta\ln v_{t+1} \equiv \ln v_{t+1} - \ln v_t = \ln\frac{v_{t+1}}{v_t} = \ln(1+g_v) \approx g_v.\]


Deriving the results
The product rule. Let \(z_t = x_t \times y_t\). Taking logs gives \(\ln z_t = \ln x_t + \ln y_t\). This holds in every year, so we can write it for year \(t+1\) and for year \(t\) and subtract the second from the first: \(\Delta\ln z = \Delta\ln x + \Delta\ln y\). Replacing each change in logs by the growth rate it approximates (Appendix C.5):
\[z = x \times y \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g_z = g_x + g_y. \tag{7}\]
The ratio rule. Let \(z_t = x_t/y_t\). Now \(\ln z_t = \ln x_t - \ln y_t\), and the same subtraction gives
\[z = \frac{x}{y} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g_z = g_x - g_y. \tag{8}\]
The power rule. Let \(z_t = x_t^a\) for any number \(a\): positive, negative or a fraction. Now \(\ln z_t = a\ln x_t\), so \(\Delta\ln z = a\,\Delta\ln x\) and
\[z = x^a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g_z = a \times g_x. \tag{9}\]
For a whole-number power you can also see it from the product rule: \(x^2 = x \times x\) grows at \(g_x + g_x = 2g_x\). Each rule replaces an operation by a simpler one, which is exactly what logs do: multiplying becomes adding, dividing becomes subtracting, and a power becomes a multiple.
How exact are the rules? With yearly data the product rule holds exactly for growth factors: \(1+g_z = (1+g_x)(1+g_y)\), so \(g_z = g_x + g_y + g_x g_y\). The leftover term is the product of two small numbers; at 2 and 1 percent it is \(0.02 \times 0.01 = 0.0002\). The same is true of the ratio rule, \(1+g_z = (1+g_x)/(1+g_y)\), and of the power rule, \(1+g_z = (1+g_x)^a\). The rules hold exactly for growth rates measured as changes in logs, or in continuous time.
Combining the rules. Joining (7) and (9), a variable \(z = x^a y^b\) grows at \(g_z = a\,g_x + b\,g_y\). The most important case in this book is the Cobb-Douglas production function of Chapter 4, \(Y_t = A_t K_t^{1/3} L_t^{2/3}\). The product rule (7), used twice for the three factors, gives \(g_Y = g_A + g_{K^{1/3}} + g_{L^{2/3}}\). The power rule (9) turns the last two terms into multiples:
\[g_Y = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}\,g_K + \tfrac{2}{3}\,g_L. \tag{10}\]
Output per person is \(y = Y/L\), so the ratio rule (8) subtracts \(g_L\):
\[g_y = g_Y - g_L = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}g_K + \tfrac{2}{3}g_L - g_L = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}\left(g_K - g_L\right) = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}\,g_k,\]
where the last step uses the ratio rule once more for capital per person, \(k = K/L\).
Intuition. Output grows as fast as productivity, plus the growth of each input weighted by its exponent. Per person, only productivity growth and the growth of capital per person are left, and capital per person counts only one third. Chapters 4 to 6 build on this decomposition.


What the results predict

Equal growth rates keep a ratio constant. If \(g_x = g_y\), the ratio rule gives \(g_{x/y} = 0\). On a ratio scale, two countries growing at the same rate draw parallel lines, as the United States and the United Kingdom do after 1950 in Fig. 6.
GDP, population and GDP per person. Total GDP is GDP per person times the population, \(Y = y \times L\), so \(g_Y = g_y + g_L\), or equivalently \(g_y = g_Y - g_L\). In the U.S. data of Fig. 9, GDP per person grew about 1.9 percent a year since 1870 and the population about 1.4 percent, so total GDP grew about 3.3 percent. Fast GDP growth with equally fast population growth leaves income per person where it was. Comparative statics of equation (10), with each growth rate raised by one percentage point while the others stay the same:









One point faster growth of …
raises \(g_Y\) by
raises \(g_y\) by




productivity \(A\)
1 point
1 point


capital \(K\)
1/3 point
1/3 point


labor \(L\)
2/3 point
\(-1/3\) point (the same capital is spread over more workers)


capital and labor together
1 point
0 (constant returns to scale)






The model in code
We now turn the tools into Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes. The cells after it check every result above with numbers.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”, and np.log is the natural logarithm.


def constant_growth(y0, g, t):
    """Value after t years of constant growth at rate g: y_t = y0 (1 + g)^t   (equation 2)."""
    return y0 * (1 + g) ** t


def growth_rate(y0, yt, t):
    """Average annual growth rate between two values t years apart: (yt / y0)^(1/t) - 1   (equation 6)."""
    return (yt / y0) ** (1 / t) - 1


def doubling_time(g):
    """Exact number of years it takes to double at growth rate g: ln 2 / ln(1 + g)   (equation 4)."""
    return np.log(2) / np.log(1 + g)

Check 1: compounding. We follow the population of Fig. 3, 6 billion people growing at 2 percent, and compare compound growth, equation (2), with simple growth, which adds the same 2 percent of the starting value every year.

Python note. A for loop repeats its indented lines once for each value in the list after in, here the years 1, 35, 70 and 100. An f-string such as f"{x:.2f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text: :.2f shows two decimals, and :8.2f also pads the number to 8 characters so the columns line up.


print("Years   compound growth, eq. (2)   simple growth")
for t in (1, 35, 70, 100):
    compound = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, t)
    simple = 6.0 * (1 + 0.02 * t)
    print(f"{t:5d}   {compound:15.2f} billion   {simple:8.2f} billion")

Years   compound growth, eq. (2)   simple growth
    1              6.12 billion       6.12 billion
   35             12.00 billion      10.20 billion
   70             24.00 billion      14.40 billion
  100             43.47 billion      18.00 billion


After 35 years compound growth has doubled the population, and after 70 years quadrupled it. Simple growth gets only to 1.7 and 2.4 times the start.
Check 2: a straight line in logs. Equation (3) says that the log of a constantly growing variable rises by the same amount, \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\), every year.

Python note. np.arange(0, 6) gives the whole numbers 0, 1, …, 5, and constant_growth then works on all of them at once. np.log takes the log of every value, np.diff subtracts each value from the next one, and .round(4) keeps four decimals.


years = np.arange(0, 6)
L = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, years)
print("Population (billions):    ", L.round(4))
print("Yearly change in ln L:    ", np.diff(np.log(L)).round(5))
print(f"Slope of eq. (3), ln(1.02): {np.log(1.02):.5f}   (close to g = 0.02)")

Population (billions):     [6.     6.12   6.2424 6.3672 6.4946 6.6245]
Yearly change in ln L:     [0.0198 0.0198 0.0198 0.0198 0.0198]
Slope of eq. (3), ln(1.02): 0.01980   (close to g = 0.02)


Check 3: the Rule of 70. We compare the exact doubling time, equation (4), with the approximations of equation (5), and confirm that the population really is twice as large after one exact doubling time.

print("Growth rate   exact, eq. (4)   69.3 / g   Rule of 70, eq. (5)")
for g in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.07):
    G = 100 * g                                     # the growth rate in percent
    print(f"{G:9.0f}%   {doubling_time(g):14.2f}   {69.3 / G:8.2f}   {70 / G:19.2f}")
print(f"At 2%, after {doubling_time(0.02):.2f} years: {constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, doubling_time(0.02)):.3f} billion")

Growth rate   exact, eq. (4)   69.3 / g   Rule of 70, eq. (5)
        1%            69.66      69.30                 70.00
        2%            35.00      34.65                 35.00
        3%            23.45      23.10                 23.33
        7%            10.24       9.90                 10.00
At 2%, after 35.00 years: 12.000 billion


The Rule of 70 is within half a year of the exact answer at these growth rates. In relative terms its error grows once growth rates go well beyond a few percent: at 7 percent it is off by more than 2 percent.
Check 4: the average annual growth rate. Equation (6) must undo equation (2), the log version of step 4 must agree with it, and the geometric mean of step 5 must give the right answer where the plain average does not.

end = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, 100)
print(f"6 billion at 2% for 100 years:          {end:.2f} billion")
print(f"Equation (6) gives back:                {growth_rate(6.0, end, 100):.4f}")
print(f"Log version, exp(slope) - 1:            {np.exp((np.log(end) - np.log(6.0)) / 100) - 1:.4f}")
print(f"One year, t = 1 (a percentage change):  {growth_rate(6.0, 6.3, 1):.4f}")
print(f"Up 10% then down 10%, two years:        {growth_rate(1.0, 1.10 * 0.90, 2):+.4f}   (not 0)")
higher = growth_rate(6.0, 1.01 * end, 100)
print(f"Final value 1% higher: the growth rate rises by {100 * (higher - 0.02):.4f} percentage points")

6 billion at 2% for 100 years:          43.47 billion
Equation (6) gives back:                0.0200
Log version, exp(slope) - 1:            0.0200
One year, t = 1 (a percentage change):  0.0500
Up 10% then down 10%, two years:        -0.0050   (not 0)
Final value 1% higher: the growth rate rises by 0.0101 percentage points


Check 5: the growth rules. We take the U.S. growth rates of Fig. 9, 1.9 percent for GDP per person and 1.4 percent for the population, and compare each rule with the exact growth over one year.

gy, gL = 0.019, 0.014                               # GDP per person and population, U.S. since 1870 (Fig. 9)
y0, L0 = 1.0, 1.0
y1, L1 = y0 * (1 + gy), L0 * (1 + gL)               # the values one year later
print(f"Product  y x L:    rule (7) {gy + gL:.5f}   exact {(y1 * L1) / (y0 * L0) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Ratio    y / L:    rule (8) {gy - gL:.5f}   exact {(y1 / L1) / (y0 / L0) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Power    y^(1/3):  rule (9) {gy / 3:.5f}   exact {y1 ** (1 / 3) / y0 ** (1 / 3) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Power    L^(-2):   rule (9) {-2 * gL:.5f}   exact {L1 ** -2 / L0 ** -2 - 1:.5f}")
change_logs = np.log(y1 * L1) - np.log(y0 * L0)
print(f"In logs the product rule is exact: {change_logs:.5f} = {np.log(1 + gy) + np.log(1 + gL):.5f}")

Each country keeps one color in every chart of this notebook, so a country is easy to follow when you add others. The function group_colors hands them out.

LIGHT = {"#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"}      # too pale on white
PALETTE = []                                                                   # 44 colors
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT and c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # too close to the book's U.S. blue: used last


Python note. group_colors gives the countries their colors one at a time. For each country, the list used collects the colors already given to the countries shown together with it, and the country takes the first palette color that is not in used, preferring one that no country has yet. If every color is taken, it takes the one that used counts least often (.count), searching from the end of the palette (reversed). dict(fixed or {}) starts from a copy of the fixed colors (or an empty dictionary), and continue skips to the next country.


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color} for the book's countries."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []                                       # the colors of the countries shown with `name`
        for group in groups:
            for other in group:
                if name in group and other in colors:
                    used.append(colors[other])
        free, unused = [], []
        for c in PALETTE:
            if c not in used:
                free.append(c)
                if c not in colors.values():
                    unused.append(c)                    # no country has this color yet: the best choice
        least = PALETTE[-1]
        for c in reversed(PALETTE):                     # no free color: the one used least, from the end
            if used.count(c) < used.count(least):
                least = c
        colors[name] = (unused + free + [least])[0]
    return colors

The eight countries of the textbook’s figures get fixed colors of our palette. Each group lists the countries that one region view shows together: the eight, plus the countries of that region.

Python note. .groupby("country").region.first() gives each country’s region, taken from its first row. region_of[region_of == region].index lists the countries of one region.

Python note. px.line draws one line per value of color=; markers=True adds a dot for each estimate, and log_y=True gives a ratio scale (Fig. 4 explains it). color_discrete_map=COLORS gives each country its own color. interact calls the function and draws the figure again every time you change a control: a Dropdown is a menu of choices, ToggleButtons is a row of buttons, and a SelectMultiple is a list from which you pick several countries by holding Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) while clicking. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text. In short, name.split(" (")[0] cuts the text at ” (” and keeps the first piece, and SHORT_NAMES.get(name, name) looks the name up in the dictionary, returning it unchanged when it is not there. a if condition else b gives a when the condition is true and b otherwise.


SHORT_NAMES = {"Republic of Korea": "South Korea", "D.R. of the Congo": "DR Congo", "Russian Federation": "Russia",
               "Taiwan, Province of China": "Taiwan", "China, Hong Kong SAR": "Hong Kong", "U.R. of Tanzania": "Tanzania",
               "Lao People's DR": "Laos", "Republic of Moldova": "Moldova", "Syrian Arab Republic": "Syria"}


def short(name):
    """A short country name for titles, e.g. 'Bolivia (Plurinational State of)' -> 'Bolivia'."""
    name = name.split(" (")[0].split(":")[0]                      # drop '(...)' and ': Mainland'
    return SHORT_NAMES.get(name, name)


def very_long_run(start=1, scale="linear", countries=tuple(BOOK_SIX)):
    """Fig. 3.1: GDP per person (multiples of $500) from the year `start` to 2022."""
    chosen = everyone[(everyone.year >= start) & everyone.country.isin(countries)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gdp", color="country", markers=True, log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(countries)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdp": "GDP per person (multiple of 500 dollars)", "country": "Country"})
    if chosen.empty:
        fig.update_layout(title=f"No data for the chosen countries since the year {start}")
        return fig
    name = "United Kingdom" if "United Kingdom" in set(chosen.country) else chosen.country.iloc[0]
    one = chosen[chosen.country == name]
    factor = one.gdp.iloc[-1] / one.gdp.iloc[0]
    label = "U.K." if name == "United Kingdom" else short(name)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{label} GDP per person in {one.year.iloc[-1]} was {factor:.0f} times "
                            f"its level in the year {one.year.iloc[0]}")
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500])
    return fig

def income_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 3.2: GDP per person (2022 dollars); the U.S. alone uses the official series to 2025."""
    if tuple(countries) == ("United States",):
        chosen = us.assign(country="United States")
    else:
        chosen = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", color_discrete_map=COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    latest = chosen.groupby("country").last()
    if chosen.empty:
        fig.update_layout(title="Choose at least one country")
    elif len(latest) == 1:
        first, last = chosen.iloc[0], chosen.iloc[-1]
        label = "U.S." if first.country == "United States" else short(first.country)
        fig.update_layout(title=f"{label} GDP per person grew about {last.gdppc / first.gdppc:.0f}-fold "
                                f"from {first.year} to {last.year}")
    else:
        rich, poor = latest.gdppc.idxmax(), latest.gdppc.idxmin()
        fig.update_layout(title=f"{latest.year.max()}: GDP per person {latest.gdppc.max() / latest.gdppc.min():.0f} "
                                f"times higher in {short(rich)} than in {short(poor)}")
    return fig

text:
The mathematics of growth
Constant growth produces a curve that bends upward, which is hard to read. These figures show why, and how a ratio scale turns that curve into a straight line.

Fig. 3: Population over time
Goal. See what constant growth looks like when we plot it.
Suppose the world population starts at \(L_0 = 6\) billion and grows at a constant rate \(\bar{n} = 2\%\) a year. Each year the population is multiplied by \((1+\bar{n})\):
\[L_{t+1} = L_t\,(1+\bar{n})\]
This is equation (1) written for the population. Applying it year after year gives \(L_t = L_0(1+\bar{n})^t\) (equation 2). The cell below checks this with a loop: it multiplies by \(1.02\) one hundred times and compares the result with the formula.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each value. range(100) gives the numbers 0, 1, …, 99, so the loop runs exactly 100 times.


L = 6.0
for year in range(100):
    L = L * (1 + 0.02)                     # equation (1), applied once per year
print(f"Year by year:  L_100 = {L:.2f} billion")
print(f"Formula (2):   L_100 = {constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, 100):.2f} billion")

Year by year:  L_100 = 43.47 billion
Formula (2):   L_100 = 43.47 billion



Python note. np.arange(0, 101) gives the whole numbers 0, 1, …, 100. go.Figure() starts an empty chart, and add_trace adds a curve to it. In the widget cell, a FloatSlider chooses a number between min and max in steps of step; readout_format=".3f" shows it with three decimals. L[-1] is the last value of the array, and max(100, 1.05 * L[-1]) is the larger of the two numbers: the vertical axis stays at 0 to 100 unless the curve would leave it.


def population_path(L0=6.0, n=0.02):
    """Fig. 3.3: population L_t = L0 (1 + n)^t over 100 years."""
    t = np.arange(0, 101)
    L = constant_growth(L0, n, t)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Population", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"L0 = {L0:.0f} billion growing at {100 * n:.1f}% a year: after 100 years, L = {L[-1]:.1f} billion",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[0, 102], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Population L (billions)", range=[0, max(100, 1.05 * L[-1])]))
    return fig

         n=FloatSlider(value=0.02, min=0.0, max=0.04, step=0.005, description="growth rate n", style=WIDE,
                       readout_format=".3f"));

What to notice.

At 2 percent a year, 6 billion people become 43.5 billion after a century, more than seven times as many. (This is only an illustration: demographers expect population growth to fall toward zero.)
The curve bends upward, just like U.S. GDP per person in Fig. 2. A constant growth rate adds a larger amount each year, because it applies to a larger base.
From this picture alone, it is hard to tell whether the growth rate is constant. Fig. 4 fixes that.

Fig. 4: Population over time, revisited
Goal. Learn to read a ratio scale, on which constant growth is a straight line.
At 2 percent a year, the population doubles about every 35 years (Rule of 70: \(70/2 = 35\)). It goes from 6 to 12, 24 and 48 billion. On a ratio scale, the vertical axis is labeled 6, 12, 24, 48: each step doubles the one before. Equal distances then mean equal percentage changes, so a constant growth rate draws a straight line.

Python note. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, ...) makes a figure with two panels side by side, and row=1, col=2 sends a trace to the second one. np.arange(0, 106, T) gives 0, T, 2T, … up to 105. On a ratio-scale axis, the range is given in powers of ten: np.log10(150).


def population_two_scales(n=0.02):
    """Fig. 3.4: the same population path on (a) a standard scale and (b) a ratio scale."""
    T = doubling_time(n)
    t = np.linspace(0, 105, 200)
    dots = np.arange(0, 106, T)                                   # every doubling time
    L, L_dots = constant_growth(6, n, t), constant_growth(6, n, dots)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) Standard scale: the curve bends upward", "(b) Ratio scale: a straight line"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Standard scale", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Ratio scale", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4)), row=1, col=2)
    for col in [1, 2]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=dots, y=L_dots, name="Each doubling", mode="markers", showlegend=(col == 1),
                                 marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Year", range=[-3, 108], tickvals=[25, 50, 75, 100])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Population L (billions)", range=[0, 85], row=1, col=1)      # fixed: room for n = 2.5%
    fig.update_yaxes(type="log", range=[np.log10(4.5), np.log10(150)], tickvals=[6, 12, 24, 48, 96], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"n = {100 * n:.1f}%: doubles every {T:.1f} years (Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n):.1f})")
    return fig

Fig. 5: U.S. per capita GDP on a ratio scale
Goal. Use the ratio scale to read the growth rate of real data.
Here are the data of Fig. 2 again, now on a ratio scale, with a dashed line that grows at a constant rate. The line’s level is chosen to fit the data as closely as possible (by least squares, in logarithms). You can also choose another country; its data then come from the Maddison Project, and the vertical axis adapts.

Python note. np.log(gdp) takes the logarithm of every value at once, and .mean() averages them. On a ratio scale, a constant growth line is a straight line in logarithms, which is why we fit it there.


Python note. For a country other than the U.S., the vertical range runs from a little below the lowest value to a little above the highest one, in powers of ten (np.log10), because the axis is a ratio scale. DOUBLINGS lists tick values that double each time.


DOUBLINGS = [250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000, 256000]


def ratio_scale_chart(g=0.02, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 3.5: GDP per person on a ratio scale, with a constant-growth line at rate g."""
    data = us if country == "United States" else world[world.country == country]
    years = data.year - data.year.iloc[0]
    level = (np.log(data.gdppc) - years * np.log(1 + g)).mean()   # best-fitting starting level
    line = np.exp(level) * (1 + g) ** years
    label = "U.S." if country == "United States" else short(country)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="gdppc", log_y=True,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), name=f"{label} data", showlegend=True)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=data.year, y=line, name=f"Constant growth at {100 * g:.2f}%",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    low, high = 2500, 140000                                      # the textbook's U.S. range
    if country != "United States":
        low, high = min(data.gdppc.min(), line.min()) / 1.3, max(data.gdppc.max(), line.max()) * 1.3
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=DOUBLINGS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{label}: dashed line at {100 * g:.2f}% a year, doubling every "
                            f"{doubling_time(g):.0f} years")
    return fig

The title compares one country with the United States: Japan when it is chosen, otherwise the first country in your list. The helper versus_us finds the first and the last year in which both have data.

Python note. category_orders fixes the order of the countries in the legend. .pivot(...) turns the long table into a wide one, with one row per year and one column per country. .dropna() then keeps the years in which both countries have data. list(countries) makes a list we can change, and .remove(...) deletes one entry from it. The vertical axis widens (once, to a fixed wider range) when a chosen country lies outside the textbook’s range.


def versus_us(name):
    """First and last year in which `name` and the U.S. both have data, and name's GDP per person relative to the U.S."""
    pair = world[world.country.isin([name, "United States"])].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
    ratio = (pair[name] / pair["United States"]).dropna()
    return ratio.index[0], ratio.iloc[0], ratio.index[-1], ratio.iloc[-1]

BENCHMARKS = sorted(decades.year.unique())                     # the textbook's years: 1870, 1890, ..., 2022


def countries_since_1870(frequency="every decade", countries=tuple(SEVEN)):
    """Fig. 3.6: GDP per person on a ratio scale (2022 dollars), by decade or every year."""
    chosen = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    if frequency == "every decade":
        chosen = chosen[chosen.year.isin(BENCHMARKS)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", log_y=True, color_discrete_map=COLORS,
                  category_orders={"country": list(countries)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)", "country": "Country"})
    others = list(countries)
    if "United States" in others:
        others.remove("United States")                            # compare the others with the U.S.
    title = "Choose a country to compare with the United States"
    if others:
        name = "Japan" if "Japan" in others else others[0]
        first, share_first, last, share_last = versus_us(name)
        title = f"{short(name)} went from {share_first:.0%} of U.S. GDP per person in {first} to {share_last:.0%} in {last}"
    low, high = 700, 90000                                        # the textbook's range ...
    if not chosen.empty and (chosen.gdppc.min() < low or chosen.gdppc.max() > high):
        low, high = 250, 300000                                   # ... or one fixed wider range
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=DOUBLINGS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    fig.update_layout(title=title)
    return fig

Now we compute, for each country, its average annual growth rate from a starting year to 2023, and its GDP per person in 2023 relative to the United States.

Python note. merge joins two tables on a common column, like matching rows by ID in a spreadsheet. Each pass of the loop adds one table to the list tables, and pd.concat(tables) stacks them into one long table. .map(SHORT) looks each country up in the dictionary SHORT; countries that are not in it get NaN, which .fillna("") replaces with an empty text. That way only a few names are printed on the chart, and POSITION puts some of them beside their dot so that labels do not overlap.

         "Botswana": "Botswana", "Singapore": "Singapore", "Japan": "Japan", "Brazil": "Brazil",
         "D.R. of the Congo": "DR Congo", "Burundi": "Burundi", "Ethiopia": "Ethiopia"}
POSITION = {"United States": "bottom right", "India": "top left", "Botswana": "bottom right",
            "Singapore": "middle left", "Japan": "bottom left", "D.R. of the Congo": "bottom center"}

end["level_2023"] = end.gdp_pc / end[end.country == "United States"].gdp_pc.iloc[0]

for start in [1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010]:
    first = sample[sample.year == start][["iso3", "gdp_pc"]]

    table["growth"] = 100 * growth_rate(table.gdp_pc_start, table.gdp_pc_2023, 2023 - start)
    table["start_year"] = start
    tables.append(table)
