text:
Counting people, not countries
Weighting each country by its population changes the picture. This figure shows how many of the world’s people live at each level of income.

Fig. 8: The world’s population by per capita GDP
Goal. Count people instead of countries.
In Fig. 7 China and Luxembourg each count as one dot. Here every person counts equally. For a given year, we sort countries from poorest to richest and add up their populations. The chart shows the percentage of the world’s population that lives in countries with GDP per person at or below each level. Income is measured relative to the U.S. level in 2019 for every year, so that the curves can be compared.

Python note. .cumsum() gives running totals: the first value, then the sum of the first two, and so on. Dividing by the total and multiplying by 100 turns them into cumulative percentages. .copy() makes a separate table, so that adding a column does not touch sample. line_shape="hv" draws the line as steps, one for each country, and add_vline draws the dashed vertical line.


def cumulative_shares(year):
    """Countries sorted from poorest to richest in `year`, with the cumulative share of world population."""
    table = sample[sample.year == year].sort_values("y_rel_us_2019").copy()
    table["share"] = 100 * table.pop_millions.cumsum() / table.pop_millions.sum()
    return table


def population_distribution(year=2019):
    """Fig. 3.8: cumulative share of world population by GDP per person (U.S. 2019 = 1), year vs 1960."""
    both = pd.concat([cumulative_shares(1960), cumulative_shares(year)])
    below = cumulative_shares(year)
    poor = below[below.y_rel_us_2019 < 0.05].pop_millions.sum() / below.pop_millions.sum()
    fig = px.line(both, x="y_rel_us_2019", y="share", color="year", line_shape="hv", hover_name="country",
                  log_x=True, range_x=[1 / 200, 2], range_y=[0, 102], color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN, BLUE],
                  labels={"y_rel_us_2019": "Per capita GDP (U.S. = 1 in 2019, ratio scale)",
                          "share": "Share of world population (percent)", "year": "Year"})
    fig.add_vline(x=0.05, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=FRACTIONS, ticktext=FRACTION_NAMES)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{year}: {poor:.0%} of people live below 5% of the 2019 U.S. level (dashed line)")
    return fig

text:
Rules for growth rates
Last, three handy rules: the growth rate of a product is a sum, of a ratio a difference, and of a power a multiple. We check them with U.S. data.

Fig. 9: U.S. population, GDP and per capita GDP
Goal. See the rules for growth rates at work.
Three rules make growth rates easy to work with (equations 7 to 9). If \(x\) grows at rate \(g_x\) and \(y\) at rate \(g_y\), then

the product \(z = x \times y\) grows at \(g_x + g_y\);
the ratio \(z = x / y\) grows at \(g_x - g_y\);
the power \(z = x^a\) grows at \(a \times g_x\).

Total GDP is GDP per person times population, so its growth rate is the sum of the two growth rates. To see this, the chart divides each series by its value in the first year, so all three lines start at 1. For the United States we use the official series of the textbook figure. For any other country we compute total GDP from the Maddison Project’s GDP per person and population.

Python note. start, end = period unpacks a pair of years into two variables. Dividing the table table.loc[start:end] by its first row divides every column by its own first value. An IntRangeSlider has two handles, so it chooses a whole period at once. country_table builds, for any country, a table with the same columns as usa. .astype(float) turns whole numbers with gaps into ordinary numbers.


usa = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-9.csv").set_index("year")


def country_table(country):
    """Population (thousands), GDP per person and total GDP (billions of 2022 dollars) by year, as in `usa`."""
    if country == "United States":
        return usa                                                # the official series of the textbook
    one = world[world.country == country].set_index("year")
    table = pd.DataFrame({"population_thousands": one.pop_thousands.astype(float), "gdppc": one.gdppc})
    table["gdp_billions"] = table.gdppc * table.population_thousands / 1e6
    return table.dropna()

If the period starts before a country’s data do, the chart starts in the country’s first year, and the title says which years it uses.

def growth_rules_chart(period=(1870, 2025), country="United States"):
    """Fig. 3.9: total GDP, GDP per person and population, each relative to its first-year value."""
    table = country_table(country)
    start, end = period
    if end == start:                                              # both handles on one year: use one year
        end = min(start + 1, 2025)
        start = end - 1
    chosen = table.loc[start:end]
    if len(chosen) < 2:                                           # no data in the period
        return go.Figure().update_layout(title=f"No data for {short(country)} in {start}–{end}")
    start, end = chosen.index[0], chosen.index[-1]
    rates = (100 * growth_rate(chosen.iloc[0], chosen.iloc[-1], end - start)).round(2) + 0.0   # + 0.0: no "-0.00"
    chosen = (chosen / chosen.iloc[0]).reset_index().rename(columns={
        "gdp_billions": "Total GDP", "gdppc": "Per capita GDP", "population_thousands": "Population"})
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y=["Total GDP", "Per capita GDP", "Population"], log_y=True,
                  color_discrete_sequence=["#e0a33b", GREEN, BLUE],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Relative to the first year (ratio scale)", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[start - (end - start) / 20, end])   # a little room: no label in the bottom-left corner
    label = "" if country == "United States" else f"{short(country)}, "
    sign = "+" if rates.population_thousands >= 0 else "−"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{label}{start}–{end}: GDP {rates.gdp_billions:.2f}% ≈ per capita {rates.gdppc:.2f}%"
                            f" {sign} population {abs(rates.population_thousands):.2f}% a year")
    return fig

title: 3. An Overview of Long-Run Economic Growth
text:
Concluding remarks

Sustained growth in living standards is very recent. It began about 200 years ago and spread unevenly, which produced the Great Divergence in incomes across countries.
A growth rate is a percentage change. Growing at a constant rate, a variable is multiplied by \(1+\bar{g}\) each year, equation (1), so after \(t\) years it equals \(y_t = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t\), the constant growth rule, equation (2). Compounding makes the yearly increase grow, and small differences in growth rates become large gaps in levels.
In logs, constant growth is a straight line, equation (3), so on a ratio scale the slope is the growth rate. A variable doubles in exactly \(\ln 2/\ln(1+\bar{g})\) years, equation (4), or in about \(70/g\) years, the Rule of 70, equation (5). U.S. GDP per person has grown at close to 2 percent a year for more than 150 years.
The average annual growth rate between two years, equation (6), is the one constant rate that links the two end points: a geometric mean of the yearly growth factors.
Growth rates differ a lot across countries, and small differences compound into huge income gaps. Counting people rather than countries, poverty has fallen dramatically, mainly because of growth in China and India.
Growth rates of products are sums, of ratios are differences, and of powers are multiples, equations (7) to (9). Applied to the production function, they split output growth into productivity growth plus weighted input growth, equation (10).
The next chapter builds a first model to explain why some countries are so much richer than others.

title: 3. An Overview of Long-Run Economic Growth
text:
Practice problems
These problems put the chapter’s tools to work in three ways: conceptual problems apply the growth-rate math to real cases, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data to find patterns and facts, and modeling problems use the chapter’s interactive charts to answer policy questions. Each problem is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it first, then open the Hint, and only then the Solution. The sliders in the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): China’s plan to double its economy. China’s 13th Five-Year Plan (2016–2020) set out to “ensure that China’s 2010 GDP and per capita personal income double by 2020”. Its table of targets has GDP rising from 67.7 trillion yuan in 2015 to more than 92.7 trillion yuan in 2020 (13th Five-Year Plan, official English translation, Chapter 3 and Box 2).

What average annual growth rate does doubling GDP in the ten years from 2010 to 2020 require?
What average annual growth rate do the plan’s GDP numbers for 2015 and 2020 imply? If the goal was to be met, what does that say about growth from 2010 to 2015?
The goal also named income per person. In this chapter’s Maddison data, China’s population grew about 0.5 percent a year from 2010 to 2020. How fast must total GDP grow for GDP per person to double in ten years?



Hint

Doubling means \(y_t/y_0 = 2\) with \(t = 10\) in equation (6). In (b), the two five-year periods must together multiply GDP by 2. In (c), GDP per person is GDP divided by the population, so the ratio rule, equation (8), applies.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Put \(y_{2020}/y_{2010} = 2\) and \(t = 10\) into equation (6):
\[\bar{g} = 2^{1/10} - 1 = 1.0718 - 1 = 0.0718.\]
Doubling in ten years takes growth of about 7.2 percent a year. The Rule of 70, equation (5), agrees: at 7.2 percent a variable doubles in about \(70/7.2 \approx 9.7\) years.
(b) Equation (6) with \(t = 5\):
\[\bar{g} = \left(\frac{92.7}{67.7}\right)^{1/5} - 1 = 1.3693^{1/5} - 1 = 0.0649,\]
about 6.5 percent a year, the “more than 6.5 percent” of the plan’s table. That is slower than the 7.2 percent of (a), so the first five years had to be faster. Call \(g_1\) the growth rate of 2010–2015. The two periods together must double GDP. Taking the fifth root of both sides of that condition, and then dividing by 1.0649:
\[(1+g_1)^5 \times 1.0649^5 = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1+g_1) \times 1.0649 = 2^{1/5}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1+g_1 = \frac{1.1487}{1.0649} = 1.0787.\]
The plan’s 6.5 percent was enough only if GDP had grown about 7.9 percent a year from 2010 to 2015.
(c) GDP per person is \(y = Y/L\), so the ratio rule, equation (8), gives \(g_y = g_Y - g_L\), or \(g_Y = g_y + g_L\). With \(g_y = 7.18\) percent from (a) and \(g_L = 0.5\) percent:
\[g_Y \approx 7.18 + 0.5 = 7.68 \text{ percent}, \qquad \text{or exactly} \quad (1.0718)(1.005) - 1 = 0.0772.\]
Total GDP must grow about 7.7 percent a year: over ten years it must rise by a factor of \(2 \times 1.005^{10} = 2.10\), not 2. A goal for income per person is harder to reach than the same goal for GDP whenever the population grows.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Greece’s slump, or why a fall needs a bigger rise. Greece’s debt crisis led to a joint rescue by the European Union and the IMF in May 2010 (IMF press release, 9 May 2010). In this chapter’s data (maddison_world.csv, from the Maddison Project Database 2023), Greek GDP per person peaked in 2008 and then fell every year until 2013:



Year
2008
2013
2022




GDP per person (2022 dollars)
37,296
28,816
32,621




By what percentage did GDP per person fall from 2008 to 2013? By what percentage must it rise from its 2013 level to get back to the 2008 level? Show that after a fall by a fraction \(x\), the rise needed is \(x/(1-x)\).
Use equation (6) to compute the average annual growth rate from 2008 to 2013, and from 2013 to 2022.
If Greece kept growing at its 2013–2022 rate after 2022, in what year would GDP per person be back at its 2008 level? How many years of that growth did the slump of 2008–2013 undo?



Hint


Write the 2013 level as \((1-x)\) times the 2008 level, and ask which factor takes it back. (c) The Model overview shows that a variable growing at the rate \(\bar{g}\) takes \(t = \ln m/\ln(1+\bar{g})\) years to grow by a factor \(m\).


Your answer:


Solution

(a) The ratio of the two levels is \(28{,}816/37{,}296 = 0.7726\), so GDP per person fell by \(1 - 0.7726 = 0.2274\), about 22.7 percent. To get back, it must be multiplied by \(37{,}296/28{,}816 = 1.2943\): a rise of 29.4 percent. In general, if \(y_{2013} = (1-x)\,y_{2008}\), the factor back is \(1/(1-x)\), and the rise is
\[\frac{1}{1-x} - 1 = \frac{1 - (1-x)}{1-x} = \frac{x}{1-x} = \frac{0.2274}{0.7726} = 0.294.\]
The rise is larger than the fall because it starts from a lower base.
(b) From 2008 to 2013, \(0.7726^{1/5} - 1 = -0.0503\): GDP per person fell about 5.0 percent a year. From 2013 to 2022, \((32{,}621/28{,}816)^{1/9} - 1 = 1.1320^{1/9} - 1 = 0.0139\), about 1.4 percent a year.
(c) In 2022 Greece was still \(1 - 32{,}621/37{,}296 = 12.5\) percent below its 2008 level. The factor still to go is \(m = 37{,}296/32{,}621 = 1.1433\), so
\[t = \frac{\ln 1.1433}{\ln 1.0139} = \frac{0.1339}{0.0138} = 9.7 \text{ years}.\]
At 1.4 percent a year, Greece gets back to its 2008 level around 2032, 24 years after the peak. The slump undid \(\ln 1.2943/\ln 1.0139 = 18.7\) years of growth at that rate. Over 2008–2022 as a whole, equation (6) gives \((32{,}621/37{,}296)^{1/14} - 1 = -0.95\) percent a year. A deep slump costs living standards for a long time, because the recovery has to climb back from a lower base.

Problem 3 (Challenge): How long until India catches up? The World Bank estimates that India’s real GDP must grow 7.8 percent a year on average for 22 years to reach the country’s goal of high-income status by 2047; from 2000 to 2024, growth averaged 6.3 percent (World Bank press release, 28 February 2025).

Suppose India’s population grows 1.05 percent a year, its rate from 2012 to 2022 in this chapter’s Maddison data. What growth rate of GDP per person does GDP growth of 7.8 percent give? By what factor do GDP and GDP per person rise in 22 years?
A poorer country P starts with the fraction \(r_0 = y^P_0/y^R_0\) of the income per person of a richer country R. P grows at the constant rate \(\bar{g}_P\) and R at \(\bar{g}_R\), with \(\bar{g}_P > \bar{g}_R\). Derive the number of years \(t\) until P reaches the fraction \(r^*\) of R’s income. Then show that the income gap halves about every \(70/(g_P - g_R)\) years, with the growth rates in percent.
In the Maddison data, India’s GDP per person was 13.28 percent of the U.S. level in 2022, and U.S. GDP per person grew 1.11 percent a year from 2000 to 2022. If the U.S. kept that pace, how many years would India need to reach half the U.S. level with the growth rate of (a)? And with its own 2000–2022 rate of 4.83 percent? (Half the U.S. level is our yardstick, not the World Bank’s definition of high income.)



Hint


Write equation (2) for both countries and divide the first by the second, so the starting levels become the ratio \(r_0\). Then take logs, as in the derivation of the doubling time, equation (4), and use \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\).
Start from \(r_0 = 0.1328\) and aim for \(r^* = 0.5\).


Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) The ratio rule, equation (8), gives \(g_y \approx 7.8 - 1.05 = 6.75\) percent, or exactly \(1.078/1.0105 - 1 = 0.0668\), about 6.7 percent a year. In 22 years GDP rises by a factor of \(1.078^{22} = 5.22\) and GDP per person by \(1.0668^{22} = 4.15\).
(b) Equation (2) for each country gives \(y^P_t = y^P_0(1+\bar{g}_P)^t\) and \(y^R_t = y^R_0(1+\bar{g}_R)^t\). Dividing the first by the second:
\[\frac{y^P_t}{y^R_t} = r_0\left(\frac{1+\bar{g}_P}{1+\bar{g}_R}\right)^t.\]
Set the left-hand side equal to \(r^*\), divide both sides by \(r_0\), and take logs:
\[\ln\frac{r^*}{r_0} = t\left[\ln(1+\bar{g}_P) - \ln(1+\bar{g}_R)\right]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
t = \frac{\ln(r^*/r_0)}{\ln(1+\bar{g}_P) - \ln(1+\bar{g}_R)} \approx \frac{\ln(r^*/r_0)}{\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R}.\]
This is the ratio rule at work: relative income \(y^P/y^R\) grows at about \(\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R\), so it behaves like any variable growing at that rate. Halving the gap means doubling the ratio, \(r^*/r_0 = 2\), so \(t \approx \ln 2/(\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R) \approx 0.70/(\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R) = 70/(g_P - g_R)\) with the rates in percent. If \(\bar{g}_P \le \bar{g}_R\), the gap never closes.
(c) The ratio must rise by the factor \(r^*/r_0 = 0.5/0.1328 = 3.77\), and \(\ln 3.77 = 1.33\).
r0 = 0.1328                                    # India relative to the U.S. in 2022 (Maddison)
for g_india in [1.078 / 1.0105 - 1, 0.0483]:
    years = np.log(0.5 / r0) / (np.log(1 + g_india) - np.log(1 + 0.0111))
    print(f"India growing {100 * g_india:.2f}% a year: half the U.S. level after {years:.1f} years, around {2022 + years:.0f}")
At 6.68 percent a year India reaches half the U.S. level after 24.7 years, around 2047; at its 2000–2022 pace of 4.83 percent it takes 36.7 years, until about 2059. The Rule-of-70 view gives the same picture: at a growth gap of \(6.68 - 1.11 = 5.57\) points the gap halves every \(70/5.57 = 12.6\) years, and it must halve \(\log_2 3.77 = 1.9\) times. Faster growth by 1.85 points a year brings the date forward by 12 years.



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): The Great Divergence in one number. The file maddison_world.csv holds GDP per person (2022 dollars) for 169 countries from the Maddison Project Database 2023. Find the richest and the poorest country in 1870 and in 2022, and the ratio of their GDP per person. How many countries have an estimate in each year, and how does that affect the comparison?


Hint

maddison[maddison.year == 1870] keeps one year. .idxmax() gives the row label of the largest value, and .loc[...] then picks that row. len(...) counts the countries. To compare like with like, you can keep in 2022 only the countries that also appear in 1870.


# Your answer here



Solution

For each year, keep its rows, find the rows of the largest and the smallest GDP per person, and divide. Then repeat 2022 with the 1870 countries only.
maddison = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
for year in [1870, 2022]:
    one_year = maddison[maddison.year == year]
    richest = one_year.loc[one_year.gdppc.idxmax()]
    poorest = one_year.loc[one_year.gdppc.idxmin()]
    print(f"{year}: {len(one_year)} countries; {richest.country} {richest.gdppc:,} / "
          f"{poorest.country} {poorest.gdppc:,} = {richest.gdppc / poorest.gdppc:.1f}")
in_1870 = maddison[maddison.year == 1870].country
same = maddison[(maddison.year == 2022) & maddison.country.isin(in_1870)]
print(f"2022, the same {len(same)} countries: {same.gdppc.max() / same.gdppc.min():.1f}")
In 1870 the richest country, the United Kingdom (7,520 dollars), was 9.1 times as rich as the poorest, Nepal (827 dollars). In 2022 Qatar (192,456 dollars) was 250 times as rich as the Central African Republic (769 dollars). But only 70 countries have an estimate for 1870, against 169 in 2022: in Sub-Saharan Africa only Liberia and South Africa have one, and Qatar is an oil exporter with fewer than 3 million people. Among the same 70 countries, the ratio in 2022 is 108.9 (Norway against Liberia). Either way, the gap between the richest and the poorest grew more than tenfold: that is the Great Divergence.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Booms, busts and the average growth rate. The file fig3-2.csv holds U.S. GDP per person (2022 dollars) from 1870 to 2025: from 1929 it comes from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, real GDP (GDPCA), via FRED and the BEA’s population, and before 1929 from the Maddison Project Database 2023.

Compute the growth rate of every year. Which five years saw the largest falls? Match them with the U.S. recessions dated by the NBER.
For 1870–2025, 1870–1949 and 1950–2025, compare the plain average of the yearly growth rates with the average annual growth rate of equation (6).
In which period is the gap between the two averages larger? Compare the standard deviations of the yearly growth rates, and explain.



Hint

.pct_change() gives the growth rate from each year to the next, and .sort_values().head(5) lists the five smallest. For (c), recall step 5 of the derivation of equation (6): a rise of 10 percent followed by a fall of 10 percent.


# Your answer here



Solution

Compute the yearly growth rates once, list the smallest, and then, for each period, compare their mean with growth_rate applied to the first and the last year.
us_gdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-2.csv").set_index("year").gdppc
yearly = us_gdp.pct_change().dropna()                 # the growth rate of each year, from 1871
print((100 * yearly.sort_values().head(5)).round(1))
for first, last in [(1870, 2025), (1870, 1949), (1950, 2025)]:
    rates = yearly.loc[first + 1:last]
    plain = 100 * rates.mean()
    eq6 = 100 * growth_rate(us_gdp[first], us_gdp[last], last - first)
    print(f"{first}-{last}: plain average {plain:.2f}%, equation (6) {eq6:.2f}%, "
          f"standard deviation {100 * rates.std():.1f}%")
(a) The five largest falls are 1932 (−13.5 percent), 1946 (−12.5), 1914 (−10.0), 1908 (−9.8) and 1930 (−9.5). 1930 and 1932 fall in the NBER’s contraction of August 1929 to March 1933: the Great Depression. 1908 and 1914 fall in the contractions of May 1907 to June 1908 and January 1913 to December 1914 (before 1929 these are estimates). 1946 is the first year after World War II, when war production was cut back.
(b) From 1870 to 2025 the plain average is 1.99 percent and equation (6) gives 1.88 percent. For 1870–1949 the two are 1.92 and 1.72 percent; for 1950–2025, 1.99 and 1.97 percent.
(c) The gap is about 0.2 points before 1950 and only 0.02 points after. The standard deviation of the yearly growth rates was 6.3 percent before 1950 and 2.2 percent after: the early economy swung far more. A fall hurts more than an equal rise helps (\(1.10 \times 0.90 = 0.99\)), so the plain average overstates growth, and more so the bigger the swings. A handy rule is that the gap is about half the variance: \(0.063^2/2 = 0.0020\), or 0.2 points. Use equation (6) for growth over a period.

Problem 6 (Intermediate): Argentina’s century of relative decline. Alan Taylor describes Argentina’s economic history as one of the most dramatic cases of divergence in modern times (Taylor 2014, NBER Working Paper 19924). Compare it in maddison_world.csv with two other countries rich in land and settled by immigrants, Australia and Canada.

Compute the GDP per person of Argentina, Australia and Canada relative to the United States in 1913 and in 2022.
Compute the average annual growth rate of the four countries from 1913 to 2022.
How rich would Argentina have been in 2022 if it had grown as fast as Australia since 1913? Compare this with its actual level.



Hint

Turn the four countries into a wide table, one column per country, with .pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc"), as in the Key numbers of Fig. 6. Then growth_rate gives (b), and constant_growth gives (c).


# Your answer here



Solution

Make the wide table, divide each year’s row by the U.S. value, then apply equation (6) and equation (2).
maddison = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
four_names = ["Argentina", "Australia", "Canada", "United States"]
four = maddison[maddison.country.isin(four_names)].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
for year in [1913, 2022]:
    print(year, (four.loc[year] / four.loc[year, "United States"]).round(2).to_dict())
for name in four_names:
    print(f"{name}: {growth_rate(four.loc[1913, name], four.loc[2022, name], 109):.2%} a year")
g_aus = growth_rate(four.loc[1913, "Australia"], four.loc[2022, "Australia"], 109)
what_if = constant_growth(four.loc[1913, "Argentina"], g_aus, 109)
print(f"Argentina at Australia's rate: {what_if:,.0f} dollars, {what_if / four.loc[2022, 'Argentina']:.1f} times its actual level")
(a) In 1913 Argentina had 60 percent of U.S. GDP per person, Canada 70 percent and Australia 81 percent. In 2022 Argentina had 31 percent, while Canada had risen to 78 percent and Australia to 89 percent.
(b) From 1913 to 2022, GDP per person grew 1.02 percent a year in Argentina, 1.71 percent in Australia, 1.72 percent in Canada and 1.62 percent in the United States.
(c) At Australia’s 1.71 percent, Argentina’s 7,808 dollars of 1913 would have become about 49,400 dollars in 2022, 2.1 times its actual 23,600 dollars. A gap of 0.7 points a year looks small, but by the ratio rule it makes Argentina’s income relative to Australia’s fall about 0.7 percent a year, which halves it in about \(70/0.7 = 100\) years. That is what happened: Argentina had 74 percent of Australia’s GDP per person in 1913 and 35 percent in 2022.

Problem 7 (Challenge): A fairer test of catch-up. Fig. 7 plots each country’s growth against its income in 2023, and the chapter warns that its upward tilt is partly built in. Patel, Sandefur and Subramanian (2021) find that poorer countries have been catching up with richer ones, slowly, since the mid-1990s (Journal of Development Economics, doi:10.1016/j.jdeveco.2021.102687). Check this with pwt_income.csv from the Penn World Table 11.0, for the 110 countries of Fig. 7 (those with in_sample true, without Venezuela).

Compute each country’s average annual growth rate of GDP per person from 1960 to 2023, and from 2000 to 2023.
For each period, compute the correlation of growth with the log of GDP per person relative to the United States in the starting year, and with the log of relative GDP per person in 2023.
What do the four correlations say about convergence? How many countries grew faster than the United States in each period?



Hint

Build one table per starting year with merge, as the code of Fig. 7 does, and add a column with np.log(...) of relative income. table.growth.corr(table.log_start) gives a correlation. For (c), ask why a country that grew fast must end up rich, whatever its start.


# Your answer here



Solution

For each starting year, merge the start-year and 2023 values, compute growth with equation (6), divide by the U.S. value of the same year, take logs and correlate.
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_income.csv")
panel = panel[panel.in_sample & (panel.country != "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)")]
last_year = panel[panel.year == 2023][["iso3", "gdp_pc"]]
for start_year in [1960, 2000]:
    pair = panel[panel.year == start_year][["iso3", "country", "gdp_pc"]].merge(last_year, on="iso3",
                                                                                suffixes=("_start", "_2023"))
    pair["growth"] = 100 * growth_rate(pair.gdp_pc_start, pair.gdp_pc_2023, 2023 - start_year)
    usa_row = pair[pair.country == "United States"].iloc[0]
    pair["log_start"] = np.log(pair.gdp_pc_start / usa_row.gdp_pc_start)
    pair["log_2023"] = np.log(pair.gdp_pc_2023 / usa_row.gdp_pc_2023)
    print(f"{start_year}-2023, {len(pair)} countries: correlation with the start level "
          f"{pair.growth.corr(pair.log_start):.2f}, with the 2023 level {pair.growth.corr(pair.log_2023):.2f}; "
          f"{(pair.growth > usa_row.growth).sum()} grew faster than the U.S. ({usa_row.growth:.2f}%)")
(a)–(b) For 1960–2023 the correlation of growth with the starting level is −0.05, and with the 2023 level +0.66. For 2000–2023 it is −0.34 with the starting level and −0.05 with the 2023 level.
(c) The +0.66 of Fig. 7’s view is mostly built in: a country that grew fast became rich by 2023, whatever its start. Against the starting level, 1960–2023 shows almost no relation: on average, poor countries in 1960 did not grow faster than rich ones, so there was no catch-up across the world as a whole. Since 2000 the correlation is negative, −0.34: poorer countries grew faster on average, as Patel, Sandefur and Subramanian find. It is still weak, so catch-up is slow and many poor countries lag. From 1960, 64 of the 110 countries grew faster than the United States (2.03 percent a year); from 2000, 85 did (the U.S. grew 1.32 percent a year).



Modeling problems
Problem 8 (Basic): Will the world’s population double again? The United Nations reports that the world population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022, twelve years after it passed 7 billion. It expects 9 billion in about 15 years, around 2037, and a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s (United Nations, Global Issues: Population). Food and energy planners want to know how soon the world will need twice as much as today. The widget is the doubling chart of Fig. 4 with a finer slider for the growth rate. It starts at 6 billion, but the doubling time does not depend on the starting level.

What was the average annual growth rate of the world population from 7 to 8 billion? Set the slider close to it: how many years would a doubling take at that rate?
Do the same for the UN’s path from 8 to 9 billion.
What average growth rate takes the world from 8 billion in 2022 to 10.3 billion around 2085? Why can a constant growth rate never produce a peak? What population in 2085 would a planner predict by extending the growth rate of (a)?



Hint

Use equation (6) with the two population levels and the number of years between them. The chart’s title then gives the exact doubling time, equation (4), and the Rule of 70. For (c), equation (1) says how much a population growing at a constant \(\bar{n}\) adds in a year.


def world_doubling(n=0.015):
    """Fig. 3.4 with a finer slider: the doubling time of equation (4) for the growth rate n."""
    fig = population_two_scales(n)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"n = {100 * n:.2f}%: doubles every {doubling_time(n):.1f} years "
                            f"(Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n):.1f})")
    return fig


interact(world_doubling,
         n=FloatSlider(value=0.015, min=0.003, max=0.025, step=0.0005, description="growth rate n", style=WIDE,
                       readout_format=".4f"));

Source. The model of Fig. 4 above, adapted from Fig. 3.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

paths = [("7 to 8 billion", 7, 8, 12), ("8 to 9 billion", 8, 9, 15), ("8 to 10.3 billion", 8, 10.3, 63)]
for name, low, high, years in paths:
    n_path = growth_rate(low, high, years)
    print(f"{name}: n = {100 * n_path:.2f}% a year, doubling time {doubling_time(n_path):.1f} years "
          f"(Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n_path):.1f})")
print(f"8 billion at the 7-to-8 rate for 63 years: {constant_growth(8, growth_rate(7, 8, 12), 63):.1f} billion")
(a) Equation (6) gives \(\bar{n} = (8/7)^{1/12} - 1 = 0.0112\), or 1.12 percent a year. On the slider, 1.10 percent gives a doubling time of 63.4 years and 1.15 percent gives 60.6 years. The exact doubling time is \(\ln 2/\ln(1+\bar{n}) = 12\ln 2/\ln(8/7) = 62.3\) years (Rule of 70: 62.6).
(b) From 8 to 9 billion in 15 years, \(\bar{n} = (9/8)^{1/15} - 1 = 0.0079\), or 0.79 percent a year. The slider at 0.80 percent shows 87.0 years; the exact doubling time is \(15\ln 2/\ln(9/8) = 88.3\) years (Rule of 70: 88.8).
(c) From 8 to 10.3 billion in 63 years, \(\bar{n} = (10.3/8)^{1/63} - 1 = 0.0040\), only 0.40 percent a year, with a doubling time of 172.8 years. But a constant growth rate can never produce a peak. By equation (1), a population growing at a constant \(\bar{n} > 0\) adds \(\bar{n}L_t\) people every year, a positive amount that grows with \(L_t\), so the population rises forever. A peak needs a growth rate that falls to zero and then turns negative, which is what the UN expects as birth rates keep falling. A planner who extended the 1.12 percent of 2010–2022 would predict 16.1 billion people in 2085, almost 6 billion more than the UN’s peak. On the UN’s projections, the world population will not double again from 8 billion, so plans built on a constant growth rate would greatly overstate future needs.

Problem 9 (Intermediate): Fewer births, faster growth? In 2022 a woman in Niger had about 6.1 children on average, against 2.2 in Bangladesh, where the fertility rate has fallen from 6.8 in 1970 (World Bank, World Development Indicators, Fertility rate, total (SP.DYN.TFRT.IN)). The widget is the chart of Fig. 9 for five countries of Africa and South Asia.

Set the period to 1990–2022. Read the growth rates of total GDP, GDP per person and population in Niger and in Bangladesh. At these rates, how many years does GDP per person take to double in each country?
A policy adviser argues: “If Niger’s population grew as slowly as Bangladesh’s, while its GDP kept growing at the same rate, its GDP per person would double within a generation.” Use the ratio rule to check the claim.
Population growth is also growth of the labor force. Use equation (10), keeping productivity growth \(g_A\) and capital growth \(g_K\) unchanged, to show why the adviser is too optimistic. How fast would Niger’s GDP per person then grow, and how long would it take to double?



Hint


Keep \(g_Y\) fixed in \(g_y = g_Y - g_L\). (c) Per person, equation (10) becomes \(g_y = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}(g_K - g_L)\), as the Model overview shows. How much does \(g_y\) change when \(g_L\) falls by one point?



interact(growth_rules_chart,
         period=IntRangeSlider(value=(1990, 2022), min=1950, max=2022, step=1, description="period", style=WIDE),
         country=Dropdown(options=["Bangladesh", "Ethiopia", "Niger", "Nigeria", "Pakistan"], value="Niger",
                          description="country", style=WIDE));

Source. The chart of Fig. 9 above, with data from the Maddison Project Database 2023 (Bolt and van Zanden 2024), inspired by Fig. 3.9 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

for country_name in ["Niger", "Bangladesh"]:
    print(growth_rules_chart((1990, 2022), country_name).layout.title.text)
gY, gL_niger, gL_bangladesh, gy_niger = 0.0410, 0.0364, 0.0141, 0.0045
gy_rule = gY - gL_bangladesh                            # (b): ratio rule, GDP growth unchanged
gy_eq10 = gy_niger + (gL_niger - gL_bangladesh) / 3     # (c): equation (10), g_A and g_K unchanged
for name, rate in [("actual", gy_niger), ("(b) ratio rule", gy_rule), ("(c) equation (10)", gy_eq10)]:
    print(f"{name}: GDP per person grows {100 * rate:.2f}% a year and doubles in {doubling_time(rate):.0f} years")
(a) From 1990 to 2022, Niger’s GDP grew 4.10 percent a year, but its population grew 3.64 percent, so GDP per person grew only 0.45 percent: it doubles in about 154 years. Bangladesh’s GDP grew 6.57 percent and its population 1.41 percent, so GDP per person grew 5.09 percent and doubles in about 14 years.
(b) With \(g_Y = 4.10\) and \(g_L = 1.41\) percent, the ratio rule gives \(g_y = 4.10 - 1.41 = 2.69\) percent, which doubles GDP per person in about 26 years. On this arithmetic the adviser is right.
(c) But GDP growth would not stay the same. Population growth falls by \(\Delta = 3.64 - 1.41 = 2.23\) points, so by equation (10) labor adds \(\tfrac{2}{3} \times 2.23 = 1.49\) points less to GDP growth. Per person, \(g_y = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}(g_K - g_L)\) rises by only \(\Delta/3 = 0.74\) points, to \(0.45 + 0.74 = 1.19\) percent a year: the same capital is spread over fewer people, but fewer workers also produce less. GDP per person then doubles in about 58 years, not 26. Slower population growth helps, but only a third as much as the adviser thinks. By the same equation, Bangladesh’s lower population growth explains only a small part of its 4.64-point lead over Niger in growth per person; the rest must come from faster growth of productivity and of capital per person, the subject of Chapters 4 to 6.

Problem 10 (Challenge): Can poverty fall to 3 percent by 2030? In 2013 the World Bank and the IMF’s Development Committee endorsed the goal of cutting the share of the world’s people in extreme poverty to 3 percent by 2030 (IMF, Transcript of the Development Committee press briefing, 20 April 2013). The World Bank now counts people living on less than $3 a day as extremely poor (World Bank, Poverty overview). Fig. 8 uses a simpler measure: the share of people who live in countries whose GDP per person is below 5 percent of the 2019 U.S. level, about 3,400 dollars a year at 2021 prices.

Use the widget to read the share of people below the line in 1990, 2010, 2019 and 2023.
A falling share has a negative growth rate. Compute its average annual growth rate from 1990 to 2019 with equation (6). Derive a halving rule like the Rule of 70: about how many years does the share take to halve at that pace? At the 1990–2019 pace, in what year would the share reach 3 percent?
Repeat (b) for 2010–2023. Which projection do you trust more, and why? Hover over the steps of the chart: what made the share fall so fast before 2010, and who is left below the line?



Hint


Put \(y_t = y_0/2\) into equation (2) and follow the steps that led to equation (4). For the 3 percent date, use \(t = \ln m/\ln(1+\bar{g})\) with \(m = 0.03\) divided by the latest share. (c) cumulative_shares(2023) lists the countries and their incomes; compare the shares of 2015 and 2019 too.



interact(population_distribution,
         year=Dropdown(options=[1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2019, 2023], value=1990, description="year", style=WIDE));

Source. The chart of Fig. 8 above, with data from the Penn World Table 11.0 (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015), inspired by Fig. 3.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

poor_share = {}
for year in [1990, 2010, 2015, 2019, 2023]:
    shares_year = cumulative_shares(year)
    below = shares_year[shares_year.y_rel_us_2019 < 0.05]
    poor_share[year] = below.pop_millions.sum() / shares_year.pop_millions.sum()
    print(f"{year}: {poor_share[year]:.1%} of people below the line")
for first, last in [(1990, 2019), (2010, 2023)]:
    g_share = growth_rate(poor_share[first], poor_share[last], last - first)
    to_3 = np.log(0.03 / poor_share[last]) / np.log(1 + g_share)
    print(f"{first}-{last}: {100 * g_share:.2f}% a year, halves in {np.log(0.5) / np.log(1 + g_share):.1f} years, "
          f"3% in {last + to_3:.0f}, {constant_growth(poor_share[last], g_share, 2030 - last):.1%} in 2030")
print(below.sort_values("pop_millions").tail(5)[["country", "pop_millions", "y_rel_us_2019"]])
(a) The chart’s titles show about 60 percent in 1990, 11 percent in 2010, 9 percent in 2019 and 8 percent in 2023 (the code gives 59.7, 11.3, 8.5 and 7.8 percent).
(b) Equation (6) gives \(\bar{g} = (0.0854/0.5973)^{1/29} - 1 = -0.0649\): the share fell 6.49 percent a year, a percentage of itself, not percentage points. For the halving time, \((1+\bar{g})^t = 1/2\) gives
\[t_{\text{half}} = \frac{\ln(1/2)}{\ln(1+\bar{g})} = \frac{-\ln 2}{\ln(1+\bar{g})} \approx \frac{0.693}{|\bar{g}|} \approx \frac{70}{|g|},\]
with \(g\) in percent, the Rule of 70 for a decline. At 6.49 percent it gives \(70/6.49 = 10.8\) years; the exact value is 10.3 years. (For a decline the rule overstates the time a little, because \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\) is more negative than \(\bar{g}\).) The share then reaches 3 percent \(\ln(0.03/0.0854)/\ln(0.9351) = 15.6\) years after 2019, in 2035; in 2030 it would still be 4.1 percent.
(c) From 2010 to 2023 the share fell only 2.78 percent a year: it halves every 24.5 years, reaches 3 percent only in 2057, and would be 6.4 percent in 2030. The second projection is the better guide, and it says that on this measure the 3 percent goal will be missed. A constant rate of decline fits these data badly, because the share falls in steps: when a very populous country crosses the line, its whole population leaves the poor group at once. Hovering shows China crossing the line in the 1990s and India in the 2000s (in these data, in 1996 and 2006), which took the share from 60 percent in 1990 to 11 percent in 2010. That cannot happen again. The largest countries still below the line in 2023 are Ethiopia (129 million people), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (106 million), Uganda, Mozambique and Madagascar. Their populations grow fast, which raises their share of the world’s people: the share even rose from 8.2 percent in 2015 to 8.5 percent in 2019. Reaching the goal requires growth in these poorest, fast-growing countries.

Setup
We first load the Python libraries we need. You only have to run this cell once.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig




Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website versions with many countries (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_menu(fig, shown, regions, label="Textbook countries"):
    """Draw the countries in `shown` and put every other country one click away in the legend.

    `regions` maps each country to its region. With more than 40 countries, a menu above the plot
    chooses the region whose countries the legend lists. Traces that are not countries stay as they are.
    """
    countries = [trace.name for trace in fig.data if trace.name in regions]
    groups = [label] + sorted(set(regions[name] for name in countries))
    if len(countries) <= 40:
        groups = [None]                                 # a short legend lists every country at once
    buttons = []
    for group in groups:
        visible = []
        for trace in fig.data:
            if trace.name in shown:
                visible.append(True)
            elif trace.name not in regions:
                visible.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)
            elif group is None or regions[trace.name] == group:
                visible.append("legendonly")
            else:
                visible.append(False)
        buttons.append(dict(label=group, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    if len(groups) > 1:
        menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
        fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig

title: 4. A Model of Production
text:
Model overview
Why does a typical person in a rich country produce dozens of times more than a typical person in a poor one? This chapter gives a first, deliberately simple answer. Output per person is high where each worker has many machines to work with and where machines and workers are combined efficiently. The model takes place in a toy economy with one good (the textbook calls it ice cream), a given number of workers and a given number of machines. Competitive firms choose how much of each input to use, and the markets for the two inputs set their prices.
We build the model in two blocks. The first block states the assumptions, solves the firm’s problem and the two input markets, and derives the equilibrium wage, rental price of capital and output, in total and per person. The second block turns the per-person result into a measuring tool, development accounting. It asks how much of the income gap between two countries comes from capital and how much from productivity, which we measure as total factor productivity (TFP). At the end, ### The model in code defines the Python functions that the rest of the notebook uses and checks each key result with numbers.
A bar over a letter marks a parameter: a number we take as given from outside the model, such as \(\bar{A}\), \(\bar{K}\) or \(\bar{L}\). Letters without a bar are endogenous variables, which the model determines, and an asterisk, as in \(w^*\), marks their equilibrium values. In the code we simply write A, K_bar and L_bar.

The production model

Assumptions
1. One good. The economy is closed and makes a single consumption good, measured in tons per year. Every price is expressed in units of this good, so the price of the good itself is 1. A good that serves as the unit of account in this way is called the numéraire.
2. Given supplies of the inputs. The economy has \(\bar{L}\) workers and \(\bar{K}\) machines. Both are parameters: this model does not ask where they come from. (The Solow model of Chapter 5 explains the capital stock.)
3. Technology. With \(K\) machines and \(L\) workers, firms can produce
\[Y = F(K, L) = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}, \tag{1}\]
which is the Cobb-Douglas production function. Here \(K\) and \(L\) carry no bars on purpose: the function gives the output of any combination of inputs, not only of the amounts this economy owns. The positive number \(\bar{A}\) is productivity. For the same machines and workers, a larger \(\bar{A}\) means more output.
4. Competitive, profit-maximizing firms. Many identical firms are too small to influence the wage \(w\) or the rental price of capital \(r\), so they treat both prices as fixed. Each chooses \(K\) and \(L\) to make its profit as large as possible. Because of constant returns to scale (shown next), the number of firms makes no difference, and we can think of one representative firm that rents all the capital and hires all the labor.
5. Markets clear. The wage and the rental price adjust until the firm wants to use exactly the machines and workers that exist.
Two properties of equation (1) matter for everything that follows. Both follow from the rules for exponents, \((ab)^c = a^cb^c\) and \(a^ca^d = a^{c+d}\) (Appendix C.3).
Constant returns to scale. Multiply both inputs by the same factor \(\lambda > 0\):
\[F(\lambda K, \lambda L) = \bar{A}(\lambda K)^{1/3}(\lambda L)^{2/3} = \lambda^{1/3}\lambda^{2/3}\,\bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3} = \lambda^{1/3+2/3}F(K,L) = \lambda F(K,L).\]
Output grows in exact proportion to the inputs because the two exponents add up to one. With exponents that sum to more than one, output would grow faster than the inputs (increasing returns to scale); with a sum below one, it would grow more slowly (decreasing returns to scale). Why is constant returns a natural benchmark? A firm can always copy itself: a second plant identical to the first, with the same staff and the same equipment, makes the same output again.
Diminishing returns to one input. Now scale capital alone:
\[F(\lambda K, L) = \bar{A}(\lambda K)^{1/3}L^{2/3} = \lambda^{1/3}F(K,L).\]
Doubling the machines while the workforce stays the same multiplies output by only \(2^{1/3} \approx 1.26\). Each new machine has fewer people to operate it, so it adds less than the machine before it. With \(\bar{A} = 1\) and the 64 workers of Fig. 1, a single machine gives \(1^{1/3}\times 64^{2/3} = 16\) tons, while eight machines give \(8^{1/3}\times 64^{2/3} = 2\times 16 = 32\) tons: eight times the capital, but only twice the output.


Solving the model
Step 1: the firm’s problem. Profit is revenue minus what the firm pays for its inputs. Revenue is simply \(Y\), because the good’s price is 1:
\[\max_{K,L}\ \Pi = F(K,L) - rK - wL.\]
Step 2: the marginal products. The marginal product of capital, \(MPK\), is the additional output from one more machine with the workforce unchanged. The marginal product of labor, \(MPL\), is the additional output from one more worker with the machines unchanged. For small changes, they are the partial derivatives of \(F\) (Appendix C.7). Treat \(L\) as a constant and apply the power rule, \(\frac{d}{dK}K^{a} = aK^{a-1}\):
\[MPK = \frac{\partial F}{\partial K} = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}K^{1/3-1}L^{2/3} = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}K^{-2/3}L^{2/3}.\]
Two rewritings make this result easy to read. First, \(K^{-2/3}L^{2/3} = (L/K)^{2/3}\). Second, \(K^{-2/3} = K^{1/3}/K\), so \(\bar{A}K^{-2/3}L^{2/3} = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}/K = Y/K\). Hence
\[MPK = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\left(\frac{L}{K}\right)^{2/3} = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{K}. \tag{2}\]
The same steps, now with \(K\) held constant and \(L^{2/3-1} = L^{-1/3}\), give
\[MPL = \frac{\partial F}{\partial L} = \frac{2}{3}\bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{-1/3} = \frac{2}{3}\bar{A}\left(\frac{K}{L}\right)^{1/3} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{L}. \tag{3}\]
Intuition. For a Cobb-Douglas function, each marginal product equals the input’s exponent times its average product: output per machine, \(Y/K\), or output per worker, \(Y/L\). The middle form of equation (2) shows the diminishing returns: with \(L\) fixed, a larger \(K\) lowers \(L/K\) and therefore lowers the MPK. More workers, on the other hand, raise the MPK, since every machine then has more hands to run it. Equation (3) is the mirror image for labor.
Step 3: the hiring rules. At the best choice of inputs, the derivative of profit with respect to each input is zero (Appendix C.8):
\[\frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial K} = MPK - r = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial L} = MPL - w = 0.\]
The logic works without calculus too. If one more machine adds more output than its rent, \(MPK > r\), renting it raises profit. So the firm keeps renting, and the MPK falls as it does. If \(MPK < r\), giving back a machine raises profit. Only at \(MPK = r\) is nothing left to gain. In the same way, the firm hires workers until \(MPL = w\). Because the MPK falls as \(K\) rises, the rule \(r = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}(L/K)^{2/3}\) is a downward-sloping demand curve for capital, drawn with capital \(K\) along the x-axis and its rental price \(r\) up the y-axis. The MPL curve is, likewise, the demand curve for labor.
Step 4: five equations in five unknowns. The model determines three quantities, \(Y\), \(K\) and \(L\), and two prices, \(r\) and \(w\):







Equation
Role




\(Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}\)
production function


\(r = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{K}\)
hiring rule for capital: demand for capital


\(w = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{L}\)
hiring rule for labor: demand for labor


\(K = \bar{K}\)
the capital market clears


\(L = \bar{L}\)
the labor market clears



The parameters are \(\bar{A}\), \(\bar{K}\) and \(\bar{L}\). Two markets clear at once, so the solution is a general equilibrium rather than the partial equilibrium of a single market.
Step 5: solve. The two market-clearing conditions give the quantities right away: \(K^* = \bar{K}\) and \(L^* = \bar{L}\). The supply curves are vertical lines at \(\bar{K}\) and \(\bar{L}\), and every machine and every worker is employed. Substituting them into the production function gives output, \(Y^* = \bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}\bar{L}^{2/3}\). Substituting \(Y^*\) into the hiring rules gives the prices. For the rental price, divide by \(\bar{K}\) and subtract exponents, \(\bar{K}^{1/3}/\bar{K} = \bar{K}^{-2/3}\):
\[r^* = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}\bar{L}^{2/3}}{\bar{K}} = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\bar{K}^{-2/3}\bar{L}^{2/3} = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{L}}{\bar{K}}\right)^{2/3}.\]
For the wage, divide by \(\bar{L}\), using \(\bar{L}^{2/3}/\bar{L} = \bar{L}^{-1/3}\):
\[w^* = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}\bar{L}^{2/3}}{\bar{L}} = \frac{2}{3}\bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}\bar{L}^{-1/3} = \frac{2}{3}\bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{K}}{\bar{L}}\right)^{1/3}.\]
Collecting the results, with each unknown on the left and only parameters on the right, gives the solution of the production model:
\[\begin{aligned}
K^* &= \bar{K}, \qquad L^* = \bar{L}, \qquad Y^* = \bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}\bar{L}^{2/3},\\
r^* &= \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{L}}{\bar{K}}\right)^{2/3}, \qquad w^* = \frac{2}{3}\bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{K}}{\bar{L}}\right)^{1/3}.
\end{aligned} \tag{4}\]
Intuition. The economy produces what its full stock of machines and workers can make, and each input is paid what the last unit of it adds to output. With the values used in Fig. 2, \(\bar{K} = \bar{L} = \bar{A} = 1\), the solution is \(Y^* = 1\), \(r^* = 1/3\) and \(w^* = 2/3\).
Step 6: who gets what. Multiply the wage by employment and divide by output. The hiring rule says \(w^* = \frac{2}{3}Y^*/L^*\), so \(L^*\) and \(Y^*\) cancel:
\[\frac{w^*L^*}{Y^*} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{Y^*}{L^*}\cdot\frac{L^*}{Y^*} = \frac{2}{3}, \qquad\text{and in the same way}\qquad \frac{r^*K^*}{Y^*} = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{Y^*}{K^*}\cdot\frac{K^*}{Y^*} = \frac{1}{3}. \tag{5}\]
These are the factor shares of income. They equal the exponents of the production function, whatever the values of \(\bar{A}\), \(\bar{K}\) and \(\bar{L}\). That is the reason for the exponent \(1/3\) on capital: in U.S. data, capital receives roughly a third of GDP and labor roughly two-thirds, and the split has been fairly stable over time (Chapter 2). Adding the two shares, \(2/3 + 1/3 = 1\), and multiplying through by \(Y^*\):
\[w^*L^* + r^*K^* = Y^*. \tag{6}\]
The payments to workers and to the owners of machines use up all of output, so economic profit is zero: \(\Pi^* = Y^* - r^*K^* - w^*L^* = 0\). That is what perfect competition leads us to expect. Equation (6) also says that total income equals total production, one of the identities of national income accounting. Since all output is consumed, production equals spending as well. What accountants call profit is the payment to capital, \(r^*K^* = Y^*/3\), and the stock market puts a value on claims to this flow of capital income (Fig. 3).
Step 7: per person. Living standards depend on output per person, \(y \equiv Y/L\). Let \(k \equiv K/L\) be capital per person. (Everyone works in this model, so “per person” and “per worker” mean the same thing.) Divide \(Y^*\) by \(\bar{L}\) and use \(\bar{L}^{2/3}/\bar{L} = \bar{L}^{-1/3}\):
\[y^* = \frac{Y^*}{L^*} = \frac{\bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}\bar{L}^{2/3}}{\bar{L}} = \bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}\bar{L}^{-1/3} = \bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{K}}{\bar{L}}\right)^{1/3},\]
so that, with \(\bar{k} = \bar{K}/\bar{L}\),
\[y^* = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}. \tag{7}\]
Intuition. Income per person is the product of two forces: productivity, and the cube root of capital per person, \(\bar{k}^{1/3}\). A higher \(\bar{A}\) raises income one for one, while extra capital raises it with diminishing returns. The two prices can be written per person too: \(w^* = \frac{2}{3}y^*\), so the wage moves in proportion to income per person, and \(r^* = \frac{1}{3}y^*/\bar{k} = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\bar{k}^{-2/3}\).
A general exponent. The code lets the exponent on capital be any \(\alpha\) between 0 and 1, so that \(Y = \bar{A}K^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}\). The same steps give \(MPK = \alpha Y/K\), \(MPL = (1-\alpha)Y/L\), factor shares \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\), and \(y^* = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{\alpha}\). Setting \(\alpha = 1/3\) brings back equations (2) to (7).


What the model predicts
Comparative statics. Take logs of the solution (4) and of equation (7) (Appendix C.4). The log of a product is the sum of the logs, and the log of a power is the exponent times the log:
\[\ln Y^* = \ln\bar{A} + \tfrac{1}{3}\ln\bar{K} + \tfrac{2}{3}\ln\bar{L}, \qquad \ln y^* = \ln\bar{A} + \tfrac{1}{3}\ln\bar{K} - \tfrac{1}{3}\ln\bar{L},\]
\[\ln w^* = \ln\tfrac{2}{3} + \ln\bar{A} + \tfrac{1}{3}\ln\bar{K} - \tfrac{1}{3}\ln\bar{L}, \qquad \ln r^* = \ln\tfrac{1}{3} + \ln\bar{A} - \tfrac{2}{3}\ln\bar{K} + \tfrac{2}{3}\ln\bar{L}.\]
Each coefficient is an elasticity: the percent change in the variable when the parameter rises by 1 percent.

\(r^*\)

\(+\tfrac{1}{3}\%\)
\(+\tfrac{1}{3}\%\)
\(+\tfrac{1}{3}\%\)
\(-\tfrac{2}{3}\%\)

\(-\tfrac{1}{3}\%\)

The factor shares of equation (5) are \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) in every row: only the exponent can change them. For \(y^* = Y^*/\bar{L}\), the elasticity with respect to \(\bar{L}\) is \(2/3 - 1 = -1/3\), because the same output is shared by more people.
What the table says:

Each input is worth more when the other one is plentiful. More machines lower their own rental price, a move down the capital demand curve, because of diminishing returns. But they raise the wage, since each worker now has more machines to work with. More workers do the opposite.
Prices depend only on the ratio \(\bar{K}/\bar{L}\). Scaling the whole economy up raises total output but changes nothing per person. A country is not richer per person just because it is bigger.
Productivity is the one parameter that raises every outcome, each with elasticity 1.
Capital per person has diminishing returns. By equation (7), doubling \(\bar{k}\) multiplies \(y^*\) by \(2^{1/3} \approx 1.26\). Large differences in capital per person therefore show up as much smaller differences in income. The second block takes this prediction to the data.

With the values of Fig. 2, doubling \(\bar{K}\) from 1 to 2 lowers the rental price from \(1/3 \approx 0.333\) to \(\frac{1}{3}(1/2)^{2/3} \approx 0.210\) and raises the wage from \(2/3 \approx 0.667\) to \(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 2^{1/3} \approx 0.840\).



Development accounting: capital and TFP across countries

Assumptions
We now apply equation (7) to whole countries. This exercise is called development accounting, and it adds three assumptions:

every country produces with the same Cobb-Douglas function, with the exponent \(1/3\) on capital that matches capital’s share of income in the data;
\(y\) is measured as real GDP per person, and \(\bar{k}\) as the stock of physical capital (buildings, machinery, equipment, computers) per person;
both are expressed relative to the United States, so the U.S. values are 1.

In a first pass we also assume that productivity is the same everywhere, \(\bar{A} = 1\).


Solving the model
Step 1: compare two countries. Write equation (7) for a country \(i\) and for the United States, and divide. A ratio of two powers with the same exponent is the power of the ratio, \(a^c/b^c = (a/b)^c\):
\[\frac{y^*_i}{y^*_{US}} = \frac{\bar{A}_i}{\bar{A}_{US}}\left(\frac{\bar{k}_i}{\bar{k}_{US}}\right)^{1/3}.\]
Step 2: equal productivity. If \(\bar{A}_i = \bar{A}_{US}\), and \(y\) and \(\bar{k}\) are both measured relative to the United States, the prediction is just
\[y^* = \bar{k}^{1/3}.\]
In logs, \(\ln y^* = \frac{1}{3}\ln\bar{k}\): a gap in capital per person becomes an income gap only one-third as large in logs. Take a country with one-eighth of U.S. capital per person. The model predicts that it has \((1/8)^{1/3} = 1/2\) of U.S. income. With \(1/27\) of U.S. capital, the prediction is \(1/3\) of U.S. income. Diminishing returns compress the predicted income differences. So a model in which only capital differs predicts that poor countries should be much richer than they are (Figs. 4 and 5).
Step 3: measure TFP. We have data on \(y\) and \(\bar{k}\) for every country, but there is no direct way to measure \(\bar{A}\). So we assume that the model is right and solve equation (7) for the one term we cannot observe, dividing both sides by \(\bar{k}^{1/3}\):
\[\bar{A} = \frac{y^*}{\bar{k}^{1/3}}. \tag{8}\]
This \(\bar{A}\) is total factor productivity (TFP): how much output a country obtains from given amounts of capital and labor. Because it is chosen to make the model fit exactly, TFP is also a residual. It collects everything that raises income other than physical capital, so it measures how much the model leaves unexplained. Suppose our example country, with one-eighth of U.S. capital per person, also has one-eighth of U.S. income. Its implied TFP is then \((1/8)/(1/2) = 1/4\).
Step 4: split an income gap. Write equation (7) for a rich and a poor country and divide:
\[\frac{y^*_{rich}}{y^*_{poor}} = \frac{\bar{A}_{rich}}{\bar{A}_{poor}}\times\left(\frac{\bar{k}_{rich}}{\bar{k}_{poor}}\right)^{1/3}. \tag{9}\]
Taking logs turns the product into a sum, so the two parts of the log gap add up exactly:
\[\underbrace{\ln\frac{y^*_{rich}}{y^*_{poor}}}_{\text{income gap}} = \underbrace{\ln\frac{\bar{A}_{rich}}{\bar{A}_{poor}}}_{\text{TFP part}} + \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{3}\ln\frac{\bar{k}_{rich}}{\bar{k}_{poor}}}_{\text{capital part}}.\]
In the example, the United States is 8 times richer: \(8 = 4\times 2\), a factor of 4 from TFP and a factor of 2 from capital. In logs, capital explains \(\ln 2/\ln 8 = 1/3\) of the gap and TFP explains \(\ln 4/\ln 8 = 2/3\).
Step 5: the return to capital across countries. Per person, equation (2) reads \(MPK = \frac{1}{3}y/\bar{k} = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\bar{k}^{-2/3}\). Dividing for two countries,
\[\frac{MPK_{poor}}{MPK_{rich}} = \frac{\bar{A}_{poor}}{\bar{A}_{rich}}\left(\frac{\bar{k}_{rich}}{\bar{k}_{poor}}\right)^{2/3}.\]
With equal TFP, a country with one-eighth of the capital would have a marginal product \(8^{2/3} = 4\) times higher, and investors would rush to move capital there. With a TFP of \(1/4\), the two effects cancel exactly, \(\frac{1}{4}\times 4 = 1\), and capital earns the same return in both countries. Low TFP thus answers the question Robert Lucas asked in 1990: why so little capital flows from rich to poor countries.


What the model predicts








Result
Elasticity
In words




income, \(y^* = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}\)
\(1/3\) for \(\bar{k}\), \(1\) for \(\bar{A}\)
capital gaps are compressed; TFP gaps pass through in full


implied TFP, \(\bar{A} = y^*/\bar{k}^{1/3}\)
\(1\) for \(y^*\), \(-1/3\) for \(\bar{k}\)
a country poorer than its capital predicts has low TFP


return to capital, \(MPK = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\bar{k}^{-2/3}\)
\(-2/3\) for \(\bar{k}\), \(1\) for \(\bar{A}\)
capital-poor countries earn high returns only if their TFP is not too low




With equal productivity, the model fails in a telling way. It gets the ranking right, since richer countries do have more capital, but its income gaps are far too small: almost every country is poorer than its capital predicts.
A bigger exponent is no fix. With \(y^* = \bar{k}^{\alpha}\) and \(\alpha = 1\), income gaps would be as large as capital gaps. That fits the poorest countries better but overshoots for the rich ones, and it contradicts a capital share of about one-third (the slider of Fig. 5 lets you try it).
TFP explains most of the gap. In typical comparisons of rich and poor countries, TFP accounts for about two-thirds or more of the log income gap, and capital for the rest (Figs. 6 and 7 and the key numbers after them).
What is TFP? The model treats \(\bar{A}\) as a parameter and does not explain it. Candidates are human capital (skills and schooling), technology, institutions (secure property rights, courts that enforce contracts, and the rule of law) and the misallocation of capital and labor across firms. Human capital can be sized with \(w^* = \frac{2}{3}y^*\): if extra schooling raises wages by some percentage, it raises income per person by the same percentage. In the data this explains part of the measured TFP gap, but far from all of it.




The model in code
We now write the key results as Python functions, which every later section reuses. To let you experiment with the shape of the function, the code writes the exponent on capital as \(\alpha\) (“alpha”), with the textbook value \(\alpha = 1/3\) as the default. Each function’s description names the equation it computes, and the cells after it check the algebra with numbers.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing A=1.0 gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”, and 1 / 3 is simply the number one third.


def production(K, L, A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Output: Y = A K^alpha L^(1 - alpha)   (equation 1; the textbook uses alpha = 1/3)."""
    return A * K ** alpha * L ** (1 - alpha)


def mpk(K, L, A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Marginal product of capital: MPK = alpha * Y / K   (equation 2)."""
    return alpha * production(K, L, A, alpha) / K


def mpl(K, L, A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Marginal product of labor: MPL = (1 - alpha) * Y / L   (equation 3)."""
    return (1 - alpha) * production(K, L, A, alpha) / L

Check 1: the production function. With \(\bar{A} = 1\) and 64 workers, 8 machines should make 32 tons. Doubling both inputs should double output, and doubling capital alone should multiply it by only \(2^{1/3}\).

Python note. An f-string such as f"Y = {Y:.2f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.2f means “show two decimals”.


print(f"8 machines and 64 workers:       Y = {production(8, 64):.2f} tons")
print(f"Double both (16 and 128):        Y = {production(16, 128):.2f} tons   (constant returns: twice as much)")
print(f"Double capital only (16 and 64): Y = {production(16, 64):.2f} tons   (2^(1/3) = {2 ** (1 / 3):.3f} times as much)")
print(f"Gain from the 2nd machine: {production(2, 64) - production(1, 64):.2f} tons; "
      f"from the 8th: {production(8, 64) - production(7, 64):.2f} tons")

8 machines and 64 workers:       Y = 32.00 tons
Double both (16 and 128):        Y = 64.00 tons   (constant returns: twice as much)
Double capital only (16 and 64): Y = 40.32 tons   (2^(1/3) = 1.260 times as much)
Gain from the 2nd machine: 4.16 tons; from the 8th: 1.39 tons


Check 2: the marginal products. Equations (2) and (3) came from derivatives. A derivative is the extra output from a very small extra amount of an input, divided by that amount, so we can compute it a second way with a tiny step.

K, L, small = 8, 64, 0.0001
print(f"MPK, equation (2), (1/3) Y/K:          {mpk(K, L):.4f}")
print(f"MPK, equation (2), (1/3) A (L/K)^(2/3): {(1 / 3) * (L / K) ** (2 / 3):.4f}")
print(f"MPK by a small step in K:              {(production(K + small, L) - production(K, L)) / small:.4f}")
print(f"MPL, equation (3), (2/3) Y/L:          {mpl(K, L):.4f}")
print(f"MPL, equation (3), (2/3) A (K/L)^(1/3): {(2 / 3) * (K / L) ** (1 / 3):.4f}")
print(f"MPL by a small step in L:              {(production(K, L + small) - production(K, L)) / small:.4f}")

Check 3: the equilibrium, the factor shares and zero profit. For three different economies, we compute the prices as marginal products and compare them with the closed forms of equation (4). Whatever the economy, capital should get one-third of output, labor two-thirds (equation 5), and nothing should be left as profit (equation 6).

Python note. A for loop repeats its indented lines once for each item of a list. Here each item is a group of three numbers in parentheses, a tuple, and for K_bar, L_bar, A in ... gives the three numbers the names K_bar, L_bar and A. abs is the absolute value: it avoids printing a tiny rounding error as -0.000.


for K_bar, L_bar, A in [(1, 1, 1), (2, 1, 1), (8, 64, 1.5)]:
    Y_star = production(K_bar, L_bar, A)
    r_star, w_star = mpk(K_bar, L_bar, A), mpl(K_bar, L_bar, A)
    r_formula = (1 / 3) * A * (L_bar / K_bar) ** (2 / 3)          # equation (4)
    w_formula = (2 / 3) * A * (K_bar / L_bar) ** (1 / 3)          # equation (4)
    profit = Y_star - r_star * K_bar - w_star * L_bar             # equation (6) says zero
    print(f"K = {K_bar}, L = {L_bar}, A = {A}:  r* = {r_star:.3f} (formula {r_formula:.3f}),  "
          f"w* = {w_star:.3f} (formula {w_formula:.3f})")
    print(f"     capital share {r_star * K_bar / Y_star:.3f},  labor share {w_star * L_bar / Y_star:.3f},  "
          f"profit {abs(profit):.3f}")

K_bar, L_bar = 8, 64

print(f"y* = Y*/L:                       {y_star:.4f}")

print(f"w* = (2/3) y*:                   {(2 / 3) * y_star:.4f}")

w* = MPL:                        0.3333
w* = (2/3) y*:                   0.3333


Check 5: the comparative statics. Starting from \(\bar{K} = \bar{L} = \bar{A} = 1\), we raise one parameter at a time by 1 percent. The table of elasticities predicts \(+1\%\) for everything when \(\bar{A}\) rises; \(+1/3\%\), \(+1/3\%\), \(+1/3\%\) and \(-2/3\%\) for \(Y^*\), \(y^*\), \(w^*\) and \(r^*\) when \(\bar{K}\) rises; and \(+2/3\%\), \(-1/3\%\), \(-1/3\%\) and \(+2/3\%\) when \(\bar{L}\) rises.

Y0, w0, r0 = production(1, 1), mpl(1, 1), mpk(1, 1)          # the starting point: y0 = Y0 because L = 1
for name, K_bar, L_bar, A in [("A", 1, 1, 1.01), ("K", 1.01, 1, 1), ("L", 1, 1.01, 1)]:
    Y_star = production(K_bar, L_bar, A)
    y_star = Y_star / L_bar
    w_star, r_star = mpl(K_bar, L_bar, A), mpk(K_bar, L_bar, A)
    print(f"1% higher {name}:  Y* {100 * (Y_star / Y0 - 1):+.3f}%,  y* {100 * (y_star / Y0 - 1):+.3f}%,  "
          f"w* {100 * (w_star / w0 - 1):+.3f}%,  r* {100 * (r_star / r0 - 1):+.3f}%")

title: 4. A Model of Production
section: The production function and its equilibrium
text:
The production function and its equilibrium
We start with the shape of the production function and then solve for the prices that clear the markets for capital and labor.

Fig. 1: The diminishing marginal product of capital
Goal. See why each extra machine adds less output than the one before.
Hold the number of workers fixed at \(L\) and draw output against capital. The curve rises, but it gets flatter: going from 1 to 2 machines adds much more output than going from 7 to 8 machines. The slope of the curve is the marginal product of capital, and it falls as \(K\) rises.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 10.4, 300) creates 300 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 10.4: the values of \(K\) at which we draw the curve. np.arange(1, 11) gives the whole numbers 1, 2, …, 10 (the end value 11 is left out). A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each value in a list. go.Figure() starts an empty chart, and each add_trace(go.Scatter(...)) adds one line or set of dots to it. add_annotation writes a piece of text at a point of the chart, here the name of the curve at its end. K[-1] is the last value of K, and max(60, 1.1 * Y_end) is the larger of the two numbers: the vertical axis stays at 0 to 60 unless the curve would leave it.


def production_curve(A=1.0, L=64, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Fig. 4.1: output against capital with labor held fixed; dots at K = 1, ..., 10."""
    K = np.linspace(0, 10.4, 300)
    dots = np.arange(1, 11)
    fig = go.Figure()
    # Dashed guides at K = 1, 2, 7 and 8: the two output gains reported in the title
    for K0 in [1, 2, 7, 8]:
        Y0 = production(K0, L, A, alpha)
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[K0, K0, 0], y=[0, Y0, Y0], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                                 line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=K, y=production(K, L, A, alpha), name="Output, Y", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=dots, y=production(dots, L, A, alpha), name="K = 1, 2, ..., 10", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)))
    # The curve's name, written above its right end
    Y_end = production(K[-1], L, A, alpha)             # the axis grows only if the curve ends above 54
    fig.add_annotation(x=K[-1], y=Y_end, text="Y = A K<sup>α</sup> L<sup>1−α</sup>",
                       showarrow=False, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", yshift=8)
    gain_1_2 = production(2, L, A, alpha) - production(1, L, A, alpha)
    gain_7_8 = production(8, L, A, alpha) - production(7, L, A, alpha)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Output gain from K = 1 to 2: {gain_1_2:.2f} tons;  from K = 7 to 8: {gain_7_8:.2f} tons",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital, K", range=[0, 10.4], tickvals=dots),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Tons of ice cream, Y", range=[0, max(60, 1.1 * Y_end)], dtick=10),
                      showlegend=False)
    return fig

The textbook does not say how many workers there are, so we pick our own round number: \(L = 64\) workers. With \(\bar{A}=1\), one machine then makes \(64^{2/3} = 16\) tons and eight machines make \(16 \cdot 8^{1/3} = 32\) tons.
For the exponent we use a SelectionSlider. It is a slider that moves through a fixed list of values, here a few simple fractions.

Python note. A dictionary such as {"1/3": 1 / 3} links a label (the key) to a value. ALPHAS.items() gives the (label, value) pairs, which is what SelectionSlider needs: it shows the label and passes the value to the function.


ALPHAS = {"1/4": 1 / 4, "1/3": 1 / 3, "1/2": 1 / 2, "2/3": 2 / 3, "3/4": 3 / 4, "1": 1.0}

Now the interactive version. Move the sliders and watch the two readouts in the title.

Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.


interact(production_curve,
         A=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=1.5, step=0.1, description="productivity A", style=WIDE),
         L=FloatSlider(value=64, min=8, max=120, step=8, description="workers L", style=WIDE),
         alpha=SelectionSlider(options=list(ALPHAS.items()), value=1 / 3, description="capital exponent α", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version

slider_figure(production_curve, "L", [8, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112], start=64,
              label="workers L")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 4.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The dots get closer together vertically as \(K\) rises: each extra machine adds less output. With the defaults, the first extra machine adds 4.16 tons and the eighth adds only 1.39 tons.
More workers lift the whole curve. Each machine is more useful when there are more people to run it.
Set \(\alpha = 1\): the curve becomes a straight line and the marginal product no longer falls. With \(\alpha = 1/4\) the curve bends even more sharply.

Your turn. With the default settings, by how much does output rise when capital goes from 9 to 10? Compute it in the cell below with the production function. Is it more or less than 1.39 tons?


Hint

Type production(10, 64) - production(9, 64). The arguments A and alpha keep their default values.


# Your turn: try it here



Fig. 2: Supply and demand for capital and labor
Goal. Solve the production model and find the equilibrium prices of capital and labor.
Firms rent capital until its marginal product equals the rental price \(r\), and hire workers until their marginal product equals the wage \(w\). So the MPK and MPL curves are the demand curves for capital and labor. The supplies are fixed at \(\bar{K}\) and \(\bar{L}\), so the supply curves are vertical lines. Where supply meets demand, the markets clear (equation 4):
\[r^* = \frac{1}{3}\,\bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{L}}{\bar{K}}\right)^{2/3} \qquad\qquad
w^* = \frac{2}{3}\,\bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{K}}{\bar{L}}\right)^{1/3}\]
Both panels have the same parts, so one function draws a panel and we call it twice.

Python note. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) creates a figure with two panels side by side, and row=..., col=... tells add_trace which panel to draw in. names[0] is the first item of the list names, and "solid" if col == 1 else "dot" gives "solid" in the first panel and "dot" in the second. demand <= 0.65 * top is True where the demand curve is in the lower part of the panel; x[low] keeps those values of x, and [0] takes the first of them: there we write the curve’s name.


def add_market(fig, col, x, demand, supply, price, top, names):
    """One panel of Fig. 4.2: the demand curve, the vertical supply line and the equilibrium."""
    dash = "solid" if col == 1 else "dot"
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=demand, name="Demand", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4, dash=dash)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[supply, supply], y=[0.05, 0.8 * top], name="Supply", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4, dash=dash)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, supply], y=[price, price], mode="lines", line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")),
                  row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[supply], y=[price], name="Equilibrium", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=12)), row=1, col=col)
    low = demand <= 0.65 * top                       # the name goes below the name of the supply line
    fig.add_annotation(x=x[low][0], y=demand[low][0], text=names[0], showarrow=False, yanchor="bottom", yshift=6,
                       row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_annotation(x=supply, y=0.8 * top, text=names[1], showarrow=False, yanchor="bottom", row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, top], row=1, col=col)


def factor_markets(K_bar=1.0, L_bar=1.0, A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Fig. 4.2: (a) the capital market and (b) the labor market, with the curve names on the plot."""
    K = L = np.linspace(0.3, 2.2, 200)               # capital and labor demanded, for the demand curves
    r_star, w_star = mpk(K_bar, L_bar, A, alpha), mpl(K_bar, L_bar, A, alpha)
    Y_star = production(K_bar, L_bar, A, alpha)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) The capital market", "(b) The labor market"))
    # Fixed vertical axes, which grow only when an equilibrium price is high
    add_market(fig, 1, K, mpk(K, L_bar, A, alpha), K_bar, r_star, max(1.15, 2.2 * r_star),
               ["Demand<br>MPK", "Supply of<br>capital"])
    add_market(fig, 2, L, mpl(K_bar, L, A, alpha), L_bar, w_star, max(1.7, 2.2 * w_star),
               ["Demand<br>MPL", "Supply of<br>labor"])
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Capital, K", range=[0, 2.2], tickvals=[0.5, 1, 1.5, 2], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Rental price, r", dtick=0.2, row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Labor, L", range=[0, 2.2], tickvals=[0.5, 1, 1.5, 2], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Real wage, w", dtick=0.5, row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"r* = {r_star:.3f}   w* = {w_star:.3f}   |   capital gets {r_star * K_bar / Y_star:.0%} "
                            f"of output, labor {w_star * L_bar / Y_star:.0%}", showlegend=False)
    return fig


interact(factor_markets,
         K_bar=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.1, description="supply of capital K̄", style=WIDE),
         L_bar=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.1, description="supply of labor L̄", style=WIDE),
         A=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=1.5, step=0.1, description="productivity A", style=WIDE),
         alpha=SelectionSlider(options=list(ALPHAS.items()), value=1 / 3, description="capital exponent α", style=WIDE));
