title: 8. Inflation
text:
Model overview
Inflation is the rate at which prices rise on average. A few percent a year hardly gets noticed, but over decades it adds up, and in some countries prices have doubled every few weeks. This chapter asks what causes inflation in the long run, how it changes interest rates, and why some governments let it get out of hand. The answer it builds on is an old one: prices rise when money grows faster than the goods and services it buys.
This section works through the chapter’s ideas in five blocks, each going from assumptions to results. First come the definitions we need to measure inflation. Then the quantity theory of money explains the price level and the inflation rate, and it shows why money is neutral in the long run. The Fisher equation links inflation to interest rates. A short block uses it to see who gains and who loses when inflation is a surprise or when taxes ignore it. The last block, the government budget constraint, explains why governments print money, and how much revenue the printing press can raise. At the end, ### The model in code turns the key results into Python functions and checks each of them with numbers.
As in the rest of the book, a bar over a letter marks something taken as given from outside the model, such as \(\bar{M}_t\) or \(\bar{V}\). Letters without a bar are determined by the model. A \(g\) with a subscript is a growth rate, \(g_X \equiv \Delta X_{t+1}/X_t\), and \(\pi\) is the inflation rate. In the text rates are in percent; in the algebra they are decimals (2 percent is 0.02). Throughout, we use one illustrative economy: money \(\bar{M} = 100\), velocity \(\bar{V} = 2\) and real GDP \(\bar{Y} = 200\) in the starting year, money growth \(\bar{g}_M = 5\) percent, real GDP growth \(\bar{g}_Y = 3\) percent (the starting value of the slider in Fig. 4), and a real interest rate of 2 percent.

Measuring inflation

Definitions
The price level. \(P_t\) is the price of a basket of goods in year \(t\), written as an index: we pick a base year and set \(P = 100\) there. The consumer price index (CPI) uses a basket that a typical household buys. The GDP deflator uses all of GDP.
The inflation rate. Inflation is the percentage change of the price level from one year to the next:
\[\pi_t = \frac{P_{t+1} - P_t}{P_t}. \tag{1}\]
When \(\pi_t < 0\) the price level falls, which is called deflation.
Nominal and real values. A nominal value is measured in the dollars of its own year. A real value is measured in the dollars of one fixed year, so that it counts goods rather than dollars.


Working with the definitions
From inflation back to the price level. Multiply both sides of equation (1) by \(P_t\) and add \(P_t\):
\[\pi_t P_t = P_{t+1} - P_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_{t+1} = (1 + \pi_t)P_t.\]
Applying this year after year chains the inflation rates together:
\[P_T = P_0(1 + \pi_0)(1 + \pi_1)\cdots(1 + \pi_{T-1}).\]
This is how Fig. 1 builds a price level from inflation rates. With a constant rate \(\pi\) the product is a power, \(P_T = P_0(1+\pi)^T\) (Appendix C.3).
Average inflation over many years. Solve \(P_T = P_0(1+\bar{\pi})^T\) for the constant rate \(\bar{\pi}\) that links the first and the last price level. Divide by \(P_0\), raise both sides to the power \(1/T\), and subtract 1:
\[\left(\frac{P_T}{P_0}\right)^{1/T} = 1 + \bar{\pi} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{\pi} = \left(\frac{P_T}{P_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1.\]
Fig. 3 measures the average growth of money and prices over decades with this formula. Taking logs gives a handy shortcut, \(\bar{\pi} \approx (\ln P_T - \ln P_0)/T\) (Appendix C.4).
How long until prices double. Set \(P_T/P_0 = 2\) in \(P_T = P_0(1+\pi)^T\) and take logs: \(T\ln(1+\pi) = \ln 2\). Since \(\ln 2 \approx 0.70\) and \(\ln(1+\pi) \approx \pi\) for small \(\pi\), the doubling time is about \(70\) divided by inflation in percent: the rule of 70 (Appendix C.3). At 2 percent a year, prices double in about 35 years.
Moving a price from one year to another. A good that cost \(X_a\) dollars in year \(a\) cost the same share of the basket as \(X_a \times P_b/P_a\) dollars in year \(b\). The “year-\(a\) dollars” cancel, like units in a conversion:
\[X_b = X_a \times \frac{P_b}{P_a}. \tag{2}\]
Only the ratio \(P_b/P_a\) matters, so the choice of base year makes no difference (Appendix C.2). If the price level doubles from 100 to 200, a 50-dollar item of the first year is a 100-dollar item of the second.


What it tells us

Small rates add up. At 2 percent a year the price level doubles in 35 years, so a dollar of today buys about half of what a dollar bought 35 years ago.
Anything fixed in dollars loses value at the rate of inflation. A pension of 1,000 dollars a year that is never raised buys, after 35 years at 2 percent, what 500 dollars bought when it started: its real value is \(1{,}000 \times P_0/P_T\).
A price index only compares years. To say whether gasoline was cheap in some past year, convert its price into today’s dollars with equation (2) before comparing it with today’s price.




The quantity theory of money

Assumptions
Money is whatever people use to pay for things. Think of it first as paper currency; Table 8.2 lists broader measures that add bank deposits. Four variables enter the theory, and four equations pin them down.
1. The quantity equation. Each dollar is spent several times a year. The velocity of money \(V_t\) counts how many times, on average. So \(M_t\) dollars buy \(M_tV_t\) dollars of goods in a year. That spending is nominal GDP, the price level times real GDP:
\[M_tV_t = P_tY_t. \tag{3}\]
On its own, equation (3) is close to a definition: given \(M\), \(P\) and \(Y\), it measures velocity, \(V = PY/M\). In our economy nominal GDP is \(1 \times 200 = 200\) and money is 100, so each dollar changes hands twice a year. It becomes a theory once we add three more equations.
2. The classical dichotomy. Real GDP is set by real forces only: capital, labor, ideas and productivity, as in the growth models of Chapters 4 to 6. Money and prices do not enter those models. So for the quantity theory real GDP is given: \(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t\).
3. Constant velocity. People’s habits of paying, and the technology they pay with, change slowly. We take velocity as a constant: \(V_t = \bar{V}\). It has no time subscript because it does not change over time.
4. The central bank sets the money supply. We do not model how the central bank decides; we take its choice as given: \(M_t = \bar{M}_t\). (Chapter 12 gives monetary policy a richer model.)








Equation
Name
What it takes as given




\(M_tV_t = P_tY_t\)
quantity equation

\(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t\)

\(\bar{M}_t\), chosen by the central bank



The endogenous variables are \(M_t\), \(V_t\), \(P_t\) and \(Y_t\). Three of the four equations simply set a variable equal to something given from outside.


Solving the model
Step 1: the price level. Put the last three equations into the quantity equation (3):
\[\bar{M}_t\bar{V} = P_t\bar{Y}_t.\]
Only \(P_t\) is unknown. Divide both sides by \(\bar{Y}_t\):
\[P_t^* = \frac{\bar{M}_t\bar{V}}{\bar{Y}_t}. \tag{4}\]
The numerator, \(\bar{M}_t\bar{V}\), is the spending power of the money in the economy; the denominator is the amount of goods there is to buy. The price level is their ratio. With \(\bar{M} = 100\), \(\bar{V} = 2\) and \(\bar{Y} = 200\), \(P^* = 100 \times 2/200 = 1\).
Step 2: from levels to growth rates. Inflation is the growth rate of \(P\), so we turn equation (3) into growth rates. A product grows at a rate equal to its factors’ growth rates added together (Appendix C.5). To see where that rule comes from, take logs of equation (3) in two years, \(t\) and \(t+1\):
\[\ln M_t + \ln V_t = \ln P_t + \ln Y_t, \qquad \ln M_{t+1} + \ln V_{t+1} = \ln P_{t+1} + \ln Y_{t+1}.\]
Subtract the first from the second. Each term becomes a change in a log, \(\Delta \ln X = \ln X_{t+1} - \ln X_t\), and the change in a log is approximately the growth rate, \(\Delta\ln X \approx g_X\) (Appendix C.4). So money growth plus velocity growth equals inflation plus real GDP growth:
\[\bar{g}_M + \bar{g}_V = g_P + \bar{g}_Y. \tag{5}\]
Step 3: inflation. Velocity is constant, so \(\bar{g}_V = 0\). Write \(\pi = g_P\) and subtract \(\bar{g}_Y\) from both sides of equation (5):
\[\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y. \tag{6}\]
Money that grows as fast as real GDP just keeps up with the extra goods; only the money growth beyond that raises prices. With \(\bar{g}_M = 5\) and \(\bar{g}_Y = 3\) percent, inflation is \(5 - 3 = 2\) percent.
How exact is the growth-rate rule? In discrete time, write each variable in year \(t+1\) as its value in year \(t\) times one plus its growth rate, and divide equation (3) for year \(t+1\) by equation (3) for year \(t\):
\[\frac{M_{t+1}V_{t+1}}{M_tV_t} = \frac{P_{t+1}Y_{t+1}}{P_tY_t} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1+\bar{g}_M)(1+\bar{g}_V) = (1+\pi)(1+\bar{g}_Y).\]
With \(\bar{g}_V = 0\) the exact inflation rate is
\[\pi = \frac{1+\bar{g}_M}{1+\bar{g}_Y} - 1 = \frac{\bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y}{1+\bar{g}_Y}.\]
It differs from equation (6) only by the factor \(1/(1+\bar{g}_Y)\), which is close to one. In our economy the exact rate is \(1.05/1.03 - 1 = 1.94\) percent instead of 2 (Appendix C.6).


What the model predicts
Comparative statics. Take logs of equation (4): \(\ln P^* = \ln\bar{M} + \ln\bar{V} - \ln\bar{Y}\). Each coefficient is an elasticity, and they are all one in size. Equation (6) is already linear in growth rates, so its effects are one for one too.

A one-time change in a level gives a one-time jump in the price level; only a change in a growth rate changes inflation for good.
Money growth drives inflation. Real GDP growth comes from the slow forces of the growth models and stays in a narrow range, a few percent a year. Money growth is a policy choice and can be anything, from 2 percent to thousands of percent. So large and lasting differences in inflation, over time or across countries, must come from differences in money growth. That is the prediction Figs. 3 and 4 test.
The neutrality of money. Suppose the central bank multiplies the money supply by a factor \(\lambda\), say \(\lambda = 2\). By equation (4), with \(\bar{V}\) and \(\bar{Y}\) unchanged, the price level is multiplied by \(\lambda\) too. If every price and every wage is multiplied by \(\lambda\), then every ratio between them is unchanged:
\[\frac{\lambda p_{\text{bread}}}{\lambda p_{\text{book}}} = \frac{p_{\text{bread}}}{p_{\text{book}}}, \qquad \frac{\lambda W}{\lambda P} = \frac{W}{P}.\]
Relative prices and the real wage tell people what to buy, how much to work and what to produce, so no one has a reason to change what they do: real GDP stays at \(\bar{Y}\). A change in the money supply that only changes nominal values is called neutral. The same algebra describes a currency reform that replaces every old note with \(\lambda\) new ones. This is why the classical dichotomy is a good description of the long run.
Only the long run. In the short run, many prices and wages are slow to change. Then more money can change relative prices and real GDP for a while. The short-run model of Chapters 9 to 13 is built around that idea. The quantity theory is a theory of the long run.



Real and nominal interest rates: the Fisher equation

Assumptions

A nominal interest rate \(i\) is paid in dollars: put 1 dollar in the bank today and get \(1+i\) dollars back next year. Banks and newspapers quote nominal rates.
A real interest rate \(R\) is paid in goods: give up 1 unit of goods today and get \(1+R\) units next year. In the long run it equals the marginal product of capital, as in the Solow model (Chapter 5), so it is set by real forces, just like \(\bar{Y}\).
Prices rise at the rate \(\pi\) between this year and the next: \(P_{t+1} = (1+\pi)P_t\).



Solving the model
Step 1: follow one dollar. A saver can buy \(1/P_t\) units of goods with 1 dollar today. If she saves the dollar instead, she gets \(1+i\) dollars next year, which buy \((1+i)/P_{t+1}\) units of goods. Her return in goods is the ratio of the two:
\[1 + R = \frac{(1+i)/P_{t+1}}{1/P_t} = (1+i)\frac{P_t}{P_{t+1}} = \frac{1+i}{1+\pi}.\]
Step 2: solve for the nominal rate. Multiply both sides by \(1+\pi\) and expand the product:
\[1 + i = (1+R)(1+\pi) = 1 + R + \pi + R\pi.\]
Step 3: drop the small term. At low rates, \(R\pi\) is the product of two small numbers, tiny next to \(R\) and \(\pi\) themselves (2 percent times 2 percent is only 0.04 percent). Dropping it gives the Fisher equation:
\[i = R + \pi. \tag{7}\]
The nominal rate must pay the real return and make up for the fall in the value of the dollars being repaid. Subtracting \(\pi\) from both sides gives the form we use with data:
\[R = i - \pi. \tag{8}\]
The real rate cannot be looked up; we compute it from a quoted nominal rate and measured inflation, as in Fig. 5. In our economy, \(R = 2\) and \(\pi = 2\) give \(i = 4\) percent (the exact formula gives 4.04).
Step 4: the long run. Combine the Fisher equation (7) with the quantity theory (6):
\[i^* = R + \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y.\]
In the long run, \(R\) is set by the marginal product of capital and \(\bar{g}_Y\) by the growth models, so one more point of money growth raises the nominal interest rate by one point.


What the model predicts








A change in …
nominal rate \(i\)
real rate \(R\)

\(+1\) point

High inflation, high nominal rates. Countries and decades with high inflation should have high nominal interest rates, even if their real rates are normal.
Real rates can be negative. If \(i\) is below \(\pi\), savers lose purchasing power. Equation (8) shows when that happens. A negative real rate could not last in the long run, because the marginal product of capital is positive. When we see one in the data, it tells us that the short run differs from the long run.
The shortcut fails at high inflation. The exact rate is \(R = (1+i)/(1+\pi) - 1\). With 14 percent nominal and 72 percent inflation, equation (8) gives \(-58\) percent but the exact formula gives \(-34\) percent (Appendix C.6).




Who gains and who loses from inflation
The book discusses the costs of inflation in words. The Fisher equation turns two of them into numbers.

Assumptions

A lender and a borrower agree on a nominal rate \(i\) for some years. They set it with the inflation they expect, \(\pi^e\), so that \(i = R^e + \pi^e\), where \(R^e\) is the real rate they both want.
Interest income is taxed at the rate \(\tau\) on its nominal amount, as in most tax systems.



Solving the model
A surprise. Once the rate is fixed, the real rate the lender actually earns comes from equation (8) with the inflation that actually happens:
\[R = i - \pi = (R^e + \pi^e) - \pi = R^e - (\pi - \pi^e).\]
Every point of unexpected inflation, \(\pi - \pi^e\), takes one point of real return from the lender and gives it to the borrower. In our economy the loan is set at \(i = 2 + 2 = 4\) percent. If inflation turns out to be 8 percent, the lender earns \(4 - 8 = -4\) percent in real terms, and the borrower repays with dollars worth less than expected.
Taxes on nominal interest. Now let inflation be expected, so that \(i = R + \pi\), but the tax applies to all of \(i\). The saver keeps \((1-\tau)i\) dollars of interest, and inflation still takes \(\pi\), so her real return after tax is
\[(1-\tau)i - \pi = (1-\tau)(R + \pi) - \pi = (1-\tau)R - \tau\pi.\]
The last step multiplies out \((1-\tau)\pi - \pi = -\tau\pi\). The tax hits the part of the interest that only makes up for inflation as well. As a share of the real return \(R\), the tax actually paid is \(\tau R + \tau\pi\), an effective tax rate of \(\tau(1 + \pi/R)\). With \(\tau = 25\) percent and \(R = 2\) percent, the effective rate is 50 percent at 2 percent inflation and 125 percent at 8 percent inflation, when the after-tax real return turns negative.


What the model predicts

Surprises redistribute. Unexpected inflation moves wealth from lenders, savers and people on fixed nominal incomes to borrowers. Unexpected disinflation does the opposite. Expected inflation that is built into contracts does neither.
Inflation raises taxes on saving. With taxes on nominal returns, higher inflation lowers the after-tax real return even when it is fully expected, which discourages saving and investment.
Indexing removes both effects. Contracts, pensions and taxes written in real terms (adjusted for \(\pi\)) would make steady, known inflation little more than a nuisance. The real cost of inflation comes from surprises, and from rules written in dollars.




Seigniorage and the fiscal causes of high inflation

Assumptions

The government spends \(G\) dollars a year. It pays with taxes \(T\), with new borrowing \(\Delta B\) (the change in its debt \(B\)), or with new money \(\Delta M\) (the change in the money stock \(M\)).
The money in this block is the money the government itself issues: currency, or the monetary base. Its velocity \(\bar{V}\) is nominal GDP divided by currency, about 12 for the United States in 2023.
The quantity theory holds, with constant velocity.



Solving the model
Step 1: the budget constraint. Uses of funds equal sources of funds:
\[G = T + \Delta B + \Delta M. \tag{9}\]
Solved for the new money, \(\Delta M = G - T - \Delta B\): whatever spending is not covered by taxes or new loans must be covered by printing money. The revenue from new money is called seigniorage, or the inflation tax.
Step 2: seigniorage as a share of GDP. Divide the new money by nominal GDP and write \(\Delta M_t = \bar{g}_M M_{t-1}\), where \(M_{t-1}\) is last year’s stock. Since \(M_t = (1+\bar{g}_M)M_{t-1}\) and, by the quantity equation (3), \(M_t = P_tY_t/\bar{V}\),
\[\frac{\Delta M_t}{P_tY_t} = \frac{\bar{g}_M M_{t-1}}{P_tY_t} = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{1+\bar{g}_M}\cdot\frac{M_t}{P_tY_t} = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{(1+\bar{g}_M)\bar{V}}.\]
For low rates \(1+\bar{g}_M \approx 1\), and the quantity theory (6) gives \(\bar{g}_M = \pi^* + \bar{g}_Y\). So
\[\frac{\Delta M_t}{P_tY_t} = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{(1+\bar{g}_M)\bar{V}} \approx \frac{\pi^* + \bar{g}_Y}{\bar{V}}. \tag{10}\]
With 2 percent inflation, 3 percent real growth and \(\bar{V} = 12\), new money pays for about \(5/12 \approx 0.4\) percent of GDP a year.
Step 3: who pays. Split equation (10) into two parts. The part \(\bar{g}_Y/\bar{V}\) is new money people want anyway, because a growing economy needs more money for its payments; it causes no inflation. The part \(\pi^*/\bar{V}\) is a tax: every dollar people hold loses the share \(\pi/(1+\pi)\) of its purchasing power each year, so the tax rate is about \(\pi\) and the tax base is the real money people hold. Holders of currency pay it. People who hold land, houses or shares do not, because those prices rise along with all the others.
Step 4: how much inflation a deficit needs. Suppose lenders stop lending, \(\Delta B = 0\), and taxes fall short of spending by a share \(\sigma\) of GDP. Then equation (10) must equal \(\sigma\). Multiply both sides by \((1+\bar{g}_M)\bar{V}\), collect the terms in \(\bar{g}_M\), and solve (Appendix C.9):
\[\sigma\bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M) = \bar{g}_M \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma\bar{V} = \bar{g}_M(1 - \sigma\bar{V}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{g}_M = \frac{\sigma\bar{V}}{1-\sigma\bar{V}}.\]
Inflation then follows from the exact quantity theory, \(\pi = (1+\bar{g}_M)/(1+\bar{g}_Y) - 1\). A deficit of 5 percent of GDP with \(\bar{V} = 12\) gives \(\sigma\bar{V} = 0.6\), money growth of \(0.6/0.4 = 150\) percent, and inflation of about 143 percent a year.


What the model predicts

Persistent high inflation is fiscal. Rich countries raise well under 1 percent of GDP with new money, because inflation is low and people hold little currency. A government that loses access to taxes and loans must print money, and the quantity theory turns that money into inflation.
The printing press has a ceiling. Since \(\bar{g}_M/(1+\bar{g}_M) < 1\), seigniorage stays below \(1/\bar{V}\) of GDP however fast money grows: about 8 percent of GDP with \(\bar{V} = 12\). In practice the ceiling is lower, because people hold less money when it loses value fast, so velocity rises. A deficit close to the ceiling needs explosive money growth: this is the arithmetic of hyperinflation.
Ending a hyperinflation needs a fiscal fix. Inflation falls when money growth falls, and by equation (9) money growth can fall only when spending falls, taxes rise or borrowing resumes. An independent central bank, one that the treasury cannot order to print, is a way to close the third option before a crisis.




The model in code
We now turn the key results into Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes. The cells after it check the algebra above with numbers.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing g_V=0.0 gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. All rates here are in percent.


def price_level(M, V, Y):
    """Equation (4): the price level that solves the quantity equation M V = P Y."""
    return M * V / Y


def qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y, g_V=0.0):
    """Equations (5)-(6): inflation = money growth + velocity growth - real GDP growth (percent)."""
    return g_M + g_V - g_Y


def nominal_rate(R, pi):
    """Equation (7), the Fisher equation: the nominal interest rate i = R + pi (percent)."""
    return R + pi


def real_rate(i, pi):
    """Equation (8): the real interest rate R = i - pi (percent)."""
    return i - pi

Check 3: the growth-rate version. We let money and real GDP grow year by year and solve equation (4) in every year. Inflation should be the exact rate \(1.05/1.03 - 1\), close to the shortcut of equation (6).

Python note. rows.append([...]) adds one row to a list, and pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[...]) turns the list into a table. .pct_change() gives the change from the previous row as a fraction, and .iloc[-1] picks the last row.


def simulate_prices(g_M=5.0, g_Y=3.0, V=2.0, years=5):
    """Equation (4) year by year: money grows at g_M percent and real GDP at g_Y percent."""
    M, Y = 100.0, 200.0
    rows = []
    for t in range(years + 1):
        rows.append([t, M, Y, price_level(M, V, Y)])
        M = M * (1 + g_M / 100)
        Y = Y * (1 + g_Y / 100)
    path = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["year", "M", "Y", "P"])
    path["inflation"] = 100 * path.P.pct_change()
    return path

So that a country keeps its color from chart to chart, and two countries shown together never share one, we give the colors with a small tool. Its palette has 44 colors: Plotly’s 24 dark ones, and the 20 darker ones of its 26 “Alphabet” colors.

Python note. PALETTE = [] starts an empty list, and .append adds one color at a time. In first_free, return inside a loop stops the function at the first color that fits, used.count(c) counts how often c appears in the list used, and reversed(PALETTE) walks through the palette from its last color.


LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]   # too pale on white
PALETTE = []
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24:                                       # 24 dark colors ...
    if c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(c)                                                     # ... and 20 more: 44 in all
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                    # a medium blue, too close to the U.S. navy: used last


def first_free(used, taken):
    """The palette color least used in `used` (the group-mates' colors), preferring one no country has `taken` yet."""
    for c in PALETTE:
        if c not in used and c not in taken:
            return c
    best = PALETTE[-1]
    for c in reversed(PALETTE):                  # from the end, far from the colors always on show
        if used.count(c) < used.count(best):
            best = c                             # a big group shares out the colors evenly
    return best


Python note. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. dict(fixed or {}) starts from a copy of the fixed colors (an empty dictionary when there are none), continue skips a country that already has a color, and used collects the colors of the countries that are shown together with this one.


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    names: every country; groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color}
    for the textbook's countries, so the default view keeps the book's colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    if other in colors:
                        used.append(colors[other])
        colors[name] = first_free(used, list(colors.values()))
    return colors

The chart has two views. The price level is shown on a ratio scale, where equal distances mean equal percentage changes, so a steeper line means faster inflation. Each country’s price level starts at 100 in the year before its first inflation rate (1959 for the United States). Inflation rates differ hugely across countries, so the top of the inflation axis moves up in steps (15, 30, 60, 120, 250, 500 percent) when a country needs it.

Python note. if ... else runs one block of code or the other, and return inside a loop stops the function at the first match. With log_y=True the vertical axis is a ratio scale; tickvals chooses the numbers printed on it, and the range of a ratio axis is given in powers of 10 (np.log10(80)).


PRICE_TICKS = [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600]
CAPS = [15, 30, 60, 120, 250, 500]               # possible tops of the inflation axis


def axis_top(value, caps):
    """The smallest number in caps that is at least value (the largest one if none is)."""
    for cap in caps:
        if value <= cap:
            return cap
    return caps[-1]


def price_index(rates):
    """Fig. 8.1: the price level implied by inflation rates (100 in the year before the first rate)."""
    return 100 * (1 + rates / 100).cumprod()


Python note. px.line(..., color="country") draws one line per country, and color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS fixes each country’s color. data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()] is the row with the highest inflation.


def rate_view(data):
    """Fig. 8.1, inflation rates: one line per country; the top of the axis rises in steps."""
    top = axis_top(data.inflation.max(), CAPS)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=2))
    if data.country.nunique() == 1:
        fig.update_traces(fill="tozeroy")               # one country: an area chart, as in the textbook
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-2 * top / 15, top])
    peak = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
    title = f"{peak.country}: inflation peaked at {peak.inflation:,.1f}% in {peak.year:.0f}"
    if peak.inflation > top:
        title = f"{peak.country}: inflation peaked at {peak.inflation:,.0f}% in {peak.year:.0f} (axis cut at {top}%)"
    elif data.country.nunique() == 1:
        title = title + f"; {data.year.iloc[-1]}: {data.inflation.iloc[-1]:.1f}%"
    return fig, title


def level_view(data):
    """Fig. 8.1, price levels on a ratio scale (100 in the year before each country's first rate)."""
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="price_level", color="country", log_y=True, hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "price_level": "Price level (start = 100, ratio scale)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    top = data.price_level.max()
    if top < 1500:
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=PRICE_TICKS, range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(1500)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(dtick=1, exponentformat="power", range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(2 * top)])   # ticks 10², 10³, ...
    peak = data.loc[data.price_level.idxmax()]
    start = data[data.country == peak.country].year.min() - 1
    factor = f"{peak.price_level / 100:,.3g}" if peak.price_level < 1e8 else f"about 10^{np.log10(peak.price_level / 100):.0f}"
    return fig, f"{peak.country}: prices rose {factor}-fold from {start} to {peak.year:.0f}"

def inflation_chart(view="inflation rate", countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 8.1: CPI inflation, or the price level it adds up to, for the chosen countries."""

    else:
        data["price_level"] = data.groupby("country").inflation.transform(price_index)

def group_share(threshold, group):
    """Fig. 8.2: the percentage of a group's reporting economies with inflation above `threshold`, by year."""
    if group == "World":
        members = countries.iso3
    elif group == "OECD members":
        members = countries.iso3[countries.oecd]
    else:
        members = countries.iso3[countries.region == group]
    sub = wdi[wdi.iso3.isin(members)]
    share = (100 * (sub.inflation > threshold).groupby(sub.year).mean()).reset_index(name="share")
    share["economies"] = sub.groupby("year").size().values
    share["group"] = group
    return share


def high_inflation_share(threshold=25, groups=("World",)):
    """Fig. 8.2: the percentage of economies with inflation above `threshold` percent, for each group."""
    if len(groups) == 0:
        groups = ("World",)                             # nothing chosen: the textbook's view
    tables = []
    for group in groups:
        tables.append(group_share(threshold, group))
    shares = pd.concat(tables)
    first = shares[shares.group == groups[0]]
    peak = first.loc[first.share.idxmax()]
    fig = px.line(shares, x="year", y="share", color="group", hover_name="group", hover_data=["economies"],
                  color_discrete_map=GROUP_COLORS, labels={"year": "Year", "share": "Fraction of countries (percent)"},
                  title=f"Inflation above {threshold}%: {groups[0]} peaked at {peak.share:.1f}% in {peak.year:.0f}")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=2))
    if len(groups) == 1:
        fig.update_traces(fill="tozeroy")               # one group: an area chart, as in the textbook
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 104], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig

money and cpi are indexes in each country’s own units, so only their growth rates can be compared across countries. Two things to notice: the other countries stop in 2020, and some have gaps. Python note. range(1870, last, years) counts 1870, 1870 + years, … up to the year before last: the first year of each period. min(a, b) is the smaller number, so the last period stops at the last year of data. x ** (1 / n) is the n-th root. and is True only when both conditions are.


def growth(x, start, end):
    """Average annual growth of x from start to end, in percent."""
    return 100 * ((x[end] / x[start]) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1)


def periods(years=10, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 8.3: average money growth and inflation in periods of `years` years since 1870, for one country."""
    data = money_panel[money_panel.country == country].set_index("year")
    last = data.index.max()
    rows = []
    for start in range(1870, last, years):
        end = min(start + years, last)
        if start in data.index and end in data.index:      # skip periods that start or end in a gap
            label = f"{start}s" if (years == 10 and end - start == 10) else f"{start}–{end}"
            if end - start < years:
                label = label + "*"                       # * marks an unfinished period
            rows.append([country, label, start, end, growth(data.money, start, end), growth(data.cpi, start, end)])
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["country", "period", "start", "end", "money_growth", "inflation"])

The quantity theory says \(\pi = g_M + g_V - g_Y\). If velocity were constant and real GDP did not grow, every point would lie on the 45-degree line \(\pi = g_M\). Real GDP does grow, so points should lie below that line, by about \(g_Y - g_V\). The chart draws both lines; the lower one is shifted down by the average gap in the data.
Germany’s 1920s are a problem for any chart: money grew by more than 1,000 percent a year on average over the decade. The axes widen once (to 70 percent) when a country needs it, and points beyond that are listed in a note instead of squeezing all the others into a corner.

Python note. .between(a, b) is True for values from a to b. table.drop(shown.index) keeps the rows that are not in shown. .corr() is the correlation of two columns: 1 for points on a rising straight line, 0 for no relation.


KEY_DECADES = ["1870s", "1930s", "1940s", "1970s", "1980s", "2010s", "2020–2025*"]
JST_COUNTRIES = sorted(money_panel.country.unique())
MONEY_COLORS = group_colors(JST_COUNTRIES, [JST_COUNTRIES], BOOK_COLORS)   # the website lists all 18 together


def period_table(years, countries):
    """Fig. 8.3: the periods of all chosen countries, split into points on the chart and points beyond 70%."""
    tables = []
    for country in countries:
        tables.append(periods(years, country))
    table = pd.concat(tables, ignore_index=True)
    inside = table.money_growth.between(-10, 70) & table.inflation.between(-10, 70)
    us_key = (table.country == "United States") & (table.period.isin(KEY_DECADES) | (years == 20))
    table["label"] = table.period.where(us_key, "")   # labels for the textbook's decades; hover shows the rest
    return table[inside], table[~inside]


def add_reference_lines(fig, xr, gap, off):
    """Fig. 8.3: the 45-degree line, the quantity-theory line pi = g_M - gap, and a note on points off the chart."""
    g_M = np.array(xr)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=g_M, mode="lines", name="π = g_M (45-degree line)", line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=qt_inflation(g_M, gap), mode="lines", name=f"π = g_M − {gap:.1f}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
    notes = []
    for row in off.itertuples():
        notes.append(f"{row.country} {row.period}: money {row.money_growth:,.0f}%, inflation {row.inflation:,.0f}%")
    if len(notes) > 0:
        fig.add_annotation(x=0.01, y=0.98, xref="paper", yref="paper", xanchor="left", yanchor="top", align="left",
                           showarrow=False, text="Off the chart:<br>" + "<br>".join(notes), font=dict(size=12))


def money_and_prices(years=10, countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 8.3: money growth against inflation, one point per period of `years` years and country."""
    shown, off = period_table(years, countries if len(countries) > 0 else ("United States",))
    gap = (shown.money_growth - shown.inflation).mean()
    r = shown.money_growth.corr(shown.inflation)
    fig = px.scatter(shown, x="money_growth", y="inflation", color="country", text="label", hover_name="period",
                     hover_data=["country"], color_discrete_map=MONEY_COLORS,
                     labels={"money_growth": "Money growth (percent per year)", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent per year)"},
                     title=f"{years}-year periods: correlation {r:.2f}, average gap g_M − π = {gap:.1f} points")
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=11), textposition="top center", textfont=dict(size=11))
    wide = shown.money_growth.max() > 18 or shown.inflation.max() > 17 or shown.inflation.min() < -5
    xr, yr = ([-8, 70], [-10, 70]) if wide else ([-3, 18], [-5, 17])   # widen once, when a country needs it
    if wide:
        fig.update_traces(mode="markers")             # zoomed out, the decade labels would pile up: hover instead
    add_reference_lines(fig, xr, gap, off)

def world_money(g_Y=3.0, period="1990–2025"):
    """Fig. 8.4: average money growth and inflation by economy, with the line pi = g_M - g_Y."""
    suffix = period.replace("–", "_")
    x, y, n_m, n_p = "money_growth_" + suffix, "inflation_" + suffix, "n_money_" + suffix, "n_infl_" + suffix
    above = (world[y] > qt_inflation(world[x], g_Y)).sum()
    fig = px.scatter(world, x=x, y=y, text="label", hover_name="country", log_x=True, log_y=True,
                     hover_data=[n_m, n_p],                       # years behind each average, shown on hover
                     labels={x: f"Money growth, {period} average (percent, ratio scale)",
                             y: "Inflation rate (percent, ratio scale)",
                             n_m: "years of money data", n_p: "years of inflation data"},
                     title=f"π = g_M − g_Y with g_Y = {g_Y:.0f}%: {above} of {len(world)} economies lie above the line")
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=8), textposition=list(world.position), textfont=dict(color=BLUE, size=11))
    g_M = np.geomspace(g_Y + 0.4, 900, 200)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y), mode="lines", name=f"Quantity theory, π = g_M − {g_Y:.0f}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=MONEY_TICKS, range=[np.log10(1.5), np.log10(900)])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=INFLATION_TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.3), np.log10(4000)])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig

RATE_RANGES = [[-10, 16], [-20, 32], [-40, 64], [-80, 128], [-200, 250]]


def rate_range(low, high):
    """The first range in RATE_RANGES that contains both low and high (the widest one if none does)."""
    for bottom, top in RATE_RANGES:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    return RATE_RANGES[-1]


def interest_rates(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 8.5: the nominal rate i, the real rate R = i - pi and inflation pi of one country."""
    data = rates_panel[rates_panel.country == country]
    named = data.rename(columns={"short_rate": "Nominal rate, i", "real_rate": "Real rate, R = i − π",
                                 "inflation": "Inflation, π"})
    negative = (data.real_rate < 0).sum()
    fig = px.line(named, x="year", y=["Nominal rate, i", "Real rate, R = i − π", "Inflation, π"], hover_name="year",
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN, ORANGE], labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent"},
                  title=f"{country}: the real rate R = i − π was negative in {negative} of {data.real_rate.count()} years")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Inflation, π"), visible="legendonly", line=dict(dash="dot"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    yr = rate_range(data[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].min().min(),
                    data[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].max().max())
    fig.update_yaxes(range=yr, tickvals=[-5, 0, 5, 10, 15] if yr == [-10, 16] else None)   # no label in the corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig

What to notice.

The nominal rate is high when inflation is high. It peaked at just over 14 percent in 1981, a year after inflation peaked.

Choose Germany. In 1974 the U.S. real rate was −3.2 percent, but Germany’s was +2.9 percent: its central bank fought the inflation of the 1970s earlier and harder, and German inflation never went above 7 percent (Fig. 1).

def disinflation(data):
    """Figs. 8.6-8.7: the highest peak among the chosen countries, and when that country fell below 25%."""
    top = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
    own = data[data.country == top.country]
    later = own[(own.year > top.year) & (own.inflation < 25)]
    if len(later) > 0:
        return f"{top.country}: {top.inflation:,.0f}% in {top.year:.0f}, below 25% by {later.year.min():.0f}"
    return f"{top.country}: {top.inflation:,.0f}% in {top.year:.0f}, still above 25% in {own.year.max():.0f}"


def inflation_paths(countries=("Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"), scale="linear"):
    """Figs. 8.6 and 8.7: inflation in the chosen countries, on a linear or a ratio scale."""
    data = paths[paths.country.isin(countries if len(countries) > 0 else ("Argentina",))]
    title = disinflation(data)
    if scale == "ratio":
        data = data[data.inflation > 0]                  # a ratio scale cannot show zero or falling prices
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", log_y=(scale == "ratio"), hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=PATH_COLORS, title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    fig.add_hline(y=500, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, annotation_text="500%: hyperinflation",
                  annotation_position="bottom left")
    peak = data.inflation.max()
    if scale == "ratio":
        top = 5000 if peak < 5000 else 200000
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=RATIO_TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.1), np.log10(top)])
    else:
        top = axis_top(1.1 * peak, LINEAR_TOPS)
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=LINEAR_TICKS if top == 3500 else None, range=[-top / 35, top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1960, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified", legend_title_text="")
    return fig

The inflation tax
Why would a government let money grow so fast? Because printing money is one way to pay its bills. The government budget constraint says that spending \(G\) is paid with taxes \(T\), new borrowing \(\Delta B\), or new money \(\Delta M\) (equation 9):
\[G = T + \Delta B + \Delta M\]
The revenue from new money is called seignorage, or the inflation tax. It is paid by everyone who holds money: when the price level doubles, a 200-dollar bill buys only what 100 dollars bought before.

def money_printed(G, T, dB):
    """Equation (9): the new money the government must issue, Delta M = G - T - Delta B."""
    return G - T - dB


print(f"Spending 25% of GDP, taxes 20%, new borrowing 2%: new money = {money_printed(25, 20, 2):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"If lenders stop lending (new borrowing 0%):        new money = {money_printed(25, 20, 0):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"Real value of 200 dollars of currency after prices double: {200 / 2:.0f} dollars of today")

text:
Concluding remarks

Inflation is the growth rate of the price level, equation (1). U.S. inflation peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980, stayed near 2 percent for two decades, and jumped to 8 percent in 2022. A price index turns past prices into today’s dollars, equation (2), and at 2 percent a year prices double in about 35 years.
The quantity theory of money adds three assumptions to the quantity equation (3) and solves for the price level, \(P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}\), equation (4), and for inflation, \(\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y\), equations (5) and (6): in the long run, faster money growth means higher inflation, one for one, and money is neutral. U.S. decades and 165 economies line up as predicted, although velocity is not really constant.
The Fisher equation, \(i = R + \pi\), equations (7) and (8), turns nominal interest rates into real ones. U.S. real rates were negative in the 1970s and in most years since 2008. Surprise inflation moves wealth from lenders to borrowers, and taxes on nominal interest make inflation a tax on saving.
The government budget constraint, equation (9), shows why governments print money, and equation (10) how much revenue it raises: well under 1 percent of GDP in the United States, and, with constant velocity, never more than \(1/\bar{V}\) of GDP. Hyperinflations happen when governments cannot pay their bills with taxes or borrowing: persistent high inflation is a fiscal problem. They can end as quickly as they start.
The next chapter starts the short-run part of the book, with an introduction to economic fluctuations.

text:
Practice problems
These problems come in three kinds: conceptual problems apply the chapter’s equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data, and modeling problems use small calculators built on the Model overview to answer policy questions. Each problem is marked Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it in the answer cells first, then open its Hint and its Solution. The calculators’ sliders run only in Colab, so open the notebook with the badge at the top to use them.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): Turkey drops six zeros. On 1 January 2005, Turkey replaced its currency with the new Turkish lira, worth 1,000,000 old liras (European Central Bank). Overnight, every banknote, price, wage, bank balance and debt was divided by one million.

In equation (4), divide the money supply \(\bar{M}\) by 1,000,000 and keep \(\bar{V}\) and \(\bar{Y}\) as they are. What happens to the price level \(P^*\)?
Take some made-up round numbers: a worker earns 600 million old liras a month, and a kilo of bread costs 1.5 million old liras. What is her real wage, in kilos of bread a month, before and after the reform?
In our data, Turkish inflation was 8.6 percent in 2004 and 8.2 percent in 2005. Use equation (6) to explain why the reform by itself could not lower inflation. What would have to change instead?



Hint

The reform is the neutrality experiment of the Model overview, with \(\lambda = 1/1{,}000{,}000\). For (c), look at the variables in equation (6): are they levels or growth rates?

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Equation (4) says \(P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}\). Put \(\bar{M}/1{,}000{,}000\) in place of \(\bar{M}\):
\[P^*_{\text{new}} = \frac{(\bar{M}/1{,}000{,}000)\,\bar{V}}{\bar{Y}} = \frac{P^*}{1{,}000{,}000}.\]
The price level is divided by one million as well: bread at 1,500,000 old liras costs 1.5 new liras.
(b) Before the reform: \(600{,}000{,}000 / 1{,}500{,}000 = 400\) kilos a month. After it: \(600 / 1.5 = 400\) kilos. The real wage is unchanged, and so is every relative price. Nobody has a reason to work, buy or produce differently, so real GDP stays at \(\bar{Y}\): the reform is neutral.
(c) Equation (6), \(\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y\), contains growth rates, not levels. Dividing the money stock by one million in every year leaves its growth rate as it was:
\[\frac{M_{t+1}/10^6 - M_t/10^6}{M_t/10^6} = \frac{M_{t+1} - M_t}{M_t}.\]
So inflation stayed where money growth put it: 8.6 percent in 2004, 8.2 percent in 2005 and 9.6 percent in 2006. To lower inflation, money growth has to slow down, and by equation (9) that needs a budget that does not lean on new money. In Turkey the big fall had come before the reform, from 45.0 percent in 2002 to 21.6 percent in 2003 and 8.6 percent in 2004 (our data). The new lira mainly made prices easier to read, write and compute.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): The 3 percent mortgage of 2021. In 2021 the average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the United States was 2.96 percent (Freddie Mac, Primary Mortgage Market Survey (MORTGAGE30US), via FRED), and the Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2 percent over the longer run (it measures inflation with another price index, but the CPI is close enough here). Your answer:


Solution

(a) By equation (8), the real rate both sides expected was \(R^e = i - \pi^e = 2.96 - 2 = 0.96\) percent.
(b) The real rate the bank earned is \(R = i - \pi\): in 2022, \(2.96 - 7.99 = -5.03\) percent; in 2023, \(2.96 - 4.13 = -1.17\) percent. With \(R = R^e - (\pi - \pi^e)\), the surprise moved \(7.99 - 2 = 5.99\) points of real return from the bank to the family in 2022, and \(4.13 - 2 = 2.13\) points in 2023. The exact real rates, \((1+i)/(1+\pi) - 1\), are −4.66 and −1.12 percent: at these rates the shortcut works well.
(c) The price level of 2024 is that of 2021 times one plus each year’s inflation rate:

Prices rose by 15.8 percent from 2021 to 2024, against 6.1 percent on the 2 percent path. By equation (2), the debt of 300,000 dollars was worth 259,141 dollars of 2021 in 2024, against 282,697 dollars with 2 percent inflation. The surprise took 23,556 dollars of real value off the debt.
(d) The family, and every borrower at a fixed nominal rate, gained. The bank, and anyone who held fixed-rate loans or bonds, lost: they were repaid in dollars that buy less. With an adjustable rate, the family’s interest rate rises when market rates rise, and by the Fisher equation (7) market rates rise with inflation. So its real rate falls by less: the surprise moves wealth only while the nominal rate is fixed in advance.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Should the inflation target be 4 percent? In 2010, three IMF economists asked whether central banks should aim for 4 percent inflation instead of 2 percent, so that interest rates would be higher in normal times and could be cut further in a deep recession (Blanchard, Dell’Ariccia and Mauro 2010). Weigh the idea for the United States with the chapter’s equations. Assume a long-run real interest rate of \(R = 1\) percent and real GDP growth of \(\bar{g}_Y = 2\) percent (round numbers for this problem, not estimates).

How many years does the price level take to double at 2 percent and at 4 percent inflation? Use the rule of 70, then the exact formula.
Use equation (7) to find the long-run nominal interest rate under each target. In 2007–2008 the Federal Reserve cut its policy rate: the federal funds rate fell from 5.26 percent in July 2007 to 0.16 percent in December 2008 (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Funds Effective Rate (FEDFUNDS), via FRED). Which target leaves room for a cut of about that size before the rate reaches zero?
Use equation (10) to compute seigniorage under each target, with the velocity of U.S. currency in 2025 from our data, \(\bar{V} = 12.9\). How much extra revenue, as a percentage of GDP, would the higher target bring?
The switch takes the holders of 10-year bonds by surprise: they bought them when everyone expected 2 percent. By how many points does their real return fall each year? By what percentage does the real value of their final payment fall?
Weigh (a) to (d). Would you support the higher target? Name one cost of inflation from the chapter that these numbers leave out.



Hint

For (a), use the doubling-time step of the Model overview, \(T\ln(1+\pi) = \ln 2\). For (c), the shortcut in equation (10) is enough. For (d), a bond pays a fixed number of dollars, so the real value of its final payment depends on how far the price level has risen after 10 years under each inflation rate.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The rule of 70 gives \(70/2 = 35\) years at 2 percent and \(70/4 = 17.5\) years at 4 percent. The exact doubling time is \(T = \ln 2/\ln(1+\pi)\): \(0.6931/0.0198 = 35.0\) years and \(0.6931/0.0392 = 17.7\) years. At 4 percent, prices double twice as fast.
(b) By equation (7), \(i^* = R + \pi\): \(1 + 2 = 3\) percent under the 2 percent target and \(1 + 4 = 5\) percent under the 4 percent target (the exact formula gives 3.02 and 5.04 percent). The cut of 2007–2008 was \(5.26 - 0.16 = 5.10\) points. With a nominal rate of 3 percent, the central bank can cut by only 3 points before it reaches zero; with 5 percent it can cut by 5 points, almost all of the 5.10 points it used in 2007–2008.
(c) With the shortcut of equation (10), seigniorage is \((\pi + \bar{g}_Y)/\bar{V}\):
\[\frac{2 + 2}{12.9} = 0.31 \text{ percent of GDP}, \qquad \frac{4 + 2}{12.9} = 0.47 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
The higher target brings in about 0.16 percent of GDP more each year (0.14 percent with the exact formula). That is a small gain.
(d) The bonds pay a nominal rate fixed for 2 percent inflation. By \(R = R^e - (\pi - \pi^e)\), their real return falls by \(4 - 2 = 2\) points each year. After 10 years, the final payment buys
\[\left(\frac{1.02}{1.04}\right)^{10} = 0.824\]
times what the holders expected: 17.6 percent less. The holders’ loss is the gain of whoever issued the bonds, often the government itself.
(e) For the higher target: two more points of room to cut rates in a deep recession, and a little more revenue. Against it: prices double in about 18 years instead of 35, so everything fixed in dollars (wages in contracts, pensions, savings in cash) loses value twice as fast; the switch takes 17.6 percent of the real value of existing 10-year bonds from their holders; and people may wonder whether 4 percent is the last increase. Costs left out of (a) to (d) include the higher tax on saving when taxes apply to nominal interest (Problem 9), and the cost of rules and contracts written in dollars. Reasonable people disagree: an answer that weighs the room to cut rates against these costs, with numbers, is a good answer.

Our data for Venezuela end in 2024 (35 years). The arithmetic average is 2,614.0 percent, as in Fig. 4, but the compound average is only 147.4 percent a year. Prices rose by a factor of about \(6 \times 10^{13}\). The five highest arithmetic averages are Venezuela (2,614.0; compound 147.4), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (995.4; 124.7), Georgia (587.7; 49.4), Angola (311.0; 99.0) and Brazil (238.7; 55.5 percent). Georgia falls furthest, from third to eighth place: its arithmetic average is dominated by three hyperinflation years, 1992–1994 (15,607 percent in 1994). A single year of 65,374 percent, like Venezuela’s 2018, adds 1,868 points to a 35-year arithmetic mean, but its gross rate of 655 enters the compound average only through its 35th root.
(c) Let \(a = \pi_1\) and \(b = \pi_2\). The squared arithmetic average of the gross rates, minus their product, is
\[\left(1 + \frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2 - (1+a)(1+b) = 1 + (a+b) + \frac{(a+b)^2}{4} - 1 - a - b - ab = \frac{(a+b)^2 - 4ab}{4} = \frac{(a-b)^2}{4} \ge 0.\]
So \(\left(1 + \frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2 \ge (1+a)(1+b)\), and taking square roots, \(1 + \frac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{(1+a)(1+b)}\): the arithmetic average is at least the compound average, with equality only when \(a = b\). (The same holds for any number of years: it is the inequality between the arithmetic and the geometric mean.) The more inflation varies, the bigger the gap.
(d) Taking logs of equation (3) in two years and subtracting gives, exactly, \(\Delta\ln M + \Delta\ln V = \Delta\ln P + \Delta\ln Y\). Averaging over the years keeps the identity exact, and the average of \(\Delta \ln P = \ln(1+\pi_t)\) is the log of one plus the compound average. So a test of the quantity theory should compare compound (or log) averages of money growth and inflation. Arithmetic averages give crisis years far too much weight: they push the high-inflation economies of Fig. 4 up and to the right, and by different amounts for money and prices when the two series cover different years.

    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[pi, pi], y=[after, indexed], mode="markers", name="at this inflation rate",
                             marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=11)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"π = {pi:.1f}%: after-tax real return {round(after, 2) + 0.0:.2f}% (indexed {indexed:.2f}%), "
                            f"effective tax {100 * (R - after) / R:.0f}%",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Inflation π (percent)", range=[0, 16]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="After-tax real return (percent)", range=[-8, 5], tickvals=[-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4]),
                      legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"))

Problem 10 (Challenge): How much can the printing press raise? A hypothetical government has lost access to loans and must pay a deficit of 3 percent of GDP with new money. The velocity of its currency is 12, and real GDP grows by 3 percent a year.

With constant velocity, use the calculator to find the money growth and the inflation rate that pay for the deficit. Check them with step 4 of the seigniorage block in the Model overview.
People hold less currency when it loses value fast, so velocity rises with money growth. Suppose that \(V = \bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^a\) with \(a > 0\). Show that seigniorage is then \(\bar{g}_M/[\bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^{1+a}]\) of GDP, and that it is largest at \(\bar{g}_M = 1/a\). How much can the press raise at most when \(a = 1\)?
With \(a = 1\), can the government still pay its deficit of 3 percent of GDP? What about a deficit of 1.5 percent? Find the two money growth rates that raise 1.5 percent. Which one would you choose, and why?
According to equation (9), what has to happen to end the inflation?



Hint

For (b), start from the exact seigniorage \(\bar{g}_M/[(1+\bar{g}_M)V]\) of equation (10), take logs, and set the derivative with respect to \(\bar{g}_M\) to zero. For (c), with \(a = 1\) the condition “seigniorage = 1.5 percent of GDP” is a quadratic equation in \(\bar{g}_M\). In the calculator, choose the velocity response \(a\) with the menu.


def press_calculator(sigma=3.0, V=12.0, a=0.0):
    """Practice: seigniorage 100 g / [V (1 + g)^(1 + a)] (equation (10), velocity V (1 + g)^a) and a deficit sigma."""
    g = np.geomspace(0.01, 200, 400)                               # money growth: 1% to 20,000% a year
    fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=100 * g, y=100 * g / (V * (1 + g) ** (1 + a)), mode="lines",
                               name="seigniorage", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_hline(y=sigma, line_dash="dash", line_color=GREEN, annotation_text=f"deficit: {sigma:.1f}% of GDP",
                  annotation_position="top left")
    rising = np.geomspace(0.001, 200 if a == 0 else 1 / a, 2001)    # seigniorage rises up to g = 1/a
    revenue = 100 * rising / (V * (1 + rising) ** (1 + a))
    best = 100 / V if a == 0 else revenue[-1]                       # the ceiling 1/V, or the peak at g = 1/a
    if sigma <= revenue[-1]:
        needed = np.interp(sigma, revenue, rising)                  # read the rising curve backwards
        pi = 100 * ((1 + needed) / 1.03 - 1)                        # exact quantity theory, real growth 3%
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[100 * needed], y=[sigma], mode="markers", name="deficit paid",
                                 marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=12)))
        title = f"Deficit {sigma:.1f}% of GDP: money growth {100 * needed:,.0f}%, inflation {pi:,.0f}% a year"
    else:
        title = f"A deficit of {sigma:.1f}% of GDP cannot be paid: the press raises at most {best:.2f}%"
    fig.update_layout(title=title, yaxis=dict(title="Seigniorage (percent of GDP)", range=[0, 14], tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]),
                      xaxis=dict(type="log", title="Money growth g_M (percent a year, ratio scale)",
                                 range=[0, np.log10(20000)], tickvals=[1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000]))
    return fig

Solution

(a) With \(\sigma = 0.03\) and \(\bar{V} = 12\), \(\sigma\bar{V} = 0.36\), so step 4 gives \(\bar{g}_M = \sigma\bar{V}/(1 - \sigma\bar{V}) = 0.36/0.64 = 56.25\) percent, and the exact quantity theory gives inflation of \(1.5625/1.03 - 1 = 51.7\) percent a year. The calculator’s title shows 56 and 52 percent.
(b) By equation (10), seigniorage is \(\bar{g}_M/[(1+\bar{g}_M)V]\). Put in \(V = \bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^a\):
\[s(\bar{g}_M) = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{(1+\bar{g}_M)\,\bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^a} = \frac{\bar{g}_M}{\bar{V}(1+\bar{g}_M)^{1+a}}.\]
Take logs, \(\ln s = \ln\bar{g}_M - (1+a)\ln(1+\bar{g}_M) - \ln\bar{V}\), and set the derivative to zero:
\[\frac{1}{\bar{g}_M} - \frac{1+a}{1+\bar{g}_M} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1 + \bar{g}_M = (1+a)\,\bar{g}_M \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{g}_M = \frac{1}{a}.\]
Over a common denominator the derivative is \((1 - a\bar{g}_M)/[\bar{g}_M(1+\bar{g}_M)]\): positive below \(1/a\) and negative above it, so this is the maximum. Putting \(\bar{g}_M = 1/a\) back in gives \(s_{\max} = a^a/[\bar{V}(1+a)^{1+a}]\). With \(a = 1\) the peak is at 100 percent money growth, and \(s_{\max} = 1/(4\bar{V}) = 1/48 = 2.08\) percent of GDP, a quarter of the constant-velocity ceiling of 8.33 percent.
(c) No: 3 percent is more than the 2.08 percent the press can raise, and the calculator says so. Printing faster than 100 percent a year only lowers the revenue, because people hold so much less money. A government that tries anyway gets ever faster money growth and inflation: a hyperinflation. A deficit of 1.5 percent can be paid. With \(a = 1\), \(\bar{V} = 12\) and \(s = 0.015\), the condition \(\bar{g}_M = 0.18\,(1+\bar{g}_M)^2\) becomes
\[0.18\,\bar{g}_M^2 - 0.64\,\bar{g}_M + 0.18 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{g}_M = \frac{0.64 \pm \sqrt{0.64^2 - 4 \times 0.18^2}}{2 \times 0.18},\]
so \(\bar{g}_M = 30.8\) percent or \(\bar{g}_M = 324.8\) percent, with inflation of 27.0 or 312.4 percent a year. Both raise the same revenue, so the government should choose the low one: the high one taxes money holders much harder for nothing. The calculator marks the low one (31 percent and 27 percent in its title); the high one is where the blue curve crosses the dashed line again on the right.
for root in (1, -1):
    g_root = (0.64 - root * (0.64 ** 2 - 4 * 0.18 ** 2) ** 0.5) / (2 * 0.18)
    print(f"money growth {100 * g_root:.1f}%, inflation {100 * ((1 + g_root) / 1.03 - 1):.1f}%, "
          f"seigniorage {100 * g_root / (12 * (1 + g_root) ** 2):.2f}% of GDP")
(d) Equation (9) says \(\Delta M = G - T - \Delta B\). Money growth, and with it inflation, can fall only if spending falls, taxes rise, or the government can borrow again. A new currency or a promise from the central bank does not change this arithmetic; a credible budget does.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

# @title Helper for the website's country legends (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def add_legend_traces(fig, traces, keep=()):
    """Website: add traces that start hidden but stay in the legend (click to show), except those named in keep.

    If the figure has a slider, its steps only switch the figure's own traces, so the countries you
    clicked on stay on the chart when you move the slider.
    """
    n = len(fig.data)
    for t in traces:
        if t.name not in keep:
            t.visible = "legendonly"
        fig.add_trace(t)
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        steps = []
        for step in slider.steps:
            steps.append(dict(method=step.method, label=step.label, args=[step.args[0], step.args[1], list(range(n))]))
        slider.steps = steps
    return fig

title: 9. An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Model overview
From one year to the next, the economy does not glide along its long-run path. It overheats and it slumps, workers lose jobs and find new ones, and inflation drifts up and down. This chapter does not yet build a complete model of these movements. Instead it sets up the frameworks that the next chapters build on, and they answer three questions. How do we split output into a trend and a cycle? What does the cycle do to inflation? And what does it do to unemployment?
The road map follows those questions. The first block defines potential output and short-run output, and shows how to work with them as percentages, as log differences and as growth rates. The second block writes down the Phillips curve and solves it forward in time, which gives the inflation cost of a boom and the output cost of bringing inflation down. The third block adds Okun’s law, which translates an output gap into an unemployment gap. The fourth block previews how the full short-run model of Chapters 11–13 connects these pieces. At the end, ### The model in code turns the key results into Python functions and checks each of them with numbers.
Notation. A bar marks a value that the short-run model takes as given: potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\), the long-run inflation rate \(\bar{\pi}\) and the natural rate of unemployment \(\bar{u}\) come from the long-run model, and parameters such as the slope \(\bar{\nu}\) (the Greek letter nu) are chosen from outside. A tilde marks a short-run deviation from the long run, as in \(\tilde{Y}_t\). The symbol \(\Delta\) is the change from the year before, for example \(\Delta\pi_t \equiv \pi_t - \pi_{t-1}\). Short-run output is measured in percent and inflation in percent, so changes in inflation are in percentage points (“points”), as in the textbook’s figures.
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook’s Figs. 9.1 and 9.6 print no numbers, so every model figure and every worked example below starts from one illustrative baseline:

potential output starts at \(\bar{Y}_0 = 100\) and grows by \(\bar{g} = 2\) percent a year;
short-run output follows a wave between \(+2\) and \(-2\) percent (the \(\pm 2\%\) marked in Fig. 9.1) that repeats every 8 years, \(\tilde{Y}_t = 2\sin(2\pi t/8)\) percent. In whole years it takes the values \(0, +1.41, +2, +1.41, 0, -1.41, -2, -1.41, 0\);
the slope of the Phillips curve is \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), the textbook’s “about 1/3” for the United States;
long-run inflation is \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, and Okun’s slope is \(-1/2\).

Fig. 9 is the worked answer to a textbook exercise, which gives its own numbers (\(\bar{\nu} = 1\), \(\tilde{Y} = +3\%\)), and we use those there.

Trend and cycle: potential output and short-run output

Definitions
Two models with two jobs. The book uses two models side by side:



Model
What it determines
Built in




long-run model
potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) and long-run inflation \(\bar{\pi}\)
Chapters 3–8 (the combined Solow–Romer model of Chapter 6, the quantity theory of Chapter 8)


short-run model
actual output \(Y_t\) and actual inflation \(\pi_t\), year by year or quarter by quarter
Chapters 9–15



In the short-run model, \(\bar{Y}_t\) and \(\bar{\pi}\) are exogenous: they are handed over from the long-run model, which is why they wear bars. The endogenous variables are \(Y_t\) and \(\pi_t\). The long-run inflation rate has no time subscript, because in the end it is a stable target that policymakers pick (Chapter 13).
Potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) is what the economy produces when capital, labor and ideas are used at rates it can keep up year after year. It is a sustainable level, not a ceiling: for a while, firms can produce more than potential by running overtime shifts or by putting off maintenance, and they can also produce less.
Shocks push actual output away from potential: a jump in oil prices, a freeze in financial markets, a tax cut, a new technology that delivers or disappoints, a natural disaster, a boom or slump abroad. The short run is the stretch of time over which such deviations last, typically about two years.
Short-run output. Any output level can be split into the trend and the deviation from it, \(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t + (Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)\). A gap of 100 million dollars is large for a small economy and tiny for a big one, so we scale the deviation by potential output:
\[\tilde{Y}_t \equiv \frac{Y_t - \bar{Y}_t}{\bar{Y}_t}. \tag{1}\]
\(\tilde{Y}_t\) is the percentage gap between actual and potential output. It is also called the output gap or detrended output, because it is what is left of output once the trend has been taken out. In a boom \(Y_t > \bar{Y}_t\) and \(\tilde{Y}_t > 0\); in a slump \(\tilde{Y}_t < 0\); at potential \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\).
Recessions. A recession starts when short-run output turns negative, and it is usually dated as over once short-run output reaches its low point and starts to climb, even though output is still below potential. In practice the U.S. dates of each peak and trough are set by a committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), which looks at employment, sales and industrial production as well as GDP.


Working with the definitions
Step 1: actual output as potential output times a factor. Multiply both sides of equation (1) by \(\bar{Y}_t\), then add \(\bar{Y}_t\) to both sides:
\[\tilde{Y}_t\bar{Y}_t = Y_t - \bar{Y}_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_t = \bar{Y}_t + \tilde{Y}_t\bar{Y}_t,\]
and factor out \(\bar{Y}_t\):
\[Y_t = \bar{Y}_t\,(1 + \tilde{Y}_t). \tag{2}\]
Actual output is the trend multiplied by a cycle factor that is a little above 1 in a boom and a little below 1 in a slump. This is exactly how the function actual_output builds the baseline: the trend \(\bar{Y}_t = 100\times(1.02)^t\) (compound growth, Appendix C.3) times the factor \(1 + 0.02\sin(2\pi t/8)\). In year 2, at the top of the boom, potential output is \(100\times1.02^2 = 104.04\) and \(\tilde{Y}_2 = +2\%\), so actual output is \(104.04\times1.02 = 106.12\). In year 6, at the bottom of the slump, potential is \(100\times1.02^6 = 112.62\) and actual output is \(112.62\times0.98 = 110.36\). Going back with equation (1): \((110.36 - 112.62)/112.62 = -0.02\), that is, \(-2\) percent.
Step 2: the trend drops out. In equation (1), the numerator and the denominator both contain the trend. In the baseline, \(Y_t - \bar{Y}_t = \bar{Y}_t\times0.02\sin(2\pi t/8)\), so dividing by \(\bar{Y}_t\) cancels the growth factor \((1.02)^t\) completely and leaves \(\tilde{Y}_t = 2\sin(2\pi t/8)\) percent, whatever the growth rate of potential output. Faster trend growth makes the cycle harder to see in a chart of \(Y_t\), but it does not change \(\tilde{Y}_t\) (Fig. 1).
Step 3: short-run output as a log difference. Take the natural log of equation (2). The log of a product is the sum of the logs (Appendix C.4):
\[\ln Y_t = \ln\bar{Y}_t + \ln(1 + \tilde{Y}_t).\]
For a small number \(x\), \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) (Appendix C.6). Using it with \(x = \tilde{Y}_t\) and moving \(\ln\bar{Y}_t\) to the left:
\[\tilde{Y}_t \approx \ln Y_t - \ln\bar{Y}_t. \tag{3}\]
The gap in percent is, to a close approximation, the difference between the logs of actual and potential output. The approximation is very good for the usual gaps: \(\ln(1.02) = 0.0198\) and \(\ln(0.98) = -0.0202\), both within 0.03 points of \(\pm 2\%\). It gets worse for very deep slumps: a gap of \(-10\%\) has a log difference of \(\ln(0.90) = -0.105\), half a point off. Many statistical agencies report gaps in logs for exactly this reason: logs turn ratios into differences.
Step 4: growth rates. Write equation (3) for year \(t\) and for year \(t-1\), and subtract the second from the first:
\[\ln Y_t - \ln Y_{t-1} \approx \left(\ln\bar{Y}_t - \ln\bar{Y}_{t-1}\right) + \left(\tilde{Y}_t - \tilde{Y}_{t-1}\right).\]
The change in the log of a variable is approximately its growth rate (Appendix C.5). With potential output growing at the rate \(\bar{g}\):
\[g_{Y,t} \approx \bar{g} + \Delta\tilde{Y}_t. \tag{4}\]
The exact version comes from dividing equation (2) for year \(t\) by equation (2) for year \(t-1\): \(Y_t/Y_{t-1} = (1+\bar{g})\times(1+\tilde{Y}_t)/(1+\tilde{Y}_{t-1})\).
Intuition. Actual growth is trend growth plus the change in the gap. When the gap widens upward, output grows faster than its trend; when the gap shrinks or turns more negative, it grows more slowly. In the baseline, from year 1 to year 2 the gap rises from \(+1.41\) to \(+2\), so output grows by about \(2 + 0.59 = 2.59\) percent. From year 4 to year 5 the gap falls from \(0\) to \(-1.41\), so output grows by only about \(2 - 1.41 = 0.59\) percent: still growing, yet sliding into a slump.
Step 5: quarterly and annualized rates. GDP is published every quarter, and quarterly growth rates are usually reported as annualized rates: the growth that would result if the quarter’s pace lasted four quarters. Compounding gives \((1+g_q)^4 - 1\), which is close to \(4g_q\) when \(g_q\) is small. A quarter with 1 percent growth is reported as \(1.01^4 - 1 = 4.06\%\), about 4 percent. Going the other way, potential output growing by 2 percent a year grows by \(1.02^{1/4} - 1 = 0.496\%\) per quarter, just under a quarter of 2 percent.


What the framework predicts
Growth alone does not reveal the state of the economy. Equation (4) has one number we observe, \(g_{Y,t}\), and two we do not, \(\bar{g}\) and \(\Delta\tilde{Y}_t\). Suppose GDP grows at an annualized 5 percent. That fits potential growth of 5 percent with an unchanged gap, but it equally fits potential growth of 2 percent with a gap that widened by 3 points. Potential output is never observed directly, so it must be estimated. The common methods are: fit a smooth trend through real GDP; average the actual GDP of the surrounding quarters; or, like the U.S. Congressional Budget Office (CBO), compute what a Solow-style production function gives when labor and capital are at their sustainable levels. Each method can be revised as new data arrive, and the measured gaps change with it (Fig. 3).
A slump does not require falling output. In the baseline, actual output never shrinks: its slowest growth is about 0.6 percent a year. Yet the economy spends four years of every eight below potential. A recession is a matter of the gap, not of the sign of growth.
The cost of a slump. Add up short-run output over the years below potential. The sum is the output lost, as a percent of one year’s potential output. In the baseline the slump years 5, 6 and 7 give \(-1.41 - 2 - 1.41 = -4.83\) percent of a year’s potential output. Over the whole cycle, though, the boom years add \(+4.83\), so the total is exactly zero. Removing fluctuations altogether would therefore gain much less than the cost of a recession on its own, because the booms would go too.

The Phillips curve

Assumptions
The short-run model rests on three premises. We state them in our own words:

Shocks never stop. Something is always hitting the economy, pushing \(Y_t\) away from \(\bar{Y}_t\) or inflation away from \(\bar{\pi}\).
Policy can move output in the short run. Monetary and fiscal policy can raise or lower spending, and so output, for a while. In this chapter we go one step further and let policymakers choose \(\tilde{Y}_t\) directly. Chapters 11 and 12 explain how they do it.
Output and inflation trade off over time. A hot economy speeds up inflation and a cold one slows it down. This is the Phillips curve:

\[\Delta\pi_t \equiv \pi_t - \pi_{t-1} = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t, \qquad \bar{\nu} > 0. \tag{5}\]
The slope \(\bar{\nu}\) is the number of points by which inflation rises in a year for each percent that output is above potential.
Why the curve slopes up. When demand runs hot, firms are working beyond their sustainable level: overtime is paid at premium wages, machines run without a break, and goods are scarce. Each firm then raises its prices by more than the inflation everyone expected, and when all firms do so at once, inflation itself goes up. When demand is weak, firms with idle capacity hold back their price increases to win customers, and inflation comes down. The curve describes the change in inflation, not its level: in Chapter 12 a full version adds a term for price shocks such as oil.


Solving the model
Step 1: a rule that moves inflation forward. Add \(\pi_{t-1}\) to both sides of equation (5):
\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t.\]
This is a difference equation (Appendix C.10): given last year’s inflation and this year’s short-run output, it gives this year’s inflation.
Step 2: apply it year after year. Start from inflation \(\pi_0\) in year 0:
\[\pi_1 = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_1,\] \[\pi_2 = \pi_1 + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_2 = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\left(\tilde{Y}_1 + \tilde{Y}_2\right),\] \[\pi_3 = \pi_2 + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_3 = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\left(\tilde{Y}_1 + \tilde{Y}_2 + \tilde{Y}_3\right),\]
and after \(t\) years
\[\pi_t = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\tilde{Y}_s. \tag{6}\]
Intuition. Inflation keeps a running total of every past gap. A boom that is over still leaves inflation higher, until a slump of the same total size brings it back.
Step 3: steady inflation. Inflation stays constant, \(\Delta\pi_t = 0\), if and only if \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\). Any inflation rate can persist as long as output sits at potential. That is why the level of long-run inflation \(\bar{\pi}\) is not pinned down by the Phillips curve: it comes from the long run and from policy.
Step 4: a boom that lasts. If policymakers hold output at the same gap \(\tilde{Y}\) every year, the sum in equation (6) is \(t\) copies of \(\tilde{Y}\), so \(\pi_t = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\,t\): inflation climbs in a straight line, by \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) points every year, without end. With the baseline slope \(0.33\) and a gap held at \(+2\) percent, inflation rises by \(0.66\) points a year: \(2 \to 2.66 \to 3.32 \to 3.98\) percent. Fig. 9 runs this experiment.
Step 5: the output cost of lowering inflation. Set \(t = T\) in equation (6), subtract \(\pi_0\) from both sides and divide by \(\bar{\nu}\):
\[\sum_{s=1}^{T}\tilde{Y}_s = \frac{\pi_T - \pi_0}{\bar{\nu}}. \tag{7}\]
To lower inflation, the gaps must add up to a negative number, and the required total is fixed by the slope alone. With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), cutting inflation by one point takes a cumulative gap of \(-1/0.33 = -3.03\) percent-years: for example \(-3.03\) percent for one year, or \(-1.01\) percent in each of three years. Policy chooses how to spread the pain over time, not how much pain there is in total. The ratio \(1/\bar{\nu}\), the output lost per point of disinflation, is often called the sacrifice ratio.
