Comparative statics. The effect of one more percent of short-run output on the change in inflation is the slope, \(\partial\Delta\pi_t/\partial\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{\nu}\). Both variables are already in percent, so the slope plays the role of an elasticity.

A steeper curve (higher \(\bar{\nu}\)) rotates the line counterclockwise around the origin. A boom then raises inflation faster, and a disinflation is cheaper: by equation (7), its output cost \(1/\bar{\nu}\) falls.
A price shock (Chapter 12) shifts the whole line up: inflation rises even at potential.
A different long-run inflation rate \(\bar{\pi}\) does not move the line at all, because the curve is about changes in inflation.

Inflation peaks as the slump begins. By equation (6), inflation rises while \(\tilde{Y}_t > 0\) and falls while \(\tilde{Y}_t < 0\). Its highest point is therefore the moment the gap crosses zero from above, which is the start of a recession. In the baseline cycle, inflation goes \(2 \to 2.47 \to 3.13 \to 3.59\) percent in years 1 to 3, stays at \(3.59\) in year 4 (where \(\tilde{Y} = 0\)), and then falls back to 2 percent by year 8, because the gaps of a full cycle add up to zero. This is the pattern of Fig. 5: U.S. inflation tends to peak close to the start of each recession and to fall during it.
No free lunch from a permanent boom. Holding output above potential buys ever-rising inflation (step 4). Lowering inflation that is too high requires a period of output below potential (equation 7), which is how the Volcker disinflation of the early 1980s worked (Fig. 6).



Okun’s law

Definitions
The unemployment rate is \(u_t\). The natural rate of unemployment \(\bar{u}\) is the rate the economy settles at in the long run (Chapter 7), the labor-market cousin of potential output. Their difference \(u_t - \bar{u}\) is cyclical unemployment. Okun’s law is a rule of thumb fitted to U.S. data (Fig. 8):
\[u_t - \bar{u} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\tilde{Y}_t. \tag{8}\]
Each percent of output below potential comes with half a point of unemployment above the natural rate. The slope is smaller than 1 in size because firms do not adjust only through jobs: in a slump they also cut hours and keep some workers they do not fully need, and some people who lose jobs stop looking for work and so are not counted as unemployed.


Working with the law
Step 1: going back from unemployment to output. Multiply both sides of equation (8) by \(-2\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = -2\,(u_t - \bar{u}).\]
In the baseline slump, \(\tilde{Y} = -2\%\) means unemployment 1 point above its natural rate, and 1 point of unemployment below the natural rate signals output 2 percent above potential.
Step 2: changes in unemployment. Write equation (8) for years \(t\) and \(t-1\) and subtract. The natural rate is constant, so it cancels:
\[\Delta u_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Delta\tilde{Y}_t.\]
Now replace \(\Delta\tilde{Y}_t\) with \(g_{Y,t} - \bar{g}\) from equation (4):
\[\Delta u_t \approx -\tfrac{1}{2}\left(g_{Y,t} - \bar{g}\right). \tag{9}\]
Intuition. Unemployment rises whenever output grows more slowly than potential, even if output is still growing. Steady growth at the trend rate only holds unemployment where it is. In the baseline, from year 4 to year 5 output grows only about 0.6 percent, so unemployment rises by about \(-\tfrac{1}{2}(0.6 - 2) = +0.7\) point.
Step 3: the Phillips curve in terms of unemployment. Substitute \(\tilde{Y}_t = -2(u_t - \bar{u})\) from step 1 into the Phillips curve, equation (5):
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\times\left[-2\,(u_t - \bar{u})\right] = -2\bar{\nu}\,(u_t - \bar{u}).\]
Inflation rises when unemployment is below its natural rate and falls when it is above. With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), each point of unemployment above the natural rate lowers inflation by \(0.66\) points a year. This is the form in which the trade-off was first found in the data, with unemployment on the horizontal axis (Chapter 12 tells that history).

A preview of the full short-run model

Assumptions
The full model keeps the long run as given (\(\bar{Y}_t\), \(\bar{\pi}\) and \(\bar{u}\) come from outside) and keeps the three premises above. It adds households, firms that invest, a government that spends, trade with the rest of the world and a central bank that runs monetary policy.


How the pieces fit together
The chain of cause and effect, built over the next chapters, runs from the interest rate to output and then to inflation and unemployment:
\[\underbrace{R_t}_{\text{real interest rate}} \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{IS curve}\ }\; \tilde{Y}_t \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{Phillips curve}\ }\; \Delta\pi_t, \qquad \tilde{Y}_t \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{Okun's law}\ }\; u_t - \bar{u}.\]

The IS curve (Chapter 11) says that a higher real interest rate \(R_t\) lowers investment and other borrowing-financed spending, and so lowers short-run output.
The MP curve (Chapter 12) shows how the central bank, by setting a short-term nominal interest rate such as the federal funds rate, sets the real interest rate in the short run.
The Phillips curve, equation (5), then turns short-run output into a change in inflation, and Okun’s law, equation (8), into unemployment.

So the signs run: a higher \(R_t\) means a lower \(\tilde{Y}_t\), falling inflation and higher unemployment. This chapter skips the first link by letting policymakers pick \(\tilde{Y}_t\) directly.


What the model predicts

Policy can lean against shocks and keep \(\tilde{Y}_t\) near zero, which keeps inflation steady (equation 5).
It cannot keep output above potential year after year without inflation climbing without limit (equation 6).
High inflation comes down only through a period of output below potential, with a total cost set by the slope (equation 7).
In practice the job is harder than in the model, because potential output is not observed (equation 4) and new shocks keep arriving.




The model in code
We now turn the key results into Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes. The cells after them check the algebra above with numbers.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing g=2.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”, and np.sin is the sine function, which draws a smooth wave (np.pi is the number π).


def potential_output(t, g=2.0, Y0=100.0):
    """Potential output Ybar_t: a smooth trend that grows g percent a year, from Y0 in year 0."""
    return Y0 * (1 + g / 100) ** t


def actual_output(t, A=2.0, g=2.0, cycle=8):
    """Actual output Y_t = Ybar_t (1 + Y~_t)   (equation 2), with a wave of +-A percent that repeats every `cycle` years."""
    return potential_output(t, g) * (1 + A / 100 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / cycle))


def short_run_output(Y, Ybar):
    """Short-run output in percent: 100 (Y - Ybar) / Ybar   (equation 1)."""
    return 100 * (Y - Ybar) / Ybar


def phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu=0.33):
    """Change in inflation, percentage points: delta pi = nu * Y_tilde   (the Phillips curve, equation 5)."""
    return nu * Y_tilde


def okun_law(Y_tilde, slope=-0.5):
    """Cyclical unemployment u - u_bar, percentage points: slope * Y_tilde   (Okun's law, equation 8)."""
    return slope * Y_tilde

The colors come from a small tool. Its palette has 44 colors: Plotly’s 24 dark ones, and the 20 darker ones of its 26 “Alphabet” colors.

Python note. PALETTE = [] starts an empty list, and .append adds one color at a time. In first_free, return inside a loop stops the function at the first color that fits, used.count(c) counts how often c appears in the list used, and reversed(PALETTE) walks through the palette from its last color.


LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]   # too pale on white
PALETTE = []
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24:                                       # 24 dark colors ...
    if c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(c)                                                     # ... and 20 more: 44 in all
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                    # a medium blue, too close to the U.S. navy: used last


def first_free(used, taken):
    """The palette color least used in `used` (the group-mates' colors), preferring one no country has `taken` yet."""
    for c in PALETTE:
        if c not in used and c not in taken:
            return c
    best = PALETTE[-1]
    for c in reversed(PALETTE):                  # from the end, far from the colors always on show
        if used.count(c) < used.count(best):
            best = c                             # a big group shares out the colors evenly
    return best


Python note. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. dict(fixed or {}) starts from a copy of the fixed colors (an empty dictionary when there are none), continue skips a country that already has a color, and used collects the colors of the countries that are shown together with this one.


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    names: every country; groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color}
    for the textbook's countries, so the default view keeps the book's colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    if other in colors:
                        used.append(colors[other])
        colors[name] = first_free(used, list(colors.values()))
    return colors

The United States keeps the chapter’s blue, and every other country gets a color that no country of its groups uses.

title: 9. An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Trend and cycle
We start with a made-up economy to see the key idea of the chapter: actual output equals potential output plus short-run fluctuations around it.

Fig. 1: Economic fluctuations and short-run output
Goal. See how removing the trend from actual output leaves the ups and downs of the business cycle.
Panel (a) draws actual output \(Y_t\) around a smooth potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\). Panel (b) draws short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\) from equation (1): the same wiggle, with the trend taken out. The gray bars in panel (a) are the gaps \(Y - \bar{Y}\) at the top of the boom and at the bottom of the slump.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 8, 200) creates 200 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 8: the years at which we draw the curves. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) makes a figure with two panels, and row=..., col=... tells add_trace where to draw. fig.add_hline draws a horizontal line. We fix the axis ranges so that you can see the curves move when a parameter changes.


def fluctuations(A=2.0, g=2.0):
    """Fig. 9.1: actual and potential output (a) and short-run output (b), over one 8-year cycle."""
    t = np.linspace(0, 8, 201)                          # time, in years: t[50] = 2 and t[150] = 6
    Y, Ybar = actual_output(t, A, g), potential_output(t, g)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) Actual and potential output",
                                                        "(b) Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Y, name="Actual output, Y", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Ybar, name="Potential output, Ȳ", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")),
                  row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[2, 2, None, 6, 6], y=[Ybar[50], Y[50], None, Ybar[150], Y[150]],   # boom and slump
                             name="Gap, Y − Ȳ", mode="lines", line=dict(color=GRAY, width=4)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=short_run_output(Y, Ybar), name="Short-run output, Ỹ",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color=GREEN, width=2, dash="dash"), row=1, col=2)      # Ỹ = 0: output at potential
    add_end_label(fig, 8, Y[-1], "Y", BLUE, "bottom", 1, 1)          # Y and Ȳ meet at t = 8: one above,
    add_end_label(fig, 8, Ybar[-1], "Ȳ", GREEN, "top", 1, 1)         # one below
    add_end_label(fig, 8, 0, "Ỹ", TEAL, "bottom", 1, 2)
    fig.add_annotation(x=2, y=A, xref="x2", yref="y2", text="Boom: Ỹ > 0", showarrow=False, yshift=14)
    fig.add_annotation(x=6, y=-A, xref="x2", yref="y2", text="Slump: Ỹ < 0", showarrow=False, yshift=-14)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Time (years)", range=[0, 8])
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Output", range=[94, 145], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5.2, 5.2], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Boom: Ỹ = +{A:.1f}%   Slump: Ỹ = −{A:.1f}%   |   potential grows {g:.1f}% a year",
                      showlegend=False)
    return fig

Now the interactive version. Move the sliders and compare the two panels.

Source. Adapted from Fig. 9.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

Panel (b) looks just like actual output in panel (a), without the upward trend. That is why economists also call \(\tilde{Y}\) detrended output.
Raise the growth of potential output to 4 percent. In panel (a) the slump almost disappears: even at the bottom of the cycle, actual output still grows by more than 2 percent a year. In panel (b) nothing changes. Strong growth hides the cycle, which is exactly what happens with real GDP in Fig. 2.
Set \(\bar{g} = 0\) and the two panels look the same: potential output is then a constant 100, so \(Y - \bar{Y}\) and \(\tilde{Y}\) are the same numbers.

The Great Depression shows up clearly: output was 23 percent below potential in 1933. During World War II it was 35 percent above potential in 1944. But look at the first row: output 25 percent above potential in 1929. That is not a real boom. Nobody published potential output for those years, so the early values are only an estimate. The trend has to start somewhere, and at the edge of the sample it is least reliable. Always ask where a number comes from, and treat the 1929–1948 gaps with care.
Now the chart. On a ratio scale (a logarithmic axis), equal distances mean equal percentage changes. You can also pick another country. Its GDP comes from the OECD, in trillions of 2021 dollars at PPP, and starts later.

Python note. rename(columns={...}) gives the columns readable names for the legend. px.line with a list y=[...] draws one line per column. log_y=True gives a ratio scale, tickvals sets the numbers printed on the axis, and on a ratio scale the axis range is given in powers of ten: np.log10(0.9).


us_levels = gdp.rename(columns={"gdp_actual": "Actual GDP", "gdp_potential": "Potential GDP"})
TICKS = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
LEVEL_COUNTRIES = ["United States"] + sorted(others.dropna(subset=["gdp_real"]).country.unique())


def gdp_levels(country):
    """Fig. 9.2: actual and potential GDP of one country (U.S.: CBO, 2022 dollars; others: OECD, 2021 PPP dollars)."""
    if country == "United States":
        return us_levels
    data = others[others.country == country].dropna(subset=["gdp_real"])
    return data.rename(columns={"gdp_real": "Actual GDP", "gdp_potential": "Potential GDP"})


def ratio_ticks(low, high):
    """Tick values 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, ... (more of them for a narrow range) from low to high."""
    steps = [1, 2, 5] if high / low > 8 else [1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 7]
    if high / low < 3:
        steps = [1, 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]       # a narrow range needs more ticks
    ticks = []
    for power in range(-3, 3):
        for step in steps:
            if low <= step * 10 ** power <= high:
                ticks.append(round(step * 10 ** power, 3))
    return ticks


Python note. .idxmin() gives the row label of the smallest value, and .notna().any() is True when a column has at least one number.


def gdp_title(country, data):
    """Fig. 9.2: a title with the finding: the deepest slump below potential output."""
    gaps = short_run_output(data["Actual GDP"], data["Potential GDP"])
    if country == "United States":
        return "Actual and potential GDP move together, except in the 1930s and 1940s"
    if gaps.notna().any():
        return f"{country}: the deepest slump was {-gaps.min():.1f}% below potential, in {data.year[gaps.idxmin()]}"
    return f"{country}: actual GDP only (the OECD estimates no potential output)"


def gdp_chart(scale="ratio", country="United States"):
    """Fig. 9.2: real GDP, actual and potential, of one country (ratio or linear scale)."""
    data = gdp_levels(country)
    unit = "Trillions of 2022 dollars" if country == "United States" else "Trillions of 2021 dollars (PPP)"
    title = gdp_title(country, data)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=["Actual GDP", "Potential GDP"], log_y=(scale == "ratio"), title=title,
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN], labels={"year": "Year", "value": unit, "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Potential GDP"), line_dash="dash")
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Actual GDP"), line_width=3)
    if country == "United States":
        ticks, ratio_range, linear_top = TICKS, [np.log10(0.9), np.log10(32)], 30
    else:
        low, high = 0.9 * data["Actual GDP"].min(), 1.1 * data["Actual GDP"].max()
        ticks, ratio_range, linear_top = ratio_ticks(low, high), [np.log10(low), np.log10(high)], 1.05 * high
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=ticks, range=ratio_range)
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, linear_top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.year.min() - 1, 2026])
    return fig

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPCA), via FRED; Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Real Potential Gross Domestic Product (GDPPOT), via FRED; and the BEA’s GDP implicit price deflator (A191RD3A086NBEA), via FRED, used to express both in 2022 dollars. No agency publishes potential output before 1949, so the 1929–1948 values are our own smooth trend. Other countries: OECD, Economic Outlook No. 119, real GDP at purchasing power parity (GDPVD) and potential output (GDPVTR, GDPV), from the OECD Data Explorer (dataflow DSD_EO@DF_EO). Prepared files: data/ch09/fig9-2.csv and data/ch09/short_run_panel.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 9.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
On the website, choose a country in the menu at the top left; choosing a country switches back to the ratio scale.
What to notice.

Since about 1950 the two lines are hard to tell apart. Growth is so large that the fluctuations become hard to see, an illusion of scale that Fig. 3 removes.
On the linear scale, everything before 1960 is squeezed near the bottom.
Potential output grows more slowly after the Great Recession of 2007–09 (see the key numbers below). The CBO builds potential output with a Solow-type model, so weak investment after 2008 meant less capital and slower potential growth.
Choose Greece. After 2008 its GDP fell far below potential, to 10.6 percent below in 2012, and the OECD now estimates that Greece’s potential output itself shrank, by 0.5 percent a year from 2007 to 2025. Choose Japan: potential output has grown by less than 1 percent a year since 1995.


Key numbers: the Depression, the war and slower potential growth

Python note. set_index("year") labels the rows by year, so potential[2007] is the value for 2007. .loc[1930:1939] keeps the rows from 1930 to 1939, and .mean() averages them.


by_year = gdp.set_index("year")
potential = by_year.gdp_potential


def potential_growth(start, end):
    """Average annual growth of potential output from year start to year end, in percent."""
    return 100 * ((potential[end] / potential[start]) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1)

print(f"Potential growth 1990-2007:         {potential_growth(1990, 2007):.1f}% a year")
print(f"Potential growth 2007-2019:         {potential_growth(2007, 2019):.1f}% a year")

Output was on average 11 percent below potential in the 1930s. Since 1950 no gap has been as large as the 1982 one, 6.2 percent below potential. The column short_run_output_book_vintage is the same calculation with the data as they were published in 2023, when the textbook was written. def fluctuations_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 9.3: short-run output; U.S. quarterly (two data vintages), other countries annual (OECD)."""
    fig = px.line(vintages, x="date", y=["Data as of 2026", "Data as published in 2023"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GRAY],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", "variable": "Data vintage"},
                  title="Short-run output falls sharply in every recession (shaded)")
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Data as of 2026"), line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Data as published in 2023"), line_dash="dot")
    if "United States" not in countries and len(countries) > 0:
        fig.update_traces(visible=False)
    data = annual_gaps[annual_gaps.country.isin(countries)]
    if len(data) > 0:
        extra = px.line(data, x="date", y="output_gap", color="country", markers=True, hover_name="year", color_discrete_map=COLORS)
        fig.add_traces(extra.data)
        low = data.loc[data.output_gap.idxmin()]

Key numbers: what does a recession cost?
The textbook adds up the output lost in a slump: about 6 percent of a year’s GDP in a typical recession. We can measure it. We walk through the quarters, and each time \(\tilde{Y}\) turns negative we start adding up the shortfall until output is back at potential. A quarter is a quarter of a year, so each quarter adds \(-\tilde{Y}/4\) percent of a year’s GDP.

Python note. series.short_run_output.items() hands over one (date, value) pair at a time. None means “no value yet”: start is None is true while we are not inside a slump. total += x is short for total = total + x.


slumps = []
start, total = None, 0.0
for date, value in series.short_run_output.items():
    if value < 0:
        if start is None:                      # a new slump begins
            start, total = date, 0.0
        total += -value / 4                    # lost output, percent of a year's GDP
    elif start is not None:                    # output is back at potential: the slump is over
        years = (date - start).days / 365.25
        slumps.append([start.strftime("%Y-%m"), date.strftime("%Y-%m"), years, total])
        start = None
slumps = pd.DataFrame(slumps, columns=["Slump starts", "Back at potential", "Years", "Lost output (% of GDP)"])

Python note. px.bar draws one bar per row. fig.add_annotation writes a label with an arrow that points at a data point; ax and ay set where the label sits, in pixels from that point. f"{date:%B %Y}" prints a date as “April 2020”, and date.quarter is its quarter of the year (1 to 4).


def employment_data(country):
    """Fig. 9.4: the employment changes of one country (U.S.: monthly payroll jobs; others: quarterly, OECD)."""
    if country == "United States":
        return jobs, "Monthly"
    return emp_q[emp_q.country == country], "Quarterly"


def employment_chart(view="full range", country="United States"):
    """Fig. 9.4: the percent change in employment from the month (or quarter) before."""
    data, freq = employment_data(country)
    low = data.loc[data.emp_change_pct.idxmin()]
    when = f"{low.date:%B %Y}" if country == "United States" else f"{low.date.year} Q{low.date.quarter}"
    title = "Employment grows in most months; 2008–09 and April 2020 stand out"
    if country != "United States":
        title = f"{country}: employment fell most in {when}, by {-low.emp_change_pct:.1f}% in one quarter"
    fig = px.bar(data, x="date", y="emp_change_pct", title=title,
                 labels={"date": "Year", "emp_change_pct": f"{freq} change in employment (percent)"})
    fig.update_traces(marker_color=BLUE, marker_line_width=0)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    if view == "full range":
        fig.add_annotation(x=low.date, y=low.emp_change_pct, text=f"{when}: {low.emp_change_pct:.1f}%",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, ax=-110, ay=0)
        if country == "United States":
            fig.update_yaxes(range=[-15, 4.5], tickvals=[-14, -12, -10, -8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[-1, 2], tickvals=[-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.date.min() - pd.DateOffset(months=6), data.date.max() + pd.DateOffset(months=6)])
    return fig

INFLATION_RANGES = [[-2.5, 15.5], [-5, 31], [-10, 62], [-20, 124], [-50, 310]]


def inflation_range(low, high):
    """The first range in INFLATION_RANGES that contains low and high (the widest one if none does)."""
    for bottom, top in INFLATION_RANGES:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    return INFLATION_RANGES[-1]


def inflation_chart(countries=("United States",)):

    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    shade_recessions(fig)

title: 9. An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
The Phillips curve
When output is above potential, inflation tends to rise. We draw this relationship in the model and then measure it in U.S. data.

Fig. 6: The Phillips curve
Goal. Draw the Phillips curve and see how short-run output moves inflation.
Think of a hot holiday toy. When demand is high, the firm that makes it runs overtime and pays its workers more, and the toy is scarce. So its price rises faster than usual. In a booming economy, it is as if every firm made the hot toy: all of them raise prices faster than the current inflation rate, so inflation goes up. In a slump the opposite happens. The Phillips curve, equation (5), puts this in one line:
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\]
When output is at potential (\(\tilde{Y} = 0\)), inflation is steady. Our function phillips_curve from “The model in code” draws the line. The black dot is the economy, at the short-run output you choose.

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="line", ...) draws a straight segment, here the dashed guides from the dot to the axes. An if ... elif ... else block picks one of three cases.


def phillips_diagram(nu=0.33, Y_tilde=0.0):
    """Fig. 9.6: the Phillips curve delta pi = nu * Y_tilde, with the economy at Y_tilde."""
    Y_end = min(6.0, 2.6 / nu)                          # stop the line where its name still fits below the top
    Y = np.linspace(-Y_end, Y_end, 100)
    dpi = phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu)
    if dpi > 0:
        verdict = "inflation rises"
    elif dpi < 0:
        verdict = "inflation falls"
    else:
        verdict = "inflation is steady"
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=phillips_curve(Y, nu), name="Phillips curve", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)))
    add_end_label(fig, Y_end, phillips_curve(Y_end, nu), "Phillips curve", TEAL, "bottom", xanchor="right")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[Y_tilde], y=[dpi], name="The economy", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=13)))
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=Y_tilde, y0=-3.2, x1=Y_tilde, y1=dpi, line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash"))
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=-6.5, y0=dpi, x1=Y_tilde, y1=dpi, line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=-3.2, y=2.8, text="← Ỹ < 0: output below potential", showarrow=False)
    fig.add_annotation(x=3.2, y=-2.8, text="Ỹ > 0: output above potential →", showarrow=False)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Ỹ = {Y_tilde:+.2f}%  →  Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_tilde:+.2f}) = {dpi:+.2f} points: {verdict}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=[-6.5, 6.5], tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Change in inflation, Δπ (points)", range=[-3.2, 3.2], tickvals=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]),
                      showlegend=False)                  # tick values: no labels in the bottom-left corner
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 9.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

To the right of zero (a boom), \(\Delta\pi > 0\): inflation rises. To the left (a slump), \(\Delta\pi < 0\): inflation falls.
The line always goes through the origin: only output at potential keeps inflation steady.
A steeper curve (a larger \(\bar{\nu}\)) means a boom raises inflation faster, but also that a slump brings it down faster.


How the short-run model works: the Volcker disinflation
In 1979 U.S. inflation was above 11 percent (Fig. 5), and the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker set out to bring it down. The Phillips curve says that the only way to lower inflation is to push output below potential. Tight monetary policy did exactly that: short-run output averaged about \(-6\) percent in 1982 (Fig. 3 shows the quarters). The model then predicts falling inflation, and inflation did fall to about 3 percent by 1983.
Let us check the model’s prediction for 1981–1983 with the annual short-run output of Fig. 7 below.

Python note. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits the best straight line \(y = a + bx\) through the points (by least squares, also called OLS) and returns the slope \(b\) first and the intercept \(a\) second.


slope, intercept = np.polyfit(phillips.short_run_output, phillips.d_inflation, 1)

OLS line: delta pi = 0.10 + 0.35 x Y~   (1961-2025)


The fitted slope is about 0.35, close to the textbook’s “about 1/3”. Now we draw the data with our model line \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\), and you choose \(\bar{\nu}\). The title adds up the squared misses, the squared vertical distances between the points and the line. The smaller that number, the better the line fits.

Python note. .where(condition, "") keeps a value where the condition is true and puts "" elsewhere, so only a few years get a text label (hover over any point to see its year). np.where(condition, a, b) picks a or b row by row.


LABELS = [1966, 1974, 1975, 1979, 1982, 1983, 2009, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
phillips["label"] = phillips.year.astype(str).where(phillips.year.isin(LABELS), "")
phillips["period"] = np.where(phillips.year <= 2022, "1961–2022 (in the textbook)", "2023–2025 (new data)")
X_RANGES, Y_RANGES = [[-8.5, 6.5], [-13, 19]], [[-5.5, 5.5], [-12, 12]]   # the textbook's ranges, and wider ones


def wider(values, ranges):
    """The first range that holds all values (the last one if none does)."""
    for low, high in ranges:
        if low <= values.min() and values.max() <= high:
            return [low, high]
    return ranges[-1]

For another country, the points are the OECD’s output gap and the change in World Bank CPI inflation.

Python note. .diff() gives the change from the row before: here, \(\Delta\pi_t = \pi_t - \pi_{t-1}\).


def phillips_data(country):
    """Fig. 9.7: one point per year, short-run output and the change in inflation (U.S.: the textbook's data)."""
    if country == "United States":
        return phillips
    data = others[others.country == country].copy()
    data["d_inflation"] = data.inflation.diff()
    data = data.rename(columns={"output_gap": "short_run_output"}).dropna(subset=["short_run_output", "d_inflation"])
    data["label"] = ""
    data["period"] = f"{data.year.min()}–{data.year.max()} (OECD data)"
    return data


def phillips_fit(nu=0.33, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 9.7: the data with the model line delta pi = nu * Y_tilde; the title measures the fit."""
    data = phillips_data(country)
    misses = data.d_inflation - phillips_curve(data.short_run_output, nu)
    ols = np.polyfit(data.short_run_output, data.d_inflation, 1)[0]
    fig = px.scatter(data, x="short_run_output", y="d_inflation", color="period", text="label", hover_name="year",
                     color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN, "#0b4f47"],
                     labels={"short_run_output": "Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)",
                             "d_inflation": "Change in inflation, Δπ (points)", "period": "Years"})
    fig.update_traces(textposition="middle right", textfont_size=11, marker_size=9)
    xr, yr = wider(data.short_run_output, X_RANGES), wider(data.d_inflation, Y_RANGES)
    Y = np.linspace(xr[0], xr[1], 50)                # the model line spans the whole x-axis
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=phillips_curve(Y, nu), name=f"Model: Δπ = {nu:.2f} × Ỹ", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    off = (~data.d_inflation.between(yr[0], yr[1]) | ~data.short_run_output.between(xr[0], xr[1])).sum()
    note = f"  |  {off} off the chart" if off > 0 else ""
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{country}, ν = {nu:.2f}: squared misses {(misses ** 2).sum():,.1f}  |  OLS slope {ols:.2f}{note}",
                      xaxis_range=xr, yaxis_range=yr)
    return fig

For other countries we need a natural rate of unemployment too. The OECD no longer publishes its estimates in the Economic Outlook, so our file has a stand-in: unemployment_trend, a smooth trend through each country’s unemployment rate (a Hodrick–Prescott trend). Cyclical unemployment is then \(u - \text{trend}\). How much does this choice matter? We can try it on the United States, where we have both:

      f"{np.polyfit(trial.Y_tilde, trial.cyclical, 1)[0]:.2f}")

The slope is smaller with the trend, because a trend follows unemployment up in long slumps and counts part of the slump as “natural”. Keep this in mind when you compare countries: their slopes use the trend, the U.S. one the CBO.

OKUN_Y_RANGES = [[-3.5, 4.5], [-7, 9]]          # the textbook's range, and a wider one


def okun_data(country):
    """Fig. 9.8: one point per year, short-run output and cyclical unemployment (U.S.: the textbook's data)."""
    if country == "United States":
        return okun
    data = others[others.country == country].copy()
    data["cyclical_unemployment"] = data.unemployment - data.unemployment_trend
    data = data.rename(columns={"output_gap": "short_run_output"}).dropna(subset=["short_run_output", "cyclical_unemployment"])
    data["label"] = ""
    return data


def okun_fit(slope=-0.5, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 9.8: the data with the model line u - u_bar = slope * Y_tilde; the title measures the fit."""
    data = okun_data(country)
    misses = data.cyclical_unemployment - okun_law(data.short_run_output, slope)
    ols = np.polyfit(data.short_run_output, data.cyclical_unemployment, 1)[0]
    fig = px.scatter(data, x="short_run_output", y="cyclical_unemployment", text="label", hover_name="year",
                     color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN],
                     labels={"short_run_output": "Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)",
                             "cyclical_unemployment": "Cyclical unemployment, u − ū (points)"})
    fig.update_traces(textposition="middle right", textfont_size=11, marker_size=9, showlegend=True,
                      name=f"{country}, {data.year.min()}–{data.year.max()}")
    xr, yr = wider(data.short_run_output, X_RANGES), wider(data.cyclical_unemployment, OKUN_Y_RANGES)
    Y = np.linspace(xr[0], xr[1], 50)                # the model line spans the whole x-axis
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=okun_law(Y, slope), name=f"Model: u − ū = {slope:.2f} × Ỹ", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{country}, slope {slope:.2f}: squared misses {(misses ** 2).sum():.2f}  |  OLS slope {ols:.2f}",
                      xaxis_range=xr, yaxis_range=yr)
    return fig

title: 9. An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Overstimulating the economy
We end with an experiment: what happens to inflation if policymakers keep output above potential year after year?

Fig. 9: The Phillips curve and the booming economy
Goal. Answer the textbook’s exercise “Overstimulating the economy”: what happens if policymakers keep output 3 percent above potential every year?
The economy starts at potential with inflation at its long-run rate, \(\bar{\pi} = 2\%\). Then output is held at \(\tilde{Y} = +3\%\). The Phillips curve (equation 5) says inflation rises by \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) every year:
\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\]
With the textbook’s slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), inflation goes from 2 to 5, 8 and 11 percent in three years, the straight-line climb that equation (6) predicts for a gap held constant. A computer can apply this equation year after year: a simulation.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each year. pi_path[-1] is the last number in the list, last year’s inflation, and pi_path.append(...) adds this year’s at the end. range(1, years + 1) counts 1, 2, …, years.


def simulate_inflation(pi_bar=2.0, nu=1.0, Y_tilde=3.0, years=5):
    """Inflation year by year when output is held at Y_tilde: pi_t = pi_(t-1) + nu * Y_tilde."""
    pi_path = [pi_bar]                                    # year 0: inflation at its long-run rate
    for year in range(1, years + 1):
        pi_path.append(pi_path[-1] + phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu))
    return np.arange(years + 1), np.array(pi_path)


years, pi_path = simulate_inflation()
print("Inflation, years 0 to 5:", pi_path)

Inflation, years 0 to 5: [ 2.  5.  8. 11. 14. 17.]


The figure has two panels: (a) the Phillips curve with the economy at potential and in the boom (the two black dots), and (b) the inflation path \(\pi\) that the boom produces, against long-run inflation \(\bar{\pi}\) (dashed).

def booming_economy(pi_bar=2.0, nu=1.0, Y_tilde=3.0):
    """Fig. 9.9: the economy held at Y_tilde on the Phillips curve (a) and the inflation path (b)."""
    years, pi_path = simulate_inflation(pi_bar, nu, Y_tilde)
    dpi = phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu)
    Y = np.linspace(-6.5, 6.5, 100)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) The Phillips curve", "(b) Inflation, year by year"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=phillips_curve(Y, nu), name="Phillips curve", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)),
                  row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, Y_tilde], y=[0, dpi], name="At potential and in the boom", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=12)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=pi_path, name="Inflation, π", mode="lines+markers",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), marker=dict(size=9)), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 5], y=[pi_bar, pi_bar], name="Long-run inflation, π̄", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")), row=1, col=2)
    up = pi_path[-1] >= pi_bar                            # does inflation end above its long-run rate?
    add_end_label(fig, 5, pi_path[-1], "π", BLUE, "bottom" if up else "top", 1, 2)
    add_end_label(fig, 5, pi_bar, "π̄", GRAY, "top" if up else "bottom", 1, 2)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=[-6.5, 6.5], tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Change in inflation, Δπ", range=[-6.5, 6.5], tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Years of the boom", range=[-0.3, 5.3], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Inflation (percent)", range=[-36, 42], tickvals=[-30, -20, -10, 0, 10, 20, 30], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_tilde:+.2f}) = {dpi:+.2f} a year: "
                            f"π = {pi_path[0]:.2f} → {pi_path[1]:.2f} → {pi_path[2]:.2f} → {pi_path[3]:.2f}%",
                      showlegend=False)
    return fig

What to notice.

Holding output above potential does not raise inflation once: it raises it every year. The cost of a permanent boom is ever-rising inflation.
The steeper the Phillips curve, the faster inflation climbs. With the U.S. slope of about 0.33, inflation rises by about 1 point a year instead of 3, slower but without end.
Set \(\tilde{Y}\) below zero and the same mechanism brings inflation down: that is how a recession fights inflation.

title: 9. An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Concluding remarks

Actual output is potential output times a cycle factor, \(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t(1+\tilde{Y}_t)\), equations (1) and (2). Short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t = (Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)/\bar{Y}_t\) is positive in a boom and negative in a recession; it is close to the log difference \(\ln Y_t - \ln\bar{Y}_t\) (equation 3), and actual growth is trend growth plus the change in the gap (equation 4).
U.S. recessions push output a few percent below potential, cost millions of jobs and, in total, several percent of a year’s GDP. Potential output is only estimated, so the measured gaps change when the data are revised.
Inflation usually falls during a recession. The Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\), equation (5), captures this, with a U.S. slope of about 1/3. Solved forward, inflation is a running total of past gaps (equation 6): a lasting boom raises it without end, and lowering it costs a cumulative slump of \(1/\bar{\nu}\) percent-years per point (equation 7).
Okun’s law, equation (8), links output and unemployment: each point of output below potential adds about half a point of unemployment, and unemployment rises whenever output grows more slowly than potential (equation 9).
The next chapter uses this short-run lens on the Great Recession and the Covid-19 pandemic.

title: 9. An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
Practice problems
The conceptual problems apply the frameworks of the Model overview to real episodes, the data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data, and the modeling problems answer policy questions with the chapter’s interactive models; each problem is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge. Try each problem before you open its Hint, and only then its Solution. The sliders in the answer cells run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): How deep was the Covid-19 collapse, really? U.S. statistics report quarterly GDP growth as an annualized rate (step 5 of the trend-and-cycle block in the Model overview). In its first, “advance” estimates, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that real GDP fell at an annual rate of 32.9 percent in the second quarter of 2020 and rose at an annual rate of 33.1 percent in the third quarter.

Convert each annualized rate into the growth rate over the quarter itself.
A reader adds the two numbers and concludes that the rebound more than made up for the fall. In the third quarter, was real GDP back at its level of the first quarter? By how many percent did it differ?



Hint

An annualized rate \(a\) and the quarterly rate \(g_q\) behind it are linked by \(1 + a = (1 + g_q)^4\), so \(g_q = (1 + a)^{1/4} - 1\). In (b), growth factors such as \(1 + g_q\) multiply from one quarter to the next; growth rates do not add up.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Second quarter: \(g_q = (1 - 0.329)^{1/4} - 1 = 0.671^{1/4} - 1 = -0.0949\), a fall of 9.49 percent within a single quarter. Third quarter: \(g_q = 1.331^{1/4} - 1 = +0.0741\), a rise of 7.41 percent.
(b) Chain the two quarterly growth factors:
\[\frac{Y_{\text{Q3}}}{Y_{\text{Q1}}} = (1 - 0.09493)\times(1 + 0.07410) = 0.90507 \times 1.07410 = 0.97213.\]
In the third quarter, real GDP was still 2.79 percent below its level of the first quarter. Adding the annualized rates misleads twice:

Compounding over four quarters stretches a rise more than a fall: a 7.41 percent quarter becomes +33.1 percent a year, while a 9.49 percent fall becomes only −32.9 percent.
A fall shrinks the base. Undoing a fall of 9.49 percent takes a rise of \(1/0.90507 - 1 = 0.1049\), that is 10.49 percent.

These were first estimates. In today’s revised data (fig9-3.csv), the fall was 7.88 percent and the rebound 7.76 percent (annualized −27.98 and +34.86 percent), so GDP in the third quarter was 0.73 percent below its first-quarter level. As in Fig. 3, the revisions changed the numbers but not the story.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Two falling quarters in 2022: was it a recession? In 2022 the BEA’s advance estimates showed real GDP falling at an annual rate of 1.4 percent in the first quarter and 0.9 percent in the second. “Two quarters of falling GDP” is a popular rule of thumb for a recession, and that summer many commentators used it. Over the same six months, the unemployment rate averaged 3.75 percent (BLS, UNRATE, via FRED), while the CBO’s natural rate for 2022 was 4.44 percent (CBO, NROUST, via FRED; nrou_short_term in fig9-8.csv).

Convert both rates into quarterly rates. Potential output grows by about 2 percent a year. With a quarterly version of equation (4), by how many points did short-run output \(\tilde{Y}\) change over the half year?
What short-run output does Okun’s law, equation (8), imply for these six months?
The NBER, which dates U.S. recessions, explains in its business-cycle FAQ why it does not use the two-quarter rule. Using (a) and (b), was the U.S. economy in a recession in the first half of 2022? What did the fall in GDP mean?



Hint


Per quarter, potential output grows by \(1.02^{1/4} - 1\). In each quarter, equation (4) gives \(\Delta\tilde{Y} \approx g_Y - \bar{g}\) with both rates per quarter. (b) Solve equation (8) for \(\tilde{Y}\), as in step 1 of the Okun’s-law block. (c) A falling \(\tilde{Y}\) is not the same thing as a negative \(\tilde{Y}\).


Your answer:


Solution

(a) First quarter: \((1 - 0.014)^{1/4} - 1 = -0.352\%\). Second quarter: \((1 - 0.009)^{1/4} - 1 = -0.226\%\). Potential output grows by \(1.02^{1/4} - 1 = 0.496\%\) a quarter. Equation (4), quarter by quarter:
\[\Delta\tilde{Y}_{\text{Q1}} \approx -0.352 - 0.496 = -0.848, \qquad \Delta\tilde{Y}_{\text{Q2}} \approx -0.226 - 0.496 = -0.722,\]
so short-run output fell by about 1.57 points in six months: a sharp slowdown.
(b) Cyclical unemployment was \(u - \bar{u} = 3.75 - 4.44 = -0.69\) points. Solving equation (8) for short-run output,
\[\tilde{Y} = -2\,(u - \bar{u}) = -2 \times (-0.69) = +1.38 \text{ percent}.\]
By Okun’s law, output was above potential, with a hot labor market.
(c) The two facts fit together. Short-run output fell by about 1.6 points, but from a high level, so it was still positive: a boom was cooling down, which is not a recession. That is the NBER’s point: GDP can dip a little in two quarters in a row without a significant, widespread decline in activity, and the 2001 recession did not even include two falling quarters in a row. The NBER did not date a recession in 2022 (our recessions.csv has none after 2020).
The revisions settle it. Today’s data (fig9-3.csv) put growth at −1.01 percent (annualized) in the first quarter and +0.56 percent in the second, so the second falling quarter has disappeared. With the CBO’s potential output, \(\tilde{Y}\) went from +2.08 percent at the end of 2021 to +0.77 percent in the second quarter of 2022, a fall of 1.31 points, close to the estimate in (a) and still above zero.

Problem 3 (Challenge): The 2023 disinflation: where was the slump? In the data of Fig. 7 (fig9-7.csv: BLS CPI inflation and short-run output from the BEA’s real GDP and the CBO’s potential output), U.S. inflation fell from 7.99 percent in 2022 to 4.13 percent in 2023 and 2.95 percent in 2024. Yet output stayed above potential: \(\tilde{Y} = +1.2\) percent in 2023 and \(+1.5\) percent in 2024, even though the Federal Reserve raised its target for the federal funds rate to 5.25–5.5 percent by July 2023.

With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), what change in inflation does the Phillips curve, equation (5), predict for 2023 and for 2024? Compare with the data.
Suppose that in early 2023 you believed equation (5) was the whole story. By equation (7), what cumulative short-run output would it have taken to bring inflation from its 2022 level to its 2024 level? With Okun’s law, how many point-years of extra unemployment is that?
Bernanke and Blanchard (2023) find that most of the inflation surge that began in 2021 came from shocks to prices, such as jumps in commodity prices and price spikes in sectors whose supply could not keep up with demand, and not from an overheated labor market. Chapter 12 adds such shocks to the Phillips curve as a term \(\bar{o}\): \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}_t\). Find the price shock \(\bar{o}_t\) that makes each year from 2021 to 2024 fit exactly, and interpret the signs.
Open question: what does this episode suggest about planning a disinflation with the sacrifice ratio \(1/\bar{\nu}\)?



Hint


Multiply \(\bar{\nu}\) by each year’s \(\tilde{Y}\), and read the actual change from the column d_inflation.
Equation (7) gives the required sum of the gaps from the change in inflation; Okun’s law turns each percent of output into half a point of unemployment. (c) Solve the full Phillips curve for \(\bar{o}_t\); then add up the shocks of 2021–22 and of 2023–24.



# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Equation (5) predicts \(\Delta\pi_{2023} = 0.33 \times 1.205 = +0.40\) points and \(\Delta\pi_{2024} = 0.33 \times 1.488 = +0.49\) points: inflation should have risen a little. In fact it fell by 3.86 points in 2023 and by 1.18 points in 2024.
(b) Equation (7) with \(\pi_{2022} = 7.99\) and \(\pi_{2024} = 2.95\):
\[\sum \tilde{Y} = \frac{\pi_{2024} - \pi_{2022}}{\bar{\nu}} = \frac{2.95 - 7.99}{0.33} = -15.27 \text{ percent-years},\]
and Okun’s law, equation (8), turns it into \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\times(-15.27) = +7.63\) point-years of extra unemployment, for example unemployment almost 4 points above its natural rate for two years. What happened instead: the gaps of 2023 and 2024 add up to +2.69 percent-years, and cyclical unemployment was negative in both years (−0.80 and −0.39 points, fig9-8.csv).
(c) Solving the full Phillips curve for the shock, \(\bar{o}_t = \Delta\pi_t - \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\):

The shocks of 2021–22 add up to +6.17 points and those of 2023–24 to −5.93 points. Read this way, the surge came mostly from positive price shocks, as Bernanke and Blanchard find, and the disinflation came mostly from the same shocks going into reverse, not from a slump.
pc = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig9-7.csv").set_index("year")
for year in [2021, 2022, 2023, 2024]:
    predicted = phillips_curve(pc.short_run_output[year])           # equation (5), nu = 0.33
    shock = pc.d_inflation[year] - predicted                         # o-bar that makes the year fit
    print(f"{year}: d_pi = {pc.d_inflation[year]:+.2f}, nu x Y~ = {predicted:+.2f}, o-bar = {shock:+.2f}")
needed_gap = (pc.inflation_cpi[2024] - pc.inflation_cpi[2022]) / 0.33    # equation (7)
print(f"Cumulative Y~ needed: {needed_gap:.2f} percent-years; Okun: {okun_law(needed_gap):+.2f} point-years")
print(f"Actual cumulative Y~ 2023-2024: {pc.short_run_output[2023] + pc.short_run_output[2024]:+.2f}")
(d) There is no single answer. Equation (7) prices the cost of removing inflation that sits in last year’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\), the inflation people have come to expect. Inflation caused by temporary price shocks can fade when the shocks reverse, at a much lower cost. The difficulty is that a central bank cannot tell in real time which kind of inflation it faces, and Bernanke and Blanchard also find that the effects of tight labor markets on wages and inflation, though not the main driver so far, last longer than those of price shocks. Waiting risks letting inflation settle in, and tightening hard risks a slump that was not needed. Chapter 12 adds expectations to this trade-off.



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): Which rule of thumb gets the direction right? Equation (5) says that inflation rises when \(\tilde{Y} > 0\) and falls when \(\tilde{Y} < 0\). Equation (8) says that unemployment is above its natural rate when \(\tilde{Y} < 0\) and below it when \(\tilde{Y} > 0\). Check both signs, year by year, in the files of Figs. 7 and 8, fig9-7.csv and fig9-8.csv (data from the BEA, the CBO and the BLS, via FRED).

In what share of the years does the change in inflation have the sign that the Phillips curve predicts?
In what share of the years does cyclical unemployment have the sign that Okun’s law predicts?
Which rule is the more reliable guide to the direction? How many of the Phillips curve’s misses come in 2000 or later?



Hint

A comparison such as pc.d_inflation > 0 gives True or False for each year. Two such columns are equal (==) in the years in which the two signs agree, and the .mean() of True/False values is the share of True. Read the files under new names, such as pc and ok: the names phillips and okun are used by the charts above.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

We compare the sign of the outcome with the sign that each equation predicts, year by year. ~ turns True into False, so ~right_pc marks the Phillips curve’s misses.
pc = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig9-7.csv")
ok = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig9-8.csv")
right_pc = (pc.d_inflation > 0) == (pc.short_run_output > 0)              # equation (5): same sign
right_ok = (ok.cyclical_unemployment > 0) == (ok.short_run_output < 0)    # equation (8): opposite signs
print(f"Phillips curve: right in {right_pc.sum()} of {len(pc)} years ({100 * right_pc.mean():.0f}%)")
print(f"Okun's law:     right in {right_ok.sum()} of {len(ok)} years ({100 * right_ok.mean():.0f}%)")
misses = pc[~right_pc & (pc.year >= 2000)]
print(f"Phillips misses since 2000: {len(misses)} of {(pc.year >= 2000).sum()} years:", list(misses.year))
(a) The Phillips curve gets the direction of inflation right in 38 of 65 years (1961–2025), 58 percent of the time: better than a coin toss, but not by much.
(b) Okun’s law gets the sign of cyclical unemployment right in 58 of 66 years (1960–2025), 88 percent of the time.
(c) Okun’s law is the far more reliable guide, as the tight cloud of Fig. 8 suggested. Since 2000 the Phillips curve has missed in 14 of 26 years: 2003, 2004, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2014, 2016, 2017, 2019, 2023, 2024 and 2025. In 11 of those 14 years \(\tilde{Y}\) was less than 1.5 percent in size, so other forces, such as price shocks (Chapter 12), could easily outweigh the pull of the output gap. The slope \(\bar{\nu}\) tells us how strong that pull is on average; the misses tell us how much else moves inflation.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): How long until the jobs come back? Use the monthly payroll jobs of payroll_employment.csv (BLS, PAYEMS, via FRED) and the NBER dates of recessions.csv (USREC, via FRED). For each recession since 1980:

In which month did payroll employment first get back to its level of the peak month, and how many months after the peak was that?
What was the largest fall in jobs before that, in percent of the peak level?
Which recovery was the slowest? Which was the fastest, given the size of its fall, and why might that be?



Hint

Make the jobs a Series indexed by date, as in the key numbers of Fig. 4, but under a new name (payroll and recessions are used above). For each recession, keep the months after the trough and pick the first one whose jobs are at least the peak-month level: after[after >= level].index[0]. The number of months between two dates is 12 times the difference in years plus the difference in months.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

We loop over the recessions, as in the key numbers of Fig. 4, and look forward from each trough for the first month with as many jobs as at the peak.
jobs_m = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "payroll_employment.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date").payroll_millions
nber = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])
rows = []
for peak, trough in zip(nber.peak, nber.trough):
    if peak.year >= 1980:
        level = jobs_m[peak]                                   # jobs in the peak month
        after = jobs_m[jobs_m.index > trough]
        back = after[after >= level].index[0]                  # first month with as many jobs again
        months = (back.year - peak.year) * 12 + back.month - peak.month
        fall = 100 * (jobs_m[peak:back].min() / level - 1)
        rows.append([peak.strftime("%Y-%m"), round(fall, 1), back.strftime("%Y-%m"), months])

(a), (b) See the table.
(c) The slowest recovery followed the Great Recession: jobs fell by 6.3 percent and took 77 months, more than six years, to come back. The recoveries after 1990–91 and 2001 were also slow for such small falls (31 and 46 months). They are often called “jobless recoveries”: output grew again, but for years no more than a little faster than potential, so by equation (9) unemployment came down only slowly.
Given the size of its fall, the Covid-19 recovery was by far the fastest: the 14.4 percent fall, more than twice the next largest, was undone in 28 months, as fast as the 3.1 percent fall of the early 1980s. One reason is that many of the jobs were paused rather than destroyed: in April 2020, 18.1 million of the 23.1 million unemployed were job losers on layoff, the BLS category for workers laid off temporarily who expect to return to their jobs (BLS, LNS13023653 and UNEMPLOY, via FRED). When the economy reopened, they could return to their old jobs.

Problem 6 (Intermediate): What did the Great Recession and the euro crisis cost, country by country? The panel short_run_panel.csv has the OECD’s short-run output for 39 economies (OECD Economic Outlook, via the OECD Data Explorer). For each economy, add up the negative gaps from 2008 to 2019. As in the key numbers of Fig. 3, the sum is the output lost below potential, in percent of one year’s potential output (“percent-years”). Also count the years below potential and find the lowest gap.

Which five economies lost the most? How much did the United States and Germany lose, and what is the median?
Compare Italy with Estonia. Which one had the deeper slump, and which one lost more output? What does that tell you about how to measure the cost of a slump?



Hint

Keep the rows with year.between(2008, 2019) and an output gap. Then loop over the countries: for each one, gaps[gaps < 0].sum() adds up the negative gaps and (gaps < 0).sum() counts them. Collect one row per country in a list and turn it into a DataFrame, which sort_values can rank.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

We loop over the countries and collect, for each one, the lost output, the years below potential and the lowest gap.
panel_9 = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "short_run_panel.csv")
crisis = panel_9[panel_9.year.between(2008, 2019)].dropna(subset=["output_gap"])
rows = []
for country in crisis.country.unique():
    gaps = crisis[crisis.country == country].output_gap
    rows.append([country, gaps[gaps < 0].sum(), (gaps < 0).sum(), gaps.min()])
cost = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["country", "lost", "years_below", "lowest_gap"]).sort_values("lost")
print(cost.head(5).round(1).to_string(index=False))
print(cost[cost.country.isin(["United States", "Germany", "Italy", "Estonia"])].round(1).to_string(index=False))
print(f"Median of {len(cost)} economies: {cost.lost.median():.1f} percent-years")
(a) The code reports each loss as a sum of negative gaps. The five largest losses were Greece (44.9 percent-years), Latvia (43.0), Lithuania (41.2), Italy (40.2) and Spain (35.8), followed by Portugal (33.7). The United States lost 14.0 percent-years and Germany 6.9, against a median of 12.0. The five hardest-hit economies lost about three times as much as the United States: between a third and a half of a year’s output each.
(b) Estonia had much the deeper slump, 11.1 percent below potential at the bottom (2009), against 6.2 percent for Italy (2013). Yet Italy lost more: 40.2 percent-years against 29.8, because its output stayed below potential in 11 of the 12 years, against 8 for Estonia. The cost of a slump depends on its depth and on how long it lasts, so a single number such as the lowest gap understates the cost of a long, moderate slump.

Problem 7 (Challenge): The Sahm rule, a real-time recession alarm. The NBER waits until the data leave no doubt before it announces a recession: for the last four recessions, its FAQ shows announcements 4 to 12 months after the peak. Claudia Sahm proposed a faster signal, and a policy built on it: automatic stimulus payments whenever the three-month average of the national unemployment rate rises by at least 0.50 points above its low of the previous 12 months. FRED tracks it as the Sahm Rule Recession Indicator. The file unemployment_monthly.csv has the monthly U.S. unemployment rate since 1948, from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS, UNRATE, via FRED).

Compute the indicator for every month: the 3-month average of the unemployment rate minus the lowest 3-month average of the previous 12 months, rounded to 2 decimals. October 2025 has no value (no estimate was published in the month of the federal government shutdown): fill it with .interpolate().
For each NBER recession in recessions.csv, in which month did the indicator first reach 0.50, how many months after the peak was that, and was it before the trough?
List the months since 1960 in which the alarm switched on (0.50 or more, after a month below 0.50). Which ones were not followed by a recession? For the most recent one, use payroll_employment.csv to see how many jobs were added in the 12 months before it. What does this suggest about why the alarm went off, and about paying stimulus automatically?



Hint

u.rolling(3).mean() averages each month with the two months before it. .shift(1) moves a series one month later, so average.shift(1).rolling(12).min() is the lowest average of the previous 12 months. With alarm = sahm >= 0.5, a switch-on month has alarm True and alarm.shift(1, fill_value=False) False; ~ turns True into False. Rounding first matters: several months sit exactly at 0.50.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The indicator, built step by step:
unemp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "unemployment_monthly.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
u = unemp.set_index("date").unrate.interpolate()        # fill October 2025 from its neighbors
average = u.rolling(3).mean()                           # 3-month moving average
sahm = (average - average.shift(1).rolling(12).min()).round(2)
alarm = sahm >= 0.5
switch_on = alarm & ~alarm.shift(1, fill_value=False)   # on now, off the month before
print(sahm[switch_on].loc["1960":])
(b) For each recession, the first alarm month at or after the peak:
nber = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])
for peak, trough in zip(nber.peak, nber.trough):
    first = sahm[(sahm.index >= peak) & alarm].index[0]
    months = (first.year - peak.year) * 12 + first.month - peak.month
    print(f"Peak {peak:%Y-%m}: alarm in {first:%Y-%m}, {months} months later; by the trough: {first <= trough}")
The alarm caught all nine recessions since 1960, between 1 and 8 months after the peak (1 month in 1980, 8 months in 1973–75), and never later than the trough month (in 2020 it came in April, the trough month itself). For the last four recessions it came 2 or 3 months after the peak, before the NBER’s announcements (4 to 12 months after the peak).
(c) The alarm switched on 11 times since 1960: in 1960-10, 1970-03, 1974-07, 1980-02, 1981-11, 1990-10, 2001-06, 2003-07, 2008-02, 2020-04 and 2024-07. Two were not followed by a new recession:

July 2003 came during the slow recovery from the 2001 recession: unemployment kept rising until June 2003 (6.3 percent), 19 months after the trough (see also Problem 5).
July 2024 had no recession after it in our data.

Both sit exactly at 0.50 in today’s revised data. In real time, as FRED’s real-time series shows, July 2003 read 0.47, so it did not set off the alarm then, while July 2024 read 0.53.
jobs_m = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "payroll_employment.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date").payroll_millions
print(f"Payroll jobs, July 2023 to July 2024: {jobs_m['2024-07-01'] - jobs_m['2023-07-01']:+.1f} million")
print(f"Unemployment rate: {u['2023-07-01']} -> {u['2024-07-01']} percent")
From July 2023 to July 2024 the economy added 1.7 million payroll jobs while the unemployment rate rose from 3.5 to 4.2 percent. So the rise in unemployment does not look like a wave of layoffs. It suggests that more people were looking for work than the new jobs could absorb, and a rule built on the unemployment rate alone cannot tell the two cases apart.
For policy, this is the trade-off of any automatic trigger. It is fast: in every recession since 1960 it switched on no later than the trough month. Even so, in a very short recession such as 2020’s, which ended in the month the alarm switched on, the payments would have arrived as the recovery began. It can also fire without a recession, as in 2024, and data revisions can move a reading across the 0.50 line. One answer is to pair the trigger with a second check, such as payroll jobs, or to make the payments small enough that a false alarm is cheap.



Modeling problems
Problem 8 (Basic): Short-time work or layoffs? Okun’s law in Germany and Spain. Germany’s short-time work scheme, Kurzarbeit, pays firms to cut hours instead of jobs, and the IMF notes that Germany was the only G7 country whose employment did not fall in 2009, despite a deep recession. Spain relied on temporary contracts that are cheap to end: Bentolila, Cahuc, Dolado and Le Barbanchon (2012) estimate that about 45 percent of the surge in Spanish unemployment after 2008 could have been avoided under France’s job-protection rules.

With the sliders below, find for each country the slope of Okun’s law, to the nearest 0.05, that makes the squared misses in the title smallest.
A shock pushes output 3 percent below potential in both countries. With your slopes, by how much does cyclical unemployment rise in each?
A minister says that “a flatter Okun’s law is always better”. Give one reason to agree and one to disagree.



Hint

Choose a country, then move the slope one step at a time and watch the squared misses: they fall, reach a low and rise again. For (b), apply equation (8) with your slope instead of \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\). Remember that both countries’ cyclical unemployment is measured from a smooth trend (Fig. 8).


interact(okun_fit,
         slope=FloatSlider(value=-0.5, min=-0.8, max=0.0, step=0.05, description="model slope", style=WIDE),
         country=Dropdown(options=["Germany", "Spain"], value="Germany", description="country", style=WIDE));

Source. The Okun’s-law chart of Fig. 8 above, with OECD data, inspired by Fig. 9.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The squared misses are smallest at a slope of −0.20 for Germany (squared misses 12.89) and −0.55 for Spain (122.71). The code below confirms it by trying every slope on the slider.
for country in ["Germany", "Spain"]:
    data_c = okun_data(country)
    best_slope, best_misses = 0.0, 1e9
    for k in range(17):                                        # slopes -0.80, -0.75, ..., 0.00
        slope_try = -0.8 + 0.05 * k
        misses_try = ((data_c.cyclical_unemployment - okun_law(data_c.short_run_output, slope_try)) ** 2).sum()
        if misses_try < best_misses:
            best_slope, best_misses = slope_try, misses_try
    print(f"{country}: slope {best_slope:.2f}, squared misses {best_misses:.2f}, "
          f"Y~ = -3% gives u - u_bar = {okun_law(-3.0, best_slope):+.2f} points")
(b) By equation (8) with these slopes, \(u - \bar{u} = -0.20 \times (-3) = +0.60\) points in Germany and \(-0.55 \times (-3) = +1.65\) points in Spain: the same slump costs Spain 2.75 times as much unemployment. The data show the gap clearly. In 2009 Germany’s output was 4.51 percent below potential, but its cyclical unemployment was only +0.06 points. In 2013 Spain’s output was 8.04 percent below potential and its cyclical unemployment +5.84 points.
(c) To agree: when firms keep their workers, people keep their incomes and their skills, and output can bounce back quickly once demand returns, without a long search for new jobs. To disagree: a flat Okun’s law can hide problems. Paying firms to keep workers they no longer need costs public money and can keep workers in firms and sectors that will not recover, which slows the move of labor to growing firms. A flatter slope is good for a temporary shock; it is less clearly good for a lasting one.

Problem 9 (Intermediate): An election boom and the bill that follows. Nordhaus (1975) argued that governments facing an election are tempted to run the economy hot just before the vote (The Political Business Cycle). Consider a hypothetical country whose Phillips curve has slope \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\). In year 0, inflation is 2 percent and output is at potential.

The government pushes output 2 percent above potential in each of the two years before an election. Use the sliders to find inflation in years 1 and 2.
After the election, a new central bank governor brings inflation back to 2 percent. The new government accepts a slump of at most 1 percent below potential, so she holds output exactly there, year after year, until inflation is back at 2 percent. How many years does the slump last? (Set the starting inflation to your answer for year 2.)
Add up short-run output over the whole cycle, from the first year of the boom to the last year of the slump. Then use equation (6) to show that this total must be zero whenever inflation ends where it started, whatever the slope \(\bar{\nu}\) and however long the slump lasts.
If the boom and the slump cancel out, why might a government still want such a cycle? What institution could stop it?



Hint

Each year inflation changes by \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y} = 0.5\,\tilde{Y}\). The title lists inflation in years 0, 1, 2 and 3, and the right panel follows it to year 5. In (b), compare how far inflation has to fall with how much one year of the slump brings it down. In (c), write equation (6) for the last year of the slump, \(t = T\), and set \(\pi_T = \pi_0\).


interact(booming_economy,
         pi_bar=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="inflation in year 0 (%)", style=WIDE),
         nu=fixed(0.5),
         Y_tilde=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-4.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="short-run output Ỹ (%)", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 9 above, adapted from Fig. 9.9 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) With \(\tilde{Y} = +2\), inflation rises by \(0.5 \times 2 = 1\) point a year: \(2 \to 3 \to 4\) percent in years 1 and 2 (the title reads π = 2.00 → 3.00 → 4.00).
(b) With \(\tilde{Y} = -1\), inflation falls by \(0.5 \times 1 = 0.5\) point a year. It has to fall by 2 points, from 4 to 2 percent, so the slump lasts \(2/0.5 = 4\) years. With the starting inflation at 4 and \(\tilde{Y} = -1\), the title reads π = 4.00 → 3.50 → 3.00 → 2.50, and the right panel reaches 2 percent in its year 4: four years after the election, six years after the boom began.
years_boom, boom = simulate_inflation(pi_bar=2.0, nu=0.5, Y_tilde=2.0, years=2)
years_slump, slump = simulate_inflation(pi_bar=boom[-1], nu=0.5, Y_tilde=-1.0, years=4)
print("Boom:", boom, " slump:", slump, " sum of Y~:", 2 * 2.0 + 4 * (-1.0))
(c) The total is \(2 + 2 - 1 - 1 - 1 - 1 = 0\). In general, equation (6) for the last year of the slump, \(t = T\), reads \(\pi_T = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\left(\tilde{Y}_1 + \tilde{Y}_2 + \dots + \tilde{Y}_T\right)\). If \(\pi_T = \pi_0\), then \(\bar{\nu}\sum\tilde{Y}_s = 0\), and since \(\bar{\nu} > 0\) the sum of the gaps is zero. The 4 percent-years of extra output before the election are paid back in full after it, here as four years of a 1 percent slump. A milder slump spreads the bill over more years, and a different slope changes how far inflation climbs, but neither changes the size of the bill.
(d) The timing is what matters politically: voters feel the boom just before they vote, and the slump arrives after the election, perhaps under the next government. The bill can also be dodged: the central bank can let inflation stay at 4 percent, but that brings the costs of higher inflation studied in Chapter 8. A central bank that is independent of the government and has an inflation target (Chapter 13) can refuse to supply the pre-election boom, which removes the temptation.

Problem 10 (Challenge): When does a slump stop showing up as falling GDP? In World Bank data, China’s real GDP has grown every year since 1977; even in 2020 it grew by 2.3 percent, after 6.1 percent in 2019. In a fast-growing economy, a slump shows up as a slowdown rather than a fall. Use the cycle of Fig. 1 for a hypothetical economy: short-run output swings between \(+A\) and \(-A\) percent and repeats every 8 years, while potential output grows by \(\bar{g}\) percent a year.

With the sliders below, find for \(A = 2\) the smallest potential growth on the slider at which actual output never falls from one year to the next. The title reports the slowest yearly growth.
Derive the exact threshold. Show that the slowest year runs from year 4 to year 5, and that output falls in that year only if \(\bar{g} < 1/(1 - A/\sqrt{2}) - 1\), with \(A\) and \(\bar{g}\) as decimals. Compute the threshold for \(A = 2\) and \(A = 4\) percent, and compare it with the shortcut that equation (4) gives.
A statistics office announces a recession only when real GDP falls over a year. When will it miss a slump, and what should it watch instead?



Hint

By equation (2), \(Y_t/Y_{t-1} = (1 + \bar{g})\,(1 + \tilde{Y}_t)/(1 + \tilde{Y}_{t-1})\). In whole years, the gap of Fig. 1 takes the values \(0, +s, +A, +s, 0, -s, -A, -s\) with \(s = A\sin(\pi/4) = A/\sqrt{2}\). Find the year pair with the smallest cycle factor \((1 + \tilde{Y}_t)/(1 + \tilde{Y}_{t-1})\); to compare \(1/(1+s)\) with \(1 - s\), multiply out \((1 + s)(1 - s)\).


def slowest_growth(A=2.0, g=1.0):
    """Fig. 9.1 with a readout: the slowest growth of actual output from one whole year to the next."""
    fig = fluctuations(A, g)
    slowest = 100.0
    for t in range(1, 9):
        growth = 100 * (actual_output(t, A, g) / actual_output(t - 1, A, g) - 1)
        slowest = min(slowest, growth)
    verdict = "output falls in the slump" if slowest < 0 else "output never falls"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"A = {A:.1f}%, g = {g:.2f}%: slowest yearly growth {slowest:+.2f}%, {verdict}")
    return fig


interact(slowest_growth,
         A=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.5, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="size of the swings A (%)", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.0, max=3.0, step=0.25, description="growth of potential g (% a year)", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 1 above, adapted from Fig. 9.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) With \(A = 2\), the title shows a slowest year of −0.18 percent at \(\bar{g} = 1.25\) and of +0.06 percent at \(\bar{g} = 1.50\). So 1.5 percent is the smallest potential growth on the slider at which output never falls.
(b) By equation (2), each year’s growth factor is the trend factor times a cycle factor:
\[\frac{Y_t}{Y_{t-1}} = (1 + \bar{g})\,\frac{1 + \tilde{Y}_t}{1 + \tilde{Y}_{t-1}}.\]
Over the cycle, with \(s = A/\sqrt{2}\), the cycle factors are \(1 + s\), \(\frac{1+A}{1+s}\), \(\frac{1+s}{1+A}\), \(\frac{1}{1+s}\), \(1 - s\), \(\frac{1-A}{1-s}\), \(\frac{1-s}{1-A}\) and \(\frac{1}{1-s}\). Only four are below 1: those of the four years in which the gap falls, from year 2 to year 6. The smallest is \(1 - s\), from year 4 to year 5:

\(\frac{1}{1+s} > 1 - s\), because \((1 + s)(1 - s) = 1 - s^2 < 1\);
\(\frac{1+s}{1+A} = 1 - \frac{A - s}{1 + A}\) and \(\frac{1-A}{1-s} = 1 - \frac{A - s}{1 - s}\), and \(A - s = 0.29A\) is much smaller than \(s = 0.71A\), so both lie closer to 1 than \(1 - s\) does (for the second, this holds for any \(A\) below 0.83).

Output therefore falls in the slowest year if and only if
\[(1 + \bar{g})\left(1 - \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\right) < 1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bar{g} < \frac{1}{1 - A/\sqrt{2}} - 1.\]
For \(A = 0.02\): \(\bar{g} < 1/0.98586 - 1 = 1.43\) percent, which is why 1.25 fails and 1.5 works in (a). For \(A = 0.04\): \(\bar{g} < 1/0.97172 - 1 = 2.91\) percent. The shortcut of equation (4), \(g_Y \approx \bar{g} + \Delta\tilde{Y}\), gets almost the same answer in one line: the largest one-year fall of the gap is \(s = 0.71A\) points, so output falls when \(\bar{g} < 0.71A\), that is 1.41 and 2.83 percent.
for A in [2.0, 4.0]:
    s = A / 100 / np.sqrt(2)
    print(f"A = {A:.0f}%: exact threshold {100 * (1 / (1 - s) - 1):.2f}%, shortcut 0.71 x A = {100 * s:.2f}%")
for t in range(1, 9):                                     # cycle factors with A = 2
    factor = (1 + short_run_output(actual_output(t), potential_output(t)) / 100) / \
             (1 + short_run_output(actual_output(t - 1), potential_output(t - 1)) / 100)
    print(f"Year {t - 1} to {t}: cycle factor {factor:.5f}")
(c) The rule misses every slump whose one-year fall in the gap, about \(0.71A\), is smaller than trend growth. An economy with potential growth of 5 percent would need swings larger than about \(\pm 7\) percent (\(5/0.71\); 6.7 with the exact formula) before a slump showed up as a falling year. Such an office should watch growth relative to the trend (equation 4), an estimate of the output gap, and the labor market, through Okun’s law. If China’s potential growth in 2020 was close to its 6.1 percent growth of 2019, equation (4) says that its gap fell by almost 4 points that year: a sharp slump, although GDP never fell.

# The data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch10/"

The next cell defines a helper that only the book website needs. Run it and move on.


Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig
