# @title Helper for the website group buttons (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def group_menu(fig, book, small=8):
    """Buttons that list one group of countries in the legend (a small group is drawn at once); `book` is always drawn."""
    names = [t.name for t in fig.data]
    short = {"Europe and Central Asia": "Europe", "Asia and Pacific": "Asia-Pacific", "Middle East and Africa": "Africa, Mideast"}
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Americas": [], "Europe": [], "Asia-Pacific": [], "Africa, Mideast": []}
    for c, r in zip(countries.country, countries.region):
        if c in names:
            groups[short.get(r, r)].append(c)
    first = ["legendonly" if len(names) <= 40 else False] * len(names)   # a short legend lists every country
    buttons = []
    for label, members in groups.items():
        if not set(members) & set(names):
            continue                                   # no country of this group in the figure
        visible = []
        for j, n in enumerate(names):
            if n in book:
                visible.append(True)
            elif n in members:
                visible.append(True if len(members) <= small else "legendonly")
            else:
                visible.append(first[j] if label == "Textbook" else False)
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=120), updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [dict(
        type="buttons", direction="right", x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", buttons=buttons)])
    return compact(fig)

text:
The short-run model at a glance
Before the details, a small live version of the whole chain: from the interest rate to output to inflation.

Fig. 1: The structure of the short-run model
Goal. See the whole short-run model at once: how the central bank’s nominal interest rate ends up changing inflation.
The textbook’s Fig. 12.1 is a chain of four circles. Each arrow is one building block:
\[i_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{MP curve}}\; R_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{IS curve}}\; \tilde{Y}_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{Phillips curve}}\; \Delta\pi_t\]
Here the chain is live. You choose the inputs: the nominal interest rate \(i\) that the central bank sets, the current (sticky) inflation rate \(\pi\), and the demand shock \(\bar{a}\). The circles show the outcomes that the model computes: the real interest rate, short-run output and the change in inflation. The baseline is normal times: inflation of 2 percent and a nominal rate of 7 percent, so that \(R = 5\% = \bar{r}\) and output is at potential.

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="circle", ...) draws a circle inside the box from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1), and add_annotation(..., showarrow=False) writes text at a point. for k in range(4): repeats the indented lines for k = 0, 1, 2, 3, so names[k] picks one name at a time. scaleanchor="x" gives both axes the same scale, so the circles stay round, and visible=False hides the axes.


def short_run_model(i=7.0, pi=2.0, a=0.0):
    """Fig. 12.1: the nominal rate sets R (MP), R sets Y~ (IS), and Y~ sets the change in inflation (PC)."""
    R = real_rate(i, pi)
    Y = is_curve(R, a)
    dpi = phillips(Y)
    names = ["Nominal<br>interest rate, i", "Real interest<br>rate, R", "Short-run<br>output, Ỹ", "Change in<br>inflation, Δπ"]
    values = [f"{i:.1f}%", f"{R:.1f}%", f"{Y:+.1f}%", f"{dpi:+.2f}"]
    links = ["MP<br>curve", "IS<br>curve", "Phillips<br>curve"]
    fig = go.Figure()
    for k in range(4):
        fig.add_shape(type="circle", x0=3.4 * k - 1.15, x1=3.4 * k + 1.15, y0=-1.15, y1=1.15,
                      line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3), fillcolor="#e6f5f1")
        fig.add_annotation(x=3.4 * k, y=0.35, text=names[k], showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12))
        fig.add_annotation(x=3.4 * k, y=-0.45, text=f"<b>{values[k]}</b>", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=20, color=BLUE))
    for k in range(3):
        add_arrow(fig, 3.4 * k + 1.2, 0.0, 3.4 * k + 2.2, 0.0)
        fig.add_annotation(x=3.4 * k + 1.7, y=0.5, text=links[k], showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12))
    fig.add_annotation(x=5.1, y=-1.7, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14),
                       text=f"Inflation next year: {pi:.2f}% + ({dpi:+.2f}) = {pi + dpi:.2f}%")
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[-1.5, 11.7])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[-2.2, 1.8], scaleanchor="x")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"i = {i:.1f}%, π = {pi:.1f}%  →  R = {R:.1f}%  →  Ỹ = {Y:+.1f}%  →  Δπ = {dpi:+.2f}")
    return fig


Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.


interact(short_run_model,
         i=FloatSlider(value=7.0, min=2.0, max=12.0, step=0.5, description="nominal interest rate i (%)", style=WIDE),
         pi=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="sticky inflation π (%)", style=WIDE),
         a=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-4.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="demand shock ā", style=WIDE));

slider_figure(short_run_model, "i", [5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0], start=7.0, label="nominal interest rate i (%)")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

Raise \(i\) from 7 to 8 percent with inflation stuck at 2 percent: \(R\) rises to 6 percent, output falls to \(-2\) percent, and inflation starts to fall by 1 point a year. This is the textbook’s summary of the model “in a nutshell”: \(\uparrow i \Rightarrow \uparrow R \Rightarrow \downarrow \tilde{Y} \Rightarrow \downarrow \Delta\pi\).
What matters is \(i - \pi\). Raise inflation and the nominal rate by the same amount: nothing real changes.
A negative demand shock lowers output at any interest rate; the central bank can offset it by cutting \(i\).

Output is at potential when \(R = \bar{r} = 5\) percent, so you need \(i - 4 = 5\). Try is_curve(real_rate(9.0, 4.0)).

The MP curve and the IS/MP diagram
The central bank sets the interest rate, and the IS/MP diagram shows what that does to output. We look at the fed funds rate, a rate hike, a housing bust and the yield curve.

Fig. 2: The federal funds rate
Goal. See how much the Federal Reserve’s main policy rate has moved since 1960, and compare it with other central banks.
The federal funds rate is the interest rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed controls it because it stands ready to lend and borrow at a stated rate: no bank pays more than the Fed charges, and no bank lends for less than the Fed pays, or others would borrow cheaply and lend back at the higher rate (an arbitrage opportunity).

Look at your data. Eleven series stop early. Germany, France, Italy, Spain and four other countries handed their monetary policy to the European Central Bank in 1999 (Greece in 2001): after that, look at the Euro area. Croatia’s series ends in 2022, just before it joined the euro, and Argentina’s in mid-2025. Two more warnings: the euro-area series switches in September 2024 from the ECB’s main refinancing rate to its deposit rate (the ECB’s new steering rate), and in a few hyperinflations policy rates reached hundreds or even thousands of percent (Brazil around 1990). The chart says so in its title when a line leaves the chart.
The chart can zoom in on three episodes of this chapter: choose one from the menu. You can also add other countries.

Python note. rates.country.isin(countries) is true for the rows of the chosen countries, and .between(a, b) keeps the dates of the period. color="country" draws one line per country, and color_discrete_map=POLICY_COLORS (made by menu_colors when we read the file) gives each its fixed color. The loop for step in [20, 40, 80] raises the top of the axis in steps, only when a chosen country needs it. ", ".join(names) glues a list of names into one text. A SelectMultiple is a list in which you can pick several entries (hold Ctrl, or Cmd on a Mac, and click); the function receives the chosen names as a tuple.


PERIODS = {"1960–2026, all the data": (["1959-06-01", "2027-01-01"], [-1.5, 20]),   # 0 clear of the corner
           "The Volcker years, 1977–1987": (["1977-01-01", "1987-12-31"], [-0.8, 20]),
           "Near-zero rates after 2008, 2006–2016": (["2006-01-01", "2016-12-31"], [-0.8, 8]),
           "Covid-19 and after, 2019–2026": (["2019-01-01", "2026-12-31"], [-0.8, 8])}


def missing_or_off(part, column, countries, low, high):
    """Title text naming the chosen countries with no data in `part`, and those whose values leave [low, high]."""
    missing, off = [], []
    for name in countries:
        values = part[column][part.country == name]
        if values.empty:
            missing.append(name)
        elif values.min() < low or values.max() > high:
            off.append(name)
    note = ""
    if missing:
        note += "; no data: " + ", ".join(missing)
    if off:
        note += "; off the chart: " + ", ".join(off)
    return note


def fed_chart(period="1960–2026, all the data", countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 12.2: the policy rates of the chosen central banks over one period, U.S. recessions shaded."""
    x_range, y_range = PERIODS[period]
    part = rates[rates.country.isin(countries) & rates.date.between(x_range[0], x_range[1])]
    top = y_range[1]
    for step in [20, 40, 80]:                    # a wider axis only when a chosen country needs it
        if part.policy_rate.max() > top:
            top = step
    title = f"The fed funds rate: {peak.fedfunds:.1f}% at its 1981 peak, near zero in 2009–15 and 2020–21"
    if list(countries) != ["United States"]:
        title = "Central bank policy rates" + missing_or_off(part, "policy_rate", countries, y_range[0], top)
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y="policy_rate", color="country", color_discrete_map=POLICY_COLORS, title=title,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "policy_rate": "Policy rate (percent)", "country": "Central bank of"})
    shade_recessions(fig, "1960-01-01")
    if "United States" in countries:
        fig.add_annotation(x=peak.date, y=peak.fedfunds, text=f"{peak.date:%B %Y}: {peak.fedfunds:.1f}%",
                           ax=90, ay=0, arrowhead=2)
        fig.add_annotation(x=latest.date, y=latest.fedfunds, text=f"{latest.date:%b %Y}: {latest.fedfunds:.2f}%",
                           ax=-40, ay=-50, arrowhead=2)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=x_range, yaxis_range=[y_range[0], top], showlegend=len(countries) > 1)
    return fig

What to notice.

The rate has ranged from about 0.05 percent (2020–2021) to 19.1 percent (June 1981): the textbook’s “nearly 20 percent”.
Under Paul Volcker (Fed chair from 1979) the rate reached 17.6 percent in April 1980 and 18.9 percent in December 1980, and above 19 percent in 1981: the tight money that ended the Great Inflation (Figs. 10–12).
The rate was close to zero in 2009–2015 and again in 2020–2021, then rose quickly in 2022–2023 to fight the return of inflation. Rate cuts followed from September 2024.
The rate usually falls during and after recessions (the shaded bands): the Fed lowers it to stimulate the economy.
Add the euro area, the United Kingdom and Japan, and choose 2019–2026: the ECB’s rate was at zero and the Bank of Japan’s at −0.1 percent before the pandemic, and the Bank of England cut its rate to 0.1 percent in March 2020. The Bank of England raised its rate first (December 2021), then the Fed (March 2022) and the ECB (July 2022); the Bank of Japan waited until March 2024.

Fig. 3: The MP curve in the IS/MP diagram
Goal. Put the MP curve and the IS curve in one diagram and read off short-run output.
With sticky inflation, the central bank picks the real interest rate. The MP curve is simply a horizontal line at that rate. The IS curve then tells us the output that goes with it: the economy is where the two curves cross. This is the IS/MP diagram. When the central bank sets \(R = \bar{r}\) and there is no demand shock, the curves cross at \(\tilde{Y} = 0\), point \(A\): output is at potential.
The textbook uses this diagram for three figures: the starting point (Fig. 12.3), a higher interest rate (Fig. 12.4), and the Volcker tightening (Fig. 12.10). So we write one function, ismp_experiment, for all three. Its arguments are the new values: the real interest rate R_new that the central bank sets, the demand shock a_new and the slope b. With the defaults nothing changes. When a curve moves, the old one stays behind as a dashed gray line.

Python note. if ... else runs one block of lines or the other. (a_new, b) != (A_BAR, B_BAR) is true as soon as one of the two numbers differs from the baseline.


def ismp_experiment(R_new=R_BAR, a_new=A_BAR, b=B_BAR):
    """Figs. 12.3, 12.4, 12.10: the economy moves from A (R = r_bar, Y~ = 0) to B, where IS' meets MP'."""
    Y_B = is_curve(R_new, a_new, b)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if (a_new, b) != (A_BAR, B_BAR):
        add_is(fig, "IS", GRAY, dash="dash")
        add_is(fig, "IS′", TEAL, a_new, b)
    else:
        add_is(fig, "IS", TEAL)
    if R_new != R_BAR:
        add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash")
        add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE)
        add_arrow(fig, -7.3, R_BAR, -7.3, R_new)                 # the central bank moves R
    else:
        add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", BLUE)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0)
    if (Y_B, R_new) != (0.0, R_BAR):
        add_point(fig, Y_B, R_new, "B", -8, 0)
        add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, Y_B, 0.6)                       # the change in output
    set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"MP: R = {R_new:.2f}%;  IS: ā = {a_new:.1f}, b̄ = {b:.2f}  →  Ỹ = {Y_B:+.1f}%")
    return fig

What to notice.

At the baseline the MP line and the IS curve cross at \(A\): \(R = \bar{r} = 5\) percent and \(\tilde{Y} = 0\).
The central bank chooses the height of the MP line, nothing else. The IS curve then decides how much output that interest rate brings.
A demand shock moves the IS curve, and with \(R\) unchanged output moves one for one with \(\bar{a}\).

Fig. 4: Raising the interest rate in the IS/MP diagram
Goal. See how the central bank can cause a recession.
Inflation is slow to adjust, so a higher nominal interest rate means a higher real interest rate. The MP line moves up to \(R'\). Borrowing now costs more than the return on new capital (\(R' > \bar{r}\)), so firms and households cut their investment, and the economy moves along the IS curve from \(A\) to \(B\). The textbook’s figure has no numbers; with our baseline, \(R' = 6\) percent gives the “\(-2\) percent” of its later examples. It is the same function as in Fig. 3.

         a_new=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="demand shock ā′", style=WIDE),
         b=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=2.5, step=0.25, description="sensitivity of investment b̄", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With \(R' = 6\) percent, output falls from 0 to \(-2\) percent: each percentage point on \(R\) costs \(\bar{b} = 2\) points of output.
The IS curve does not move: a change in \(R\) is a movement along it. Only the MP line shifts.
A flatter IS curve (a larger \(\bar{b}\)) makes the same rate increase more painful: with \(\bar{b} = 2.5\) output falls to \(-2.5\) percent.

Fig. 5: Stabilizing the economy after a housing bubble
Goal. See how monetary policy can offset an aggregate demand shock.
When a housing bubble bursts, households lose wealth and confidence, and spend less: the demand shock \(\bar{a}\) falls to \(\bar{a}' < 0\). The IS curve shifts left, and at an unchanged interest rate the economy moves from \(A\) to \(B\), a recession (panel a; the textbook uses \(-2\) percent as its example). The central bank can respond by cutting the real interest rate to the level of equation (3),
\[R' = \bar{r} + \frac{\bar{a}'}{\bar{b}},\]
the rate at which the new IS curve gives \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) (our rate_for_output). Cheaper borrowing raises investment and makes up for the fall in \(\bar{a}\): the economy moves to \(C\), back at potential (panel b).

Python note. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=(...)) makes a figure with two panels side by side. Our drawing functions take row and col, so add_point(..., 1, 2) draws in the panel of row 1, column 2. for col in [1, 2]: draws the parts that both panels share.


def housing_bubble(a_new=-2.0, b=B_BAR):
    """Fig. 12.5: (a) a fall in demand moves the economy from A to B; (b) the Fed lowers R to R' and reaches C."""
    Y_B = is_curve(R_BAR, a_new, b)
    R_new = rate_for_output(0.0, a_new, b)          # the rate at which IS' gives Y~ = 0
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, horizontal_spacing=0.12,
                        subplot_titles=("(a) The bubble bursts: A → B", "(b) The Fed lowers R: B → C"))
    for col in [1, 2]:
        add_is(fig, "IS", GRAY, A_BAR, b, "dash", 1, col)
        add_is(fig, "IS′", TEAL, a_new, b, "solid", 1, col)
        add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0, 1, col)
        add_point(fig, Y_B, R_BAR, "B", -8, 0, 1, col)
        set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE, 1, col)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", BLUE, "solid", 1, 1)
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, Y_B, 0.6, 1, 1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash", 1, 2)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE, "solid", 1, 2)
    add_arrow(fig, -7.3, R_BAR, -7.3, R_new, 1, 2)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_new, "C", -8, 0, 1, 2, where="bottom left")    # below left, clear of A
    add_arrow(fig, Y_B, 0.6, 0.0, 0.6, 1, 2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"ā′ = {a_new:.1f}: B at Ỹ = {Y_B:+.1f}%;  R′ = {R_new:.2f}% brings C back to Ỹ = 0.0%")
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The bust alone (panel a) takes output to \(-2\) percent. Cutting \(R\) from 5 to 4 percent (panel b) brings it back to potential: in the model, monetary policy can fully offset a demand shock.
The larger the shock, the larger the cut. The flatter the IS curve (larger \(\bar{b}\)), the smaller the cut needed.
In practice this is hard. It takes time to see how large the shock is, and Milton Friedman’s “long and variable lags” mean that interest rates need 6–18 months to have their main effect. In 2008 the housing bust turned out to be much more than an ordinary demand shock (Chapter 14).

text:
The Phillips curve
The Phillips curve links output to changes in inflation. We add a price shock, such as an oil price increase, and look at U.S. inflation over the long run.

Fig. 7: The Phillips curve
Goal. Draw the Phillips curve and see how the state of the economy changes inflation.
Imagine you run a firm and inflation has been 5 percent a year. You expect it to stay there, so normally you raise your prices by 5 percent. If demand for your products is weak, you raise them by less, to win back customers; if demand is strong, by more. When all firms do this, inflation equals last year’s inflation plus an adjustment for demand (equation 5):
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}.\]
A booming economy (\(\tilde{Y} > 0\)) raises inflation; a slumping one lowers it. The slope \(\bar{\nu}\) measures how strongly prices react to demand. As with the IS diagram, one function draws three textbook figures: the Phillips curve itself (Fig. 7), an oil shock (Fig. 8) and a recession (Fig. 11). Its arguments are short-run output Y_new, the price shock o_new and the slope nu.

Python note. for x, y, anchor, text in REGIONS: takes the list of (x, y, anchor, text) groups one at a time and unpacks each into four names. dict(X_OUTPUT, title=...) copies the settings of X_OUTPUT and replaces the title. Y_DPI if fits else Y_DPI_WIDE is a one-line if: it gives the first axis when fits is true (both conditions joined by and hold) and the wider one otherwise. yaxis["range"][1] looks up the axis range and takes its second number, the top of the axis.


REGIONS = [(-7.6, 3.4, "left", "Δπ > 0:<br>inflation rises"), (7.6, -3.4, "right", "Δπ < 0:<br>inflation falls")]
X_SLUMP_BOOM = dict(X_OUTPUT, title="←  Below potential (slump)          Short-run output, Ỹ (%)          Above potential (boom)  →")


def pc_experiment(Y_new=0.0, o_new=O_BAR, nu=NU):
    """Figs. 12.7, 12.8, 12.11: the Phillips curve, a price shock o' that shifts it, and the economy at Y~."""
    dpi = phillips(Y_new, nu, o_new)
    fits = abs(dpi) <= 3.4 and abs(phillips(2.0, nu, o_new)) <= 3.4
    yaxis = Y_DPI if fits else Y_DPI_WIDE                  # a wider axis only when B or the shift would not fit
    top = yaxis["range"][1]
    fig = go.Figure()
    if o_new != O_BAR:
        add_pc(fig, "PC", GRAY, nu, O_BAR, "dash", top=top)
        add_pc(fig, "PC′", GREEN, nu, o_new, top=top)
        add_arrow(fig, 2.0, phillips(2.0, nu), 2.0, phillips(2.0, nu, o_new))      # the shift of the curve
    else:
        add_pc(fig, "Phillips curve", GREEN, nu, top=top)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, phillips(0.0, nu, o_new), "A", -8, -top, where="top left")  # top left: off the rising curve
    if Y_new != 0.0:
        add_point(fig, Y_new, dpi, "B", -8, -top, where="top left")
        add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.3 - top, Y_new, 0.3 - top)                            # the change in output
    for x, y, anchor, text in REGIONS:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor=anchor, font=dict(size=13, color=GRAY))
    set_axes(fig, X_SLUMP_BOOM, yaxis)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Ỹ = {Y_new:+.1f}%, ō = {o_new:+.1f}  →  Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_new:+.1f}) + ({o_new:+.1f}) = {dpi:+.2f}")
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

At potential (\(\tilde{Y} = 0\), point \(A\)) inflation is steady: this year’s inflation equals last year’s.
An economy 2 percent above potential raises inflation by \(0.5 \times 2 = 1\) point a year, and it keeps rising as long as the boom lasts.
A steeper curve (larger \(\bar{\nu}\)) means prices react more to demand. With a flat curve it takes a deep recession to lower inflation by one point.

A brief history. A. W. Phillips first related the level of (wage) inflation to economic activity. In the 1960s many economists concluded that a country could keep output high for ever by accepting, say, 5 instead of 2 percent inflation. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that firms would soon build the higher inflation into their prices: holding output above potential would make inflation rise year after year, which is the version of the curve used here. The rising inflation of the 1970s proved them right.

Fig. 8: An oil price increase
Goal. See how a price shock moves inflation even when output is at potential.
When oil prices jump, gasoline, airline tickets and heating cost more at once, and firms that use oil as an input pass the higher cost on to their prices. In the model this is a positive price shock \(\bar{o}\): the Phillips curve shifts up by \(\bar{o}\) for one period. Even at potential, inflation now rises by \(\bar{o}\). Economists call such increases cost-push inflation, and the \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) term demand-pull inflation. Price shocks can also come from other inputs (steel), from large union wage settlements (\(\bar{o} > 0\)), or from a large inflow of workers that holds wages down (\(\bar{o} < 0\)). The textbook’s figure has no number; we use \(\bar{o} = 1\) point.

What to notice.

The whole curve moves up by \(\bar{o}\): at \(\tilde{Y} = 0\), inflation rises by 1 point.
To keep inflation steady after the shock, output would have to fall to \(\tilde{Y} = -\bar{o}/\bar{\nu} = -2\) percent: a price shock confronts the central bank with a hard choice.
Quantity theory or Phillips curve? Chapter 8 found that faster growth of real GDP lowers inflation; here a boom raises it. The two are about different things: the quantity theory is a long-run model in which more output means more supply of goods; here higher short-run output means more demand than the economy’s potential.


Key numbers: demand-pull and cost-push
The change in inflation has two parts, \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) and \(\bar{o}\). A loop computes them for a few cases.

            low, high = wider_low, wider_high
    title = f"{country}: inflation peaked at {worst.inflation:.1f}% in {worst.year}"
    if country == "United States":
        title = f"Inflation peaked at {worst.inflation:.1f}% in {worst.year} and tends to fall after shaded recessions"
    if part.inflation.max() > high or part.policy_rate.max() > high or part.real_rate.min() < low:
        title += " (off the chart)"
    fig = px.area(part, x="date", y="inflation", labels={"date": "Year", "inflation": "Percent"}, title=title)
    fig.update_traces(name="Inflation (CPI)", showlegend=True, line_color=TEAL)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.policy_rate, visible="legendonly", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2),
                             name="Fed funds rate, i" if country == "United States" else "Policy rate, i"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.real_rate, name="Real interest rate, R = i − π",
                             visible="legendonly", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=2, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    if country == "United States":
        shade_recessions(fig, "1960-01-01")
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["1959-01-01", "2026-12-31"], yaxis_range=[low, high],
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.98, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

text:
Using the short-run model: disinflation and the Great Inflation
Now we put the three pieces together and run the model through time, first for the Volcker disinflation of the early 1980s and then for a policy mistake of the 1970s.

Fig. 10: Tightening monetary policy
Goal. Follow the first step of the Volcker disinflation in the IS/MP diagram.
By 1979 inflation exceeded 10 percent. Paul Volcker’s Fed slowed money growth, which means raising the nominal interest rate. Because inflation is sticky, the real rate rises too: \(R' = i' - \pi\) (equation 1). With inflation at 10 percent, a nominal rate of 15 percent keeps \(R = 5\% = \bar{r}\); raising it to 16 percent lifts the real rate to 6 percent, and output falls to the textbook’s \(-2\) percent. The function reuses ismp_experiment and only adds the Fisher step.

def tightening(i_new=16.0, pi=10.0):
    """Fig. 12.10: with sticky inflation pi, a higher nominal rate i' raises R' = i' - pi and lowers output."""
    R_new = real_rate(i_new, pi)
    fig = ismp_experiment(R_new=R_new)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"i′ = {i_new:.1f}% and sticky π = {pi:.1f}%  →  R′ = {R_new:.1f}%  →  Ỹ = {is_curve(R_new):+.1f}%")
    return fig


interact(tightening,
         i_new=FloatSlider(value=16.0, min=13.0, max=17.5, step=0.5, description="new nominal interest rate i′ (%)", style=WIDE),
         pi=FloatSlider(value=10.0, min=9.0, max=11.0, step=0.5, description="sticky inflation π (%)", style=WIDE));

What to notice.

Only the real rate matters for output: \(i' = 16\) with \(\pi = 10\) has the same effect as \(i' = 7\) with \(\pi = 1\).
If inflation were not sticky (if the classical dichotomy held even in the short run), a higher nominal rate could simply come with lower inflation and leave output alone. Stickiness is what gives monetary policy real effects.
In 1981 the effective fed funds rate averaged 16.4 percent, and the real rate was about 6 percent (Fig. 9): the deepest recession in decades followed.

Fig. 11: A recession and falling inflation
Goal. Follow the second step: the recession lowers inflation through the Phillips curve.
The Fed’s recession takes output to \(\tilde{Y}' = -2\) percent. Firms see demand fall, so they raise prices less aggressively, and the economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\) on the Phillips curve, where \(\Delta\pi' < 0\). It is the pc_experiment function again, now with output below potential.

What to notice.

With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\), a recession of 2 percent lowers inflation by 1 point: from 10 to 9 percent in the first year.
The textbook’s example, “instead of raising prices by 10 percent, they may raise them by only 8 percent”, is a fall of 2 points; it corresponds to \(\bar{\nu} = 1\). Move the slope slider to 1 to see it.
The cost of lower inflation is lost output; the steeper the curve, the cheaper the disinflation.

# Your turn: try it here



Fig. 12: The disinflation over time
Goal. Run the Volcker policy year by year and watch inflation come down.
The Fed raises the real interest rate in year 0 and keeps it high until year \(t^*\), when inflation has fallen enough; then it returns \(R\) to \(\bar{r}\). Each year the model takes three steps: the MP curve sets \(R_t\), the IS curve gives \(\tilde{Y}_t\), and the Phillips curve gives \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\) (equation 4 with \(\bar{o} = 0\)). That is exactly our simulate function. Inflation starts at the textbook’s 10 percent. Inflation in year 0 already falls, because \(\pi_0 = (P_1 - P_0)/P_0\): firms set next year’s prices when they see this year’s recession.

Python note. np.arange(-2, 10) is the years \(-2, -1, \ldots, 9\). np.where(condition, a, b) gives a where the condition is true and b elsewhere: here a high rate from year 0 to \(t^* - 1\) and \(\bar{r}\) otherwise. & means “and”. line_shape="hv" draws steps: a flat line, then a jump. IntSlider is a slider for whole numbers. pi_path.min() is the smallest number in the array: if a long, deep recession pushes inflation below zero (deflation), the inflation axis extends below zero to show it.


def disinflation(Y_rec=-2.0, t_star=5, nu=NU):
    """Fig. 12.12: the Fed holds R high from year 0 to t*; output is Y_rec and inflation falls from 10%."""
    years = np.arange(-2, 10)
    R_path = np.where((years >= 0) & (years < t_star), rate_for_output(Y_rec), R_BAR)
    Y_path, pi_path = simulate(R_path, pi_start=10.0, nu=nu)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=3, horizontal_spacing=0.09,
                        subplot_titles=("(a) R held high until t*", "(b) Output below potential", "(c) Inflation steps down"))
    paths = [R_path, Y_path, pi_path]
    colors, shapes = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN], ["hv", "hv", "linear"]
    axes = [dict(title="Real interest rate, R (%)", range=[2.5, 7.5]), dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (%)", range=[-4.5, 1.5]),
            dict(title="Inflation, π (%)", range=[min(0.0, pi_path.min() - 1.0), 11.5])]   # widens only below zero
    for k in range(3):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=paths[k], mode="lines+markers", showlegend=False, line_shape=shapes[k],
                                 line=dict(color=colors[k], width=4), marker=dict(color="black", size=9)), row=1, col=k + 1)
        set_axes(fig, dict(title="Year", tickvals=[0, t_star], ticktext=["0", "t*"], range=[-2.5, 9.5]), axes[k], 1, k + 1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"π: 10.0% → {pi_path[-1]:.1f}% with Ỹ = {Y_rec:+.1f}% until t* = {t_star};"
                            f"  output lost: {-Y_path.sum():.1f} %-years")
    return fig

What to notice.

Five years at \(\tilde{Y} = -2\) percent bring inflation from 10 to 5 percent, one point a year. When the Fed returns \(R\) to \(\bar{r}\), output goes back to potential and inflation stays at its new, lower level.
The price is 10 “percent-years” of lost output: 2 percent of GDP for five years, or 2 percent-years for each point of inflation removed.
A deeper recession gets there faster, at about the same total cost: with \(\tilde{Y} = -4\) it takes 2.5 years. Only a steeper Phillips curve makes the disinflation cheaper.
In reality, inflation fell from 13.5 percent in 1980 to 3.2 percent in 1983 (Fig. 9), faster than in this example, and the recession of 1981–1982 was the deepest in decades.

Fig. 13: Mistaking a slowdown in potential for a recession
Goal. See how a slowdown in potential output, mistaken for a recession, can feed inflation.
From the early 1970s, U.S. productivity growth slowed down, so potential output grew more slowly. At the time, policymakers thought potential output was still growing at its old rate. They saw actual output fall behind that believed path, read it as a recession (\(\tilde{Y}_{\text{perceived}} < 0\)), and lowered interest rates. In truth output was then above its true potential (\(\tilde{Y}_{\text{true}} > 0\)), and through the Phillips curve inflation rose.
The textbook’s figure is stylized, so we describe it with three numbers: potential growth before 1973 (g_old), after 1973 (g_new), and how far the stimulus eventually pushes output above true potential (gap_max, reached gradually). Output is an index with 1973 = 100. This small model is used only here, so we define it in this section.

Python note. np.exp is the exponential function: an index growing at g percent a year is \(100\,e^{g\,(t - 1973)/100}\). np.minimum(x, 0) keeps the negative values of x and sets the others to 0, and np.maximum(x, 0) does the opposite. continue skips the rest of the loop for the current item.


def output_paths(g_old=3.5, g_new=2.5, gap_max=4.0):
    """Fig. 12.13: believed potential, true potential and actual output (1973 = 100)."""
    years = np.arange(1965, 1986)
    before, after = np.minimum(years - 1973, 0), np.maximum(years - 1973, 0)
    believed = 100 * np.exp(g_old * (years - 1973) / 100)
    true = 100 * np.exp((g_old * before + g_new * after) / 100)
    gap_true = gap_max * (1 - np.exp(-after / 4))      # the stimulus pushes output above true potential
    actual = true * (1 + gap_true / 100)
    return years, believed, true, actual


def slowdown(g_old=3.5, g_new=2.5, gap_max=4.0):
    """Fig. 12.13 with readouts: the perceived and the true output gap, and the rise in inflation."""
    years, believed, true, actual = output_paths(g_old, g_new, gap_max)
    perceived_gap, true_gap = 100 * (actual / believed - 1), 100 * (actual / true - 1)
    dpi = phillips(true_gap[(years > 1973) & (years <= 1980)]).sum()   # Phillips curve, 1974-1980
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=believed, name=f"Believed potential ({g_old:g}% a year)", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=actual, name="Actual output (with the stimulus)", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=true, name=f"True potential ({g_new:g}% a year after 1973)", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4, dash="dash")))
    gaps = [(actual[-1], believed[-1], "seen as Ỹ < 0"), (true[-1], actual[-1], "true Ỹ > 0")]
    for low, high, text in gaps:
        if high - low < 4:                             # no bracket (and no false label) for a gap that is not there
            continue
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1985.4, 1985.4], y=[low, high], mode="lines", showlegend=False, line=dict(color="black", width=2)))
        fig.add_annotation(x=1985.6, y=(low + high) / 2, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(size=13))
    k = 1980 - 1965                                    # the position of 1980 in the arrays
    fig.add_vline(x=1973, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"1980: perceived Ỹ = {perceived_gap[k]:+.1f}%, true Ỹ = {true_gap[k]:+.1f}%;"
                            f" inflation +{dpi:.1f} points since 1973",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[1964, 1990], tickvals=[1965, 1970, 1973, 1980, 1985]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Output (index, 1973 = 100)", range=[60, 190]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.13 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

By 1980 actual output is 3.7 percent below the believed path, so policymakers see a recession and keep stimulating. Yet it is 3.3 percent above true potential.
The true gap is positive every year after 1973, so the Phillips curve raises inflation every year: about 8 points by 1980 with \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\). Actual U.S. inflation rose from 6.3 percent in 1973 to 13.5 percent in 1980, also helped by the oil shocks of 1974 and 1979.
Set the growth rate after 1973 equal to the one before: there is no slowdown, the two dashed paths coincide, and the stimulus is plainly a boom.
Policymakers learn of their mistake through rising inflation, but oil shocks also raise inflation, which made the lesson slow to learn.


The short-run model in a nutshell
The textbook sums up how monetary policy works through the three building blocks:







Building block
Step




MP curve
\(\uparrow i_t \Rightarrow \uparrow R_t\)


IS curve
\(\uparrow R_t \Rightarrow \downarrow \tilde{Y}_t\)


Phillips curve
\(\downarrow \tilde{Y}_t \Rightarrow \downarrow \Delta\pi_t\)

What to notice.

Before Covid, real GDP grew by about 2.5 percent a year.


Real GDP in other countries
GDP levels in different currencies cannot be compared directly, but their changes can.     part = cpi_world[cpi_world.country == country].rename(

    title = "No all-items CPI data for this country"
    every = part.set_index("date")["All items"].dropna()
    if not every.empty:

        later = every[every.index > dip.idxmin()]
        title = f"CPI inflation fell to {round(dip.min(), 1) + 0.0:.1f}% in {dip.idxmin():%B %Y}"
        if not later.empty:

What to notice.

At the start of the pandemic, inflation fell, as the Phillips curve predicts for a weak economy: from 2.6 percent in January 2020 to 0.2 percent in May 2020.

title: 12. Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
section: How central banks control the nominal interest rate
text:
How central banks control the nominal interest rate
So far the central bank simply chose the interest rate. The money market shows how it does so: by supplying whatever money is demanded at its target rate.

Fig. 18: How the central bank sets the nominal interest rate
Goal. See where “money” comes in: the central bank sets the interest rate through the money market.
Holding money has a price, and the nominal interest rate is that price: it is what you give up by keeping cash. cash and checking accounts pay nothing, while a savings or money-market account pays \(i\). At 1 percent you might as well hold cash; at 20 percent you would keep as little as possible. So money demand \(M^d\) falls as \(i\) rises. The central bank decides how much money to supply, \(M^s\): a vertical line. The interest rate \(i^*\) is where people want to hold exactly the money supplied (equation 12). If \(i\) were higher, people would want less money than there is, and the rate would fall; if lower, the opposite.
As before, one function draws two textbook figures: this one (Fig. 18) and a change in the money supply (Fig. 19). Its arguments are the new money supply M_new and the new level of money demand m0_new (demand is \(M^d = m_0 - i\)).

Python note. "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ" is a one-line if: it gives the first text when the condition is true and the second otherwise.


def money_experiment(M_new=M_BAR, m0_new=M0):
    """Figs. 12.18 and 12.19: money supply and demand set the nominal rate; a change moves i* to i**."""
    i_star, i_new = market_rate(M_BAR), market_rate(M_new, m0_new)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if m0_new != M0:
        add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ", GRAY, M0, "dash")
    add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ", BLUE, m0_new)
    if M_new != M_BAR:
        add_line(fig, [M_BAR, M_BAR], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ", GRAY, "dash")
        add_arrow(fig, M_BAR, 1.0, M_new, 1.0)                     # the change in the money supply
    add_line(fig, [M_new, M_new], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ′" if M_new != M_BAR else "Mˢ", TEAL)
    where = "bottom left" if m0_new > M0 else "top right"      # keep i* clear of a higher demand curve
    add_point(fig, M_BAR, i_star, "i*", 0, 0, where=where)
    if i_new != i_star:
        where = "bottom left" if m0_new < M0 else "top right"  # ... and i** clear of the old, higher one
        add_point(fig, M_new, i_new, "i**", 0, 0, where=where)
        add_arrow(fig, 0.5, i_star, 0.5, i_new)                    # the change in the interest rate
    set_axes(fig, X_MONEY, Y_NOMINAL)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Money supply {M_new:.1f}, demand Mᵈ = {m0_new:.1f} − i  →  i = {i_star:.1f}% → {i_new:.1f}%",
                      margin=dict(r=90))
    return fig

With a supply of 5 and demand \(M^d = 10 - i\), the market clears at \(i^* = 5\) percent.
Move money demand: with the money supply fixed, every shift of demand moves the interest rate one for one. People need more money when prices or output are higher, or less when they pay by card, so demand shifts all the time.
In the short run inflation is sticky, so the money market clears through the interest rate (and the velocity of money), not through the price level as in the quantity theory of Chapter 8.

Fig. 20: Targeting the nominal interest rate
Goal. See why central banks set an interest rate rather than a quantity of money.
Money demand shifts all the time (Fig. 18). If the central bank kept the money supply fixed, every shift would move the interest rate, and with it the real rate and output. Instead, modern central banks peg the interest rate: they supply whatever money is demanded at the target rate \(i^*\). The money supply curve becomes horizontal at \(i^*\), and shifts in money demand change the quantity of money, not the rate. Compare the two policies with the toggle.

Python note. ToggleButtons shows one button per option, and the function receives the text of the chosen button.


def rate_target(m0_new=M0, i_target=5.0, policy="peg the interest rate"):
    """Fig. 12.20: pegging i makes money supply horizontal; fixing M lets money-demand shocks move i."""
    fig = go.Figure()
    if m0_new != M0:
        add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ", GRAY, M0, "dash")
    add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ", BLUE, m0_new)
    if policy == "peg the interest rate":
        i_eq, M_eq = i_target, money_demand(i_target, m0_new)
        add_line(fig, [0.5, 10.5], [i_target, i_target], "Mˢ", TEAL)
    else:
        M_eq = money_demand(i_target)                  # the supply that gave i_target before the shock
        i_eq = market_rate(M_eq, m0_new)
        add_line(fig, [M_eq, M_eq], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ", TEAL)
    add_point(fig, M_eq, i_eq, "", 0, 0)
    set_axes(fig, X_MONEY, Y_NOMINAL)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Policy: {policy};  demand shift {m0_new - M0:+.1f}  →  i = {i_eq:.1f}%, M = {M_eq:.1f}",
                      margin=dict(r=90))
    return fig

What to notice.

With the rate pegged at 5 percent, a rise in money demand from \(m_0 = 10\) to 11 is met by more money (6 instead of 5), and the interest rate does not move.
Switch to “fix the money supply”: the same shift raises the interest rate to 6 percent, which would push the real rate up and output down although nothing real happened. Pegging the rate shields the economy from money-demand shocks.
The IS/LM model. An older version of the short-run model keeps the money supply fixed. Then higher output raises money demand and the interest rate, which gives an upward-sloping “LM” curve instead of our flat MP curve. Since central banks in fact adjust the money supply to keep the interest rate at its target, the two approaches lead to the same analysis.


Key numbers: bond prices and interest rates
In an open-market operation the Fed buys or sells bonds, and the interest rate is hidden in the bond’s price. A bond that pays 100 dollars in one year and sells for 97 dollars today yields \(3/97 = 3.1\) percent.

def bond_yield(price, face=100.0):
    """The one-year interest rate implied by a bond's price: (face - price) / price, in percent."""
    return 100 * (face - price) / price


for price in [95.0, 96.0, 97.0, 98.0, 99.0]:

text:
Worked exercise: the Great Inflation
The last figure is the textbook’s answer to Exercise 12: what happens when policymakers mistake a slowdown in potential output for a demand shock and keep stimulating.

Fig. 21: The Great Inflation
Goal. Answer Exercise 12 of the textbook: how mistaking the productivity slowdown for a demand shock could have caused the Great Inflation.
The four panels tell the story of Fig. 13 with the model’s diagrams:


Policymakers believe a negative demand shock \(\bar{a}' < 0\) caused the slowdown: they think the IS curve shifted to IS′, and the economy is at \(B\), below potential.


So they lower the real interest rate to \(R' = \bar{r} + \bar{a}'/\bar{b}\) (equation 3), which, they believe, takes the economy back to potential at \(C\).


Demand never actually fell, so the IS curve is where it was. The lower rate moves the economy down the true IS curve, to \(C\), above potential.


With output above potential, the Phillips curve raises inflation: \(\downarrow R \Rightarrow \uparrow \tilde{Y} \Rightarrow \uparrow \pi\).


The figure has four panels, so we split the work: perceived_panels draws the two panels of what policymakers believe, and great_inflation adds the truth and the readout.

def perceived_panels(fig, a_perc, R_new):
    """Fig. 12.21 (a) and (b): the IS/MP diagram as policymakers see it."""
    for col in [1, 2]:
        add_is(fig, "IS", GRAY, dash="dash", row=1, col=col)
        add_is(fig, "IS′", TEAL, a_perc, row=1, col=col)
        add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0, 1, col)
        add_point(fig, a_perc, R_BAR, "B", -8, 0, 1, col)
        set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE, 1, col)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", BLUE, row=1, col=1)
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, a_perc, 0.6, 1, 1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash", 1, 2)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE, row=1, col=2)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_new, "C", -8, 0, 1, 2, where="bottom left")    # below left, clear of A
    add_arrow(fig, a_perc, 0.6, 0.0, 0.6, 1, 2)


def great_inflation(a_perc=-2.0, nu=NU):
    """Fig. 12.21: the Fed sees a demand shock a' that never happened, cuts R, and inflation rises."""
    R_new = rate_for_output(0.0, a_perc)           # the cut that would close the perceived gap
    Y_true = is_curve(R_new)                       # but the true IS curve never moved
    dpi = phillips(Y_true, nu)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=2, horizontal_spacing=0.12, vertical_spacing=0.14,
                        subplot_titles=("(a) Belief: demand fell, IS → IS′", "(b) Belief: a cut to R′ restores Ỹ = 0",
                                        "(c) Reality: IS unchanged, Ỹ overshoots", "(d) Reality: Ỹ > 0 pushes Δπ up"))
    perceived_panels(fig, a_perc, R_new)
    add_is(fig, "IS", TEAL, row=2, col=1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash", 2, 1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE, row=2, col=1)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0, 2, 1)
    add_point(fig, Y_true, R_new, "C", -8, 0, 2, 1, where="bottom left")  # clear of the old MP line
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, Y_true, 0.6, 2, 1)
    add_pc(fig, "Phillips curve", GREEN, nu, row=2, col=2)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, 0.0, "A", -8, -4, 2, 2, where="top left")
    add_point(fig, Y_true, dpi, "B", -8, -4, 2, 2, where="top left")
    set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE, 2, 1)
    set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_DPI, 2, 2)
    fig.update_layout(height=820, title=f"Believed ā′ = {a_perc:.1f}  →  R′ = {R_new:.2f}%  →  true Ỹ = {Y_true:+.1f}%"
                                        f"  →  Δπ = {dpi:+.2f} a year")
    return fig


interact(great_inflation,
         a_perc=FloatSlider(value=-2.0, min=-3.0, max=-0.5, step=0.5, description="demand shock policymakers believe in ā′", style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=1.0, step=0.05, description="slope ν̄", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.21 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., the worked answer to Exercise 12.
What to notice.

Believing in a shock of \(-2\), the Fed cuts \(R\) from 5 to 4 percent. On the true IS curve this takes output to \(+2\) percent, not 0, and inflation rises by 1 point a year for as long as the mistake lasts.
The bigger the shock policymakers believe in, the bigger the cut, the bigger the boom, and the faster inflation rises.
How can policymakers find out? Rising inflation with no other shock is the sign that output is above potential. In the 1970s the oil shocks also raised inflation, so the mistake took years to see.

Your turn. Suppose the Fed recognizes its mistake and wants to stop inflation from rising. To what real interest rate should it return? What if, in addition, it wants to bring inflation back down by 1 point a year?


Hint

Steady inflation needs \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) on the true IS curve: rate_for_output(0.0). Lowering inflation by 1 point a year needs \(\tilde{Y} = -1/\bar{\nu}\): try rate_for_output(-2.0).

title: 12. Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
Concluding remarks

The short-run model has three building blocks. Through the MP curve, the central bank’s nominal interest rate sets the real interest rate, \(R_t = i_t - \pi_t\) (equation 1), because inflation is sticky. Through the IS curve, equation (2), the real rate sets short-run output. Through the Phillips curve, equations (4) and (5), \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\), output changes inflation over time, and inflation adds up every past gap and shock (equation 6).
In the IS/MP diagram, monetary policy can in principle offset demand shocks such as a housing bust by setting the rate of equation (3), but long and variable lags make this hard in practice.
Combined, the three blocks give one difference equation for inflation, equation (7). Lowering inflation requires a temporary recession whose total cost, \((\pi_{-1} - \pi^T)/\bar{\nu}\) percent-years, does not depend on how fast it is done (equations 8 and 9): the Volcker disinflation brought inflation from 13.5 percent in 1980 to 3.2 percent in 1983, at the cost of the deepest recession in decades. Oil shocks, the belief in a permanent trade-off, and a productivity slowdown mistaken for a recession all contributed to the Great Inflation of the 1970s.
Central banks set the interest rate by supplying whatever money is demanded at their target. Through the term structure, the short rate also moves longer-term rates.
The next chapter adds the central bank’s policy rule and expectations, leading to the AS/AD framework. Our preview, equations (10) and (11), already shows that such a rule closes a fixed share of the inflation gap every year.

title: 12. Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve
text:
Practice problems
These twelve problems practise the chapter in three ways: conceptual problems apply its equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to its data, and modeling problems use its interactive models to answer policy questions. Each problem is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it on your own first, then open the Hint and the Solution. The sliders of the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of the figure that each problem names.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): What did “at least through mid-2013” do to interest rates? In August 2011 the federal funds rate was already close to zero: it averaged 0.10 percent that month (Fig. 2). On August 9 the Federal Open Market Committee said that economic conditions were “likely to warrant exceptionally low levels for the federal funds rate at least through mid-2013”. It changed no interest rate that day. Yet the 2-year Treasury yield fell from 0.27 percent on August 8 to 0.19 percent on August 9, and the 5-year yield from 1.11 to 0.91 percent (Board of Governors, Treasury constant-maturity yields DGS2 and DGS5, via FRED). Use the term structure of interest rates from Model overview, with 0.10 percent as the one-year rate of the first year.


Which one-year rate for the second year did the 2-year yield imply on August 8, and on August 9?


Which average one-year rate for years 2 to 5 did the 5-year yield imply on each day?


Why did longer-term yields fall on a day when the Fed left its rate unchanged?




Hint

A 2-year rate is about the average of this year’s one-year rate and the one expected for next year. Solve that average for the unknown rate. For the 5-year yield, the unknown is the average of the four rates expected for years 2 to 5.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The 2-year yield is about \(i^{(2)} \approx (i_1 + i^e_2)/2\). Multiply by 2 and subtract \(i_1\): \(i^e_2 \approx 2\,i^{(2)} - i_1\).

August 8: \(i^e_2 \approx 2 \times 0.27 - 0.10 = 0.44\) percent.
August 9: \(i^e_2 \approx 2 \times 0.19 - 0.10 = 0.28\) percent.

In one day, markets lowered the rate they expected for the second year by 0.16 points.
(b) Write \(\bar{x}\) for the average of \(i^e_2, \dots, i^e_5\). Then \(i^{(5)} \approx (i_1 + 4\bar{x})/5\), so \(\bar{x} \approx (5\,i^{(5)} - i_1)/4\).

August 8: \(\bar{x} \approx (5 \times 1.11 - 0.10)/4 = 1.36\) percent.
August 9: \(\bar{x} \approx (5 \times 0.91 - 0.10)/4 = 1.11\) percent.

The short rates expected for the following four years fell by 0.25 points on average.
(c) A long-term rate is an average of the short-term rates expected over its life. The statement told markets that the short rate would stay near zero for about two more years, longer than they had expected. Expected future short rates fell, so longer-term yields fell at once. With inflation sticky, longer-term real rates fell too, and those are the rates at which firms and households borrow (the IS curve). Central banks call this forward guidance: moving long rates by announcing the future path of the short rate. (The calculation ignores the extra return that investors ask for holding long bonds, the term premium.)

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Who gained from a 3 percent mortgage in 2021? In 2021 the rate on a new 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the United States averaged 2.96 percent (Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey, series MORTGAGE30US via FRED). Suppose a family took such a loan, and both the family and its bank expected inflation to stay at the Fed’s 2 percent target. U.S. CPI inflation then turned out to be 4.68 percent in 2021, 7.99 percent in 2022 and 4.13 percent in 2023 (Fig. 9).


What was the ex ante real interest rate on the loan?


What was the ex post real rate in each of the three years, and on average?


Who gained from the surprise, and who lost? Use the gap between the ex post and the ex ante rate from Model overview.


In 2021 the fed funds rate averaged only 0.08 percent (Fig. 2). Why was the mortgage rate so much higher?




Hint

The ex ante real rate subtracts the inflation people expect; the ex post real rate subtracts the inflation that actually happened. For (d), ask yourself what a 30-year interest rate is an average of.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) \(R^{\text{ex ante}} = i - \pi^e = 2.96 - 2 = 0.96\) percent.
(b) \(R^{\text{ex post}} = i - \pi\):

On average over the three years the ex post real rate was \(-2.64\) percent.
(c) \(R^{\text{ex post}} - R^{\text{ex ante}} = \pi^e - \pi\), the last column: the loan cost the family far less than both sides had planned. The family repays in dollars that buy much less than it expected, so it gains. The lender (the bank, or the investors who bought the mortgage) loses the same purchasing power. Inflation that nobody expected moves wealth from lenders to borrowers; inflation that everyone expected would have been built into the 2.96 percent.
(d) A mortgage lasts up to 30 years. By the term structure, its rate is about the average of the short rates expected over those years, plus extra pay for lending for so long. In 2021 the Fed’s rate sat at its floor, but nobody expected it to stay there for 30 years. The overnight rate reaches long-term borrowers only through the short rates that markets expect in the future.

The Federal Reserve’s review of its failure explains that the bank had invested its deposits mainly in securities with long maturities, and that in 2022, as interest rates rose, deposits flowed out and the losses on those securities grew fast. Extend the bond price of Model overview, \(P_B = 100/(1 + i)\), to a bond that pays 100 dollars in \(n\) years.


What did a 1-year bond and a 10-year bond cost on January 3, 2022?


On March 1, 2023, the 10-year bond bought in January 2022 had about 9 years left. Value it at that day’s 10-year yield: what share of its value had it lost? What happened to the 1-year bond bought on the same day?


Why is a bank that holds long-term bonds, paid for with deposits that customers can withdraw at any time, exposed when the central bank raises interest rates?




Hint

Money invested at the annual rate \(i\) grows to \(P(1 + i)^n\) after \(n\) years. For the 1-year bond, ask what it paid in January 2023.

Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) Buying at \(P\) and earning \(i\) a year for \(n\) years must give the 100 dollars that the bond pays: \(P(1 + i)^n = 100\), so
\[P = \frac{100}{(1 + i)^n}.\]
A rise in \(i\) is compounded \(n\) times, so the price of a long bond reacts much more than that of a short one.
(b) On January 3, 2022: \(100/1.0040 = 99.60\) dollars for the 1-year bond and \(100/1.0163^{10} = 85.07\) dollars for the 10-year bond.
(c) On March 1, 2023: \(100/1.0401^{9} = 70.20\) dollars, 17.5 percent less than the price paid. The 1-year bond did not lose anything: it paid its 100 dollars in January 2023, and that money could be lent again at the new 1-year yield of 4.72 percent.
for years, y_pct in [(1, 0.40), (10, 1.63), (9, 4.01)]:
    print(f"{years} years at {y_pct:.2f}%: price {100 / (1 + y_pct / 100) ** years:.2f} dollars")
loss = 100 * (1 - (100 / 1.0401 ** 9) / (100 / 1.0163 ** 10))
print(f"Loss on the 10-year bond: {loss:.1f}%")
(d) Deposits must be repaid in full, whenever customers ask; long bonds are worth less when rates rise. As long as the bank can keep its bonds to maturity, the loss stays on paper (“unrealized”, in the review’s words). As deposits flowed out, SVB had to sell: on March 8, 2023, it announced that it had sold 21 billion dollars of securities, at a loss of 1.8 billion dollars after tax, and its depositors ran the next day (the review). In the chapter’s terms: the Fed raised its rate from 0.20 percent in March 2022 to 4.65 percent in March 2023 (Fig. 2), and by the term structure the whole yield curve moved up with it (Fig. 6), which cut the price of every long bond.

Problem 4 (Challenge): What if the nominal rate stays put while inflation rises? Between August 2021 and February 2023 the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye cut its policy rate from 19 to 8.5 percent, while 12-month CPI inflation rose from 19.3 percent to a peak of 85.5 percent in October 2022 (our data, in the files of Figs. 2 and 15). The chapter’s MP curve holds the real rate where the central bank wants it. Here, instead, suppose the central bank holds the nominal rate at \(\bar{i}\), and spending reacts to the ex ante real rate with adaptive expectations: \(R_t = \bar{i} - \pi^e_t = \bar{i} - \pi_{t-1}\). The IS curve, equation (2), and the Phillips curve, equation (4), hold as before, with \(\bar{o} = 0\).


Combine the three equations into one equation for \(\pi_t\) in terms of \(\pi_{t-1}\).


Find the inflation rate \(\pi^*\) at which inflation stays constant, and show that \(\pi_t - \pi^* = (1 + \bar{\nu}\bar{b})(\pi_{t-1} - \pi^*)\). Does inflation return to \(\pi^*\) after a shock?


Take the notebook’s baseline (\(\bar{a} = 0\), \(\bar{b} = 2\), \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\), \(\bar{r} = 5\)), a nominal rate held at 14 percent (the rate of December 2021) and last year’s inflation of 19.6 percent (Türkiye’s average for 2021). Compute inflation for the next three years. (The baseline is illustrative: read the result as a mechanism, not as a forecast for Türkiye.)


What must the nominal rate do to stop the spiral? Compare with what the central bank did from June 2023.




Hint

For (a), put \(R_t\) into the IS curve, then the IS curve into equation (4). For (b), write the equation for \(\pi^*\) (set \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} = \pi^*\)) and subtract it from the equation of (a). For (d), look at equation (1) and at the Taylor principle in Model overview.

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) The IS curve with the ex ante real rate is \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(\bar{i} - \pi_{t-1} - \bar{r})\). Put it into equation (4) and collect the terms in \(\pi_{t-1}\):
\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\bar{a} - \bar{\nu}\bar{b}(\bar{i} - \bar{r}) + \bar{\nu}\bar{b}\,\pi_{t-1}
= (1 + \bar{\nu}\bar{b})\,\pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\left[\bar{a} - \bar{b}(\bar{i} - \bar{r})\right].\]
(b) Constant inflation means \(\pi^* = (1 + \bar{\nu}\bar{b})\,\pi^* + \bar{\nu}[\bar{a} - \bar{b}(\bar{i} - \bar{r})]\). Subtract \(\pi^*\) from both sides, \(0 = \bar{\nu}\bar{b}\,\pi^* + \bar{\nu}\bar{a} - \bar{\nu}\bar{b}(\bar{i} - \bar{r})\), and divide by \(\bar{\nu}\bar{b}\):
\[\pi^* = \bar{i} - \bar{r} - \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}}.\]
At \(\pi^*\) the real rate is \(\bar{r} + \bar{a}/\bar{b}\), the rate of equation (3), so output is at potential. Now subtract the equation for \(\pi^*\) from the equation of (a): the constant drops out, and
\[\pi_t - \pi^* = (1 + \bar{\nu}\bar{b})(\pi_{t-1} - \pi^*).\]
Since \(1 + \bar{\nu}\bar{b} > 1\), any gap grows every year: \(\pi^*\) is unstable, and inflation never returns to it. The intuition is a spiral. Inflation above \(\pi^*\) lowers the real rate, which raises output, which raises inflation further. (Below \(\pi^*\) the same spiral runs downward, toward deflation.)
(c) \(\pi^* = 14 - 5 - 0 = 9\) percent and \(1 + \bar{\nu}\bar{b} = 1 + 0.5 \times 2 = 2\). The gap of \(19.6 - 9 = 10.6\) points doubles every year, to 21.2, 42.4 and 84.8 points, so inflation runs 30.2, 51.4 and 93.8 percent.
pi_now = 19.6                                   # inflation last year, percent
for year in [1, 2, 3]:
    R_ante = 14.0 - pi_now                      # the ex ante real rate, with adaptive expectations
    pi_now = pi_now + phillips(is_curve(R_ante))
    print(f"Year {year}: R = {R_ante:+.1f}%, inflation {pi_now:.1f}%")
The real rate falls from \(-5.6\) to \(-16.2\) and \(-37.4\) percent as inflation climbs.
(d) The spiral stops only if the real rate does not fall when inflation rises: \(R_t = i_t - \pi_{t-1} \ge \bar{r} + \bar{a}/\bar{b}\). So the nominal rate must rise at least point for point with inflation, and by more to bring inflation down. This is the Taylor principle of Model overview. From June 2023 the central bank raised its rate step by step, from 8.5 to 50 percent in March 2024. In our data, 12-month inflation peaked again at 75.4 percent in May 2024, and then fell to 30.9 percent by December 2025.

With calculus, write \(d = R - 5\) and
\[L(d) = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(-2 - 1.5d)^2 + (-2 - 2.5d)^2\right].\]
By the chain rule, \(L'(d) = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[2(-1.5)(-2 - 1.5d) + 2(-2.5)(-2 - 2.5d)\right] = (3 + 2.25d) + (5 + 6.25d) = 8 + 8.5d\). Setting \(L'(d) = 0\) gives \(d = -8/8.5 = -0.94\), so \(R = 4.06\) percent: a cut of 0.94 points, smaller than the 1 point that ignores the uncertainty. In general the best change is \(d^* = \bar{a}'\,E[\bar{b}]/E[\bar{b}^2]\). Since \(E[\bar{b}^2] = E[\bar{b}]^2 + \text{Var}(\bar{b})\) is larger than \(E[\bar{b}]^2\) whenever \(\bar{b}\) is uncertain, the best cut is smaller than \(\bar{a}'/E[\bar{b}]\). Here \(E[\bar{b}] = 2\) and \(E[\bar{b}^2] = 4.25\).
(d) The cut is multiplied by the unknown \(\bar{b}\), so a bigger cut also spreads the two possible outcomes further apart. A slightly smaller cut leaves output a little below potential on average (at \(R = 4.05\), the average gap is \(-0.1\) percent) but makes the outcome less uncertain. This is one reason why central banks tend to move their rates in small steps.

Problem 11 (Intermediate): How long must a disinflation last if output may fall only 1.5 percent? A hypothetical central bank inherits 10 percent inflation, as in Fig. 12, and wants to bring it down to 4 percent. The government will not accept output more than 1.5 percent below potential in any year.


With the sliders, find how many years of tight policy the central bank needs.


How much output does the disinflation cost in total? Compare with a fast disinflation that reaches 4 percent in two years.


Which real interest rate must the central bank hold in each case?


Equation (9) says that the speed does not change the total cost. Give one reason, outside the model, to prefer the slow path, and one to prefer the fast path.




Hint

With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\), how many points does inflation fall each year at \(\tilde{Y} = -1.5\) percent? The fast path needs an output gap beyond the slider: use rate_for_output and simulate.


interact(disinflation,
         Y_rec=FloatSlider(value=-1.5, min=-3.0, max=-0.5, step=0.5, description="output in the recession (%)", style=WIDE),
         t_star=IntSlider(value=4, min=1, max=9, step=1, description="years of tight policy t*", style=WIDE),
         nu=fixed(0.5));

Source. The model of Fig. 12 above, adapted from Fig. 12.12 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) At \(\tilde{Y} = -1.5\) percent, inflation falls by \(0.5 \times 1.5 = 0.75\) points a year, so a fall of 6 points takes \(6/0.75 = 8\) years. With \(t^* = 8\) the title reads “π: 10.0% → 4.0%” and “output lost: 12.0 %-years”.
(b) 12 percent-years either way. The fast path needs inflation to fall 3 points a year, so \(\tilde{Y} = -3/0.5 = -6\) percent for two years: again 12 percent-years. Equation (9) gives the same number directly, \((10 - 4)/0.5 = 12\).
(c) By the IS curve, \(R = \bar{r} - \tilde{Y}/\bar{b}\): \(R = 5 + 1.5/2 = 5.75\) percent for eight years, or \(R = 5 + 6/2 = 8\) percent for two years.
for Y_floor, years in [(-1.5, 8), (-6.0, 2)]:
    R_tight = rate_for_output(Y_floor)                     # the IS curve solved for R
    Y_seq, pi_seq = simulate([R_tight] * years + [R_BAR], pi_start=10.0)
    print(f"Y~ = {Y_floor:+.1f}% for {years} years: R = {R_tight:.2f}%, inflation {pi_seq[-1]:.1f}%,"
          f" output lost {-Y_seq.sum():.1f} percent-years")
(d) For the slow path: a deep recession brings bankruptcies and long spells of unemployment, which can do lasting harm that the model’s straight-line Phillips curve leaves out, and a deep recession is hard to sustain politically. For the fast path: a quick, visible disinflation may convince people sooner that inflation is coming down, so that expected inflation falls faster than the adaptive rule \(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\) assumes, which would make the disinflation cheaper. Eight years of tight policy also leave plenty of time for a government to give up halfway.

Problem 12 (Challenge): What does a policy mistake cost from start to finish? A hypothetical central bank wrongly believes that a demand shock \(\bar{a}' = -1.5\) has hit the economy, as in Fig. 21. For four years (years 0 to 3) it sets the real rate by equation (3) for that shock, while in truth \(\bar{a} = 0\). Inflation was 2 percent before year 0. In year 4 the central bank sees its mistake, and it brings inflation back to 2 percent over the next four years (years 4 to 7) with a constant real rate.


With the slider: which real rate does it set, what is true output, and how fast does inflation rise?


What is inflation at the end of year 3?


Which real rate brings inflation back to 2 percent in four years (equation (8))? What is output then?


Add up the output gaps of all eight years. Show with equation (6) that the sum had to be zero. If the mistake costs no output in total, what does it cost?




Hint

Equation (6) links the inflation of year 7 to the inflation before year 0 and to the sum of all the output gaps in between. For the numbers, pass a list of eight real interest rates to simulate.


interact(great_inflation,
         a_perc=FloatSlider(value=-1.5, min=-3.0, max=-0.5, step=0.5, description="demand shock policymakers believe in ā′", style=WIDE),
         nu=fixed(0.5));

Source. The model of Fig. 21 above, adapted from Fig. 12.21 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Equation (3) for the believed shock: \(R' = 5 + (-1.5)/2 = 4.25\) percent. On the true IS curve, \(\tilde{Y} = -2\,(4.25 - 5) = +1.5\) percent, so inflation rises by \(0.5 \times 1.5 = 0.75\) points a year (the slider’s title shows \(\Delta\pi = +0.75\)).
(b) \(2 + 4 \times 0.75 = 5.0\) percent.
(c) Equation (8) with \(\pi_{-1} = 5\), \(\pi^T = 2\) and \(T = 4\): \(R = 5 + (5 - 2)/(0.5 \times 2 \times 4) = 5.75\) percent. Output is then \(-2\,(5.75 - 5) = -1.5\) percent for four years, and inflation runs 4.25, 3.5, 2.75 and 2.0 percent.
R_mistake = rate_for_output(0.0, a=-1.5)                   # equation (3) for a shock that never happened
R_back = R_BAR + (5.0 - 2.0) / (NU * B_BAR * 4)            # equation (8): from 5 to 2 percent in 4 years
Y_trip, pi_trip = simulate([R_mistake] * 4 + [R_back] * 4, pi_start=2.0)
print(f"R = {R_mistake:.2f}% for 4 years, then {R_back:.2f}% for 4 years")
print("Output gaps:", Y_trip)
print("Inflation:  ", pi_trip)
print(f"Sum of the gaps {Y_trip.sum():.1f}; sum of the squared gaps {(Y_trip ** 2).sum():.1f}")
(d) The gaps are \(+1.5\) in years 0 to 3 and \(-1.5\) in years 4 to 7, so they add up to \(4 \times 1.5 - 4 \times 1.5 = 0\). This had to happen. With no price shocks, equation (6) says \(\pi_7 = \pi_{-1} + \bar{\nu}\sum_{s=0}^{7}\tilde{Y}_s\), and since \(\pi_7 = \pi_{-1} = 2\), the sum must be zero: every round trip of inflation needs booms and slumps that cancel. The cost of the mistake is not lost output on balance but instability: four years of boom must be paid for with four years of recession of the same size (the squared gaps add up to 18), and inflation stays above 2 percent for seven years. In practice a recession hurts more than an equal boom helps, because the job losses fall on some families, so the mistake is costly even though the gaps add up to zero. This is the story of the 1970s and the early 1980s in miniature (Figs. 13, 21 and 12).

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: 13. Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework
text:
Model overview
What happens to output and inflation when the central bank stops choosing the interest rate case by case and commits to a fixed rule instead? This chapter answers with the AS/AD model. A simple rule links the real interest rate to inflation. Put into the IS curve of Chapter 11, it gives a downward-sloping aggregate demand (AD) curve. The Phillips curve of Chapter 12, written in levels, is an upward-sloping aggregate supply (AS) curve. Two equations then pin down two unknowns, this period’s output and inflation. Because firms expect last period’s inflation, the AS curve moves from one period to the next, and the model becomes dynamic: it tells us how the economy finds its way home to the steady state once a shock has hit.
We build the model in five blocks, each going from its assumptions to its solution and then to its predictions. The first block derives the AD curve and the second the AS curve. The third puts them together: the steady state, the solution for one period, the path over time, the total output cost of an episode, and the chapter’s three events (an inflation shock, a disinflation and a demand shock). The fourth writes the rule for the nominal interest rate that central banks actually set, and adds a rule that also reacts to output. The fifth lets expectations look ahead, which is why credibility matters. At the end, ### The model in code turns the results into Python functions and checks each of them with numbers.
Notation and numbers. A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number we take from outside the model: \(\bar{a}\), \(\bar{b}\), \(\bar{m}\), \(\bar{\nu}\), \(\bar{o}\), \(\bar{r}\), \(\bar{\pi}\). A tilde marks short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\), the percentage gap between actual and potential output. The subscript \(t\) counts periods (years). All worked examples, and every diagram of this notebook, use one baseline: an inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent (the target of the U.S., the U.K., the euro area and Japan), John Taylor’s policy response \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) (used again in Fig. 16), the interest sensitivity \(\bar{b} = 2\) of Chapter 11’s example, and an illustrative Phillips-curve slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\). The shocks are an inflation shock \(\bar{o} = 2\) points for one period, a demand shock \(\bar{a} = 2\) points for nine periods, and a cut in the target from 4 to 2 percent (the numbers of textbook Fig. 13.20).

The policy rule and the AD curve

Assumptions
1. The IS curve (Chapter 11). Short-run output depends on the real interest rate \(R_t\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}).\]
Spending falls below normal when borrowing costs more than the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\), and \(\bar{b} > 0\) says how strongly it reacts. The aggregate demand shock \(\bar{a}\) moves spending at every interest rate.
2. A monetary policy rule. In Chapter 12 the central bank picked \(R_t\) through the MP curve. Now it follows a rule, a fixed recipe that maps what it observes into an interest rate:
\[R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \tag{1}\]
Here \(\bar{\pi}\) is the inflation target and \(\bar{m} > 0\) is the policy response. The recipe has two steps: measure how far inflation is from the target, then set the real interest rate \(\bar{m}\) times that many points above \(\bar{r}\). With \(\bar{m} = 1/2\), inflation of 3 percent, one point above the target, calls for a real rate half a point above \(\bar{r}\), and inflation of 1 percent calls for a rate half a point below it. The rule looks at inflation only; the fourth block lets it look at output too.


Solving the model
The rule (1) gives exactly the interest-rate gap \(R_t - \bar{r}\) that appears in the IS curve, so we substitute it (Appendix C.9):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,\underbrace{(R_t - \bar{r})}_{=\ \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})} = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}).\]
This is the AD curve:
\[\text{AD:}\quad \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \tag{2}\]
The interest rate has disappeared: the AD curve links two endogenous variables, output and inflation. In the diagram output goes on the horizontal axis and inflation on the vertical axis, so we also solve (2) for \(\pi_t\). Move the inflation term to the left and \(\tilde{Y}_t\) to the right, then divide by \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\):
\[\bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) = \bar{a} - \tilde{Y}_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_t = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a} - \tilde{Y}_t}{\bar{b}\bar{m}}.\]
In the diagram the AD curve is a straight line through the point \((\tilde{Y}, \pi) = (\bar{a}, \bar{\pi})\) with slope \(-1/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\). In the baseline \(\bar{b}\bar{m} = 2 \times 0.5 = 1\): each point of inflation above the target costs one point of output.
Follow the chain for inflation of 3 percent: the rule raises \(R_t - \bar{r}\) to \(0.5 \times (3 - 2) = 0.5\), and the IS curve turns that into \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0 - 2 \times 0.5 = -1\) percent.
Intuition. The AD curve slopes down because of the central bank, not because buyers react to prices as on a market demand curve. When the bank sees inflation above its target, it raises the real interest rate, spending falls, and output drops below potential. A weaker economy brings inflation down later, and that is the bank’s aim.


What the model predicts
The AD curve is a straight line, so each effect below is the same at every point of it (Appendix C.7):

Two facts are worth keeping. First, \(\bar{b}\) and \(\bar{m}\) enter only through their product \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\), so a tougher central bank and a more interest-sensitive economy give the same AD curve. Second, inflation on target always goes with \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a}\): whatever \(\bar{m}\) is, with no demand shock the bank wants output at potential when inflation is on target.



The Phillips curve as the AS curve

Assumptions
3. The Phillips curve (Chapter 12). The change in inflation rises with short-run output and with inflation shocks \(\bar{o}\), such as a jump in oil prices:
\[\Delta\pi_t \equiv \pi_t - \pi_{t-1} = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}, \qquad \bar{\nu} > 0.\]
4. Adaptive expectations. Firms expect this period’s inflation to equal last period’s: \(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\). When period \(t\) begins, \(\pi_{t-1}\) is already known, so it is a given number for the period, not an unknown.


Solving the model
Write out \(\Delta\pi_t\) and add \(\pi_{t-1}\) to both sides:
\[\pi_t - \pi_{t-1} = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{AS:}\quad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}. \tag{3}\]
Using \(\pi_{t-1} = \pi^e_t\), the same equation reads \(\pi_t = \pi^e_t + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\): inflation is what firms expected, plus a push from a hot economy, plus any shock. In the diagram the AS curve is a straight line with slope \(\bar{\nu}\) that crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at the height \(\pi_{t-1} + \bar{o}\).
Intuition. Firms raise their prices in step with the inflation they expect. When demand pushes output above potential, they pay overtime and run machines harder, so they raise prices faster than that to cover the extra cost. In a slump they raise them more slowly.


What the model predicts








A change in …

in the AS/AD diagram
