title: 13. Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework
text:
Practice problems
These problems put the chapter to work in three ways: conceptual problems apply the AS/AD model to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data, and modeling problems use the chapter’s interactive diagrams to answer policy questions. Each problem is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it on your own first, then open the Hint, and open the Solution only at the end. The sliders of the modeling problems run when you open this notebook in Colab (badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of the figure that each problem names.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): One rule, two mortgage markets. The headline rate of the U.S. mortgage market is the rate on a 30-year fixed-rate loan, which Freddie Mac publishes every week (Primary Mortgage Market Survey). A household with such a loan keeps paying the same rate when the Fed raises its own. Compare two hypothetical countries that differ only in the interest sensitivity \(\bar{b}\) of their IS curve. In Fixia every mortgage has a fixed rate and \(\bar{b} = 1\); in Floatia mortgage rates are reset every year and \(\bar{b} = 3\). Both central banks follow the rule (1) with \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent and \(\bar{m} = 1/2\), and there is no demand shock (\(\bar{a} = 0\)).

Write the AD curve (2) of each country. Which one is flatter in the AS/AD diagram?
Inflation rises to 4 percent in both countries. How far below potential does each AD curve put output?
Fixia’s central bank wants each point of inflation above the target to cost as much output as it costs in Floatia. Which \(\bar{m}\) must it choose? By how much must it then raise its real interest rate when inflation is 4 percent?



Hint

The AD curve contains \(\bar{b}\) and \(\bar{m}\) only through their product \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\), so compute that product for each country first. In the diagram, with inflation on the vertical axis, the AD curve has the slope \(-1/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\).

Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution


Put each \(\bar{b}\) into the AD curve (2), with \(\bar{a} = 0\):

\[\text{Fixia: } \tilde{Y}_t = -1 \times \tfrac{1}{2}\,(\pi_t - 2) = -0.5\,(\pi_t - 2), \qquad
\text{Floatia: } \tilde{Y}_t = -3 \times \tfrac{1}{2}\,(\pi_t - 2) = -1.5\,(\pi_t - 2).\]
Solved for inflation, the slopes in the diagram are \(-1/0.5 = -2\) in Fixia and \(-1/1.5 \approx -0.67\) in Floatia. Floatia’s AD curve is flatter: the same rise in inflation moves its output three times as much, because a higher interest rate reaches its households’ budgets at once.

At \(\pi_t = 4\) both rules raise the real interest rate by \(\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) = 0.5 \times 2 = 1\) point. Fixia’s output falls by \(\bar{b} \times 1 = 1\) percent, Floatia’s by \(3 \times 1 = 3\) percent.
The two AD curves are the same when the products are equal: \(1 \times \bar{m} = 3 \times 0.5\), so \(\bar{m} = 1.5\). At 4 percent inflation, Fixia’s central bank must then raise the real rate by \(1.5 \times 2 = 3\) points, three times Floatia’s 1 point. With \(\bar{r} = 2\), the nominal rule (10) gives \(i = 2 + 4 + 3 = 9\) percent in Fixia and \(i = 2 + 4 + 1 = 7\) percent in Floatia.

Interpretation. Where interest rates reach spending only weakly, a central bank must move its rate further to get the same effect on output. The structure of the economy (\(\bar{b}\)) and the toughness of the central bank (\(\bar{m}\)) are two halves of one number. A check with the notebook’s AD function:
print(ad_output(4.0, b=1.0), ad_output(4.0, b=3.0), ad_output(4.0, m=1.5, b=1.0))
It prints -1.0 -3.0 -3.0.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): The Great Inflation and the Taylor principle. Richard Clarida, Jordi Galí and Mark Gertler estimated how strongly the Fed’s interest rate responded to expected inflation (NBER Working Paper 6442, Table 1, with the output gap measured from GDP). In their estimates, one more point of expected inflation raised the fed funds rate by 0.80 points from 1960 to mid-1979, and by 1.80 points from mid-1979, when Paul Volcker took over the Fed, to 1996. Use the notebook’s baseline \(\bar{b} = 2\) and \(\bar{\nu} = 1\).

In the nominal rule (10), one point of inflation raises \(i_t\) by \(1 + \bar{m}\) points. Which \(\bar{m}\) does each estimate imply?
Compute \(\lambda = 1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\) for each period.
Inflation starts 1 point above the target, and no other shock hits. Use equation (7) to find the inflation gap after 4 periods under each policy.
What do your numbers suggest about U.S. inflation in the 1970s (Fig. 19), and after 1979?



Hint

A response below one means that the real rate \(R = i - \pi\) falls when inflation rises, so \(\bar{m}\) is negative. Equation (7) says that after \(t\) periods the inflation gap is \(\lambda^t\) times the gap it started from.

Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution


Before 1979, \(1 + \bar{m} = 0.80\), so \(\bar{m} = -0.20\): one point of inflation lowered the real rate by 0.2 points. After 1979, \(1 + \bar{m} = 1.80\), so \(\bar{m} = 0.80\): one point of inflation raised the real rate by 0.8 points.
Before 1979, \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 2 \times (-0.20) \times 1 = -0.40\), so \(\lambda = 1/(1 - 0.40) = 1/0.60 \approx 1.667\). After 1979, \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 2 \times 0.80 \times 1 = 1.60\), so \(\lambda = 1/2.60 \approx 0.385\).
The gap after 4 periods is \(\lambda^4 \times 1\). Before 1979 it is \(1.667^4 \approx 7.72\) points: the gap grows by two-thirds every period, to 1.67, 2.78, 4.63 and 7.72 points. After 1979 it is \(0.385^4 \approx 0.022\) points: the gap almost disappears.
With \(\bar{m} < 0\) the AD curve slopes up. Higher inflation lowers the real rate, raises spending, and pushes inflation up further, so any inflation shock feeds on itself. That fits the drift of U.S. inflation from between 1.1 and 1.6 percent a year in 1960–1965 to more than 11 percent in 1974 and in 1979–1980 (the data of Fig. 17), with the oil shocks on top. After 1979 the Fed moved its rate more than one for one with inflation, the Taylor principle of equation (10), and \(\lambda < 1\) made every inflation gap die out. One caution: an estimate is not a certainty. The paper reports a standard error of 0.09 for the pre-1979 response, so 0.80 lies about two standard errors below one.

A check with solve_asad, period by period:
for beta in [0.80, 1.80]:
    m_est = beta - 1                                  # i rises by 1 + m points per point of inflation
    lam_est = 1 / (1 + B_BAR * m_est * NU_BAR)
    pi_e = PI_BAR + 1.0                               # start 1 point above the target
    for t in range(1, 5):
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, m=m_est)
        pi_e = pi                                     # adaptive expectations
    print(f"beta = {beta:.2f}: m = {m_est:+.2f}, λ = {lam_est:.3f}, gap after 4 periods = {pi - PI_BAR:.3f}")
It prints a gap of 7.716 points for \(\beta = 0.80\) and 0.022 points for \(\beta = 1.80\).

Problem 3 (Intermediate): A policy rule in real time. Athanasios Orphanides showed that the advice of a Taylor rule computed with revised data can differ a lot from the advice policymakers could compute at the time (American Economic Review, 2001). The file of Fig. 17 shows the problem for 2021. CPI inflation was 4.68 percent. The output gap was −1.29 percent in the data published in March 2023, but +0.81 percent in today’s data. Use the richer rule of assumption 9 with the weights of John Taylor’s 1993 rule, \(\bar{m} = \bar{x} = 1/2\) (Taylor 1993), and \(\bar{r} = \bar{\pi} = 2\) percent.

Compute the real-rate gap \(R - \bar{r}\) that the rule asks for with each vintage, and the nominal rate \(i = R + \pi\).
By how much do the two recommendations differ? Show that the difference equals \(\bar{x}\) times the revision of the output gap.
The fed funds rate averaged 0.08 percent in 2021 (Fig. 16). Does the vintage change the verdict that policy was loose? What does the example teach about rules that react to the output gap?



Hint

Assumption 9 reads \(R - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi - \bar{\pi}) + \bar{x}\tilde{Y}\). Only the term \(\bar{x}\tilde{Y}\) changes from one vintage to the other. For the nominal rate, add \(\bar{r}\) and \(\pi\) to the real-rate gap.

Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution


The inflation term is the same in both vintages: \(\bar{m}(\pi - \bar{\pi}) = 0.5 \times (4.68 - 2) = 1.34\).


March 2023 data: \(R - \bar{r} = 1.34 + 0.5 \times (-1.29) = 1.34 - 0.645 = 0.695\), so \(i = \bar{r} + \pi + (R - \bar{r}) = 2 + 4.68 + 0.695 = 7.375\) percent.
Today’s data: \(R - \bar{r} = 1.34 + 0.5 \times 0.81 = 1.745\), so \(i = 2 + 4.68 + 1.745 = 8.425\) percent.


\(8.425 - 7.375 = 1.05\) points. When we subtract one rule from the other, every term except the output term cancels: \(\Delta i = \bar{x}\,\Delta\tilde{Y} = 0.5 \times (0.81 - (-1.29)) = 0.5 \times 2.10 = 1.05\) points.
Both recommendations lie more than 7 points above the actual 0.08 percent, so “too loose in 2021” holds with either vintage. Potential output cannot be observed, so a rule that reacts to the output gap inherits the errors of its estimate. A rule on inflation alone, like the chapter’s rule (1), avoids that problem, but it answers a demand shock only after the shock has raised inflation. A check in Python:

Write the AS curve for the baseline and for the tougher policy and subtract: \(\Delta\pi_1 = \bar{\nu}\,\Delta\tilde{Y}_1\), so \(\Delta\tilde{Y}_1 = \Delta\pi_1/\bar{\nu}\). Solution


With \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), period-1 output is \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -2\bar{m}\lambda \times 2 = -4\bar{m}/(1 + 2\bar{m})\). The limit \(4\bar{m}/(1 + 2\bar{m}) \le 0.9\) means \(4\bar{m} \le 0.9 + 1.8\bar{m}\), so \(\bar{m} \le 0.9/2.2 \approx 0.41\). On the slider, \(\bar{m} = 0.40\) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -0.89\) percent, while \(\bar{m} = 0.45\) gives −0.95 percent, too deep. Period 1 is the deepest because then the whole 2-point gap between expected inflation (4 percent) and the new target is still there. From then on the gap, and with it the recession \(\tilde{Y}_t = -\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}')\), shrinks by the factor \(\lambda\) each period.
With \(\bar{m} = 0.40\) (\(\lambda \approx 0.56\)), inflation first falls below 2.1 percent in period 6 (2.06 percent; it is still 2.11 in period 5). With \(\bar{m} = 0.5\) it gets there in period 5, and with \(\bar{m} = 1\) in period 3.
The total is −2.00 percent of a year’s output under all three policies. By equation (8), the loss is \((\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')/\bar{\nu} = 2\) whatever \(\bar{m}\) is. The minister’s limit buys a shallower recession spread over more periods, and more periods of inflation above the target; it does not make the disinflation cheaper. Only a smaller gap between expected inflation and the target would (Fig. 20). The numbers in Python:

for m in [0.4, 0.5, 1.0]:
    path_m = simulate(NO_SHOCK, NO_SHOCK, PI_OLD, 2.0, m=m)
    below = path_m[(path_m.period > 0) & (path_m.pi < 2.1)]
    print(f"m = {m}: Y1 = {path_m.Y[1]:.2f}%, first period below 2.1%: {below.period.iloc[0]}, "
          f"total output = {total_output(pi_start=PI_OLD, pi_bar=2.0, m=m):.2f}")

Problem 11 (Intermediate): How tough must the central bank be during a stimulus? In March 2021 the United States enacted the American Rescue Plan Act, a large fiscal package (Public Law 117-2, via GovInfo). Model a stimulus like it as a demand shock of \(\bar{a} = 2\) points (an illustrative size) that lasts 4 periods. The central bank wants inflation to stay at or below 3 percent throughout.

Congress could have voted a smaller stimulus instead. Keep the baseline \(\bar{m} = 0.5\): what is the largest demand shock \(\bar{a}\), lasting 4 periods, that keeps inflation at or below 3 percent? Use equation (9) and the fact that, while the shock lasts, the gap \(\pi_t - \pi^c\) shrinks by the factor \(\lambda\) each period. Check your answer with simulate.
Now keep the full stimulus \(\bar{a} = 2\). Find the smallest \(\bar{m}\) on the slider that keeps the peak at or below 3 percent.
Compare the baseline \(\bar{m} = 0.5\) with your \(\bar{m}\) from (b). Add up output over the 4 periods of the stimulus, and over the periods after it ends. How much of the boom does the tougher central bank take away? Does the stimulus raise output over the whole cycle under either policy? Use equation (8).



Hint

For (a), inflation starts at \(\bar{\pi}\), where its gap to \(\pi^c = \bar{\pi} + \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\) is \(-\bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\). After \(t\) periods the gap is \(\lambda^t\) times as large, so \(\pi_t - \bar{\pi} = (1 - \lambda^t)\,\bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\), highest in the last period of the shock. For (b), the title shows peak inflation. For (c), hover over panel (b) to read output period by period, or add up the column Y of a simulation.


interact(demand_shock_summary, a=fixed(2.0),
         last=IntSlider(value=4, min=2, max=9, step=1, description="last period of the shock", style=WIDE),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=1.5, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
         nu=fixed(1.0));

Source. The model of Fig. 15 above, adapted from Fig. 13.15 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution


With \(\bar{m} = 0.5\), \(\lambda = 0.5\) and \(\bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m}) = \bar{a}\), so \(\pi_t - \bar{\pi} = (1 - 0.5^t)\,\bar{a}\). Inflation climbs while the shock lasts, so it peaks in period 4 with \(\pi_4 - \bar{\pi} = (15/16)\,\bar{a}\); for \(\bar{a} = 2\) that is 1.875 points, the peak of 3.88 percent in the chart title. The ceiling allows 1 point above the target: \((15/16)\,\bar{a} \le 1\), so \(\bar{a} \le 16/15 \approx 1.07\). A stimulus about half as large would have kept inflation at or below 3 percent with the baseline policy; simulate confirms a peak of 3.00 percent.
With \(\bar{m} = 0.75\) the peak is still 3.30 percent (\(\pi^c \approx 3.33\)). With \(\bar{m} = 1\) it is 2.99 percent, so \(\bar{m} = 1\) is the smallest value on the slider that meets the ceiling.
While the stimulus lasts, output adds up to 1.875 percent of a year’s output with \(\bar{m} = 0.5\), and to 0.988 percent with \(\bar{m} = 1\): the tougher central bank takes away 47 percent of the boom. After the stimulus ends, output adds up to −1.875 and −0.988 percent, so the recession that follows shrinks by the same share. Over the whole cycle the sum is 0.000 under both policies. Inflation starts and ends at 2 percent and there is no inflation shock, so equation (8) gives \(\sum\tilde{Y}_t = 0\): in this model a temporary stimulus does not raise output in total, it only moves output forward in time and leaves a spell of higher inflation behind. The tougher central bank cuts the boom, the bust and the extra inflation together, because by equation (9) it needs less excess inflation to offset the same shock: \(\pi^c\) is 3 percent with \(\bar{m} = 1\), against 4 percent with \(\bar{m} = 0.5\). The numbers in Python:

a_max = 1 / (1 - 0.5 ** 4)                         # (15/16) a = 1 point above the target
small = simulate(shock_list(a_max, 4), NO_SHOCK)   # the baseline m = 0.5
print(f"(a) largest stimulus a = {a_max:.2f}; its peak = {small.pi.max():.2f}%")
for m in [0.5, 1.0]:
    boom = simulate(shock_list(2.0, 4), NO_SHOCK, m=m)
    during = boom.Y.loc[1:4].sum()                 # periods 1 to 4, while the stimulus lasts
    after = boom.Y.loc[5:].sum()                   # from period 5 on
    print(f"m = {m}: peak pi = {boom.pi.max():.2f}%, output during = {during:.3f}, after = {after:.3f}, "
          f"whole cycle = {round(boom.Y.sum(), 3) + 0.0:.3f}")

Problem 12 (Challenge): How much credibility does a cheap disinflation need? Central banks build credibility with laws and track records. The Bank of England Act 1998, for example, makes price stability the Bank’s first objective in monetary policy (section 11). Take a hypothetical central bank that cuts its target from 4 to 2 percent, as in Fig. 20. In period 1 a share \(c\) of the cut, the credibility, enters expected inflation; after period 1 firms again expect last period’s inflation.

With \(\bar{m} = 0.5\), find the smallest credibility on the slider that keeps the period-1 recession at or below 0.25 percent.
Redo (a) with \(\bar{m} = 1\). Why does a tougher central bank need more credibility to meet the same limit?
Derive the total output cost of the whole disinflation: show that \(\sum_t \tilde{Y}_t = -(1 - c)(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')/\bar{\nu}\), where \(\bar{\pi} = 4\) and \(\bar{\pi}' = 2\) are the old and the new target.
Check your formula for \(c = 0.5\) with a loop over solve_asad.



Hint

Period-1 output is \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda(1 - c)(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')\). For (c), add up the AS curve (11) with \(\bar{o} = 0\), written as \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t = \pi_t - \pi^e_t\), over all periods, as in equation (8). From period 2 on, \(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\), so the middle terms cancel. For (d), set expected inflation to \(c \times 2 + (1 - c) \times 4\) before the loop, and to this period’s inflation at the end of each pass.


interact(credible_disinflation,
         credibility=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.0, max=1.0, step=0.05, description="credibility of the new target",
                                 style=WIDE),
         pi_new=fixed(2.0),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
         nu=fixed(1.0));

Source. The model of Fig. 20 above, adapted from Fig. 13.20 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution


With \(\bar{m} = 0.5\), \(\lambda = 0.5\) and \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -2 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 \times (1 - c) \times 2 = -(1 - c)\). The limit needs \(1 - c \le 0.25\), so \(c \ge 0.75\). The title reads \(\tilde{Y} = -0.25\) percent at credibility 0.75, and −0.30 percent at 0.70.
With \(\bar{m} = 1\), \(\lambda = 1/3\) and \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -2 \times 1 \times \tfrac{1}{3} \times (1 - c) \times 2 = -\tfrac{4}{3}(1 - c)\). The limit needs \(1 - c \le 0.1875\), so \(c \ge 0.8125\); on the slider, \(c = 0.85\) gives −0.20 percent, while \(c = 0.80\) gives −0.27 percent. Every point of the cut that firms do not believe must be squeezed out by the rule. A tougher rule squeezes it out faster, with a deeper recession in period 1: each unbelieved point costs \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda = 2/3\) of a point of output instead of \(1/2\). So the same limit needs more belief.
With \(\bar{o} = 0\), the AS curve (11) gives \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t = \pi_t - \pi^e_t\). Add it up over \(t = 1, \dots, T\), using \(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\) from period 2 on:

\[\bar{\nu}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\tilde{Y}_t = (\pi_1 - \pi^e_1) + (\pi_2 - \pi_1) + \dots + (\pi_T - \pi_{T-1}) = \pi_T - \pi^e_1.\]
As \(T\) grows, the economy returns to its new steady state, so \(\pi_T \to \bar{\pi}'\) (equation 4). With \(\pi^e_1 = c\,\bar{\pi}' + (1 - c)\,\bar{\pi}\):
\[\sum_t \tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{\pi}' - c\,\bar{\pi}' - (1 - c)\,\bar{\pi}}{\bar{\nu}} = -\frac{(1 - c)(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')}{\bar{\nu}}.\]
With \(c = 0\) this is the cost of 2 of equation (8); with \(c = 0.75\) it is 0.5, and with \(c = 1\) it is zero. Credibility cuts the total cost in proportion to the share of the cut that people believe, even though belief lasts only one period here. That is why central banks invest in laws, independence and a track record.

The loop gives the same number as the formula, −1.0000:

c = 0.5
pi_e = c * 2.0 + (1 - c) * PI_OLD          # period 1: a share c of the cut is believed
total = 0.0
for t in range(1, 201):
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, pi_bar=2.0)
    total = total + Y
    pi_e = pi                              # from period 2 on: adaptive expectations
print(f"sum of Y~ = {total:.4f}; formula: {-(1 - c) * (PI_OLD - 2.0) / NU_BAR:.4f}")

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: 14. Financial Crises and the Short-Run Model
text:
Model overview
Why did the 2008 financial crisis cause such a deep recession, even though the Federal Reserve cut its interest rate to zero? This chapter adds one idea to the short-run model of Chapters 11 to 13. Firms and households do not borrow at the central bank’s rate but at a higher one, and the gap between the two, a risk premium or financial friction, jumps when lenders get scared. A bigger friction raises borrowing costs even while the central bank is cutting, so it hurts the economy just like a fall in aggregate demand. Add the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates, and falling inflation can push the real interest rate up and deepen the slump.
The section builds the model in four blocks, each going from assumptions to solution to predictions. The first puts the friction into the IS/MP model. The second derives the new AD curve and solves the AS/AD model period by period. The third adds the Fisher equation and the zero lower bound, and shows how a deflationary spiral starts. The fourth writes down the simple algebra behind the policy debate: balance sheets and leverage, the value of assets, the Fed’s balance sheet, forward guidance and fiscal stimulus. At the end, ### The model in code turns the results into Python functions and checks each one with numbers. It is followed by the drawing tools for the diagrams and two tools for the data figures (recession shading and a peak-to-trough calculator).
Notation. A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number set outside the model, such as \(\bar{a}\), \(\bar{b}\), \(\bar{f}\) or \(\bar{\pi}\). Short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\) is the percentage gap between actual and potential output. All interest and inflation rates are in percent per year. In the code we write a, f, m, B_BAR, NU, and so on.
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers, apart from a few examples. The algebra below, the checks and every diagram of this notebook use one illustrative set of values:

the IS curve: a marginal product of capital \(\bar{r} = 2\) percent and \(\bar{b} = 1\), so each point of interest rate above \(\bar{r}\) costs 1 percent of output;
the policy rule and the Phillips curve: an inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, \(\bar{m} = 1\) and \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\);
2008: the housing bust lowers demand by \(\bar{a}' = -2\) and the crisis adds a risk premium \(\bar{f} = 4\) points;
1929: the Fed raises the interest rate by 3 points and the stock market crash lowers demand by \(\bar{a}' = -3\).

With these values the model reproduces the textbook’s example numbers: \(-2\) and \(-4\) percent in Fig. 2, and \(-3\), \(-6\) and \(-9\) percent in Figs. 12 and 13.

The IS/MP model with a financial friction

Assumptions
1. The IS curve (Chapter 11). Short-run output falls when the real interest rate \(R_t\) that firms and households pay rises above the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}).\]
The demand shock \(\bar{a}\) collects everything that moves spending at a given interest rate: consumer confidence, household wealth, government purchases, exports. The parameter \(\bar{b} > 0\) measures how strongly investment reacts to the interest rate.
2. The central bank sets the fed funds rate. The Fed controls the (real) fed funds rate \(R^{ff}_t\), the rate at which banks lend to each other overnight. In Chapters 11 to 13 we assumed that this was the rate firms pay. Not any more.
3. The financial friction. Lenders charge private borrowers a premium \(\bar{f} \geq 0\) on top of the fed funds rate, to cover the risk of not being repaid:
\[R_t = R^{ff}_t + \bar{f}. \tag{1}\]
In calm times \(\bar{f}\) is close to zero and the Fed sets the borrowing rate directly. In a financial crisis \(\bar{f}\) jumps. Fig. 1 measures it in the data as the spread between corporate and government bonds.


Solving the model
Step 1: the IS curve in terms of the Fed’s rate. Substitute equation (1) into the IS curve and split the bracket:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff}_t + \bar{f} - \bar{r}) = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff}_t - \bar{r}),\]
so that
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \underbrace{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}}_{\text{demand shock}} - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff}_t - \bar{r}). \tag{2}\]
Measured against the rate the Fed controls, the friction looks exactly like a lower \(\bar{a}\). Intuition: firms do not care why their loan is expensive. A higher premium cuts investment just as a loss of confidence would.
Step 2: the rate that restores potential output. Suppose the Fed wants \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\). Set the left side of (2) to zero, move \(\bar{b}(R^{ff}_t - \bar{r})\) to the other side and divide by \(\bar{b}\) (Appendix C.9):
\[0 = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff}_t - \bar{r}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R^{ff}_t - \bar{r} = \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}} - \bar{f},\]
so
\[R^{ff,*} = \bar{r} + \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}} - \bar{f}. \tag{3}\]
The Fed must offset the demand shock (the term \(\bar{a}/\bar{b}\)) and cut by one extra point for every point of risk premium.
Step 3: the 2008 example in numbers. With \(\bar{a}' = -2\) and \(\bar{b} = 1\):

housing bust, the Fed does nothing (\(R^{ff} = \bar{r} = 2\), \(\bar{f} = 0\)): \(\tilde{Y} = -2 - 0 = -2\) percent (point \(B\) of Fig. 2);
the Fed cuts to the rate (3) with \(\bar{f} = 0\): \(R^{ff} = 2 + (-2)/1 = 0\) percent and \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) (point \(C\));
the crisis adds \(\bar{f} = 4\) but the Fed stays at 0: firms pay \(R = 0 + 4 = 4\) percent, and \(\tilde{Y} = -2 - 1\times(4 - 2) = -4\) percent (point \(D\)).

To bring output back to potential, (3) asks for \(R^{ff} = 2 - 2 - 4 = -4\) percent. The third block shows why the Fed could not get there.


What the model predicts
Comparative statics. Equation (2) is linear, so each effect is a constant: the derivative of \(\tilde{Y}_t\) with respect to that parameter (Appendix C.7).









A one-point rise in …
changes \(\tilde{Y}_t\) by
What moves in the IS/MP diagram
What the Fed must do, from (3)




the risk premium \(\bar{f}\)
\(-\bar{b} = -1\) point
the MP line (the rate firms pay) shifts up by 1
cut \(R^{ff}\) by 1 point


the fed funds rate \(R^{ff}\)
\(-\bar{b} = -1\) point
the MP line shifts up by 1
(this is the Fed’s tool)


the demand shock \(\bar{a}\)
\(+1\) point
the IS curve shifts right by 1
raise \(R^{ff}\) by \(1/\bar{b} = 1\) point




A friction is a demand shock. With the Fed’s rate held fixed, a rise of \(\bar{f}\) by one point costs \(\bar{b}\) points of output, exactly like a fall of \(\bar{a}\) by \(\bar{b}\).
The Fed can offset it, point for point, as long as it can cut \(R^{ff}\) far enough. With \(\bar{f} = 2\) in our example, the friction exactly undoes the Fed’s cut of 2 points, and \(D\) lands on \(B\).
Two shocks add up. In the example, the housing bust and the friction together cost \(\bar{a}' - \bar{b}\bar{f}\) relative to the Fed’s starting rate; after the cut that offsets the bust, what is left is \(-\bar{b}\bar{f} = -4\) percent.




The new AD curve: a financial friction in the AS/AD model

Assumptions
Keep the IS curve and equation (1). Add the two remaining pieces of the AS/AD model of Chapter 13:
4. A monetary policy rule. The Fed moves its rate with the gap between inflation and its target,
\[R^{ff}_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}), \qquad \bar{m} > 0.\]
5. The AS curve. The Phillips curve with adaptive expectations (\(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\)): inflation rises above last year’s when output is above potential,
\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t.\]
The unknowns in each period are \(\tilde{Y}_t\), \(\pi_t\), \(R^{ff}_t\) and \(R_t\). Last year’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\) is already known.


Solving the model
Step 1: the borrowing rate under the rule. Put the rule into equation (1). Subtract \(\bar{r}\) from both sides of (1) first:
\[R_t - \bar{r} = (R^{ff}_t - \bar{r}) + \bar{f} = \bar{f} + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}).\]
Firms pay the premium on top of whatever the rule sets.
Step 2: the new AD curve. Substitute this into the IS curve:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\left[\bar{f} + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\right] = \underbrace{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}}_{\text{AD shock}} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \tag{4}\]
This is the familiar AD curve of Chapter 13 with \(\bar{a}\) replaced by \(\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}\). It slopes down: higher inflation makes the Fed raise rates, which lowers output. To draw it with inflation on the vertical axis, solve (4) for \(\pi_t\):
\[\pi_t = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \tilde{Y}_t}{\bar{b}\bar{m}}.\]
Step 3: this period’s output and inflation. The economy sits where AD and AS cross. Replace \(\pi_t\) in (4) by the AS curve \(\pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}) - \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t.\]
Collect the \(\tilde{Y}_t\) terms on the left, \((1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\,\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi})\), and divide:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}, \qquad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t. \tag{5}\]
In numbers. With \(\bar{b} = \bar{m} = 1\) and \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\) the denominator is \(1.5\). In the first year of the crisis, \(\pi_{t-1} = \bar{\pi} = 2\), so \(\tilde{Y}_1 = (-2 - 4 - 0)/1.5 = -4\) percent and \(\pi_1 = 2 + 0.5\times(-4) = 0\) percent: point \(B\) of Fig. 3. The rule cushions the blow a little (without it the AD shock of \(-6\) would cost 6 percent of output), because falling inflation makes the Fed cut.
Step 4: the long run. If the shocks last, the economy comes to rest where inflation stops changing. By the AS curve, \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1}\) requires \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\). Put \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) into (4) and solve for inflation:
\[0 = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_C - \bar{\pi}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_C = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}}{\bar{b}\bar{m}}. \tag{6}\]
With our numbers, \(\pi_C = 2 + (-6)/1 = -4\) percent: output returns to potential at point \(C\), but with deflation. Inflation falls until the Fed’s rule has cut the borrowing rate enough to offset the shocks.
Step 5: how fast the economy gets there. Measure inflation as its distance from the long run, \(x_t \equiv \pi_t - \pi_C\). Equation (6) says \(\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} = \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_C - \bar{\pi})\). Substitute this into the numerator of (5):
\[\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_C - \bar{\pi}) - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}) = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \pi_C) = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\,x_{t-1},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad \tilde{Y}_t = \frac{-\bar{b}\bar{m}\,x_{t-1}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.\]
Now subtract \(\pi_C\) from both sides of the AS curve and use this expression for \(\tilde{Y}_t\):
\[x_t = x_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t = x_{t-1}\left(1 - \frac{\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}\right) = \frac{x_{t-1}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.\]
Applying this \(t\) times (Appendix C.10):
\[\pi_t - \pi_C = \left(\frac{1}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}\right)^{t}(\pi_0 - \pi_C). \tag{7}\]
With \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1.5\), each period the economy closes one third of the remaining gap: \(\pi_0 - \pi_C = 2 - (-4) = 6\), so \(\pi_1 = -4 + 6\times\tfrac{2}{3} = 0\), \(\pi_2 = -4 + 6\times\tfrac{4}{9} \approx -1.3\), and so on toward \(-4\). Output follows from the formula for \(\tilde{Y}_t\) above: \(-4\), then \(-2.7\), then \(-1.8\) percent.

The friction is an AD shock. A higher \(\bar{f}\) shifts the AD curve toward lower output at every inflation rate, exactly like a lower \(\bar{a}\); the AS curve does not move at first. That is Fig. 3.
The recession is temporary, the disinflation is lasting. Output returns to potential, but inflation ends lower by \(1/\bar{m}\) for each point of premium. Starting from only 2 percent, a large enough shock ends in deflation: \(\pi_C < 0\) whenever \(\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} < -\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\pi}\), here whenever the AD shock is worse than \(-2\).
A more aggressive rule helps. A larger \(\bar{m}\) makes AD flatter. The first-year recession \((\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f})/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\) shrinks, \(\pi_C\) falls less, and by (7) the economy also converges faster.
The hidden assumption. The rule must always be able to deliver the real rate it asks for. The next block shows that deflation and the zero lower bound break this. That is why the textbook prefers the IS/MP diagram for such times (Figs. 12 and 13).




Deflation and the zero lower bound

Assumptions
6. The Fisher equation (Chapter 12). The nominal interest rate \(i_t\) equals the real rate plus inflation, \(i_t = R_t + \pi_t\). Subtract \(\pi_t\) from both sides to get the real rate, the one that enters the IS curve:
\[R_t = i_t - \pi_t. \tag{8}\]
(The textbook’s display of this rearranged equation has a plus sign in place of the minus; that is a typo, and the text around it uses the minus.) The same link holds for the Fed’s own rate: the nominal fed funds rate is \(i^{ff}_t = R^{ff}_t + \pi_t\).
7. The zero lower bound. A nominal rate cannot go (much) below zero, \(i^{ff}_t \geq 0\), because savers can always hold cash, which earns exactly zero.


Solving the model
Step 1: the nominal rate a rule asks for. Add \(\pi_t\) to both sides of the policy rule, and allow the rate to respond to output too (the Taylor rule of Chapter 13, with weight \(\bar{x}\) on output):
\[i^{ff}_t = R^{ff}_t + \pi_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) + \bar{x}\,\tilde{Y}_t. \tag{9}\]
Taylor’s original values, \(\bar{r} = \bar{\pi} = 2\) and \(\bar{m} = \bar{x} = 0.5\), give \(i^{ff}_t = 2 + \pi_t + 0.5\pi_t - 1 + 0.5\tilde{Y}_t = 1 + 1.5\,\pi_t + 0.5\,\tilde{Y}_t\), the rule of Fig. 4. In our AS/AD baseline (\(\bar{m} = 1\), \(\bar{x} = 0\)) it is \(i^{ff}_t = 2 + \pi_t + (\pi_t - 2) = 2\pi_t\): the rule asks for a negative nominal rate as soon as inflation turns negative. In the path of equation (7) that happens from period 2 on, so Fig. 3 quietly assumes something the Fed could not do.
Step 2: the floor on the real rate. Put \(i^{ff}_t \geq 0\) into \(R^{ff}_t = i^{ff}_t - \pi_t\): the lowest real fed funds rate is \(-\pi_t\). With equation (1), the lowest rate firms can pay is \(\bar{f} - \pi_t\).
Step 3: the best output the Fed can reach. Put this lowest borrowing rate into the IS curve and simplify:
\[\tilde{Y}^{\max}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(\bar{f} - \pi_t - \bar{r}), \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \tilde{Y}^{\max}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} + \bar{b}\,(\bar{r} + \pi_t). \tag{10}\]
Compare it with equation (3): the zero lower bound binds when the rate the Fed needs is below the floor, \(R^{ff,*} < -\pi_t\), which is the same as \(\tilde{Y}^{\max}_t < 0\). In numbers (2008, \(\bar{a}' = -2\), \(\bar{f} = 4\)): with inflation at 2 percent, \(\tilde{Y}^{\max} = -2 - 4 + 1\times(2 + 2) = -2\) percent, so even a zero nominal rate only brings output back to \(B\). With zero inflation the best is \(-4\) percent, and with 2 percent deflation it is \(-6\) percent.
Step 4: the deflationary spiral. Now suppose the nominal rate is stuck at some \(\bar{i}\), either at the bound or because the central bank refuses to move it (the Fed in the early 1930s). Borrowers judge the real rate by the inflation they expect, and with adaptive expectations that is last year’s: \(R_t = \bar{i} - \pi_{t-1} + \bar{f}\). The IS curve becomes
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(\bar{i} + \bar{f} - \bar{r}) + \bar{b}\,\pi_{t-1}.\]
Write the same equation one year earlier and subtract. Everything with a bar cancels:
\[\tilde{Y}_t - \tilde{Y}_{t-1} = \bar{b}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \pi_{t-2}) = \bar{b}\bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_{t-1},\]
where the last step uses the AS curve one year earlier, \(\pi_{t-1} - \pi_{t-2} = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_{t-1}\). Adding \(\tilde{Y}_{t-1}\) to both sides:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = (1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu})\,\tilde{Y}_{t-1}. \tag{11}\]
In numbers. \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu} = 1.5\), so a gap of \(-6\) percent becomes \(-9\), then \(-13.5\): each year the slump is 50 percent deeper. This is the step from \(C\) to \(D\) in Figs. 12 and 13: the crash leaves output at \(-6\) percent with inflation at zero, the slump pushes inflation to \(0 + 0.5\times(-6) = -3\) percent, the real rate rises by 3 points, and output falls to \(-9\) percent.


What the model predicts

Deflation raises the real rate. By (8), with \(i_t\) fixed, each point of lower inflation adds one point to the real rate. Normally the Fed simply cuts \(i_t\); at the zero lower bound it cannot.
Comparative statics at the bound, from equation (10): \(\partial\tilde{Y}^{\max}/\partial\pi = +\bar{b}\) (each point of deflation costs \(\bar{b} = 1\) point of reachable output), \(\partial\tilde{Y}^{\max}/\partial\bar{f} = -\bar{b}\), and \(\partial\tilde{Y}^{\max}/\partial\bar{a} = +1\). In the IS/MP diagram, deflation and a higher premium both shift the lowest possible MP line up.
Stable versus unstable. Compare equations (7) and (11). Under a rule with \(\bar{m} > 0\), falling inflation lowers the real rate, and the gap shrinks by the factor \(1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) < 1\) each year. With the nominal rate frozen, falling inflation raises the real rate, and the gap grows by the factor \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu} > 1\). There is no point of rest except \(\tilde{Y} = 0\), and the economy moves away from it: a deflationary spiral. In the language of equation (4), a frozen nominal rate behaves like a rule with a negative \(\bar{m}\).
Ways out. Anything that raises \(\tilde{Y}^{\max}\) in (10) helps: a higher \(\bar{a}\) (fiscal stimulus), a lower \(\bar{f}\) (rescuing the financial system), or higher expected inflation (anchored expectations, money growth). Lower long-term rates through asset purchases and forward guidance work in the same direction. The next block puts numbers on these. Secular stagnation is the case in which \(R^{ff,*}\) in (3) stays below the floor for years.




Balance sheets, leverage and the policy responses

Definitions
Balance sheet. For a bank, a household or the Fed, what it owns equals what it owes plus what is left for the owners:
\[\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Net worth}.\]
Leverage (Chapter 10) is the ratio of liabilities to net worth, \(\lambda \equiv \text{Liabilities}/\text{Net worth}\). A capital requirement sets a minimum for the capital ratio \(\kappa \equiv \text{Net worth}/\text{Assets}\).
Present value. An asset that pays profits \(E\) next year, growing at the rate \(g\) each year after that, is worth the discounted sum of those profits at the interest rate \(R > g\) (Appendix C.12).
The term structure (Chapter 12). An \(n\)-year interest rate is approximately the average of the short rates expected over the next \(n\) years.


Solving the model
Step 1: leverage and the capital ratio. Divide the balance sheet by net worth: \(\text{Assets}/\text{Net worth} = \lambda + 1\), and since \(\kappa\) is the inverse of that ratio,
\[\kappa = \frac{1}{1 + \lambda} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \lambda = \frac{1 - \kappa}{\kappa}.\]
A capital requirement is a cap on leverage. A 7 percent requirement allows \(\lambda = 0.93/0.07 \approx 13.3\); a 20 percent requirement allows only \(\lambda = 4\).
Step 2: why leverage magnifies losses. Liabilities are debts fixed in dollars. If the value of the assets falls by the share \(x\), the whole loss, \(x\cdot\text{Assets}\), comes out of net worth. In percent of net worth:
\[\frac{\Delta\,\text{Net worth}}{\text{Net worth}} = -\,x\,\frac{\text{Assets}}{\text{Net worth}} = -(1 + \lambda)\,x = -\frac{x}{\kappa}. \tag{12}\]
A bank with a 7 percent capital ratio loses \(3/0.07 \approx 43\) percent of its net worth when its assets lose 3 percent, and it is insolvent (net worth below zero) once they lose more than \(\kappa = 7\) percent. A 20 percent ratio absorbs a 20 percent fall. Intuition: the capital ratio is the cushion; leverage is how thin it is. A capital injection (as under TARP) raises net worth and so lowers \(\lambda\).
Step 3: asset prices. The present value of the growing profit stream is a geometric series with ratio \(q = (1+g)/(1+R) < 1\):
\[P = \frac{E}{1+R} + \frac{E(1+g)}{(1+R)^2} + \frac{E(1+g)^2}{(1+R)^3} + \dots = \frac{E}{1+R}\cdot\frac{1}{1 - q} = \frac{E}{1+R}\cdot\frac{1+R}{R - g},\]
so the price-earnings ratio is
\[\frac{P}{E} = \frac{1}{R - g}. \tag{13}\]
With \(R = 7\) percent and \(g = 2\) percent, \(P/E = 1/0.05 = 20\). A one-point rise in the discount rate, for example a higher risk premium, gives \(1/0.06 \approx 16.7\): prices fall by about 17 percent. Taking logs (Appendix C.4), \(\ln P = \ln E - \ln(R - g)\), so \(d\ln P/dR = -1/(R - g) = -20\): a rise in \(R\) of 0.01 (one point) lowers \(\ln P\) by about 0.2. That is the slope at the baseline; for a whole point the exact fall is the 17 percent above, because the slope flattens as \(R - g\) grows. A ratio far above what plausible values of \(R - g\) can explain is a sign of a bubble (Figs. 7 and 8). When such prices collapse, household wealth falls and \(\bar{a}\) drops.
Step 4: the Fed’s balance sheet. For the central bank the identity reads
\[\text{Treasuries} + \text{MBS} + \text{other assets} = \text{Currency} + \text{Reserves} + \text{other liabilities}.\]
Quantitative easing buys assets other than short-term government bonds, such as mortgage-backed securities (MBS) or long-term Treasuries. The Fed pays by crediting the sellers’ banks with reserves, so both sides grow by the same amount, without printing currency. Table 14.1 (in the Key numbers of Fig. 9) checks this identity with data.
Step 5: forward guidance. Write the \(n\)-year rate as the average of the expected short rates,
\[i^{L}_t \approx \frac{i_t + i^e_{t+1} + \dots + i^e_{t+n-1}}{n}. \tag{14}\]
Even with today’s rate \(i_t\) stuck at zero, the Fed can lower the long rate by promising to keep future rates low. Take a 4-year bond. If markets expect short rates of 0, 1, 2 and 3 percent, the long rate is \(6/4 = 1.5\) percent. A credible promise of zero for three years (0, 0, 0, 2) lowers it to \(2/4 = 0.5\) percent. Fig. 10 shows such a shift in market expectations.
Step 6: fiscal stimulus at the bound. Government purchases are part of \(\bar{a}\). At the zero lower bound the interest rate does not rise when \(\bar{a}\) rises, so by equation (10) a stimulus raises reachable output one for one: closing the gap needs \(\Delta\bar{a} = -\tilde{Y}^{\max}\). In the 2008 example that is 2 percent of potential output with inflation at 2 percent, but 6 percent if deflation of 2 percent has set in. Waiting makes the job bigger.

The model in code
We now turn the key results into Python functions, then check the algebra above with numbers. The constants hold the baseline values. Every later section of the notebook reuses these functions.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing a=0.0 gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. Names in capital letters, such as R_BAR, are constants we set once and never change.


R_BAR, B_BAR = 2.0, 1.0            # marginal product of capital 2%, interest sensitivity b = 1
PI_BAR, M_BAR, NU = 2.0, 1.0, 0.5  # inflation target 2%, policy response m = 1, Phillips slope nu = 0.5
A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS = -2.0, 4.0    # 2008: the housing bust a' = -2 and a risk premium f = 4 points
HIKE, A_CRASH = 3.0, -3.0          # 1929: the Fed's hike of 3 points and the crash a' = -3


def is_output(R, a=0.0):
    """IS curve: short-run output Y~ = a - b (R - r_bar), in percent."""
    return a - B_BAR * (R - R_BAR)


def is_rate(Y, a=0.0):
    """The IS curve solved for the real interest rate, R = r_bar + (a - Y) / b (used to draw it)."""
    return R_BAR + (a - Y) / B_BAR


def borrowing_rate(R_ff, f=0.0):
    """Equation (1): firms and households borrow at R = R_ff + f."""
    return R_ff + f


def real_rate(i, pi):
    """The Fisher equation (8): the real interest rate R = i - pi."""
    return i - pi

The AS/AD part of the model needs three more functions: the new AD curve (4), the AS curve and the point where they cross, equation (5).

def ad_output(pi, a=0.0, f=0.0, m=M_BAR):
    """Equation (4), the new AD curve: Y~ = (a - b f) - b m (pi - pi_bar)."""
    return a - B_BAR * f - B_BAR * m * (pi - PI_BAR)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_prev=PI_BAR):
    """The AS curve (the Phillips curve): pi = pi_prev + nu Y~, with pi_prev last period's inflation."""
    return pi_prev + NU * Y


def solve_asad(pi_prev, a=0.0, f=0.0, m=M_BAR):
    """Equation (5): where the AD and AS curves cross, this period's output and inflation."""
    Y = (a - B_BAR * f - B_BAR * m * (pi_prev - PI_BAR)) / (1 + B_BAR * m * NU)
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_prev)

Three small functions for the zero lower bound and for balance sheets:

def zlb_best_output(pi, a=0.0, f=0.0):
    """Equation (10): the highest output the Fed can reach with its nominal rate at zero."""
    return a - B_BAR * f + B_BAR * (R_BAR + pi)


def net_worth_change(asset_fall, capital_ratio):
    """Equation (12): the percent change in net worth when assets lose asset_fall percent."""
    return -asset_fall / capital_ratio


def price_earnings(R, g):
    """Equation (13): the price-earnings ratio 1 / (R - g), with R and g in percent."""
    return 1 / ((R - g) / 100)

pi = +0%: best output -4.0% (step by step), -4.0% (equation 10); rule (9) asks for i = +0.0%
pi = -2%: best output -6.0% (step by step), -6.0% (equation 10); rule (9) asks for i = -4.0%


Check 5: the deflationary spiral. We freeze the nominal rate at the 1929 level, \(\bar{i} = \bar{r} + 3 = 5\) percent, start from the crash (\(\bar{a}' = -3\), inflation zero) and let the real rate follow last year’s inflation. Equation (11) says each year’s gap is 1.5 times the last.

i_fixed = R_BAR + HIKE                            # the nominal rate the Fed kept (inflation was about zero)
pi_prev = 0.0
Y_prev = is_output(real_rate(i_fixed, pi_prev), A_CRASH)         # year 1: the crash, point C
print(f"Year 1: Y~ = {Y_prev:6.2f}%")
for year in range(2, 5):
    pi_prev = as_inflation(Y_prev, pi_prev)                      # last year's slump lowered inflation ...
    Y = is_output(real_rate(i_fixed, pi_prev), A_CRASH)          # ... which raises this year's real rate
    print(f"Year {year}: Y~ = {Y:6.2f}%   ratio to last year = {Y / Y_prev:.2f}  (equation 11: {1 + B_BAR * NU:.2f})")
    Y_prev = Y

Year 1: Y~ =  -6.00%
Year 2: Y~ =  -9.00%   ratio to last year = 1.50  (equation 11: 1.50)
Year 3: Y~ = -13.50%   ratio to last year = 1.50  (equation 11: 1.50)
Year 4: Y~ = -20.25%   ratio to last year = 1.50  (equation 11: 1.50)


The first two years are the points \(C\) and \(D\) of Figs. 12 and 13, \(-6\) and \(-9\) percent.
Check 6: leverage and asset prices. Equation (12) against a balance sheet written out in dollars, and equation (13) against a long sum of discounted profits.

Python note. total += ... is short for total = total + ...: it adds one more term each time the loop runs.


bank_assets, bank_capital = 100.0, 7.0            # a bank with a 7% capital ratio
bank_debts = bank_assets - bank_capital           # liabilities stay fixed in dollars
new_capital = bank_assets * (1 - 0.03) - bank_debts                  # assets lose 3%
print(f"Leverage = {bank_debts / bank_capital:.1f}; net worth {bank_capital:.0f} -> {new_capital:.0f}: "
      f"{100 * (new_capital / bank_capital - 1):.1f}% (balance sheet), {net_worth_change(3, 0.07):.1f}% (equation 12)")
total = 0.0
for year in range(1, 2001):                       # profits of 1 next year, growing 2% a year, discounted at 7%
    total += 1.02 ** (year - 1) / 1.07 ** year
print(f"P/E: {total:.2f} (sum of 2,000 years), {price_earnings(7, 2):.2f} (equation 13); "
      f"with R = 8%: {price_earnings(8, 2):.2f}, a change of {100 * (price_earnings(8, 2) / price_earnings(7, 2) - 1):.0f}%")
print(f"Forward guidance, equation (14): {(0 + 1 + 2 + 3) / 4:.2f}% -> {(0 + 0 + 0 + 2) / 4:.2f}%")

Drawing tools
All model diagrams use the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

add_curve draws one curve and writes its name at its right end; add_label skips a name that would sit on top of another one;
add_point marks a point with dashed guides to the axes, and add_arrow draws an arrow;
model_figure starts a figure with one or two panels, and model_axes fixes the axes and writes the title.


Python note. np.linspace(-7.5, 4.5, 121) creates 121 evenly spaced numbers from −7.5 to 4.5. Because our model functions work on a whole array at once, one call gives a whole curve. (x >= x0) & (y <= y1) is true where both conditions hold, x[inside] keeps the values where inside is true, and [-1] takes the last of them. A for loop over fig.layout.annotations looks at every label already written, and return inside the loop stops the function early.


FADED_TEAL, FADED_BLUE = "rgba(0,128,112,0.35)", "rgba(22,82,140,0.35)"   # curves before a shock


def axis_names(col):
    """The names Plotly gives the axes of panel col: x and y in panel 1, x2 and y2 in panel 2."""
    if col == 1:
        return "x", "y"
    return f"x{col}", f"y{col}"


def add_label(fig, x, y, text, color, col=1):
    """Write a curve name at (x, y), unless another name already sits within 0.6 axis units."""
    xref, yref = axis_names(col)
    for old in fig.layout.annotations:
        if old.xref == xref and old.showarrow is False and abs(old.x - x) < 1.5 and abs(old.y - y) < 0.6:
            return
    fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, xref=xref, yref=yref, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                       yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, box, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw a curve in panel col and write its name at its last point inside box = (x range, y range)."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)), row=1, col=col)
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = box
    inside = (x >= x0) & (x <= x1 - 1.2) & (y >= y0) & (y <= y1)    # leave room for the text
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        add_label(fig, x[inside][-1], y[inside][-1], label, color, col)


def add_point(fig, x, y, label, box, guides="v", col=1, where="top right"):
    """Mark (x, y) with a dot and a letter placed `where`; dashed guides to the x-axis ("v"), both axes ("both") or none."""
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = box
    xs, ys = [x, x], [y, y0]
    if guides == "both":
        xs, ys = [x0, x, x], [y, y, y0]
    if guides != "none":
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=xs, y=ys, mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition=where,
                             name=label, showlegend=False, textfont=dict(size=16),
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, col=1):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; nothing if the two points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref=xref, yref=yref, axref=xref, ayref=yref, text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="black")


Python note. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) creates a figure with two panels side by side, and add_trace(..., row=1, col=2) draws in the second panel. fig.update_xaxes(..., row=1, col=col) changes the horizontal axis of one panel only.


def model_figure(cols=1, titles=None):
    """An empty figure with cols panels side by side (titles: one short title per panel)."""
    return make_subplots(rows=1, cols=cols, subplot_titles=titles, horizontal_spacing=0.1)


def model_axes(fig, title, box, y_title, x_ticks, y_ticks, panels=1):
    """Fixed axes in every panel, so that you can see the curves move, and the title readout."""
    for col in range(1, panels + 1):
        fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Output, Ỹ (%)", range=box[0], tickvals=x_ticks, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
        fig.update_yaxes(title_text=y_title, range=box[1], tickvals=y_ticks, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_layout(title=title)



Tools for the data figures
Two data tools are used by several figures. shade_recessions shades the U.S. recessions, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). The file recessions.csv lists, for each recession since 1953, the peak (the last month before the recession) and the trough (its last month). peak_to_trough finds the highest value of a series between two dates, the lowest value after it, and the fall in percent between the two.

Python note. pd.read_csv reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns, and parse_dates=[...] turns text such as "2007-12-01" into real dates. zip(a, b) hands over one pair of values at a time. data[(data.date >= start) & (data.date <= end)] keeps the rows between two dates, .idxmax() gives the row label of the largest value, and .loc[label] picks that row.


recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start):
    """Shade every NBER recession that ends after the date start (Figs. 4 and 6)."""
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    return fig


def peak_to_trough(data, column, start, end):
    """The peak of column between two dates, the lowest value after it, and the fall in percent (Figs. 7, 8)."""
    window = data[(data.date >= start) & (data.date <= end)]
    peak = window.loc[window[column].idxmax()]
    after = window[window.date >= peak.date]
    trough = after.loc[after[column].idxmin()]
    return peak, trough, 100 * (1 - trough[column] / peak[column])

Beyond the United States. The textbook’s data figures are about the United States, but most of their series exist for other countries too. Where they do, a subsection called Beyond the United States draws the same series for many countries, with the textbook’s countries picked to start with. Two more tools serve those charts: group_colors gives every country a color that stays the same whichever countries you pick, and that no other country shown with it uses, and fit_axis chooses the narrowest of a few fixed axis ranges that still holds every point, so the axis only widens when a country needs it.

Python note. px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 and Alphabet are lists of colors that Plotly ships with, and PALETTE.append(color) adds a color at the end of a list. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. colors.get(other) is the color of other, or None if it has none yet. new + free + PALETTE joins three lists and [0] takes the first item: a color that no country uses yet if there is one, else one that no country of the same groups uses.


LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]      # too pale on a white page
PALETTE = list(px.colors.qualitative.Dark24)                                     # 24 dark colors ...
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:                                     # ... and 20 more
    if color not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.remove("#2E91E5")
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                          # this blue is close to the U.S. navy: use it last


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country of its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.
    groups: lists of countries shown together (the website menus); fixed: {country: color} for the book's countries."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []                                    # colors of the countries already shown with this one
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    used.append(colors.get(other))
        free, new = [], []                           # free: not used in its groups; new: not used by any country
        for color in PALETTE:
            if color not in used:
                free.append(color)
                if color not in colors.values():
                    new.append(color)
        colors[name] = (new + free + PALETTE)[0]
    return colors


Python note. for bottom, top in ranges: unpacks each pair of the list ranges.


def fit_axis(low, high, ranges):
    """The first range (bottom, top) in the list that holds every value from low to high; else a range that just fits."""
    for bottom, top in ranges:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    pad = 0.05 * (high - low)
    return [low - pad, high + pad]

The website cannot run Python, so its versions of these charts draw every country at once and let you switch them on in the legend. The next helper does that. Run it and move on.


Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the multi-country website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def legend_menu(fig, shown, groups=None):
    """Website version of a country picker: the countries in `shown` are drawn, the others wait in the legend.

    Without groups, every other country is in the legend ('legendonly'), one click away, and a menu offers
    "Show all". With groups ({menu label: [countries]}), the menu puts one group at a time in the legend.
    Traces that are not countries (showlegend=False) always stay visible. The y-axis rescales to what is shown.
    """
    def visibility(members):
        out = []
        for t in fig.data:
            if t.showlegend is False or t.name in shown:
                out.append(True)
            elif members is None or t.name in members:
                out.append("legendonly")
            else:
                out.append(False)
        return out
    if groups is None:
        buttons = [dict(method="restyle", label="Textbook view", args=[{"visible": visibility(None)}]),
                   dict(method="restyle", label="Show all", args=[{"visible": [True] * len(fig.data)}])]
    else:
        buttons = [dict(method="restyle", label="Textbook view", args=[{"visible": visibility([])}])]
        for label, members in groups.items():
            buttons.append(dict(method="restyle", label=label, args=[{"visible": visibility(members)}]))
    for trace, visible in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = visible
        compact(trace)
    fig.layout.yaxis.range = None
    fig.update_yaxes(autorange=True)
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=0, direction="down", x=1, y=1.02, xanchor="right",
                                        yanchor="bottom")], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig


def compact(trace):
    """Shorter website files: dates without the time of day, values rounded to 2 decimals."""
    if trace.x is not None and len(trace.x) > 0 and hasattr(trace.x[0], "strftime"):
        trace.x = pd.to_datetime(trace.x).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    if trace.y is not None and np.asarray(trace.y).dtype.kind == "f":
        trace.y = np.round(np.asarray(trace.y), 2)


def region_groups(data):
    """{region: [countries]} for the website menus of long country lists."""
    groups = {}
    for region, rows in data.groupby("region"):
        groups["Add: " + region] = sorted(rows.country.unique())
    return groups

Financial frictions in the short-run model
We first measure the financial friction in the data, then add it to the IS/MP and AS/AD diagrams to see why a crisis acts like a large negative demand shock.

Fig. 1: The spread between corporate bonds and 10-year Treasuries
Goal. See the financial friction \(\bar{f}\) in the data: the gap between what companies and the government pay to borrow.
The U.S. government almost surely repays its debt, so its 10-year bonds (Treasuries) are the safe benchmark. Companies with a “BAA” rating are solid but not risk-free, so investors ask for a higher yield on their bonds. The difference between the two yields, the spread, is a measure of the risk premium \(\bar{f}\) in equation (1). In normal times it is about 2 percentage points.

What to notice.

The spread averaged about 2 points from 1996 to 2007, then jumped to 6 points in December 2008, three times its usual size.
In 2007–2008 the Treasury yield fell, as the Fed cut rates and investors fled to safety, but the BAA yield rose. Lower policy rates did not reach the companies that borrow.
Smaller spikes come with other moments of stress: 2002, after the 2001 recession and the dot-com crash; the oil-price collapse of early 2016; and the Covid-19 shock of spring 2020.


Beyond the United States: government bond spreads in the euro area
Moody’s BAA index covers U.S. companies, and long, free series of corporate bond yields exist only for the United States: indexes for other countries are sold by private data firms. But the euro area offers a clean risk premium of another kind. Its governments all borrow in euros, so when Italy pays more than Germany on a 10-year bond, the difference cannot come from the currency: it is the premium investors ask for the risk of default. The textbook notes that during the European debt crisis the rates on the debt of Greece, Ireland, Italy and Spain rose “as high as 7 percent” (Chapter 20 returns to that crisis). Fig. 2: A housing bubble and a financial crisis
Goal. See why a rise in the financial friction can defeat the central bank’s interest-rate cut.
Panel (a) repeats an example from Chapter 12. The housing bubble bursts, households feel poorer and spend less, so \(\bar{a}\) falls and the IS curve shifts back to IS′. If the Fed did nothing, the economy would move from \(A\) to \(B\), a recession. The Fed answers by cutting the fed funds rate from \(\bar{r}\) to \(R^{ff}\) (MP′), just enough to bring output back to potential at \(C\).
Panel (b) adds the financial crisis. Firms now borrow at \(R = R^{ff} + \bar{f}\) (equation 1). With a large enough friction, the rate they pay ends above \(\bar{r}\) despite the Fed’s cut (MP″), and the economy lands at \(D\), a deeper recession than \(B\). Two shocks conspire: the fall in consumption, and the rise in borrowing costs.

Python note. np.full_like(IS_Y, R) makes an array as long as IS_Y in which every value is R: a flat line, our MP curve. "..." if col == 1 else "..." picks the first value when the condition holds, the second otherwise.


IS_BOX = ([-7.5, 4.5], [-4.5, 9.5])            # the fixed axes: output from -7.5 to 4.5, R from -4.5 to 9.5
IS_Y = np.linspace(-7.5, 4.5, 121)             # output levels at which we draw the curves


def draw_housing_panel(fig, col, a_new, R_ff, R):
    """One panel of Fig. 14.2: IS and IS', and the MP lines at r_bar, R_ff and (panel b) R = R_ff + f."""
    add_curve(fig, IS_Y, is_rate(IS_Y, a_new), "IS′", TEAL, IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_curve(fig, IS_Y, is_rate(IS_Y), "IS", FADED_TEAL, IS_BOX, col=col)
    if col == 2:
        add_curve(fig, IS_Y, np.full_like(IS_Y, R), "MP″", BLUE, IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_curve(fig, IS_Y, np.full_like(IS_Y, R_ff), "MP′", BLUE if col == 1 else FADED_BLUE, IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_curve(fig, IS_Y, np.full_like(IS_Y, R_BAR), "MP", FADED_BLUE, IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_point(fig, is_output(R_BAR, a_new), R_BAR, "B", IS_BOX, col=col)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_ff, "C", IS_BOX, col=col)


def housing_crisis(a_new=A_HOUSING, f=F_CRISIS):
    """Fig. 14.2: (a) a housing bust and the Fed's cut, (b) the same with a financial crisis on top."""
    R_ff = R_BAR + a_new / B_BAR                   # the cut that brings output back to potential on IS'
    R = borrowing_rate(R_ff, f)                    # equation (1): the rate firms pay
    Y_B, Y_D = is_output(R_BAR, a_new), is_output(R, a_new)
    fig = model_figure(2, ("(a) The housing bust and the Fed's cut", "(b) Add a financial crisis"))
    for col in [1, 2]:
        draw_housing_panel(fig, col, a_new, R_ff, R)
    add_arrow(fig, -7.0, R_BAR, -7.0, R_ff, col=1)          # the Fed cuts its rate ...
    add_arrow(fig, Y_B, -3.8, 0.0, -3.8, col=1)              # ... and output returns to potential
    add_arrow(fig, -7.0, R_ff, -7.0, R, col=2)               # the risk premium pushes R back up
    add_point(fig, Y_D, R, "D", IS_BOX, col=2, where="bottom left")   # readable when D meets B or C
    title = (f"B: Ỹ = {Y_B:.1f}%;  the Fed cuts R<sup>ff</sup> to {R_ff:.1f}%;  "
             f"R = R<sup>ff</sup> + f̄ = {R:.1f}%, so D: Ỹ = {Y_D:.1f}%")
    model_axes(fig, title, IS_BOX, "Real interest rate, R (%)", [-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4], [-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8], panels=2)
    return fig

What to notice.

With \(\bar{f} = 0\), points \(C\) and \(D\) coincide: the Fed’s cut fully offsets the housing bust.
With \(\bar{f} = 2\), \(D\) sits exactly at \(B\): the friction cancels the cut, and the economy is back where it would be if the Fed had done nothing. Any friction above 2 points leaves the economy worse off than \(B\).
In this baseline, output at \(D\) equals \(-\bar{b}\bar{f}\) whatever the housing shock: the Fed removed the housing shock, so only the friction is left.


Key numbers: the zero lower bound
Why not cut the fed funds rate further, to \(R^{ff} = \bar{r} + \bar{a}'/\bar{b} - \bar{f}\) (equation 3), so that firms again pay what brings output back to potential? Because \(R^{ff}\) here is a real rate. The nominal fed funds rate is \(i = R^{ff} + \pi\), and it cannot go below zero. With inflation at 2 percent, the lowest possible real fed funds rate is \(-2\) percent.

The cut needed would require a nominal rate of \(-2\) percent. At the zero lower bound the best the Fed can do is \(R = 2\) percent, which only brings output back to \(B\), \(-2\) percent. This is why the Fed turned to other tools (Figs. 9 and 10).

Fig. 3: The financial crisis in the AS/AD framework
Goal. Follow the crisis over time in the AS/AD diagram, and see how it can lead to deflation.
By the new AD curve, equation (4), the housing bust (a lower \(\bar{a}\)) and the risk premium \(\bar{f}\) both shift the AD curve down to AD′. In period 1 the economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\): a deep recession, and inflation below the 2 percent target. Firms expect last period’s inflation, so the AS curve then shifts down period by period, and the economy slides along AD′ toward \(C\), where output is back at potential but inflation is far below target. Because inflation started at only 2 percent, it can turn negative: deflation. Point \(D\) is where the economy would jump if the shocks suddenly ended: today’s AS curve meets the old AD curve.
As in Chapter 13, one function crisis_path solves the model period by period, and the figure shows period t.

Python note. rows.append(dict(...)) adds one dictionary of named values to the list rows, and rows[-1]["pi"] is the value named "pi" in the last one. pd.DataFrame(rows) turns the list into a table, one row per period, and path.loc[t] is the row of period t.


AD_BOX = ([-7.5, 7.5], [-7.5, 5.5])            # the fixed axes: output and inflation
AD_Y = np.linspace(-7.5, 7.5, 151)             # output levels at which we draw the curves
PERIODS = 15                                   # periods simulated after the shock


def ad_inflation(Y, a=0.0, f=0.0, m=M_BAR):
    """The new AD curve (4) solved for inflation, pi = pi_bar + (a - b f - Y) / (b m) (used to draw it)."""
    return PI_BAR + (a - B_BAR * f - Y) / (B_BAR * m)


def crisis_path(a=A_HOUSING, f=F_CRISIS, m=M_BAR):
    """Fig. 14.3: the AS/AD model period by period after a lasting shock; period 0 is the old steady state."""
    rows = [dict(period=0, pi_prev=PI_BAR, Y=0.0, pi=PI_BAR)]
    for t in range(1, PERIODS + 1):
        pi_prev = rows[-1]["pi"]                  # adaptive expectations: last period's inflation
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_prev, a, f, m)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, pi_prev=pi_prev, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def add_crisis_path(fig, path, t, a, f, m):
    """The AD shift, the jump from A to B in period 1, then the slide along AD' up to period t."""
    x = ad_output(5.0, m=m)                       # where the old AD curve reaches 5% inflation
    add_arrow(fig, x, 5.0, x, max(ad_inflation(x, a, f, m), AD_BOX[1][0]))
    add_point(fig, path.Y[1], path.pi[1], "B", AD_BOX, guides="both")
    for s in range(2, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s])
        add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], "", AD_BOX, guides="none")


def crisis_asad(t=8, a=A_HOUSING, f=F_CRISIS, m=M_BAR):
    """Fig. 14.3: the economy t periods into a lasting crisis, with the old and new AS and AD curves."""
    path = crisis_path(a, f, m)
    now = path.loc[t]
    pi_C = PI_BAR + (a - B_BAR * f) / (B_BAR * m)        # long run: Y~ = 0 on the new AD curve
    fig = model_figure()
    add_curve(fig, AD_Y, ad_inflation(AD_Y, a, f, m), "AD′", BLUE, AD_BOX)
    add_curve(fig, AD_Y, ad_inflation(AD_Y, m=m), "AD", FADED_BLUE, AD_BOX)
    add_curve(fig, AD_Y, as_inflation(AD_Y, now.pi_prev), "AS′", TEAL, AD_BOX)
    add_curve(fig, AD_Y, as_inflation(AD_Y), "AS", FADED_TEAL, AD_BOX)
    add_crisis_path(fig, path, t, a, f, m)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, PI_BAR, "A", AD_BOX, guides="both")
    add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_C, "C", AD_BOX, guides="both")
    if t > 1:
        Y_D, pi_D = solve_asad(now.pi_prev, m=m)         # D: today's AS curve meets the old AD curve
        add_point(fig, Y_D, pi_D, "D", AD_BOX, guides="none")
    Y, pi = round(now.Y, 1) + 0.0, round(now.pi, 1) + 0.0   # + 0.0 turns a rounded -0.0 into 0.0
    title = f"Period {t}: Ỹ = {Y:.1f}%, π = {pi:.1f}%   |   long run at C: π = {pi_C:.1f}%"
    model_axes(fig, title, AD_BOX, "Inflation, π (%)", [-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6], [-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4])
    return fig

What to notice.

In period 1 the AD shock of \(\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} = -6\) costs 4 percent of output, and inflation falls from 2 to 0 percent at \(B\).
From then on inflation keeps falling, period after period, and the economy approaches \(C\), with inflation at \(-4\) percent: deflation. Each period the economy closes one third of the remaining gap to \(C\) (equation 7).
A larger \(\bar{m}\) makes AD′ flatter: the policy rule cuts the real rate more as inflation falls. The first recession is milder, and \(C\) has less deflation.
The model assumes that the policy rule can always lower the interest rate. Deflation and the zero lower bound break that assumption, which is why the textbook prefers the IS/MP diagram for such times (Figs. 12 and 13).

Monetary policy, the output gap and money
How did the Fed respond, and how big was the hole it had to fill? These figures compare the fed funds rate with the Taylor rule, look at estimates of potential GDP, and track the growth of the money supply.

Fig. 4: The fed funds rate and the Taylor rule
Goal. Compare the Fed’s actual interest rate with the rate a Taylor rule recommends.
The Taylor rule is the policy rule of Chapter 13 with one more term: the real rate also responds to short-run output. With equal weights of one half and the Fisher equation, the nominal rate it recommends is
\[i_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + 0.5\,(\pi_t - 2) + 0.5\,\tilde{Y}_t,\]
(equation 9 with \(\bar{m} = \bar{x} = 0.5\)), which is \(i_t = 1\% + 1.5\,\pi_t + 0.5\,\tilde{Y}_t\) for the traditional \(\bar{r} = 2\) percent. Many economists now think the long-run real rate has fallen to about 1 percent, so the textbook also shows the rule with \(\bar{r} = 1\). Inflation is core PCE inflation over the last four quarters, and short-run output uses the CBO’s estimate of potential GDP.

def taylor_rule(pi, Y, r_bar=2.0, weight=0.5):
    """Fig. 14.4: the Taylor rule, i = r_bar + pi + 0.5 (pi - 2) + weight Y~, in percent."""
    return r_bar + pi + 0.5 * (pi - PI_BAR) + weight * Y

Our function reproduces the rule in the data file. Now we draw it, and let you change \(\bar{r}\) and the weight on output.

def taylor_chart(r_bar=2.0, weight=0.5):
    """Fig. 14.4, first panel: the actual fed funds rate and the rate the Taylor rule recommends."""
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"date": taylor.date, "Actual fed funds rate": taylor.fed_funds,
                          "Taylor rule": taylor_rule(taylor.core_pce_inflation, taylor.short_run_output, r_bar, weight)})
    boom = chart[(chart.date >= "2002-01-01") & (chart.date < "2007-01-01")]
    gap = round((boom["Taylor rule"] - boom["Actual fed funds rate"]).mean(), 1) + 0.0   # + 0.0 avoids -0.0
    fig = px.line(chart, x="date", y=["Actual fed funds rate", "Taylor rule"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"Taylor rule with r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}: rule minus actual rate in 2002–2006 = {gap:+.1f} points")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    shade_recessions(fig, "2000-01-01")
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["1999-07-01", "2026-12-31"], legend_title_text="",
                      yaxis=dict(range=[-5, 11.5], tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

What to notice.

From 2009 to 2015 the fed funds rate sat at zero. In 2009 the rule itself was near or below zero, so the Fed looked generous; but the risk premium of Fig. 1 meant firms did not borrow at those low rates.
From 2002 to 2006 the fed funds rate was well below the rule: policy may have been too loose for too long, helping the housing boom.
Inflation was low after 2008 but did not keep falling, although output was far below potential. A credible 2 percent target may have held expectations up.
Move \(\bar{r}\) down to 1: the rule is lower by 1 point in every quarter. From late 2021 to 2022, with core inflation near or above 5 percent, even that rule called for rates far above the actual ones.


Beyond the United States: the Taylor rule for 14 central banks
The same rule can be computed for any central bank, given its policy rate, inflation and an estimate of short-run output. The file taylor_world.csv holds them for 14 central banks with their own currency and an inflation target of 2 to 2.5 percent, as annual averages from 1999: the policy rate from the BIS, and core inflation, headline inflation and the output gap from the OECD’s Economic Outlook. Two differences from the U.S. chart above: the data are annual, and the output gap is the OECD’s estimate, not the CBO’s. The rule keeps the 2 percent target.

# @title Helper for the website country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with a dropdown menu.

    Like slider_figure, but each choice also sets its own axis ranges.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            compact(trace)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "xaxis.range": f.layout.xaxis.range,
                  "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range}
        buttons.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))

                          "Taylor rule": taylor_rule(data.inflation, data.output_gap, r_bar)})
    late = chart[chart.year == 2022].dropna()
    gap = "no data for 2022"
    if not late.empty:

        gap = f"rule minus actual in 2022 = {diff:+.1f} points"
    fig = px.line(chart, x="year", y=["Policy rate", "Taylor rule"], markers=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"},

    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)

Python note. np.exp undoes np.log: if GDP grows at the log rate g per year, after t years it is np.exp(g * t) times larger. rows.year - end counts the years since 2007 (negative before it), and .where(rows.year >= end) keeps the values from 2007 on and leaves the earlier cells empty. In the title, 'below' if gap < 0 else 'above' picks one of two words.


TREND = "Trend of 1997–2007, extended"


def old_trend(rows, start=1997, end=2007):
    """GDP if it had kept growing at its average 1997-2007 rate after 2007 (a log-linear trend)."""
    x = rows.set_index("year").gdp
    g = np.log(x[end] / x[start]) / (end - start)
    return (x[end] * np.exp(g * (rows.year - end))).where(rows.year >= end)


def potential_world_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 5 for OECD countries: actual GDP, the OECD's potential GDP and the 1997-2007 trend (2007 GDP = 100)."""
    rows = potential_world[(potential_world.country == country) & (potential_world.year >= 1995)]
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"year": rows.year, "Actual GDP": rows.gdp, "Potential GDP (OECD, latest)": rows.potential_gdp})
    title = f"{country}: no GDP data for 1997, so no trend"
    if 1997 in rows.year.values:
        chart[TREND] = old_trend(rows)
        y2019 = chart[chart.year == 2019].iloc[0]
        gap = 100 * (y2019["Actual GDP"] / y2019[TREND] - 1)
        title = f"{country}: in 2019 GDP was {abs(gap):.1f}% {'below' if gap < 0 else 'above'} its 1997–2007 trend"
    lines = list(chart.columns[1:])
    fig = px.line(chart, x="year", y=lines, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN], title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Index, actual GDP in 2007 = 100", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(line_dash="dash", selector=dict(name=TREND))
    y_range = fit_axis(chart[lines].min().min(), chart[lines].max().max(), [(60, 140), (40, 200), (20, 300), (20, 450)])
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[1994.5, 2025.5], yaxis_range=y_range, legend_title_text="",
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig
