title: 15. DSGE Models: The Frontier of Business Cycle Research
section: Real shocks: productivity, taxes and government purchases
text:
Real shocks: productivity, taxes and government purchases
We shift one curve at a time: lower TFP and a sales tax move labor demand, while more government purchases work through consumption and labor supply. Notes in these sections also describe the matching responses in a large estimated DSGE model.

Fig. 3: A negative TFP shock in the DSGE model
Goal. See why a fall in TFP looks like a recession in the labor market.
A temporary fall in TFP from \(\bar{A}\) to \(\bar{A}'\) lowers the marginal product of labor at every level of employment, so labor demand shifts down. Labor supply does not contain \(\bar{A}\), and because the shock is temporary it barely changes consumption, so the supply curve stays put. The economy moves from \(A\) to \(B\).
This figure function will serve four textbook figures: a TFP shock (here), a sales tax (Fig. 4), government purchases (Fig. 5) and good news about the future (Fig. 9). Its three arguments are the three things a shock can change: TFP \(\bar{A}'\), the sales tax \(\tau\) and consumption \(c'\). When a curve moves, its old position stays behind as a dashed gray line.

Python note. abs(x) is the absolute value of x. Slider values are not always exact (0.6 can arrive as 0.6000000000000001), so we ask whether a value differs from the baseline by more than 0.001 rather than testing !=. a if condition else b picks a when the condition holds and b otherwise. min(a, b) is the smaller of two numbers.


def labor_shock(A_new=A_BAR, tau=0.0, c_new=C_BAR):
    """Figs. 15.3-15.5 and 15.14: a shock to TFP, a sales tax or consumption moves the economy from A to B."""
    L0, w0 = equilibrium()
    L1, w1 = equilibrium(A_new, tau, c_new)
    demand_moves = abs(A_new - A_BAR) > 0.001 or tau > 0.001
    supply_moves = abs(c_new - C_BAR) > 0.001
    d_label = "L<sup>d</sup>′" if demand_moves else "L<sup>d</sup>"     # a prime marks a curve that moved
    s_label = "L<sup>s</sup>′" if supply_moves else "L<sup>s</sup>"
    fig = go.Figure()
    d_end = add_curve(fig, L_GRID, demand_wage(L_GRID, A_new, tau), d_label, BLUE)
    s_end = add_curve(fig, L_GRID, supply_wage(L_GRID, c_new), s_label, TEAL, avoid=d_end)
    if demand_moves:
        add_curve(fig, L_GRID, demand_wage(L_GRID), "L<sup>d</sup>", GRAY, "dash", avoid=d_end)
        add_arrow(fig, 1.45, demand_wage(1.45), 1.45, demand_wage(1.45, A_new, tau))
    if supply_moves:
        add_curve(fig, L_GRID, supply_wage(L_GRID), "L<sup>s</sup>", GRAY, "dash", avoid=s_end)
        w_arrow = min(0.95, 1.75 * c_new / ELL_BAR)     # low enough that the arrow ends inside the axes
        add_arrow(fig, labor_supply(w_arrow), w_arrow, labor_supply(w_arrow, c_new), w_arrow)
    add_point(fig, L0, w0, "A")
    if demand_moves or supply_moves:
        add_point(fig, L1, w1, "B")
        add_arrow(fig, 0.05, w0, 0.05, w1)          # the real wage moves ...
        add_arrow(fig, L0, 0.05, L1, 0.05)          # ... and so does employment
    return labor_axes(fig, f"Employment {L0:.2f} → {L1:.2f},   real wage {w0:.2f} → {w1:.2f}")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 15.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With \(\bar{A}' = 0.8\), employment falls from 1.00 to 0.85 and the real wage from 0.67 to 0.56. Both fall, just as in a recession.
Both fall by the same 15 percent. In equation (7), TFP has the power \(3/4\), so \(0.8^{3/4} = 0.85\); and the wage is proportional to employment along the unchanged supply curve.
Move \(\bar{A}'\) above 1: a positive TFP shock raises employment and the wage, like a boom. This is why the first DSGE models focused on TFP shocks.

Your turn. How large a fall in TFP cuts employment by exactly 10 percent? Find it with the slider, then compute it with the formula.


Hint

You need \((\bar{A}')^{3/4} = 0.9\). Raise both sides to the power \(4/3\): try 0.9 ** (4 / 3), then check with equilibrium(A=...).

Textbook Fig. 15.11: a TFP shock in an estimated DSGE model
Textbook Fig. 15.11 is not recomputed in this notebook. It shows how GDP, consumption, hours worked and inflation respond, quarter by quarter for five years, to a 1 percent rise in TFP in the estimated model of Frank Smets and Rafael Wouters, “Shocks and Frictions in U.S. Business Cycles: A Bayesian DSGE Approach,” American Economic Review 97(3), 2007, pp. 586–606 (doi:10.1257/aer.97.3.586). Its curves are the output of a large model, with sticky prices and wages, many shocks and dozens of parameters estimated from U.S. data, solved with specialized software. They are not data that we could download, and reading numbers off the printed curves would invent a precision that we do not have. So we only report what the textbook says: GDP rises by more than 1 percent at its peak, because capital accumulates as in the Solow model; consumption rises by much less, because people smooth it; hours worked fall at first, because with sticky prices firms need fewer workers to meet a demand that rises only slowly; and inflation falls.
The one number we can check is the persistence of the shock. The textbook says that after 4 years (16 quarters) the TFP shock has decayed to about half its size. If a shock keeps the fraction \(\rho\) of its size each quarter, then by equation (1) \(\rho^{16} = 1/2\):

rho = 0.5 ** (1 / 16)
print(f"Quarterly persistence rho = {rho:.3f}: the shock keeps {100 * rho:.1f}% of its size each quarter")
print(f"Left after 1 year: {100 * rho ** 4:.0f}%,  after 4 years: {100 * rho ** 16:.0f}%,  after 8 years: {100 * rho ** 32:.0f}%")

Quarterly persistence rho = 0.958: the shock keeps 95.8% of its size each quarter
Left after 1 year: 84%,  after 4 years: 50%,  after 8 years: 25%





Fig. 4: The imposition of a sales tax in the DSGE model
Goal. See that a tax on firms’ sales works exactly like a fall in TFP.
With a sales tax \(\tau\), firms keep only \(1-\tau\) of each dollar of sales, so they hire until the after-tax marginal product equals the wage (equation 5):
\[w = (1-\tau)\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}}{L^{1/3}}.\]
The tax shifts labor demand down, and labor supply stays put. We use the same function as in Fig. 3, now with the tax slider set to 20 percent and TFP at its baseline.

         tau=FloatSlider(value=0.2, min=0.0, max=0.5, step=0.05, description="sales tax τ", style=WIDE),

slider_figure(labor_shock, "tau", [0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4], start=0.2, label="sales tax τ")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 15.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

A 20 percent sales tax moves the economy to exactly the same point as a fall in TFP to 0.8 in Fig. 3: employment 0.85 and a real wage of 0.56. Both lower the term \((1-\tau)\bar{A}\) from 1 to 0.8.
So a recession-like fall in employment and wages does not require that people “forget” technology. A policy change, or another distortion that acts like a tax, can play the role of a negative TFP shock.

print(f"TFP falls to 0.8: employment {L_tfp:.4f},  real wage {w_tfp:.4f}")

TFP falls to 0.8: employment 0.8459,  real wage 0.5639

Hint

Only the product \((1-\tau)\bar{A}\) matters. Compare equilibrium(tau=0.3) with equilibrium(A=...).

Fig. 5: A rise in government purchases
Goal. See how expectations about future taxes reach today’s labor market through consumption.
Government purchases appear in neither labor curve. But a rise in purchases must be paid for with taxes at some point, so households are poorer over their lifetimes, and by the permanent-income hypothesis they consume less today. Consumption is the variable that lets future events affect the economy now. In \(L^s = \bar{\ell}w/c\), a lower \(c\) raises labor supply at every wage: people are poorer, so they also “buy” less leisure. Labor supply shifts down and to the right. Here consumption falls from 0.6 to 0.5, which corresponds to a permanent rise in purchases of 0.1 (10 percent of output); a temporary rise would cut consumption by less.

What to notice.

Employment rises from 1.00 to 1.15, but the real wage falls, from 0.67 to 0.64, and so does consumption. With capital fixed, the extra workers run into diminishing returns.
The wage falls much less than employment rises, because labor demand is flat (Fig. 2).
A boom in employment with falling wages and consumption does not look like a normal business cycle. Shocks to government purchases are part of the story, but they cannot be its main driver.

Textbook Fig. 15.12 is not recomputed in this notebook. title: 15. DSGE Models: The Frontier of Business Cycle Research
section: Monetary policy with sticky wages and sticky prices
text:
Monetary policy with sticky wages and sticky prices
If all prices adjusted at once, money would not affect employment. Making wages or prices sticky changes that, and lets a monetary expansion raise employment and output.

Fig. 6: Sticky wages in the DSGE model
Goal. See how a nominal wage that does not fall creates involuntary unemployment.
Monetary policy needs a distinction between nominal and real variables. Let \(W\) be the nominal wage (dollars per hour) and \(P\) the price level, so that \(w = W/P\) is the real wage. Suppose the nominal wage is sticky: it is stuck at \(W = \bar{W}\). With the price level at \(P_0 = 1\) and \(\bar{W} = 0.75\), the real wage is 0.75, above the market-clearing wage of 0.67.
At that wage, people want to supply more labor than firms want to hire. Trade needs both sides, so the short side of the market decides (equation 8): firms hire along their demand curve, at point \(A\). The gap between the two curves is involuntary unemployment: people who would like to work at the going wage but cannot find a job. The unlabelled dot marks where the market would clear.
This figure function covers one event in three periods, and Fig. 7 reuses it:

period 0: the nominal wage is stuck at \(\bar{W}\) (textbook Fig. 15.6);
period 1: a monetary expansion raises the price level to \(P'\), and the real wage falls to \(\bar{W}/P'\) (Fig. 15.7);
period 2: eventually the nominal wage adjusts and the market clears again (this last step is not in the textbook figures; it is what happens once wages are flexible).


Python note. real_wages[t] takes element number t of a list, counting from 0, and "ABC"[t] the letter number t of a text. min(a, b) is the smaller of two numbers and max(a, b) the larger. An IntSlider is a slider for whole numbers, here the period. A function may have several return lines: it stops at the first one it reaches.


P0 = 1.0          # the price level before the monetary expansion


def add_wage_line(fig, w, label, color, dash="solid", above=False):
    """A horizontal line at the real wage w, labelled just right of the axes (above or below the line)."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0.02, L_RANGE[1]], y=[w, w], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    fig.add_annotation(x=L_RANGE[1], y=w, text=label, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                       yanchor="bottom" if above else "top", font=dict(color=color, size=15))


def add_gap(fig, L_from, L_to, w, text):
    """A bracket from L_from to L_to above the real wage w (clear of the point letters), with a text over it."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_from, L_from, L_to, L_to], y=[w + 0.07, w + 0.1, w + 0.1, w + 0.07],
                             mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip", line=dict(color="black", width=1.5)))
    fig.add_annotation(x=(L_from + L_to) / 2, y=w + 0.1, text=text, showarrow=False, yanchor="bottom",
                       font=dict(size=13))


def letter_side(w, w_old, w_star):
    """Where to write a point's letter, so that it stays clear of the old wage line w_old above it."""
    if w > w_old - 0.01:
        return "top right"             # no old line just above the point
    if w > w_star + 0.01:
        return "bottom left"           # the point lies on labor demand
    return "bottom right"              # the point lies on labor supply


def sticky_wages(t=0, P_new=1.05, W_bar=0.75):
    """Figs. 15.6-15.7: period 0 sticky wage W_bar; period 1 prices rise to P_new; period 2 W has adjusted."""
    L_star, w_star = equilibrium()
    real_wages = [W_bar / P0, W_bar / P_new, w_star]          # W/P in periods 0, 1 and 2
    labels = ["W̄/P<sub>0</sub>", "W̄/P′", "W′/P′"]
    w = real_wages[t]
    employed = min(labor_demand(w), labor_supply(w))          # the short side of the market decides
    gap = max(labor_supply(w) - labor_demand(w), 0.0)
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, L_GRID, demand_wage(L_GRID), "L<sup>d</sup>", BLUE, start=True)   # top label, clear of W/P
    add_curve(fig, L_GRID, supply_wage(L_GRID), "L<sup>s</sup>", TEAL)
    add_point(fig, L_star, w_star, "", guides=False)          # where the market would clear
    if t > 0:
        w_A = real_wages[0]
        L_A = min(labor_demand(w_A), labor_supply(w_A))
        add_wage_line(fig, w_A, labels[0], GRAY, "dash", above=w_A >= w)    # labels on the outer sides
        add_point(fig, L_A, w_A, "A")
        add_arrow(fig, 0.05, w_A, 0.05, w)
        add_arrow(fig, L_A, 0.05, employed, 0.05)
    add_wage_line(fig, w, labels[t], GREEN, above=t > 0 and real_wages[0] < w)
    add_point(fig, employed, w, "ABC"[t], where=letter_side(w, real_wages[0], w_star))
    if gap > 0.02:
        add_gap(fig, labor_demand(w), labor_supply(w), w, "Unemployment")
    return labor_axes(fig, f"Period {t}: real wage W/P = {w:.2f}, employment {employed:.2f}, "
                           f"unemployment {gap:.2f}", "Real wage, W/P")

         W_bar=FloatSlider(value=0.75, min=0.6, max=0.9, step=0.05, description="sticky nominal wage W̄", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Fig. 15.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

At the sticky real wage of 0.75, firms hire 0.70, while people would like to supply 1.125: unemployment is 0.42.
The higher \(\bar{W}\), the larger the gap. Labor demand reacts strongly to the wage, so even a modest excess of the wage over its market-clearing level costs many jobs.
Set \(\bar{W}\) below 0.67 and the picture flips: now labor supply is the short side, firms cannot hire all the workers they want, and there is no unemployment.

Your turn. Find the sticky nominal wage \(\bar{W}\) at which unemployment disappears, with \(P_0 = 1\).


Hint

Unemployment is zero when the real wage \(\bar{W}/P_0\) equals the market-clearing wage. Print equilibrium() to see that wage.

Fig. 7: A monetary expansion with sticky wages
Goal. See how monetary policy can raise employment when nominal wages are sticky.
A monetary expansion, a lower fed funds rate, raises spending. In this example only wages are sticky, so the other prices rise, from \(P_0 = 1\) to \(P' = 1.05\). With the nominal wage still at \(\bar{W}\), the real wage \(\bar{W}/P'\) falls. At the lower real wage firms want more workers and fewer people want to work, so employment rises from \(A\) to \(B\) and unemployment shrinks. This is the same function as in Fig. 6, now in period 1. Move the period slider to 2 to let the nominal wage adjust.

         W_bar=FloatSlider(value=0.75, min=0.6, max=0.9, step=0.05, description="sticky nominal wage W̄", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Fig. 7 with a precomputed slider for the period
slider_figure(sticky_wages, "t", [0, 1, 2], start=1, label="period t")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 15.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

A 5 percent rise in prices lowers the real wage from 0.75 to 0.71 and raises employment from 0.70 to 0.81; unemployment falls from 0.42 to 0.26.
The real wage and employment move in opposite directions. In actual business cycles, booms do not usually come with low real wages, so sticky wages alone cannot be the whole story of how monetary policy works.
In period 2 the nominal wage has caught up with prices, the real wage is back at 0.67 and the market clears: in the long run, money does not change employment (the classical dichotomy).

Your turn. Which price level \(P'\) removes unemployment completely in period 1? What happens to employment if prices rise even further?


Hint

You need \(\bar{W}/P' = 2/3\) with \(\bar{W} = 0.75\). Above that price level the real wage is below the market-clearing wage: which side of the market is short now?


# Your turn: try it here



Fig. 8: A monetary expansion with sticky prices
Goal. See why, with sticky prices, labor demand is vertical and a monetary expansion raises both employment and the real wage.
Now wages are flexible, but firms change their prices only slowly. At its sticky price, each firm agrees to supply whatever customers demand. So spending decides output \(Y\), and the production function decides how much labor firms must hire to produce it (equation 9):
\[Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L = \left(\frac{Y}{\bar{A}K^{1/3}}\right)^{3/2}.\]
Labor demand no longer depends on the wage: it is a vertical line. We start from the flexible-price output \(Y_0 = 1\), so point \(A\) is the baseline. A monetary expansion raises the output demanded to \(Y' = 1.15\), labor demand shifts right, and to attract the extra workers the nominal wage must rise. With prices stuck, the real wage \(W/P\) rises too: the economy moves up along the labor supply curve to \(B\).

Y0 = 1.0          # output demanded before the shock: the flexible-price output of the baseline


def add_vertical(fig, L, label, color, dash="solid"):
    """A vertical labor demand curve at L (sticky prices), labelled just above the top of the axes."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L, L], y=[0.02, W_RANGE[1]], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    fig.add_annotation(x=L, y=W_RANGE[1], text=label, showarrow=False, yanchor="bottom",
                       font=dict(color=color, size=15))


def sticky_prices(Y_new=1.15, c_new=C_BAR):
    """Figs. 15.8 and 15.15: labor demand is the vertical line at the labor needed for the output demanded."""
    L0, L1 = labor_needed(Y0), labor_needed(Y_new)
    w0, w1 = supply_wage(L0), supply_wage(L1, c_new)
    demand_moves, supply_moves = abs(Y_new - Y0) > 0.001, abs(c_new - C_BAR) > 0.001
    d_label = "L<sup>d</sup>′" if demand_moves else "L<sup>d</sup>"
    s_label = "L<sup>s</sup>′" if supply_moves else "L<sup>s</sup>"
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_vertical(fig, L1, d_label, BLUE)
    if demand_moves:
        add_vertical(fig, L0, "L<sup>d</sup>" if abs(L1 - L0) > 0.1 else "", GRAY, "dash")
    end = add_curve(fig, L_GRID, supply_wage(L_GRID, c_new), s_label, TEAL)
    if supply_moves:
        add_curve(fig, L_GRID, supply_wage(L_GRID), "L<sup>s</sup>", GRAY, "dash", avoid=end)
    add_point(fig, L0, w0, "A")
    if demand_moves or supply_moves:
        add_point(fig, L1, w1, "B", where="bottom right")     # below-right of B no curve passes
        add_arrow(fig, L0, 0.05, L1, 0.05)
        add_arrow(fig, 0.05, w0, 0.05, w1)
    title = f"Output {Y0:.2f} → {Y_new:.2f}: employment {L0:.2f} → {L1:.2f}, real wage {w0:.2f} → {w1:.2f}"
    return labor_axes(fig, title, "Real wage, W/P")

What to notice.

Output demanded rises by 15 percent, employment from 1.00 to 1.23 and the real wage from 0.67 to 0.82.
Employment and the real wage now move in the same direction, as they do over the business cycle. That is why models with sticky prices and monetary shocks, the new Keynesian models, became so important. Together with TFP shocks, they are the two “flavors” that modern DSGE models combine.

Textbook Figs. 15.9, 15.10 and 15.13: monetary and financial shocks in the Smets–Wouters model
A full DSGE model reports impulse response functions: how one variable, such as GDP, responds over time to one shock, such as a rise in the fed funds rate. Textbook Figs. 15.9, 15.10 and 15.13 show such responses from the estimated model of Smets and Wouters, “Shocks and Frictions in U.S. Business Cycles: A Bayesian DSGE Approach,” American Economic Review 97(3), 2007, pp. 586–606 (doi:10.1257/aer.97.3.586). They are not recomputed here: they are the solution of a model with sticky prices and wages, investment adjustment costs and many shocks, whose parameters were estimated from U.S. data, and they cannot be rebuilt from public data series or read precisely off the page. What the textbook reports:

Fig. 15.9: the response of GDP to a temporary 1 percentage point rise in the fed funds rate. GDP is about 0.2 percent lower in the first quarter, the peak fall of about 0.33 percent comes 3 to 4 quarters after the shock, and most of the effect is gone after 5 years (20 quarters).
Fig. 15.10: the same shock, for GDP, consumption, hours worked and inflation. All four fall, as with sticky prices in Fig. 8 run in reverse. Consumption falls nearly as much as GDP, and inflation is slightly less than 0.2 percentage points lower for about 2 years.
Fig. 15.13: a financial friction shock that raises the interest rate households face by 1 percentage point above the fed funds rate. It looks much like a monetary policy shock, with its largest effect on consumption.

text:
Good news about the future
Last, we look at news: people learn that the future will be better, raise their consumption today, and the labor market responds differently with flexible and with sticky prices.

Fig. 9: Good news in the DSGE model: flexible prices
Goal. See how news about the future changes the labor market today (textbook Exercise 1).
People learn of a discovery that will make the economy more productive in 5 years. Today nothing changes in production, so labor demand stays put. But people expect to be richer, so by the permanent-income hypothesis they consume more today: consumption rises from 0.6 to \(c' = 0.7\). Richer people want more of every good, including leisure, so labor supply shifts up and to the left.
The function good_news handles this event twice: with flexible prices it calls labor_shock from Fig. 3, and with sticky prices (Fig. 10) it calls sticky_prices from Fig. 8. With sticky prices, firms must also produce the extra consumption, so the output demanded rises by the same amount as consumption.

Python note. A ToggleButtons widget shows a row of buttons, one per option; the function receives the text of the selected button.


def good_news(c_new=0.7, prices="flexible"):
    """Figs. 15.14-15.15: good news raises consumption today from 0.6 to c_new."""
    if prices == "flexible":
        return labor_shock(c_new=c_new)
    return sticky_prices(Y_new=Y0 + (c_new - C_BAR), c_new=c_new)     # demand rises with consumption

         c_new=FloatSlider(value=0.7, min=0.5, max=0.8, step=0.05, description="consumption after the news c′", style=WIDE),
         prices=ToggleButtons(options=["flexible", "sticky"], value="flexible", description="prices"));



Show the code of the website version

slider_figure(good_news, "c_new", [0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8], start=0.7, label="consumption after the news c′")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 15.14 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., which illustrates the worked solution to its Exercise 1.
What to notice.

With flexible prices, the good news lowers employment today, from 1.00 to 0.89, and raises the real wage a little, from 0.67 to 0.69. People work less because they feel richer.
Nothing about technology has changed yet: the whole effect comes through expectations and consumption, the forward-looking variable of the model.

Fig. 10: Good news in the DSGE model: sticky prices
Goal. Compare the same good news with sticky prices (textbook Exercise 1(d)).
With sticky prices, firms supply whatever is demanded. The good news raises consumption, so firms must produce more and need more workers: the vertical labor demand curve shifts right, from \(Y_0 = 1\) to \(Y' = 1.1\). At the same time labor supply still shifts up, because people feel richer. Firms must pay a higher wage to get the labor they need. Use the buttons to switch between the two cases.

The same shock moves employment in opposite directions depending on whether prices are sticky. This is why macroeconomists argue so much about how sticky prices really are.

title: 15. DSGE Models: The Frontier of Business Cycle Research
text:
Concluding remarks

DSGE models are dynamic (they trace the economy over time), stochastic (shocks hit it) and general equilibrium (prices clear the markets). Their shocks fade as impulse responses, equation (1), and adjustment costs delay their peak effects.
They grew out of real business cycle models, which added TFP shocks to the Solow model, equation (2). TFP is measured as a Solow residual, equation (3); U.S. TFP growth swings a lot, but once utilization is removed, equation (4), it does not fall in most recessions.
The labor market is a key block of every DSGE model. Labor demand and supply, equations (5) and (6), give employment and the wage in equation (7). With consumption taken as given, a TFP fall or a sales tax lowers employment and the wage together, like a recession; a rise in government purchases or good news acts through consumption and labor supply instead.
Nominal rigidities decide how monetary policy works. With sticky wages, equation (8), an expansion raises employment but lowers the real wage; with sticky prices, equation (9), labor demand is vertical and an expansion raises both. Estimated DSGE models such as Smets–Wouters are quantitative: their impulse response functions say how much and how fast GDP, consumption, hours and inflation respond to each shock.
The next chapter studies consumption itself: the permanent-income hypothesis and the microfoundations behind the consumption that this chapter took as given.

title: 15. DSGE Models: The Frontier of Business Cycle Research
text:
Practice problems
These ten problems put the chapter’s tools to work: conceptual problems apply its equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to Fernald’s data and the Penn World Table, and modeling problems answer policy questions with the labor-market diagrams. Each problem is marked Basic, Intermediate or Challenge. Try it on your own before you open the Hint and the Solution; the sliders of the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top), and on the website you can use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): How long do shocks last in an estimated DSGE model? Smets and Wouters (2007) estimated their model on quarterly U.S. data from 1966 to 2004. Each of its shocks fades like the shock process of the Model overview, \(x_{t+1} = \rho\,x_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}\). The table lists five of their estimates of \(\rho\) (the posterior modes in Table 1b of the working-paper version; the article is doi:10.1257/aer.97.3.586).

Use the half-life formula of the Model overview to compute the half-life of each shock, in quarters.
Use equation (1) to compute the share of each shock that is still left one year (4 quarters) after it hits.
The monetary policy shock is almost gone after a single quarter, yet the chapter reports that GDP falls most 3 to 4 quarters after a monetary shock. Which features of a DSGE model can give a short-lived shock long-lived effects?



Hint

The half-life is \(h = \ln 2/(-\ln\rho)\), and by equation (1) the share left after \(n\) quarters is \(\rho^n\); np.log gives the natural log. For (c), reread the frictions in “The building blocks of a DSGE model”, the adjustment-cost rule after equation (1), and ask how a central bank moves its interest rate from one quarter to the next.

Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) and (b). For productivity, \(h = \ln 2/(-\ln 0.95) = 0.6931/0.0513 = 13.5\) quarters, and after a year \(0.95^4 = 0.81\) of the shock is left. The same two steps for every shock give:

The productivity estimate of 0.95 is close to the \(\rho = 0.958\) that the Model overview derived from a half-life of 16 quarters. In Python:
shocks = {"productivity": 0.95, "government spending": 0.97, "investment technology": 0.71,
          "risk premium": 0.18, "monetary policy": 0.12}
for name, rho_shock in shocks.items():
    half_life = np.log(2) / -np.log(rho_shock)
    print(f"{name:22s} half-life {half_life:5.2f} quarters, left after a year {rho_shock ** 4:.4f}")
shocks.items() walks through the pairs of a dictionary, one name and one value at a time.
(c) A shock and its effects are not the same thing. Three features spread a short shock over many quarters:

Adjustment costs. With the rule \(y_t = y_{t-1} + \lambda(x_t - y_{t-1})\), the economy closes only part of the gap each quarter, so its response keeps growing after the shock has faded. With \(\rho = 0.8\) and \(\lambda = 0.3\) it peaks 3 quarters later (the Model overview’s check).
Sticky prices and wages. Prices adjust slowly, so a higher nominal interest rate is also a higher real rate for several quarters, and spending stays low.
A smooth policy rule. In the estimated rule the interest rate puts a weight of 0.81 on its own value of the quarter before (Table 1a of the same paper), so a rate that jumps comes back down only slowly, long after the shock itself is gone.

So the long swings of a DSGE model come either from shocks that are very persistent themselves (productivity, government spending) or from frictions that stretch short-lived shocks, like the monetary one, over many quarters.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Two recessions, two stories: 1974 and 1982. John Fernald’s data in tfp_annual.csv (Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco) give, for the U.S. business sector (percent per year):



Year
Output growth
Raw Solow residual
Utilization




1974
−1.56
−3.72
−2.62


1982
−2.31
−2.76
−2.94




Use equation (4) to compute true TFP growth in each year.
In 1973–74 an oil embargo nearly quadrupled the price of oil, from $2.90 to $11.65 a barrel (Federal Reserve History). Our production function has no oil in it. Explain why a jump in the price of oil can act like a fall in \(\bar{A}\), and use the table “Which way do employment and the real wage move?” of the Model overview to say what the flexible-price labor market predicts.
In 1981–82 the Federal Reserve tightened money until the federal funds rate approached 20 percent, and unemployment reached nearly 11 percent late in 1982 (Federal Reserve History). Which row of the same table fits 1982? Why did the raw Solow residual fall that year anyway?
What do the two years say about the claim that TFP shocks drive business cycles?



Hint

Equation (4) says raw residual = true TFP growth + utilization growth, so subtract. For (b), think about what the same workers and machines can produce once energy is much more expensive. For (c), a monetary contraction is a monetary expansion run in reverse; which friction lets money change employment?

Your answer:


Solution

(a) From equation (4), \(g_A = (\text{raw residual}) - g_u\):

1974: \(g_A = -3.72 - (-2.62) = -1.10\) percent (Fernald’s adjusted series has \(-1.09\); the identity holds only approximately for annual averages);
1982: \(g_A = -2.76 - (-2.94) = +0.18\) percent.

True TFP fell in 1974 and was roughly flat in 1982, although the raw residual fell in both years.
(b) Output in equation (2) is value added: what capital and labor produce beyond the materials and energy that firms buy. When oil costs nearly four times as much, firms use less of it and switch to slower, less energy-intensive ways of working, and some energy-hungry machines stop paying their way. The same \(K\) and \(L\) then produce less value added, which the model reads as a lower \(\bar{A}\). With flexible prices, labor demand shifts down: employment and the real wage both fall, the first row of the table. This is the real business cycle story, and in 1974 it fits: true TFP fell by about 1.1 percent in a recession year.
(c) A monetary contraction with sticky prices: the output demanded falls, the vertical labor demand curve of equation (9) shifts left, and employment and the real wage both fall (the “monetary expansion, sticky prices” row, in reverse). The sticky-wage row, run in reverse, fits as well: with nominal wages stuck, a lower price level raises the real wage \(\bar{W}/P\), and firms hire fewer workers. Either way a nominal rigidity lets money cut employment, and TFP plays no role. The raw residual fell by 2.76 percent only because utilization fell by 2.94 percent: firms kept workers and machines on hand but ran them less intensively, and equation (3) counts that as lost productivity.
(d) The evidence is mixed. Some recessions, like 1974, come with a true fall in TFP; others, like 1982, have flat TFP and a clear monetary cause. Measured with the raw residual, both years look like TFP recessions, which is why the first RBC models looked so successful. A model of the cycle needs both TFP shocks and monetary shocks with nominal rigidities: the two flavors that modern DSGE models combine.

Problem 3 (Challenge): How elastic must labor supply be? Economists measure how strongly hours respond to a temporary change in the wage, holding consumption fixed, with the Frisch elasticity \(\eta\). Chetty, Guren, Manoli and Weber (NBER Working Paper 16729) note that business-cycle models need much larger labor supply elasticities than studies of individual workers find; their synthesis of the micro evidence points to Frisch elasticities of about 0.5 for the hours of people who work and 0.25 for the decision to work at all.

Show that the labor supply curve (6) has a Frisch elasticity of 1.
Replace the disutility of work in the household’s utility by \(\frac{\eta}{\eta+1}\,\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{(\eta+1)/\eta}\). Derive the new labor supply curve and check that it is equation (6) when \(\eta = 1\). Then solve the labor market with labor demand (5) and no tax, and show that the elasticity of \(L^*\) with respect to \(\bar{A}\) is \(3\eta/(3+\eta)\).
In Fernald’s data for 1950–2025, the growth of hours worked has a standard deviation of 2.57 percentage points and the growth of utilization-adjusted TFP one of 1.40 points (files tfp_inputs.csv and tfp_annual.csv, from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco). If TFP shocks in the flexible-price labor market were the only reason hours move, how large would \(\eta\) have to be? Compare it with the micro estimate of 0.5 and with the chapter’s \(\eta = 1\).



Hint


Take logs of equation (6) and change \(\ln w\) with \(c\) fixed. (b) The derivative of the new disutility with respect to \(L\) is \((L/\bar{\ell})^{1/\eta}\); set it equal to \(w/c\). Then repeat steps 1–4 of the labor market’s “Solving the model”, with the power \(1/\eta\) in place of 1. (c) If \(\ln L\) always moves \(\epsilon\) times as much as \(\ln\bar{A}\), its standard deviation is \(\epsilon\) times as large. Solve \(3\eta/(3+\eta) = \epsilon\) for \(\eta\).


Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) Taking logs of (6), \(\ln L^s = \ln\bar{\ell} + \ln w - \ln c\). With \(c\) fixed, a 1 percent higher wage raises \(\ln L^s\) by 1 percent: \(\partial\ln L^s/\partial\ln w = 1\), so the Frisch elasticity is 1.
(b) Utility is now \(U = \ln c - \frac{\eta}{\eta+1}\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{(\eta+1)/\eta}\), with \(c = wL - \bar{S}\). The power rule brings down \((\eta+1)/\eta\), which cancels the factor in front, and lowers the power by one, to \(1/\eta\):
\[\frac{dU}{dL} = \frac{w}{c} - \bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{1/\eta} = \frac{w}{c} - \left(\frac{L}{\bar{\ell}}\right)^{1/\eta} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L^s = \bar{\ell}\left(\frac{w}{c}\right)^{\eta}.\]
With \(\eta = 1\) the disutility is \(\frac{1}{2}\bar{\ell}^{-1}L^2\) and \(L^s = \bar{\ell}\,w/c\): equation (6). Written as a wage, supply is \(w = c\,(L/\bar{\ell})^{1/\eta}\). Set it equal to labor demand (5):
\[c\,\bar{\ell}^{-1/\eta}L^{1/\eta} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}}{L^{1/3}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L^{1/\eta + 1/3} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}\,\bar{\ell}^{1/\eta}}{c}.\]
The power on the left is \(\frac{1}{\eta} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{3+\eta}{3\eta}\), so raise both sides to \(\frac{3\eta}{3+\eta}\):
\[L^* = \left[\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}\,\bar{\ell}^{1/\eta}}{c}\right]^{3\eta/(3+\eta)}.\]
In logs, \(\ln L^* = \text{const} + \frac{3\eta}{3+\eta}\ln\bar{A}\): the elasticity is \(3\eta/(3+\eta)\), which is \(3/4\) for \(\eta = 1\), as in the comparative-statics table. It is 0.429 for \(\eta = 0.5\) and 1.5 for \(\eta = 3\), and it can never reach 3, however elastic labor supply is: the falling marginal product caps it.
(c) The required elasticity is \(\epsilon = 2.57/1.40 = 1.84\). Solving \(3\eta/(3+\eta) = \epsilon\) gives \(3\eta = \epsilon(3+\eta)\), so \(\eta = 3\epsilon/(3-\epsilon) = 4.7\). That is nearly ten times the micro estimate of 0.5. With \(\eta = 0.5\), TFP shocks would move hours with a standard deviation of only \(0.429 \times 1.40 = 0.60\) points, under a quarter of the 2.57 in the data; with the chapter’s \(\eta = 1\), about \(0.75 \times 1.40 = 1.05\) points. Problem 4 adds a second difficulty: hours and adjusted TFP do not even move in the same direction.
inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
ratio = inputs.hours_growth.std() / inputs.tfp_util.std()
print(f"standard deviations: hours {inputs.hours_growth.std():.2f}, adjusted TFP {inputs.tfp_util.std():.2f}")
print(f"elasticity needed {ratio:.2f}, so eta = {3 * ratio / (3 - ratio):.1f}")
for eta in (0.5, 1.0, 3.0):
    print(f"eta = {eta}: employment elasticity {3 * eta / (3 + eta):.3f}")
This is the labor-supply puzzle of real business cycle models: to let TFP shocks drive hours, they need labor supply far more elastic than studies of workers find. DSGE models answer with other shocks and with nominal rigidities.



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): Do hours rise when TFP rises? The file tfp_inputs.csv holds John Fernald’s growth-accounting data for the U.S. business sector, 1950–2025 (Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco; see the data notes): the growth of output, hours, capital and labor quality, capital’s share, and both TFP measures with utilization. Compute the correlation of hours growth with the raw Solow residual and with utilization-adjusted TFP growth. The flexible-price labor market predicts that hours rise with TFP (an elasticity of 0.75); with sticky prices and unchanged demand, equation (9) predicts that they fall (an elasticity of −3/2). Which prediction do the numbers support, and why do the two TFP measures disagree?


Hint

inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.tfp_util) gives one correlation. To see why the measures disagree, also correlate hours with utilization, and remember equation (4).


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

Read the file and compute three correlations:
inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
print(f"hours and raw TFP:      {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.tfp_solow):+.2f}")
print(f"hours and adjusted TFP: {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.tfp_util):+.2f}")
print(f"hours and utilization:  {inputs.hours_growth.corr(inputs.utilization):+.2f}")
Hours growth has a correlation of +0.38 with the raw residual but −0.39 with adjusted TFP. Once utilization is removed, years of fast TFP growth tend to be years in which hours fall. That is the sign that sticky prices predict: when TFP rises and demand does not keep up, firms need fewer workers. Basu, Fernald and Kimball (2006), “Are Technology Improvements Contractionary?”, reach the same answer with careful estimates: inputs fall at first when technology improves, which fits simple sticky-price models but not the standard RBC model.
The raw residual disagrees because it contains utilization (equation 4), and utilization rises and falls with hours: their correlation is +0.65. Firms that hire more also run their workers and machines harder, and plain growth accounting records the extra intensity as higher TFP.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Growth accounting by hand. Fernald computes the raw Solow residual (tfp_solow) from the columns of tfp_inputs.csv. Rebuild it yourself.

Use equation (3), with the weights 1/3 and 2/3, to compute the residual in every year from output, capital and hours growth; the notebook’s solow_residual function works on whole columns. Compare your residual with tfp_solow in 2009 and 2020.
Over 1950–2025, what are the correlation and the average gap between your residual and Fernald’s?
Fernald’s formula differs from equation (3) in two ways: capital’s share \(\alpha\) is measured every year (capital_share), and labor input also grows with labor quality \(g_q\) (labor_quality), the skill and experience mix of the hours worked: \(g_A = g_Y - \alpha g_K - (1-\alpha)(g_L + g_q)\). Recompute the residual with this formula. How large is the largest gap now?
In which two years did labor quality grow fastest, and why might it jump in those years?



Hint

solow_residual(inputs.gdp_growth, inputs.capital_growth, inputs.hours_growth) returns a whole column; store it as a new column. inputs.year.isin([2009, 2020]) picks the two years, and .nlargest(3, "labor_quality") the years with the fastest labor-quality growth. Look at hours growth in those years.


# Your answer here



Solution

inputs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_inputs.csv")
inputs["simple"] = solow_residual(inputs.gdp_growth, inputs.capital_growth, inputs.hours_growth)
alpha = inputs.capital_share
inputs["full"] = (inputs.gdp_growth - alpha * inputs.capital_growth
                  - (1 - alpha) * (inputs.hours_growth + inputs.labor_quality))
print(inputs[inputs.year.isin([2009, 2020])][["year", "simple", "full", "tfp_solow"]].round(2).to_string(index=False))
gap = inputs.simple - inputs.tfp_solow
print(f"equation (3): correlation {inputs.simple.corr(inputs.tfp_solow):.3f}, average gap {gap.mean():.2f}")
print(f"with alpha and labor quality: largest gap {(inputs.full - inputs.tfp_solow).abs().max():.2f}")
print(inputs.nlargest(3, "labor_quality")[["year", "hours_growth", "labor_quality"]].to_string(index=False))
(a) In 2009, equation (3) gives \(-3.75 - \tfrac{1}{3}\times 1.76 - \tfrac{2}{3}\times(-7.74) = +0.82\) percent with these rounded numbers (+0.83 from the unrounded data), against Fernald’s −0.15; in 2020 it gives +1.27 against −0.23. In both deep recessions the simple formula even turns the sign.
(b) Over all 76 years the two residuals have a correlation of 0.988, but the simple one is on average 0.23 points higher.
(c) With the measured capital share and labor quality, the residual is −0.25 in 2009 and −0.29 in 2020, and the largest gap in any year is 0.10 points; it is not zero only because the identity is exact for quarterly data and approximate for annual averages. Most of the average gap of (b) is labor quality: it grows by 0.38 percent a year on average, and equation (3) leaves its contribution, \(\tfrac{2}{3} \times 0.38 = 0.25\), inside TFP.
(d) The fastest years are 2020 (1.63 percent) and 2009 (1.19 percent), the two years in which hours fell by about 7.7 percent. Labor quality weights each hour by what that kind of worker earns. When it jumps, the hours of less experienced and lower-paid workers have fallen much more than the others, so the average quality of the hours still worked rises. Without that correction, equation (3) counts the better mix of workers as higher TFP.

The correlation can therefore run from GDP to measured TFP, not from TFP to GDP. For the United States, the one country here with a utilization-adjusted series, Problem 4 found that adjusted TFP and hours move in opposite directions.

    return fig

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each model figure gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: 16. Consumption
text:
Model overview
Earlier chapters let consumption be a fixed share of income. This chapter turns it into a choice. A household decides how much to spend now and how much to carry into the future, and it decides by weighing what an extra unit of spending is worth in each period against the price of moving resources from one period to the other. The neoclassical consumption model makes this trade-off precise. Its one character is a consumer called Irving, after the economist Irving Fisher.
The overview has three blocks, each built from assumptions to solution to predictions. The first block is the two-period model: two period budgets merge into a single lifetime budget, Irving maximizes lifetime utility, the best plan satisfies the Euler equation, and with log utility we solve for consumption in closed form. The same block derives the real interest rate that a given growth rate of consumption requires. The second block stretches the model to many periods and reads it as the permanent-income and life-cycle hypotheses. The third adds taxes, a limit on borrowing and uncertain income, which deliver Ricardian equivalence, a much higher marginal propensity to consume for constrained households, the random walk of consumption and precautionary saving. Finally, ### The model in code turns the results into Python functions and checks each one with numbers.
Notation. Irving takes his financial wealth \(f_{\text{today}}\), his labor incomes \(y_{\text{today}}\) and \(y_{\text{future}}\), the real interest rate \(R\) and his patience \(\beta\) as given, and he chooses consumption \(c_{\text{today}}\) and \(c_{\text{future}}\). As in the textbook, the bar in \(\bar{X}\) marks total wealth as a number that Irving cannot change. A prime marks marginal utility, \(u'(c)\). The worked numbers use the baseline Irving of every figure in this notebook: \(f_{\text{today}}=0\), \(y_{\text{today}}=1\), \(y_{\text{future}}=5\), \(\beta=1\), and \(R=0\) or \(R=0.05\). Think of one unit as 10,000 dollars, so Irving looks like a student who expects to earn much more later.

The two-period consumption model

Assumptions
1. Two periods. Time has only two periods, today and the future. The future is the last period of Irving’s life, so he has no reason to leave anything over at the end.
2. A budget in each period. Irving starts today with financial wealth \(f_{\text{today}}\) (a bank balance, stocks, bonds) and earns labor income \(y_{\text{today}}\). What he does not spend raises his financial wealth to \(f_{\text{future}}\):
\[c_{\text{today}} + \underbrace{(f_{\text{future}} - f_{\text{today}})}_{\text{saving today}} = y_{\text{today}}.\]
In the future he earns \(y_{\text{future}}\), his savings come back with interest, and he spends everything:
\[c_{\text{future}} = y_{\text{future}} + (1+R)\,f_{\text{future}}.\]
Each line says “spending plus saving equals income” for one period. Saving can be negative: \(f_{\text{future}} < 0\) means that Irving borrows today and pays back the loan with interest, \((1+R)\) times the amount, in the future.
3. Free borrowing and lending. Irving can save or borrow as much as he likes at the same real interest rate \(R\). The third block drops this assumption.
4. Flow utility with diminishing marginal utility. Consuming \(c\) in a period gives Irving \(u(c)\) units of utility. More is always better, \(u'(c) > 0\), but each extra unit adds less than the one before: the marginal utility \(u'(c)\) falls as \(c\) rises. The workhorse case is log utility,
\[u(c) = \log c \qquad\text{with}\qquad u'(c) = \frac{1}{c},\]
where \(u'(c)\) is the derivative of the log (Appendix C.7). As a second example we use the square root, \(u(c) = c^{1/2}\), whose marginal utility by the power rule is \(u'(c) = \tfrac{1}{2}c^{-1/2} = 1/(2\sqrt{c})\). Fig. 1 draws both curves.
5. Lifetime utility. Irving adds up the utility of the two periods and gives the future a weight \(\beta\):
\[U = u(c_{\text{today}}) + \beta\,u(c_{\text{future}}). \tag{1}\]
The weight \(\beta\) measures patience. With \(\beta = 1\) a unit of utility counts the same whenever it arrives; with \(\beta < 1\), say \(0.9\), Irving would rather have it sooner.
6. Optimization. Irving chooses \(c_{\text{today}}\) and \(c_{\text{future}}\) to make \(U\) as large as possible while paying for his plan.

Solving the model
Step 1: one budget for a whole lifetime. The two budgets are linked by \(f_{\text{future}}\), the wealth Irving carries from today into the future. Solve the future budget for it: subtract \(y_{\text{future}}\) from both sides and divide by \(1+R\),
\[f_{\text{future}} = \frac{c_{\text{future}} - y_{\text{future}}}{1+R}.\]
Put this into today’s budget:
\[c_{\text{today}} + \frac{c_{\text{future}} - y_{\text{future}}}{1+R} - f_{\text{today}} = y_{\text{today}}.\]
Split the fraction into \(c_{\text{future}}/(1+R) - y_{\text{future}}/(1+R)\), then move the income terms and \(f_{\text{today}}\) to the right-hand side:
\[c_{\text{today}}+\frac{c_{\text{future}}}{1+R} \;=\; \underbrace{f_{\text{today}}}_{\text{financial wealth}}+\underbrace{y_{\text{today}}+\frac{y_{\text{future}}}{1+R}}_{\text{human wealth}} \;\equiv\; \bar{X}. \tag{2}\]
This is the intertemporal budget constraint. Dividing a future amount by \(1+R\) turns it into a present value (Appendix C.12): one dollar put aside today grows to \(1+R\) dollars, so \(1+R\) future dollars are worth exactly one dollar now. Both sides of equation (2) are present values. The left side is the present value of everything Irving will spend. The right side is his total wealth \(\bar{X}\): his financial wealth plus his human wealth, the present value of his labor income.
Intuition. Equation (2) does not tie spending in a period to income in that period. It only requires the lifetime plan to be paid for. A student who earns little today can spend more than he earns, as long as his later income can repay the loan with interest. For the baseline Irving, \(\bar{X} = 0 + 1 + 5 = 6\) when \(R = 0\), and \(\bar{X} = 1 + 5/1.05 = 5.762\) when \(R = 0.05\).
Equation (2) can also be read as a straight line in a diagram with \(c_{\text{today}}\) on the horizontal axis: \(c_{\text{future}} = (1+R)(\bar{X} - c_{\text{today}})\). Its slope is \(-(1+R)\). Each unit consumed today costs \(1+R\) units of future consumption, so \(1+R\) is the price of consumption today in terms of consumption later.
Step 2: the condition for the best plan. We find it in two ways, first with a thought experiment and then with calculus.
A small move. Start from any plan that satisfies the budget and let Irving spend one unit less today and save it. He loses \(u'(c_{\text{today}})\) units of utility today. The saved unit becomes \(1+R\) units in the future, and each of those is worth \(\beta\,u'(c_{\text{future}})\) units of utility measured from today. If the gain is larger than the loss, the move raises \(U\) and Irving should save more. If it is smaller, the opposite move, borrowing one more unit to spend today, raises \(U\). Only when the two are equal is no move left that helps:
\[u'(c_{\text{today}}) = \beta(1+R)\,u'(c_{\text{future}}). \tag{3}\]
This is the Euler equation for consumption.
With calculus (Appendix C.8). Use the budget line to replace \(c_{\text{future}}\) by \((1+R)(\bar{X} - c_{\text{today}})\). Lifetime utility then depends on one choice only:
\[U(c_{\text{today}}) = u(c_{\text{today}}) + \beta\,u\big((1+R)(\bar{X}-c_{\text{today}})\big).\]
At the best \(c_{\text{today}}\) the derivative of \(U\) is zero. By the chain rule the derivative of the second term is \(\beta\,u'(c_{\text{future}})\) times the derivative of the inside, \(-(1+R)\). So
\[\frac{dU}{dc_{\text{today}}} = u'(c_{\text{today}}) - \beta(1+R)\,u'(c_{\text{future}}) = 0,\]
which is equation (3). Since \(u'\) falls as consumption rises, this derivative is positive when \(c_{\text{today}}\) is small and negative when it is large, so the zero is a maximum.
Intuition. The left side of equation (3) is the value of spending a marginal unit now; the right side is the value of saving it. A plan is best when Irving is indifferent at the margin. Because marginal utility falls with consumption, the Euler equation is also a statement about the shape of the plan: if \(\beta(1+R) = 1\), it forces \(u'(c_{\text{today}}) = u'(c_{\text{future}})\), and so equal consumption in both periods.
Step 3: the Euler equation with log utility. Put \(u'(c) = 1/c\) into equation (3):
\[\frac{1}{c_{\text{today}}} = \beta(1+R)\,\frac{1}{c_{\text{future}}}.\]
Multiply both sides by \(c_{\text{future}}\):
\[\frac{c_{\text{future}}}{c_{\text{today}}} = \beta(1+R). \tag{4}\]
The left side is one plus the growth rate of consumption, \(1 + g_c\) with \(g_c \equiv (c_{\text{future}} - c_{\text{today}})/c_{\text{today}}\). Taking logs of both sides (Appendix C.4) gives \(\log(1+g_c) = \log\beta + \log(1+R)\), and since \(\log(1+x) \approx x\) for small \(x\) (Appendix C.6),
\[g_c \approx R + \log\beta.\]
Intuition. Consumption grows faster when saving pays more (a higher \(R\)) and when Irving cares more about the future (a higher \(\beta\); impatience makes \(\log\beta\) negative and pulls growth down). Equation (4) fixes the slope of the consumption path, but not its level. Income does not appear in it at all.
Step 4: solving for consumption. Equations (4) and (2) are two equations in the two unknowns \(c_{\text{today}}\) and \(c_{\text{future}}\). From (4), \(c_{\text{future}} = \beta(1+R)\,c_{\text{today}}\). Substitute this into (2); the factor \(1+R\) cancels:
\[c_{\text{today}} + \frac{\beta(1+R)\,c_{\text{today}}}{1+R} = c_{\text{today}} + \beta\,c_{\text{today}} = (1+\beta)\,c_{\text{today}} = \bar{X}.\]
Divide by \(1+\beta\), then return to equation (4) for the future:
\[c_{\text{today}} = \frac{1}{1+\beta}\,\bar{X}, \qquad c_{\text{future}} = \frac{\beta(1+R)}{1+\beta}\,\bar{X}. \tag{5}\]
The textbook solves the case \(\beta = 1\), where \(1+\beta = 2\):
\[c_{\text{today}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\bar{X}, \qquad c_{\text{future}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,(1+R)\,\bar{X}. \tag{6}\]
Intuition. With log utility Irving spends a fixed share of his total wealth today, \(1/(1+\beta)\), whatever the interest rate and whatever the timing of his income. A patient Irving (\(\beta = 1\)) spends half; a less patient one spends more than half. The rest he saves in present-value terms, and in the future he spends it together with the interest it earned.
For the baseline Irving with \(R = 0\): \(c_{\text{today}} = c_{\text{future}} = 6/2 = 3\). He earns 1 but spends 3, so he borrows 2 today and repays 2 out of the 5 he earns later. With \(R = 0.05\): \(c_{\text{today}} = 5.762/2 = 2.881\) and \(c_{\text{future}} = 1.05 \times 2.881 = 3.025\). He borrows \(2.881 - 1 = 1.881\) and repays \(1.05 \times 1.881 = 1.975\), which leaves \(5 - 1.975 = 3.025\) to spend, exactly the plan.
Step 5: the interest rate that matches a growth rate. Irving takes \(R\) as given and picks the growth of his consumption. For the economy as a whole the logic runs the other way. The long-run growth models, such as the Solow–Romer model of Chapter 6, pin down how fast output and consumption per person grow. The Euler equation then tells us which real interest rate makes households content to consume along that path. Write \(1 + g_c\) for the left side of equation (4), divide both sides by \(\beta\) and subtract 1:
\[1+R = \frac{1+g_c}{\beta} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad R = \frac{1+g_c}{\beta} - 1. \tag{7}\]
Take one period to be one year and let consumption grow by 2 percent a year, \(g_c = 0.02\):

with \(\beta = 1\): \(R = 1.02/1 - 1 = 0.02\), so the interest rate equals the growth rate, 2 percent;
with \(\beta = 0.99\): \(R = 1.02/0.99 - 1 = 0.0303\), about 3.0 percent. The log approximation of step 3 gives the same answer, \(R \approx g_c - \log\beta = 0.02 + 0.01005 \approx 3.0\%\).

Intuition. An impatient household must be paid a premium, about \(-\log\beta\) per year, to accept a consumption path that rises over time. Since \(\beta\) is close to 1, the premium is small, which is why real interest rates and growth rates tend to be numbers of the same size, a few percent a year. Faster growth raises the required interest rate roughly one for one.
Step 6: what a higher interest rate does. With log utility, \(R\) does not appear directly in \(c_{\text{today}} = \bar{X}/(1+\beta)\). It works only through total wealth: a higher \(R\) shrinks the present value of future income, \(y_{\text{future}}/(1+R)\), so \(\bar{X}\) and \(c_{\text{today}}\) fall. This is the wealth effect of the interest rate.
Underneath, two other forces pull in opposite directions. The substitution effect: a higher \(R\) raises the price of consumption today, \(1+R\), so Irving shifts spending toward the future. The income effect: a saver earns more on what he saves and can afford more in both periods, including today. With log utility the two cancel exactly. To see it, take an Irving whose wealth is all financial, \(y_{\text{today}} = y_{\text{future}} = 0\). Then \(\bar{X} = f_{\text{today}}\) does not depend on \(R\), and neither does \(c_{\text{today}} = f_{\text{today}}/(1+\beta)\).
With square-root utility the two effects no longer cancel. Put \(u'(c) = 1/(2\sqrt{c})\) into equation (3); the factors \(1/2\) cancel:
\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{c_{\text{today}}}} = \beta(1+R)\frac{1}{\sqrt{c_{\text{future}}}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt{\frac{c_{\text{future}}}{c_{\text{today}}}} = \beta(1+R) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{c_{\text{future}}}{c_{\text{today}}} = \beta^2(1+R)^2.\]
Substitute \(c_{\text{future}} = \beta^2(1+R)^2 c_{\text{today}}\) into equation (2); one factor \(1+R\) cancels, leaving \(c_{\text{today}}\,[1 + \beta^2(1+R)] = \bar{X}\), so
\[c_{\text{today}} = \frac{\bar{X}}{1+\beta^2(1+R)}.\]
Now \(R\) sits in the denominator too: even when \(\bar{X}\) does not change, a higher \(R\) lowers \(c_{\text{today}}\). With this utility function the substitution effect wins. In general the sign of the effect of \(R\) on consumption today depends on the shape of \(u\), so it can go either way. For the baseline Irving with \(R = 0.05\), square-root utility gives \(c_{\text{today}} = 5.762/2.05 = 2.811\), a little less than the 2.881 of log utility.


What the model predicts
Comparative statics. Equation (5) gives the effect of every parameter on consumption. Income and wealth enter \(\bar{X}\) linearly, so their effects are constant numbers: the marginal propensities to consume (MPC), the rise in \(c_{\text{today}}\) per extra unit of resources. For \(R\) and \(\beta\) we take logs of equation (5): \(\log c_{\text{today}} = \log\bar{X} - \log(1+\beta)\) and \(\log c_{\text{future}} = \log\beta + \log(1+R) + \log\bar{X} - \log(1+\beta)\). Write \(\sigma \equiv [y_{\text{future}}/(1+R)]/\bar{X}\) for the share of total wealth that comes from future income. A 1 percent rise in \(1+R\) lowers \(y_{\text{future}}/(1+R)\) by about 1 percent, and so lowers \(\bar{X}\) by about \(\sigma\) percent. A 1 percent rise in \(\beta\) raises \(1+\beta\) by \(\beta/(1+\beta)\) percent.

The model’s main predictions.

Consumption follows total wealth, not current income. What matters is \(\bar{X}\), so a student with low income and high prospects consumes far more than he earns.
Windfalls are spread out. With \(\beta = 1\), an extra unit of income today raises consumption today by only one half; the other half is saved for the future.
Future income counts for a little less, because it is discounted by \(1+R\) before it enters total wealth.
The growth of consumption is set by \(\beta(1+R)\) (equation 4), whatever the timing of income.
Interest rates and growth rates are linked (equation 7): with \(\beta = 1\) they are equal, and impatience adds a small premium.
A higher interest rate lowers consumption today through the wealth effect when Irving has future labor income. Its full effect depends on the substitution and income effects, which cancel only with log utility.




Permanent income and the life cycle

Assumptions
Keep log utility and the Euler equation, but let Irving live for \(T\) periods, \(t = 1, 2, \dots, T\), with labor income \(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_T\). To keep the algebra transparent, set \(R = 0\) and \(\beta = 1\). Irving can still borrow and lend freely, and he starts with financial wealth \(f_{\text{today}}\).


Solving the model
Step 1: a flat consumption path. The small-move argument of step 2 above works between any two neighboring periods, so equation (4) holds for each pair: \(c_{t+1}/c_t = \beta(1+R) = 1\). Consumption is the same number \(c\) in every period.
Step 2: the lifetime budget. With \(R = 0\) no present values are needed, and the budget of equation (2) becomes a simple sum: the total spent over a lifetime, \(T \times c\), equals financial wealth plus all labor income, \(\bar{X} = f_{\text{today}} + y_1 + y_2 + \dots + y_T\). Dividing by \(T\):
\[c = \frac{\bar{X}}{T} = \frac{f_{\text{today}} + y_1 + y_2 + \dots + y_T}{T}. \tag{8}\]
With \(T = 2\) this is equation (6) with \(R = 0\).
Intuition. Irving spends the per-period average of his lifetime resources, his permanent income, in every period. An extra unit of income in any single period raises \(\bar{X}\) by 1 and consumption by only \(1/T\): the MPC out of a temporary windfall is \(1/T\), one half with two periods and \(1/40\) with 40 periods left. A permanent raise of 1 in every period raises \(\bar{X}\) by \(T\) and consumption by \(T/T = 1\).
Step 3: saving for retirement. Let Irving work for the first \(W\) periods at income \(y\) and then retire, with no labor income, for the last \(T - W\) periods. By equation (8), \(c = Wy/T\). While he works he saves \(y - c = y(T-W)/T\) each period, so his wealth climbs to \(W \times y(T-W)/T\) on the day he retires; in retirement he spends \(c\) out of that wealth until it reaches zero in the last period. With \(T = 60\), \(W = 40\) and \(y = 1\): \(c = 40/60 = 0.667\), he saves \(0.333\) a year, and his wealth peaks at \(40 \times 0.333 = 13.3\), more than 13 years of income.


What the model predicts

Permanent-income hypothesis (Friedman). Consumption depends on an average of lifetime resources, the present value of income, rather than on this period’s income. Temporary changes in income have small effects on consumption (MPC \(1/T\)); permanent changes have large ones (MPC near 1).
Anticipated changes do not move consumption when they arrive. A raise that Irving expected is already part of \(\bar{X}\), so his consumption does not jump on the day it is paid.
Life-cycle hypothesis (Modigliani). Because income has a hump over life and consumption is flat, people save in their working years and run down their wealth in retirement. Wealth is hump-shaped too, peaking around retirement.




Taxes, borrowing constraints and uncertainty

Assumptions
Go back to two periods and log utility, and change one assumption at a time.
1. Taxes. The government collects taxes \(\tau_{\text{today}}\) and \(\tau_{\text{future}}\), so the incomes in the budgets are incomes after tax, \(y_{\text{today}} - \tau_{\text{today}}\) and \(y_{\text{future}} - \tau_{\text{future}}\). The government borrows and lends at the same rate \(R\) as Irving.
2. A borrowing constraint. Irving cannot borrow at all: \(f_{\text{future}} \ge 0\). By today’s budget, \(f_{\text{future}} = f_{\text{today}} + y_{\text{today}} - c_{\text{today}}\), so the constraint says \(c_{\text{today}} \le f_{\text{today}} + y_{\text{today}}\): he can spend no more than he has today. With no financial wealth, this is simply \(c_{\text{today}} \le y_{\text{today}}\).
3. Uncertainty. Future income is not known today. Irving maximizes expected lifetime utility.


Solving the model
Ricardian equivalence. With taxes, total wealth is
\[\bar{X} = f_{\text{today}} + (y_{\text{today}} - \tau_{\text{today}}) + \frac{y_{\text{future}} - \tau_{\text{future}}}{1+R}.\]
Let the government cut today’s tax by \(\Delta\) and borrow to pay for it. In the future it must repay \((1+R)\Delta\), so it raises the future tax by that amount. The change in total wealth is
\[\Delta\bar{X} = +\Delta - \frac{(1+R)\Delta}{1+R} = \Delta - \Delta = 0.\]
Total wealth does not change, so by equation (5) neither does consumption. Irving saves the whole tax cut, and the saving, with its interest, exactly pays the higher future tax. This is Ricardian equivalence: for a given path of government spending, the timing of taxes does not matter.
The borrowing constraint. The unconstrained plan of equation (5) is still the best choice whenever it is affordable today. When it is not, Irving gets as close to it as he can, by spending everything he has today. In one line:
\[c_{\text{today}} = \min\left\{\frac{\bar{X}}{1+\beta},\; f_{\text{today}} + y_{\text{today}}\right\}. \tag{9}\]
When does the constraint bind? Take \(\beta = 1\). The plan \(\bar{X}/2\) is larger than \(f_{\text{today}} + y_{\text{today}}\) exactly when
\[f_{\text{today}} + y_{\text{today}} + \frac{y_{\text{future}}}{1+R} > 2\,(f_{\text{today}} + y_{\text{today}}) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{y_{\text{future}}}{1+R} > f_{\text{today}} + y_{\text{today}}.\]
The constraint binds when the present value of future income is larger than what Irving has today: then he would like to borrow, and he cannot. The baseline Irving is such a case: \(5/1.05 = 4.76 > 1\). Constrained, he spends \(c_{\text{today}} = 1\) instead of 2.881, and \(c_{\text{future}} = y_{\text{future}} = 5\). When the constraint binds, an extra unit of income today is spent in full, an MPC of 1, extra future income does nothing for him today, and a tax cut today raises his consumption one for one, so Ricardian equivalence fails.
Uncertain income: the random walk. With risky future income the small-move argument still works, but the gain from saving is now uncertain, so it is the expected marginal utility of the future that must balance:
\[u'(c_{\text{today}}) = \beta(1+R)\,E\big[u'(c_{\text{future}})\big],\]
where \(E[\cdot]\) is the average over the possible outcomes. When \(\beta(1+R) = 1\) and marginal utility is close to a straight line over the relevant range, this says that the best forecast of tomorrow’s consumption is today’s consumption: \(c_{\text{future}} = c_{\text{today}} + \text{surprise}\). Everything Irving knows today is already in his consumption, so only news moves it. Robert Hall called this the random walk of consumption.
Uncertain income: precautionary saving. Marginal utility \(1/c\) is not a straight line; it is steeper at low consumption. A spread of possible outcomes therefore raises the average of \(1/c_{\text{future}}\) above \(1/E[c_{\text{future}}]\): the bad outcome raises marginal utility by more than the good outcome lowers it. A higher right-hand side calls for a lower \(c_{\text{today}}\), that is, for more saving. A worked example with \(R = 0\), \(\beta = 1\) and the baseline incomes: if \(y_{\text{future}}\) is 3 or 7 with equal chance instead of a sure 5, then \(c_{\text{future}}\) is \(4 - c_{\text{today}}\) or \(8 - c_{\text{today}}\), and the expected Euler equation reads
\[\frac{1}{c_{\text{today}}} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4 - c_{\text{today}}} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{8 - c_{\text{today}}}.\]
Multiply both sides by \(c_{\text{today}}(4-c_{\text{today}})(8-c_{\text{today}})\) and collect terms (Appendix C.9): \(32 - 12c_{\text{today}} + c_{\text{today}}^2 = 6c_{\text{today}} - c_{\text{today}}^2\), or \(c_{\text{today}}^2 - 9c_{\text{today}} + 16 = 0\). The root below 4 is \(c_{\text{today}} = (9 - \sqrt{17})/2 = 2.44\). The risk lowers consumption today from 3 to 2.44, although average future income is still 5.

The timing of taxes does not matter for households that can borrow and that pay the future taxes themselves. It does matter when they are constrained, and when the later taxes fall on someone else, such as other income groups or future generations.
Constrained households spend what they earn. Their consumption tracks their current income, and their MPC is 1, far above the \(1/T\) of the permanent-income consumer. With a mix of both kinds of households, the economy’s average MPC lies in between.
Consumption should be hard to predict. Under the random walk view, expected changes in income are already in today’s consumption, and only surprises move it.
Risk makes people save, even when their income is low. Precautionary savers act much like constrained households, and their consumption also responds strongly to current income.




The model in code
We now turn the key results into Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes, and the cells after it check the algebra above with numbers. The figures below reuse these functions.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing form="log" gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. if ... : runs the indented line only when the condition is true; otherwise Python moves on. np.log and np.sqrt work on a single number and on a whole array of numbers.


def utility(c, form="log"):
    """Flow utility u(c) (Fig. 16.1): log c, or the square root of c."""
    if form == "log":
        return np.log(c)
    return np.sqrt(c)


def marginal_utility(c, form="log"):
    """Marginal utility u'(c): 1/c for log utility, 1/(2 sqrt c) for the square root."""
    if form == "log":
        return 1 / c
    return 1 / (2 * np.sqrt(c))


def lifetime_utility(c_today, c_future, beta=1.0, form="log"):
    """Lifetime utility U = u(c_today) + beta u(c_future)   (equation 1)."""
    return utility(c_today, form) + beta * utility(c_future, form)

The next three functions hold the solution with log utility. A function can return two results at once, separated by a comma.

def total_wealth(f_today, y_today, y_future, R):
    """Total wealth X = f_today + y_today + y_future / (1 + R)   (equation 2)."""
    return f_today + y_today + y_future / (1 + R)


def consumption_plan(f_today, y_today, y_future, R, beta=1.0):
    """Irving's choice with log utility: c_today = X/(1 + beta), c_future = beta (1 + R) c_today   (equations 5 and 6)."""
    X = total_wealth(f_today, y_today, y_future, R)
    c_today = X / (1 + beta)
    return c_today, beta * (1 + R) * c_today


def euler_interest_rate(g, beta=1.0):
    """The real interest rate that makes consumption grow at rate g: R = (1 + g) / beta - 1   (equation 7)."""
    return (1 + g) / beta - 1
