title: 18. The Government and the Macroeconomy
text:
Practice problems
The problems come in three types: conceptual problems apply the accounting relations of the Model overview to real cases, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data, and modeling problems use small calculators built on those relations to answer policy questions. Each one is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge; try it on your own first, then open the Hint and the Solution. The calculators run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, the website version of Fig. 6 above shows the debt projection.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): Who lends to the German government? In 2025 Germany reformed its constitutional debt brake, the rule that limits government borrowing. The IMF’s 2025 Article IV press release on Germany projects a general government balance of −2.4 percent of GDP for 2025 and −3.4 percent for 2026, while the current account surplus shrinks from 4.5 to 4.0 percent of GDP. Foreign saving is minus the current account balance: a country with a surplus lends to the rest of the world.

In our data (gov_finance.csv, from the OECD national accounts via the OECD Data Explorer, the file behind the country menus of Figs. 1 and 5), Germany’s private investment was 17.6 percent of GDP in 2024 and its budget balance −2.6 percent. The same IMF release puts the 2024 current account surplus at 5.8 percent of GDP. Use equation (9) to compute German private saving in 2024.
Suppose the 2026 projections come true and private saving stays at the same share of GDP. By how much does private investment change from 2025 to 2026? Which values of \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) in equation (10) describe this case?
What would private saving have to do for investment not to fall at all?



Hint

In equation (9), government saving is the budget balance \(T - G\) and foreign saving is \(IM - EX\), which is minus the current account. For (b), take the change of every term of equation (9) from 2025 to 2026, and watch the signs: a larger deficit is a fall in government saving, and a smaller current account surplus is a rise in foreign saving.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Solve equation (9) for private saving:
\[Y - T - C = I - (T - G) - (IM - EX) = 17.6 - (-2.6) - (-5.8) = 26.0 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
German households and firms saved 26.0 percent of GDP. Only 17.6 points financed private investment at home: 2.6 points went to the government’s deficit and 5.8 points were lent abroad. (The budget balance in our file is net lending, which already subtracts the government’s own investment. That is why it pairs with private investment in the identity.)
(b) Take changes of equation (9). Private saving does not change, government saving falls by 1.0 point (\(-3.4 - (-2.4)\)) and foreign saving rises by 0.5 point (the surplus falls from 4.5 to 4.0):
\[\Delta I = 0 + (-1.0) + 0.5 = -0.5 \text{ point of GDP}.\]
This is equation (10) with \(\Delta = 1\), \(\theta = 0\) and \(\phi = 0.5\): \(\Delta I = -(1 - 0 - 0.5) \times 1 = -0.5\). Half of the extra deficit is financed by lending less abroad, and the other half crowds out private investment.
(c) Investment does not fall when \(\theta + \phi = 1\), so with \(\phi = 0.5\) private saving must rise by \(\theta\Delta = 0.5\) point of GDP. That happens if households save part of their higher incomes, or save for the higher taxes they expect later (Ricardian equivalence).
Interpretation. Because Germany starts with a large current account surplus, much of its new borrowing can come from saving that now goes abroad, so crowding out can be small. Equation (9) is an identity, though: it says how the deficit must be financed, not why. The projected fall in the surplus could also come from higher investment rather than from the deficit.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Greece in 2011: could any surplus have stopped the debt? At the end of 2010, Greece’s gross government debt was 147.85 percent of GDP (gross_debt.csv, from the IMF’s Public Finances in Modern History database, as in Fig. 2). In 2011 investors lost confidence: the yield on 10-year Greek government bonds averaged 15.75 percent (OECD, via FRED, series IRLTLT01GRM156N), and nominal GDP fell by 9.0 percent (World Bank, GDP in current local currency, NY.GDP.MKTP.CN).

Suppose the whole debt paid the 2011 market yield. Use equation (7) to compute the primary surplus that would have held the debt ratio at 147.85 percent of GDP in 2011. Compare it with Greek government revenue, which was 44.6 percent of GDP in 2011 (gov_finance.csv).
Now suppose the interest rate were zero. What primary surplus would still have been needed? What does this say about the role of growth?
In our data, the ratio rose to 175.1 percent of GDP in 2011, and fell to 164.3 percent in 2012, the year in which Greece restructured its privately held bonds (Zettelmeyer, Trebesch and Gulati 2013). Use the “confidence and default” argument of the Model overview to explain why a high debt can become impossible to stabilize, and why lowering the interest rate on the debt had to be part of the solution.



Hint

Write both rates as decimals: \(i = 0.1575\) and \(g = -0.090\). A falling GDP makes \(i - g\) larger than \(i\). For (c), follow a rise in \(i\) through equation (7), and ask what a larger required surplus does to the lenders’ belief that they will be repaid.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Equation (7) with \(i = 0.1575\), \(g = -0.090\) and \(b = 147.85\):
\[-d = \frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.1575 - (-0.090)}{1 - 0.090} \times 147.85 = \frac{0.2475}{0.910} \times 147.85 = 0.272 \times 147.85 = 40.2 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
With revenue of 44.6 percent of GDP, a primary surplus of 40.2 percent would have left only 4.4 percent of GDP for all spending other than interest: no schools, no pensions, no police. No government can do that.
(b) With \(i = 0\):
\[-d = \frac{0 - (-0.090)}{1 - 0.090} \times 147.85 = \frac{0.090}{0.910} \times 147.85 = 14.6 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
Even free borrowing would have required a surplus of 14.6 percent of GDP, because a shrinking GDP raises the ratio by itself: the denominator falls. In equation (7), a fall in \(g\) weighs as much as a rise in \(i\). Growth is the “magic elixir” of Fig. 2 in reverse.
(c) When lenders start to doubt repayment, they ask for a higher \(i\). By equation (7), a higher \(i\) raises the surplus needed to stop the ratio from rising. Raising that surplus means tax increases and spending cuts, which lower GDP in the short run, so \(g\) falls as well. The required surplus grows again, repayment looks even less likely, and lenders ask for a still higher rate. The fear fulfills itself: at a yield of 15.75 percent and a shrinking GDP, no feasible primary surplus could stabilize the ratio. The way out is to lower \(i\) or the debt itself, by a restructuring (a partial default, as in 2012) or by borrowing from official lenders instead of the market. The ratio fell from 175.1 to 164.3 percent in 2012 even though GDP kept falling, because the restructuring cut the face value of the debt.
One detail: only new bonds pay the market yield, while old bonds keep the rate at which they were sold. The average rate on the whole debt was therefore much lower than 15.75 percent, and (a) is an upper bound. That is also why the ratio rose by 27.2 points in 2011, primary deficit included, and not by the 40.2 points that interest minus growth alone would have added at the market yield.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Norway’s oil fund and the generations to come. Norway’s government owns far more than it owes: in our data (net_debt.csv, the OECD’s government balance sheets via the OECD Data Explorer, as in Fig. 4), its net debt was −413.8 percent of GDP in 2024, most of it the oil fund. Norway’s fiscal rule says that, over time, the budget may spend only the fund’s expected real return, now estimated at 3 percent a year, and never the fund itself. Work in real terms: by the inflation argument of the Model overview, replace \(i\) by the real return \(r = 3\%\) and \(g\) by real GDP growth, which we assume is 1.5 percent a year (an illustrative value, not a forecast). Treat all net assets as one fund, and leave out new oil revenue.

Rewrite equation (4) for a government that starts with assets, \(B_1 < 0\). What does it allow the government to do?
Under the 3 percent rule, how large is the primary deficit (spending above non-oil taxes) in the first year, 2025? Give it in percent of that year’s GDP, as \(d_t\) in equation (5); the fund’s 413.8 percent is measured against the GDP of 2024. What happens to the real value of the fund, and to its ratio to GDP after 30 years?
Use equation (7) to find the primary deficit that would keep the fund at 413.8 percent of GDP forever.
The deficit allowed by the 3 percent rule shrinks as a share of GDP. After how many years does it fall below the deficit of (c)? Which rule treats future generations better? (This last question has no single right answer: argue for one.)



Hint

For (a), look at the sign of the right side of equation (4) when \(B_1 < 0\). For (b), spending exactly the real return leaves the fund’s real value unchanged, while real GDP grows 1.5 percent a year, already in the first year. For (c), put \(b = -413.8\) into equation (7) and read the sign of \(d\). For (d), compare the two deficits in the first year, then ask how long it takes GDP to grow by that factor; the rule of 70 gives a quick answer.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) With \(B_1 < 0\), equation (4) reads
\[(T_1 - G_1) + \frac{T_2 - G_2}{1+i} = (1+i)B_1 < 0.\]
The present value of the budget balances is negative: the government may run primary deficits, as long as their present value equals its assets plus the interest on them, \((1+i)\lvert B_1\rvert\). With many periods it can do so forever: a deficit equal to the return on the fund leaves the fund intact.
(b) The first-year deficit is the real return on the fund, \(0.03 \times 413.8 = 12.4\) percent of 2024 GDP. Equation (5) divides it by the GDP of 2025, which is 1.5 percent larger:
\[d_{2025} = \frac{0.03 \times 413.8}{1.015} = \frac{12.4}{1.015} = 12.2 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
The fund’s real value does not change, but real GDP grows, so the ratio shrinks by the growth rule for a ratio, \(g_b = 0 - 1.5\%\):
\[\frac{413.8}{1.015^{30}} = 264.7 \text{ percent of GDP after 30 years},\]
and the deficit the rule allows in that thirtieth year is \(0.03 \times 264.7 = 7.9\) percent of that year’s GDP.
(c) Equation (7) in real terms, with \(b = -413.8\):
\[-d = \frac{r - g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.03 - 0.015}{1.015} \times (-413.8) = -6.1, \qquad\text{so } d = 6.1 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
A permanent primary deficit of 6.1 percent of GDP keeps the assets at 413.8 percent of GDP. Check with the steady state: \(b^* = \frac{1+g}{g-r}\,d = \frac{1.015}{-0.015} \times 6.115 = -413.8\).
(d) The 3 percent rule’s first deficit, 12.2 percent of GDP from (b), is exactly twice the 6.1 percent of (c), since \(r/(r-g) = 0.03/0.015 = 2\). Its deficit shrinks with the ratio, at the rate of real growth, so it falls to the level of (c) once GDP has doubled from its level in the first year. By the rule of 70 that takes about \(70/1.5 \approx 47\) years (\(\ln 2 / \ln 1.015 = 46.6\) exactly): the rule’s deficit is larger than that of (c) in each of the first 47 years and smaller from the 48th year on.

The 3 percent rule gives every generation the same real amount (in kroner of today’s value). The generations living in the next half century get more than under the rule of (c), and those after them less, as a share of their (larger) incomes.
The constant-ratio rule gives every generation the same share of GDP. It spends less today and lets the fund grow with the economy.

Future generations will be richer, which is an argument for spending more now (the 3 percent rule). Expected returns are uncertain, which is an argument for spending less (if the real return turns out lower than 3 percent, the 3 percent rule eats into the fund). The arithmetic of equations (4) and (7) shows the trade-off; choosing between the two rules is a value judgment. In reality the fund has kept growing: Norway’s net debt was −154.9 percent of GDP in 2011 and −413.8 percent in 2024 in our data. According to the page linked above, the state’s net oil revenue is paid into the fund every year (this problem leaves it out), and the fund’s investments have earned large returns.

(b) Greece fits the story: the largest average deficit (−6.5 percent of GDP) and the lowest investment rate (14.3 percent). South Korea fits it too, with an average surplus of 1.5 percent of GDP and high investment, 26.8 percent. The United States does not: it has the second-largest deficit, −6.1 percent of GDP, but an average investment rate of 17.7 percent. Nor does China, which invests by far the most, 36.6 percent of GDP, with an average deficit of 2.0 percent of GDP.
(c) First, equation (10) allows private and foreign saving to fill the gap: in open economies, foreigners can finance a deficit (\(\phi > 0\)), as Fig. 5 suggests they did for the United States. Second, many other things differ across countries: households’ saving habits (very high in China), demography, the stage of development, and the business cycle, which moves deficits and investment at the same time. A correlation across countries cannot separate these forces from the effect of the deficit.

Solution

We line up the two files by year, compute the debt in dollars, the effective rate, growth and the primary deficit, and then apply equation (5).
fed = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "federal_budget.csv")
fed = fed[fed.release == "actual (FY2027 Budget)"].set_index("year")
debt_end = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-2.csv").set_index("year").debt_public_gdp_pct
rates = pd.DataFrame({"Y": fed.gdp_billions, "b": debt_end})
rates["B"] = rates.b / 100 * rates.Y                          # debt at the end of the year, billions of dollars
rates["i"] = fed.net_interest * rates.Y / rates.B.shift(1)    # interest paid / debt at the start, percent
rates["g"] = 100 * (rates.Y / rates.Y.shift(1) - 1)
rates["d"] = -fed.balance - fed.net_interest                  # primary deficit, percent of GDP
rates["predicted"] = (1 + rates.i / 100) / (1 + rates.g / 100) * rates.b.shift(1) + rates.d   # equation (5)
rates = rates.loc[1950:2025]
gap = rates.i - rates.g
print(f"(a) i < g in {(gap < 0).sum()} of {len(rates)} years; average i - g {gap.mean():.2f} points")
for start in range(1950, 2030, 10):
    part = rates.loc[start:start + 9]
    print(f"(b) {start}s: i {part.i.mean():.2f}%, g {part.g.mean():.2f}%")
print(f"(c) FY2022: i {rates.i[2022]:.2f}%, g {rates.g[2022]:.2f}%, i - g {gap[2022]:.2f}; rank {int(gap.rank()[2022])} of {len(gap)}")
print(rates.loc[2019:2025, ["i", "g", "d", "b", "predicted"]].round(2))

(b) By decade, \(i\) was far below \(g\) in the 1950s (2.31 against 6.29 percent), the 1960s and the 1970s, when the debt ratio fell from its war peak to 23.2 percent of GDP (FY1974). It was above \(g\) in the 1980s (9.13 against 8.05 percent), the 1990s (6.93 against 5.49) and, narrowly, the 2000s (4.81 against 4.35). In those decades the term \((i-g)\,b\) pushed the ratio up, on top of the deficits of the 1980s. Since 2010 \(i\) is again below \(g\): 2.12 against 3.94 percent in the 2010s, and 2.56 against 6.13 percent in 2020–2025.
(c) In FY2022, \(i = 2.14\) percent and \(g = 10.94\) percent, so \(i - g = -8.81\) points, the second-lowest value since 1950, after FY1951. Inflation surged in 2021–22 (Chapter 8), so nominal GDP grew fast, while most of the debt had been sold earlier at low fixed rates. Unexpected inflation lowered the real value of the debt, as the Model overview predicts: the ratio fell from 96.7 to 94.9 percent although the primary deficit was 3.51 percent of GDP.
(d) Equation (5) predicts the ratio within about 1 point in FY2019 and FY2023–2025, but it misses by 5.28 points in FY2020 (predicted 93.22, actual 98.5), by −6.54 points in FY2021 (103.24 against 96.7) and by 2.36 points in FY2022. In those years the Treasury did not borrow exactly its deficit. It borrowed more than it needed in FY2020 and held the cash at the Federal Reserve, where its balance rose from about 0.3 trillion dollars in September 2019 to 1.7 trillion in September 2020; it spent the cash down to 0.2 trillion by September 2021, and raised it to 0.7 trillion by September 2022 (Federal Reserve Board, H.4.1, U.S. Treasury General Account, week averages, via FRED, WTREGEN). The flow budget constraint holds once we count changes in the government’s cash as a use of funds. Our \(i\) is also approximate: net interest is interest paid minus some interest received.

    return fig

Solution

(a) With \(i = g\), the term \(\frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b\) of equation (6) is zero, so the ratio changes by exactly the primary deficit: \(b_t - b_{t-1} = d_t\). A primary surplus of 1.0 percent of GDP (\(d = -1.0\)) meets the rule exactly, and the slider confirms it: an average change of −1.00 point a year, to 109.15 percent of GDP in 2028.
(b) With \(i = 4\%\), interest adds \(\frac{0.04 - 0.03}{1.03} \times 113.15 = 1.10\) points to the ratio in the first year, so the surplus must cover that as well: about \(1 + 1.10 = 2.1\) percent of GDP. On the slider, \(d = -2.1\) gives an average change of −1.02 point a year, and \(d = -2.0\) only −0.91. The exact constant surplus is 2.08 percent of GDP (a little less than 2.10, because the debt, and with it the interest effect, falls along the way):
for d in [-2.0, -2.08, -2.1]:
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_france, 0.04, 0.03, [d] * 4)
    print(f"d = {d}: debt in 2028 {path[-1]:.2f}%, average change {(path[-1] - b_france) / 4:.3f} points a year")
One point more interest costs France about 1.1 points of GDP of extra surplus every year, because its debt is larger than its GDP. A rise in the interest rate makes the EU rule much harder to meet.

Problem 9 (Intermediate): Growth or austerity? A hypothetical country pays an interest rate of 4 percent on its debt, its nominal GDP grows by 3 percent a year, and its primary budget is balanced. Its government can choose one of two reforms, each kept for 20 years:

Plan A (austerity): a primary surplus of 1 percent of GDP every year (\(d = -1\)), with growth unchanged;
Plan B (growth): reforms that raise nominal growth to 4 percent a year, with a balanced primary budget (\(d = 0\)).


The debt starts at 100 percent of GDP. Which plan leaves the lower debt ratio after 20 years?
Repeat for a starting ratio of 50 percent and of 150 percent of GDP.
Find the starting ratio at which the two plans tie. Explain the result with equation (6), and use equation (8) to show why the tie is exact.



Hint

Plan A is g = 3, d = -1; Plan B is g = 4, d = 0. Compare the two “after 20 years” numbers in the title. For (c), compare what each plan subtracts from the change in the ratio in the first year, using equation (6): one of the two effects grows with the debt, the other does not.


def growth_or_austerity(b0=100.0, g=3.0, d=0.0):
    """Equation (5) for 20 years with i = 4%: the debt ratio with growth g and a constant primary deficit d."""
    path = [b0] + debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, g / 100, [d] * 20)
    no_reform = [b0] + debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.03, [0.0] * 20)
    end = round(path[-1], 1) + 0.0               # + 0.0 prints a tiny negative number as 0.0, not -0.0
    low, high = 0, 150
    if b0 > 100:
        high = 300                               # a second, fixed scale for high debts
    if min(path) < 10:
        low = -50                                # room below zero: the government may end up owning more than it owes
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(21)), y=no_reform, mode="lines", name="No reform (g = 3%, d = 0)",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(21)), y=path, mode="lines", name="This plan",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"After 20 years: {end:.1f}% of GDP (no reform: {no_reform[-1]:.1f}%)",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Years from now", range=[0, 20]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Debt (% of GDP)", range=[low, high]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Starting from 100 percent, with no reform the ratio rises to 121.3 percent after 20 years. Plan A ends at 99.4 percent and Plan B at 100.0 percent: austerity wins, but only just.
(b) From 50 percent, Plan A ends at 38.7 and Plan B at 50.0 percent: austerity wins clearly. From 150 percent, Plan A ends at 160.0 and Plan B at 150.0 percent: now growth wins, and austerity does not even stop the ratio from rising.
for b0 in [50, 100, 103, 150]:
    plan_a = debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.03, [-1.0] * 20)[-1]
    plan_b = debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.04, [0.0] * 20)[-1]
    print(f"start {b0}%: Plan A {plan_a:.1f}%, Plan B {plan_b:.1f}%")
(c) The two plans tie at a starting ratio of 103 percent of GDP. By equation (6), Plan A lowers the change in the ratio by 1 point a year, whatever the debt. Plan B removes the interest-minus-growth term \(\frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.01}{1.03}\,b\), which is proportional to the debt: it is worth \(0.0097\,b\) points, so more than 1 point when \(b > 103\). Growth works on the whole stock of debt; a surplus is a fixed amount.
The tie is exact, by equation (8). Under Plan B, \(i = g\) and \(d = 0\), so the ratio stays at \(b_0\). Under Plan A, the steady state is
\[b^* = \frac{1+g}{g-i}\,d = \frac{1.03}{0.03 - 0.04} \times (-1) = 103,\]
and equation (8), \(b_{20} = b^* + \left(\frac{1.04}{1.03}\right)^{20}(b_0 - b^*)\), keeps the ratio at \(b^*\) when it starts there. Since \(i > g\) under Plan A, \(b^*\) is the tipping point of the Model overview: below 103 percent the ratio falls further and further below \(b^*\), above it the ratio rises without limit. In this example, for highly indebted countries such as Italy (135.3 percent of GDP in 2024 in our data) or Japan, a lasting rise in growth is worth more than a surplus of the same size.

Problem 10 (Challenge): Health costs and the debt in 2056. CBO’s projections of Figs. 6 and 7 assume a path for Medicare and Medicaid, which reach 8.1 percent of GDP in FY2056. Health costs are hard to forecast. Suppose the cost per recipient grows by extra points a year faster (or slower, if negative) than CBO assumes, from FY2026 on. By equation (11), the health share then grows by extra points a year faster too, and the extra spending adds to CBO’s primary deficits. The calculator draws the debt ratio (with nominal growth \(g = 4\%\)) next to CBO’s path with \(i = g = 4\%\).

With \(i = 4\%\), what are health spending and the debt ratio in FY2056 if costs grow 1 point a year faster than CBO assumes? Compare the effect on the debt with that of an interest rate one point above growth (\(i = 5\%\)) and CBO’s health path.
Congress wants the FY2056 debt ratio below 150 percent of GDP (\(i = 4\%\)). What is the smallest slowdown of health costs, on the slider, that achieves it?
Could cost control alone bring the FY2056 ratio back to its FY2025 level of 99.5 percent? Try the largest slowdown on the slider, and explain what you find with the primary deficits of Fig. 6.



Hint

Read the title: it shows the FY2056 debt ratio and the health share. For (a), set the extra cost growth to 1, then set it back to 0 and move the interest rate to 5. For (c), compare the health share in FY2056 at the largest slowdown with its FY2025 level in Fig. 7 (6.0 percent of GDP), and remember that CBO projects primary deficits even without any rise in health spending.


cbo_health = components[components.projection == 1].medicare_medicaid.tolist()   # FY2026-2056, % of GDP
cbo_path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, 0.04, 0.04, cbo_deficits)                     # CBO's deficits, i = g = 4%


def health_and_debt(extra=0.0, i=4.0, g=4.0):
    """Equations (11) and (5): the debt ratio when health costs grow `extra` points a year faster than CBO's."""
    deficits = []
    for t in range(len(cbo_deficits)):
        share = cbo_health[t] * (1 + extra / 100) ** (t + 1)        # after the loop: the FY2056 share
        deficits.append(cbo_deficits[t] + share - cbo_health[t])
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, i / 100, g / 100, deficits)
    fig = go.Figure()
    years = [2025] + cbo.year.tolist()           # start the lines at the FY2025 ratio
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=[b_2025] + cbo_path, mode="lines", name="CBO, i = g = 4%",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=[b_2025] + path, mode="lines", name="This scenario",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"FY2056: debt {path[-1]:.1f}% of GDP, Medicare and Medicaid {share:.1f}% of GDP",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Fiscal year", range=[2025, 2057]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Debt held by the public (% of GDP)", range=[0, 400],
                                 tickvals=[50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

Solution

Equation (11) says the health share grows at \(g_{N_r/N} + (g_c - g_y)\). Adding extra points to \(g_c\) multiplies CBO’s share in year \(t\) after FY2025 by \((1 + \text{extra}/100)^t\). With \(i = g\), equation (5) simply adds up the primary deficits, so every extra point of health spending stays in the debt ratio.
for extra, i in [(0.0, 4.0), (1.0, 4.0), (0.0, 5.0), (-0.25, 4.0), (-0.5, 4.0), (-2.0, 4.0)]:
    fig = health_and_debt(extra, i)
    print(f"extra {extra:+.2f}, i = {i}%:", fig.layout.title.text)
debt_cbo = health_and_debt(0.0, 4.0).data[1].y[-1]     # the FY2056 end of the blue line, unrounded
print(f"Extra FY2056 debt: health costs +1 point {health_and_debt(1.0, 4.0).data[1].y[-1] - debt_cbo:.1f}, "
      f"i = 5% {health_and_debt(0.0, 5.0).data[1].y[-1] - debt_cbo:.1f} points of GDP")
(a) With CBO’s path and \(i = 4\%\), the FY2056 ratio is 164.2 percent of GDP, with health spending at 8.1 percent. If costs grow 1 point a year faster, health spending reaches 11.0 percent of GDP in FY2056 (\(8.085 \times 1.01^{31}\)) and the debt 205.3 percent: 41.1 points more. An interest rate one point above growth, with CBO’s health path, gives 208.8 percent, 44.7 points more. (The last line of the code subtracts the unrounded ratios, so a gap can differ by 0.1 from the difference of the rounded titles.) One point of extra health-cost growth weighs about as much as one point of \(i - g\), because both compound year after year.
(b) A slowdown of 0.25 point a year leaves the ratio at 155.2 percent; a slowdown of 0.5 point a year brings it to 146.6 percent, below 150. Health spending is then 6.9 percent of GDP in FY2056 instead of 8.1.
(c) No. Even a slowdown of 2 points a year, which pushes health spending down to 4.3 percent of GDP in FY2056, below its FY2025 level of 6.0 percent, leaves the debt at 103.4 percent of GDP, after a peak of 116.5 percent. Cost control works slowly: the slowdown saves only 0.12 point of GDP in FY2026 and builds up year after year, while CBO’s primary deficits, about 2 percent of GDP a year (Fig. 6), start right away. Health is the part of the budget that grows, but closing the gap quickly also needs higher revenue or lower spending elsewhere, the two “possible solutions” of the chapter.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


Every figure of this chapter can also show other countries. On the website, the many-country versions get a menu, built by two more helpers.


Show the helper code

EMERGING = ["China", "India", "Brazil", "Russia", "Mexico", "Indonesia", "Türkiye", "South Africa",
            "Saudi Arabia", "Argentina"]


def country_groups(regions, book):
    """Menu groups: the textbook's countries, the G7, large emerging economies, then the World Bank regions."""
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Large emerging": EMERGING}
    for region in sorted(regions.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = list(regions[regions.region == region].country)
    return groups


def group_menu(fig, groups, start, title):
    """Show one group of countries at a time. A trace belongs to the country named before ', ' in its legendgroup.
    Each group gets a y range that covers its values; in groups of more than 15 countries it leaves out extreme
    outliers (double-click the chart to show them)."""
    owners = [t.legendgroup.split(", ")[0] for t in fig.data]
    buttons = []
    for name, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in members for o in owners]
        ys = np.concatenate([np.asarray(t.y, dtype=float) for t, v in zip(fig.data, visible) if v] or [np.zeros(1)])
        ys = ys[np.isfinite(ys)] if np.isfinite(ys).any() else np.zeros(1)
        lo, hi = ys.min(), ys.max()
        if len(set(o for o, v in zip(owners, visible) if v)) > 15:     # large groups: leave out extreme outliers
            q5, q95 = np.percentile(ys, [5, 95])
            lo, hi = max(lo, q5 - 0.3 * (q95 - q5)), min(hi, q95 + 0.3 * (q95 - q5))
        pad = 0.06 * (hi - lo) + 0.5
        buttons.append(dict(label=name, method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": visible}, {"yaxis.range": [lo - pad, hi + pad], "yaxis.autorange": False}]))
    first = list(groups).index(start)
    for t, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[first]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        t.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(title=title, yaxis_range=buttons[first]["args"][1]["yaxis.range"], yaxis_tickvals=None,
                      margin=dict(t=115), updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=first, direction="down",
                                                             x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])
    return fig

title: 19. International Trade
text:
Model overview
Why do countries trade with each other, and what does it mean when a country buys more from abroad than it sells? This chapter answers with two kinds of tools. The first is a set of accounting identities: rules that hold by definition, in every country and every year. They tie exports and imports to saving, investment, the government budget and the stock of foreign debt, so that every trade chart below can be read as a statement about lending and borrowing. The second is a set of small trade models, economies simple enough to solve with pencil and paper, that show where the gains from trade come from and who receives them.
The road map has two parts. We build the accounting first: the trade balance and the national income identity, then its saving–investment form, then the stock of net foreign assets and the budget constraint that a country faces over time. Then come four small models: two islands that swap two goods, two islands that lend to each other across time, a North and a South that trade by comparative advantage, and free migration as an alternative to trade in goods. At the end, ### The model in code writes each rule once as a Python function, recomputes the textbook’s tables of the trade examples and checks every result with numbers. The figure sections reuse these functions.
A word on notation. Capital letters are flows of goods during a year: output \(Y\), consumption \(C\), investment \(I\), government purchases \(G\), taxes \(T\), exports \(EX\), imports \(IM\), net exports \(NX\) and saving \(S\). Lower-case letters are the same flows as fractions of GDP, such as \(c = C/Y\) or \(nx = NX/Y\). A bar marks a parameter chosen from outside, such as the interest rate \(\bar{r}\) or the growth rate \(\bar{g}\). In the North–South model the subscripts \(n\) and \(s\) stand for North and South, and the productivities \(x\) and \(z\) and the labor forces \(L\) are fixed numbers.

The trade balance and the national income identity

Definitions

Exports \(EX\) are goods and services produced at home and sold to buyers abroad. Imports \(IM\) are goods and services produced abroad and bought by households, firms or the government at home.
The trade balance, also called net exports, is the difference \(NX \equiv EX - IM\). A positive value is a trade surplus, a negative value a trade deficit.
A flow \(X\) as a share of GDP is \(100 \times X/Y\) (Appendix C.2). Shares let us put a small and a large economy, or 1950 and 2025, on the same axis.
The national income identity splits production into its uses: \(Y = C + I + G + NX\). Why net exports and not exports? Spending \(C + I + G\) includes goods made abroad, which are not part of domestic production, so imports are subtracted. Goods made at home and sold abroad are part of production but appear in no domestic spending, so exports are added. Hence \(Y = (C + I + G) + EX - IM\).



Solving the identity
Step 1: net exports as production minus domestic spending. Subtract \(C + I + G\) from both sides of the identity:
\[NX = Y - (C + I + G). \tag{1}\]
The sum \(C + I + G\) is everything that households, firms and the government use at home, sometimes called domestic absorption. Equation (1) gives two cases:
\[NX < 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; C + I + G > Y, \qquad\qquad NX > 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; C + I + G < Y.\]
Intuition. A country with a trade deficit uses more goods than it makes. The extra goods arrive from abroad, and since nobody hands goods over for free, they come with a promise to pay later. A country with a surplus sends part of its output abroad and collects such promises. When a deficit country pays back, the inequality has to flip: for a while it must make more than it uses.
Step 2: the same identity in GDP shares. Divide every term of equation (1) by \(Y\):
\[\frac{NX}{Y} = \frac{Y}{Y} - \frac{C}{Y} - \frac{I}{Y} - \frac{G}{Y}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad nx = 1 - c - i - g. \tag{2}\]
The Penn World Table reports the shares \(c\), \(i\) and \(g\) but not \(nx\), so equation (2) is how we get the trade balances of Figs. 3 and 4. For example, \(c = 0.55\), \(i = 0.25\) and \(g = 0.18\) add up to \(0.98\), which leaves a surplus of 2 percent of GDP.
Step 3: the world as a whole. Split the world into two regions, the United States (US) and the rest of the world (RoW). Each U.S. import is a rest-of-world export and each U.S. export is a rest-of-world import, \(IM_{US} = EX_{RoW}\) and \(EX_{US} = IM_{RoW}\). Therefore
\[NX_{US} = EX_{US} - IM_{US} = IM_{RoW} - EX_{RoW} = -NX_{RoW}.\]
The world trades only with itself, so the trade balances of all countries add up to zero. To see which countries cover the U.S. deficit, both sides must be measured against the same GDP. Multiplying and dividing by country \(j\)’s GDP \(Y_j\) gives
\[\frac{NX_j}{Y_{US}} = \frac{NX_j}{Y_j}\times\frac{Y_j}{Y_{US}}.\]
This is the second bar of Fig. 3. A surplus of 2 percent of its own GDP in an economy three quarters the size of the United States covers \(2 \times 0.75 = 1.5\) percent of U.S. GDP.


What the identity predicts
An identity does not tell us what causes what. It tells us which combinations of numbers can occur together. For a given level of output \(Y\):







A change in …
effect on the trade balance




\(C\), \(I\) or \(G\) up by 1
\(NX\) down by 1


\(c + i + g\) up by 1 point of GDP
\(nx\) down by 1 point


U.S. deficit up by 1 point of U.S. GDP
surpluses elsewhere up by 1 point of U.S. GDP in total



All three effects are one for one, because the identity is a sum. The direction of cause is open: a spending boom at home can open a deficit, and cheap credit from abroad can also feed a spending boom. The models below and the data sections look at which story fits.



Saving, investment and the trade balance

Definitions

Private saving is income after taxes minus consumption, \(Y - T - C\). Here \(T\) is taxes net of transfers, as in Chapter 18.
Government saving is the budget surplus, \(T - G\). It is negative when the government runs a deficit.
Foreign saving is \(IM - EX = -NX\): the goods that the rest of the world sends us beyond what we send back, which is lending to us.
Domestic saving adds the first two: \(S \equiv (Y - T - C) + (T - G)\).



Solving the identity
Step 1. Solve the national income identity for investment: \(I = Y - C - G - NX\).
Step 2. Subtract and add taxes, which changes nothing: \(I = (Y - T - C) + (T - G) - NX\).
Step 3. Write \(-NX\) as \(IM - EX\):
\[I = \underbrace{(Y - T - C)}_{\text{private saving}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{government saving}} + \underbrace{(IM - EX)}_{\text{foreign saving}}. \tag{3}\]
Every unit of investment is paid for by one of three savers: households, the government or foreigners.
Step 4. The taxes cancel inside domestic saving, \(S = (Y - T - C) + (T - G) = Y - C - G\). So Step 1 reads \(I = S - NX\). Moving \(NX\) to the left and \(I\) to the right:
\[\underbrace{NX}_{\text{trade balance}} = \underbrace{S - I}_{\text{net capital outflow}}. \tag{4}\]
Intuition. Equation (4) describes one set of transactions in two ways. On the goods side, a country with \(NX < 0\) receives more goods than it ships. On the financial side, it saves less than it invests, \(S < I\), and the difference is lent to it by foreigners, who receive bonds, shares or dollars in return. Net capital outflow \(S - I\) is the net amount that a country lends to the rest of the world. A trade deficit and net borrowing from abroad are the same thing, seen from the goods side and from the financial side.
Step 5: the twin deficits. Split domestic saving into its two parts:
\[NX = \underbrace{(Y - T - C - I)}_{\text{private saving minus investment}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{government saving}}.\]
If private saving and investment stay roughly in line, the first term is close to zero, and the trade balance moves with the budget balance: a budget deficit comes with a trade deficit of about the same size. These are the twin deficits of Fig. 5.

Net foreign assets and the intertemporal budget constraint

Definitions

Net foreign assets \(F_t\) are what a country’s residents own abroad minus what foreigners own in the country, at the end of year \(t\). The data call it the net international investment position (Fig. 6). When \(F_t < 0\), minus \(F_t\) is the net foreign debt.
The current account adds to the trade balance the net income earned on foreign assets: \(CA_t \equiv NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1}\), where \(\bar{r}\) is the return on foreign assets. (The data also include remittances and aid, which we leave out.) The textbook’s trade examples ignore this income, so in them the current account and the trade balance are the same.



Solving the model
Step 1: assets accumulate the current account. A current account surplus is new lending to the rest of the world, so it raises the stock of foreign assets by the same amount:
\[F_t - F_{t-1} = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} + NX_t. \tag{5}\]
This is a difference equation (Appendix C.10). With \(\bar{r} = 0\), as in the island example below and in the dotted line of Fig. 6, it becomes \(F_t = F_{t-1} + NX_t\), so that \(F_t = F_0 + NX_1 + NX_2 + \dots + NX_t\): the stock is the starting stock plus the sum of all trade balances since.
Step 2: the budget constraint over many years. Divide both sides of equation (5) by \((1 + \bar{r})^t\), and use \((1 + \bar{r})/(1 + \bar{r})^t = 1/(1 + \bar{r})^{t-1}\):
\[\frac{F_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = \frac{F_{t-1}}{(1 + \bar{r})^{t-1}} + \frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t}.\]
Write this line for \(t = 1, 2, \dots, T\) and add all the lines. Each term \(F_t/(1+\bar{r})^t\) from \(t = 1\) to \(T - 1\) appears once on the left and once on the right, so it cancels, and only the two ends survive:
\[\frac{F_T}{(1 + \bar{r})^T} = F_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t}.\]
No lender lets a debt grow forever without repayment, and no country gives goods to the world forever without ever using the claims. So, looking far enough ahead, the present value of the final stock is zero, \(F_T/(1 + \bar{r})^T = 0\). Then
\[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = -F_0. \tag{6}\]
This is the country’s intertemporal budget constraint. The terms on the left are present values (Appendix C.12). The math is the same as for the government’s budget constraint in Chapter 18, but it now applies to the whole country.
Intuition. A country that starts with no foreign assets, \(F_0 = 0\), must run trade balances whose present value is zero: every deficit today has to be matched by surpluses later, worth as much in present value. A country that starts as a debtor, \(F_0 < 0\), has to run surpluses on average.
Step 3: the foreign debt as a share of GDP. Let GDP grow at the rate \(\bar{g}\), so that \(Y_t = (1 + \bar{g})Y_{t-1}\), and write \(f_t \equiv F_t/Y_t\). Divide equation (5) by \(Y_t\):
\[f_t = \frac{(1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1}}{(1 + \bar{g})Y_{t-1}} + \frac{NX_t}{Y_t} = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx_t.\]
If GDP grows faster than the return, \(\bar{g} > \bar{r}\), the coefficient on \(f_{t-1}\) is below one and, for a constant trade balance \(nx\), the ratio settles down. In the long run \(f_t = f_{t-1} = f^*\), so \(f^* - \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}f^* = nx\), that is \(f^*\,\frac{\bar{g} - \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = nx\), and
\[f^* = \frac{(1 + \bar{g})\,nx}{\bar{g} - \bar{r}}. \tag{7}\]
Both \(F\) and \(Y\) are in dollars here, so \(\bar{g}\) is the growth rate of nominal GDP. A deficit of 3 percent of GDP every year, with nominal GDP growing 4 percent and no net income on foreign assets, leads to \(f^* = 1.04 \times (-0.03)/0.04 = -0.78\): a net foreign debt of 78 percent of GDP. The U.S. debt of about 70 percent of GDP in Fig. 6 is of that order.


What the model predicts

Deficits are borrowing, and they add up. By equation (5), the foreign debt is roughly the sum of past current account deficits. Fig. 6 tests this. It also shows that the data have one more source of change: the value of foreign assets moves with stock prices and the dollar.
Trade must balance over time, in present value. By equation (6), no country can run deficits forever. A deficit is a promise of future surpluses, not a free gift of goods.

Gains from exchange: two islands, two goods

Assumptions

Two islands have the same population. Each person likes bananas and fish, and only in equal amounts: think of a meal as one banana with one fish.
Nothing is produced. Each year, every person on island 1 receives 200 bananas and 800 fish, and every person on island 2 the reverse, 800 bananas and 200 fish.
The two goods can be swapped between the islands. By symmetry, they swap one for one.



Solving the model
Without trade, a person on island 1 can put together only \(\min(200, 800) = 200\) meals: the 600 extra fish add nothing. Suppose island 1 swaps \(q\) fish for \(q\) bananas. It then holds \(200 + q\) bananas and \(800 - q\) fish. Equal amounts require
\[200 + q = 800 - q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2q = 600 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q = 300.\]
Each person on both islands ends with 500 bananas and 500 fish. In general, with endowments \((a, b)\) on one island and \((b, a)\) on the other, the swap is \(q = (b - a)/2\), and everyone ends with \((a + b)/2\) of each good.


What the model predicts

Both islands gain. Meals per person rise from 200 to 500 on each island, although nothing more is produced. The gain comes only from moving each good to the people who value it more at the margin.
Trade here is balanced. In every year each island ships as much as it receives, so \(NX = 0\). The next block shows how deficits and surpluses arise.
Trade between countries works like trade between people. Inside a country, people specialize and buy most of what they consume from others. Trade across borders extends the same idea.




Trade across time: Oddtopia and Eventopia

Assumptions

There is one good, wheat, and it cannot be stored from one year to the next.
Oddtopia harvests 100 bushels in odd years and nothing in even years. Eventopia has the opposite pattern.
People prefer a smooth path of consumption to a path that swings: because of diminishing marginal utility, the last bushel eaten in a good year is worth less than the first bushel in a bad year (the consumption smoothing of Chapter 16).
There is no investment and no government, \(I = G = 0\). An island that lends wheat is paid back the same amount a year later, so \(\bar{r} = 0\). Both islands start with no foreign assets, \(F_0 = 0\).



Solving the model
Step 1: the trade balance. With \(I = G = 0\), equation (1) becomes \(NX_t = Y_t - C_t\): the harvest minus what is eaten.
Step 2: consumption. The two islands together harvest 100 bushels every year. Wheat cannot be stored, so the 100 bushels are eaten within the year, and the smoothest split of a constant total that is also the same each year is 50 bushels for each island: \(C_t = 50\).
Step 3: the trade balances. For Oddtopia, \(NX_t = 100 - 50 = +50\) in odd years and \(NX_t = 0 - 50 = -50\) in even years. Eventopia’s trade balance is the exact mirror image, so the two balances add to zero in every year, as Step 3 of the first block requires.
Step 4: the assets. By equation (5) with \(\bar{r} = 0\) and \(F_0 = 0\), Oddtopia’s net foreign assets are \(F_1 = 50\), \(F_2 = 50 - 50 = 0\), \(F_3 = 50\), and so on: after each good year it holds a claim of 50 bushels on Eventopia, which is repaid the next year. Eventopia’s assets are \(-50, 0, -50, \dots\)
Step 5: the budget constraint. With \(\bar{r} = 0\) and \(F_0 = 0\), equation (6) says that the trade balances must add up to zero. Over any two years they do: \(+50 - 50 = 0\).


What the model predicts

Risk sharing. Each island eats 50 bushels every year, even though its harvest swings between 0 and 100. Without trade it would feast and starve in turns.
A deficit can be good news for welfare. Each island runs a deficit exactly when its harvest fails. The deficit is a loan that lets it keep eating.
Balanced on average. Each island’s average trade balance is zero, in line with equation (6). A deficit today is the counterpart of a surplus tomorrow.
A guide for the data. The same logic says that a country should borrow, and run deficits, when its income is temporarily low, when it expects to grow faster than the rest of the world, or when it has good investment projects. Fig. 4 asks whether fast-growing countries really borrow.




Comparative advantage: the North and the South

Assumptions

Two countries, the North (\(n\)) and the South (\(s\)), produce and consume two goods, apples and computers. Labor is the only input, and each worker supplies one unit of labor for a wage \(w\), which is the worker’s whole income.
In country \(j\), a worker can make either \(x_j\) apples or \(z_j\) computers, and there are \(L_j\) workers. The values used throughout this notebook are those of the textbook’s example:

Workers can switch freely between the two sectors of their own country, but they cannot cross the border (the migration block below drops this assumption).
Everyone spends half of income on apples and half on computers. Prices are measured in apples (the numéraire): an apple costs 1, and a computer costs \(p\) apples. With \(c_A\) and \(c_C\) the apples and computers that one person consumes, the two spending shares give

\[\frac{1 \times c_A}{w} = \frac{1}{2} \;\;\text{and}\;\; \frac{p \times c_C}{w} = \frac{1}{2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad c_A = \frac{w}{2}, \qquad c_C = \frac{w}{2p}. \tag{8}\]
The North is more productive in both goods, \(x_n > x_s\) and \(z_n > z_s\): it has an absolute advantage in both. But its lead is much larger in computers, \(z_n/z_s = 16/2 = 8\), than in apples, \(x_n/x_s = 160/100 = 1.6\). Cross-multiplying, \(z_n/z_s > x_n/x_s\) is the same as \(x_s/z_s > x_n/z_n\): the number of apples given up to make one computer is \(160/16 = 10\) in the North and \(100/2 = 50\) in the South. A computer is relatively cheaper to make in the North, so the North has a comparative advantage in computers, and the South in apples.


Solving the model: autarky
Under autarky, each country is closed to trade.
Step 1: the wage. A worker in the apple sector makes \(x\) apples, and an apple costs 1, so the wage is \(w = x\).
Step 2: the price of a computer. A worker in the computer sector makes \(z\) computers and earns \(p\,z\) apples. People want both goods, so both sectors must hire workers, and then both must pay the same: \(p\,z = x\). If \(p\,z\) were higher, every worker would move to computers and nobody would grow apples; if lower, nobody would make computers. So
\[w = x, \qquad p = \frac{x}{z}. \tag{9}\]
The price of a computer equals its opportunity cost, the apples given up to make it (Appendix C.9 on solving such conditions).
Step 3: consumption. Put equation (9) into equation (8): \(c_A = x/2\) and \(c_C = \dfrac{x/2}{x/z} = \dfrac{z}{2}\).
Step 4: who works where. The \(L_A\) workers in the apple sector make \(L_A\,x\) apples, and the \(L\) people eat \(L\,x/2\). Setting the two equal gives \(L_A = L/2\): half of the workers make apples and half make computers.
With our numbers, the North has \(w = 160\), \(p = 10\), \(c_A = 80\) and \(c_C = 8\), and it makes \(50 \times 160 = 8{,}000\) apples and \(50 \times 16 = 800\) computers. The South has \(w = 100\), \(p = 50\), \(c_A = 50\) and \(c_C = 1\), and it makes \(200 \times 100 = 20{,}000\) apples and \(200 \times 2 = 400\) computers.


Solving the model: free trade
Step 1: arbitrage. Under autarky a computer costs 10 apples in the North and 50 in the South. A trader could buy computers in the North and sell them in the South at a profit (arbitrage). With free trade there is one world price \(p\).
Step 2: a guess. Suppose each country makes only the good of its comparative advantage: the North only computers and the South only apples. The world then makes \(L_n z_n = 1{,}600\) computers and \(L_s x_s = 40{,}000\) apples.
Step 3: the world price. World income, measured in apples, is the value of everything produced, \(L_s x_s + p\,L_n z_n\). Half of it is spent on computers, and in equilibrium the computers bought equal the computers made:
\[p\,L_n z_n = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(L_s x_s + p\,L_n z_n\right)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tfrac{1}{2}\,p\,L_n z_n = \tfrac{1}{2}\,L_s x_s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n}. \tag{10}\]
With equal spending shares, the two goods must have the same total value, so the price of a computer is the ratio of world apples to world computers: \(40{,}000/1{,}600 = 25\) apples.
Step 4: wages. A southern worker still makes 100 apples, so \(w_s = x_s = 100\). A northern worker makes 16 computers worth 25 apples each, so \(w_n = p\,z_n = 400\) apples. Using equation (10), \(w_n = L_s x_s/L_n\).
Step 5: consumption. By equation (8): in the North, \(c_A = 400/2 = 200\) and \(c_C = 400/(2 \times 25) = 8\); in the South, \(c_A = 100/2 = 50\) and \(c_C = 100/(2 \times 25) = 2\).
Step 6: check the guess. Northern workers stay in computers only if that pays at least as well as apples, \(p\,z_n \ge x_n\), that is \(p \ge x_n/z_n\). Southern workers stay in apples only if \(x_s \ge p\,z_s\), that is \(p \le x_s/z_s\). With strict inequalities, complete specialization requires
\[\frac{x_s}{z_s} \;>\; p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n} \;>\; \frac{x_n}{z_n}. \tag{11}\]
The world price must lie between the two autarky prices. Here \(50 > 25 > 10\), so the guess is right. If, say, the South were so large that \(p\) rose above 50, southern workers would also make some computers, and the South would keep its autarky price.

Free migration: moving workers instead of goods

Assumptions
Keep the North–South model, but now let workers move across the border. Technologies stay where they are: a worker in the North makes \(x_n\) apples or \(z_n\) computers, wherever he or she was born. Production has constant returns, so output per worker does not depend on how many workers a country has.


Solving the model
Step 1: who moves. With free trade a computer costs the same everywhere, so a higher wage in apples is a higher real wage. The northern wage, 400 apples, is four times the southern one, 100 apples (under autarky it is 160 against 100). Southern workers keep moving as long as any gap remains. Because the North is more productive in both goods, a worker makes more of either good there, and the South empties out.
Step 2: the new world economy. The world is now the North under autarky, with \(L_n + L_s = 500\) workers. By equation (9), \(w = x_n = 160\) and \(p = x_n/z_n = 10\). By equation (8), everybody eats \(c_A = 80\) apples and has \(c_C = 8\) computers.
Step 3: production. Half of the 500 workers make each good: \(250 \times 160 = 40{,}000\) apples and \(250 \times 16 = 4{,}000\) computers.


What the model predicts

Migration follows absolute advantage, while trade in goods follows comparative advantage. Workers go where productivity is highest in absolute terms.
The world produces more than with free trade: the same 40,000 apples, and 4,000 computers instead of 1,600. The gains go to the migrants. What one worker consumes under each arrangement:

There is room to compensate the North. Moving from free trade to free migration, each of the 100 northerners loses 120 apples, 12,000 apples in all. Each of the 400 migrants gains 30 apples and 6 computers, 12,000 apples and 2,400 computers in all. The gains are larger than the losses. If every migrant handed 30 apples to the North, each northerner would get back exactly the free-trade bundle of 200 apples and 8 computers, and each migrant would still have 50 apples and 8 computers, four times the computers of free trade.
Moving labor versus moving capital. The production and Solow models (Chapter 4, Chapter 5) found that poor countries are poor mostly because of low total factor productivity, not because of too little capital. Sending capital to a low-productivity economy leaves that problem in place. Letting workers move to where productivity is high attacks it directly, which is why the possible gains from migration are so large.
The costs of trade. In the model, apple growers in the North become computer makers overnight and nobody loses. In reality, switching jobs takes time and new skills, so trade creates winners and losers inside each country. Because the gains to the winners are larger than the losses, the winners could, in principle, compensate the losers, for example through retraining and a social safety net.




The model in code
We now turn the accounting rules into Python functions, check each derivation above with numbers, and recompute the textbook’s tables for the trade examples. Each function’s description names the equation it computes. The figure sections reuse these functions.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description. The same function works for single numbers and for whole columns of a data table, because pandas does arithmetic on every row at once.


def share_of_gdp(x, gdp):
    """Any variable as a percent of GDP: 100 x / Y."""
    return 100 * x / gdp


def net_exports(exports, imports):
    """The trade balance (net exports): NX = EX - IM."""
    return exports - imports


def net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G):
    """The national income identity solved for net exports: NX = Y - (C + I + G)   (equation 1)."""
    return Y - (C + I + G)


def trade_balance_share(c, i, g):
    """NX as a percent of GDP from the GDP shares of C, I and G: 100 (1 - c - i - g)   (equation 2)."""
    return 100 * net_exports_from_uses(1, c, i, g)


def share_of_us_gdp(share, gdp, gdp_us):
    """Rescale a share of a country's own GDP to a share of U.S. GDP (Fig. 19.3, second bar)."""
    return share * gdp / gdp_us

Four more functions handle saving and the data over time: two forms of equation (4), an average over a window of years, and the sum of past flows, which turns yearly trade balances into a stock of foreign assets or debt (equation 5 with \(\bar{r} = 0\)).

Python note. For a table whose rows are years, data.loc[start:end] keeps the rows from start to end, both included, and .mean() averages them (one average per column). .cumsum() is the cumulative sum: row by row, the sum of all values so far.


def domestic_saving(I, NX):
    """Domestic saving S = Y - C - G, from equation (4): S = I + NX."""
    return I + NX


def net_capital_outflow(S, I):
    """Equation (4): the trade balance equals domestic saving minus investment, NX = S - I."""
    return S - I


def period_average(data, start, end):
    """Simple average over the years start to end (rows are years): one number per column."""
    return data.loc[start:end].mean()


def accumulate(start_value, flows):
    """Net foreign assets with no interest: start from start_value and add each year's trade balance (equation 5)."""
    return start_value + flows.cumsum()

NX_row = -NX_us                                  # every U.S. import is a rest-of-world export

print(f"World trade balance: {NX_us + NX_row}")
print(f"Rest of the world: a surplus of {row_share:.0f}% of its own GDP, "
      f"or {share_of_us_gdp(row_share, gdp_row, gdp_us):.0f}% of U.S. GDP")

World trade balance: 0
Rest of the world: a surplus of 1% of its own GDP, or 3% of U.S. GDP


Check 3: the intertemporal budget constraint. A country with no foreign assets borrows 50 in year 1 and repays the loan with 5 percent interest in year 2. Equation (5) should bring its assets back to zero, and the present value of its two trade balances should be zero, as equation (6) says.

Python note. range(1, 3) counts 1, 2. A list is numbered from 0, so trade_balance[t - 1] is the trade balance of year t. x = x + ... replaces the old value of x with the new one.


r = 0.05
trade_balance = [-50, 50 * (1 + r)]              # borrow 50, then repay 50 plus interest
F = 0.0                                          # no foreign assets at the start
present_value = 0.0
for t in range(1, 3):
    F = (1 + r) * F + trade_balance[t - 1]                     # equation (5)
    present_value = present_value + trade_balance[t - 1] / (1 + r) ** t
    print(f"Year {t}: NX = {trade_balance[t - 1]:+.1f}, F = {F:+.2f}")
print(f"Present value of the trade balances = {present_value:.6f}   (equation 6: -F0 = 0)")

Year 1: NX = -50.0, F = -50.00
Year 2: NX = +52.5, F = +0.00
Present value of the trade balances = 0.000000   (equation 6: -F0 = 0)


Check 4: the long-run debt ratio. We apply the ratio form of equation (5) year after year with a constant deficit of 3 percent of GDP, and compare where it ends with the formula of equation (7).

def debt_ratio_steady_state(nx, g, r=0.0):
    """Long-run net foreign assets as a share of GDP: f* = (1 + g) nx / (g - r)   (equation 7)."""
    return (1 + g) * nx / (g - r)


for g, r in [(0.04, 0.0), (0.05, 0.0), (0.04, 0.02)]:
    f = 0.0                                          # start with no foreign assets
    for year in range(1000):
        f = (1 + r) / (1 + g) * f + (-0.03)          # equation (5) divided by GDP
    print(f"g = {g:.0%}, r = {r:.0%}: simulated f = {100 * f:.1f}% of GDP, "
          f"formula = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, g, r):.1f}%")

g = 4%, r = 0%: simulated f = -78.0% of GDP, formula = -78.0%
g = 5%, r = 0%: simulated f = -63.0% of GDP, formula = -63.0%
g = 4%, r = 2%: simulated f = -156.0% of GDP, formula = -156.0%

Autarky. The function follows Steps 1 to 4 of the autarky solution.

Python note. pd.Series({...}) builds a list of numbers with labels from a dictionary. pd.DataFrame then puts two such lists side by side as the columns “North” and “South”. pd.concat([...], axis=1, keys=[...]) places two tables next to each other under two headings.


def autarky(x, z, L):
    """Table 19.3: a closed economy whose L workers each make x apples or z computers."""
    w = x                        # the wage in apples: what a worker makes in the apple sector (equation 9)
    p = x / z                    # the price of a computer: both sectors must pay the same wage (equation 9)
    return pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w,
                      "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                      "Apples per person": w / 2,              # equation (8): an apple costs 1
                      "Computers per person": w / 2 / p,       # equation (8)
                      "Workers making apples (%)": 50,
                      "Workers making computers (%)": 50,
                      "Apples produced": L / 2 * x,
                      "Computers produced": L / 2 * z})

Free trade. The function follows Steps 2 to 5 of the free-trade solution: complete specialization, the world price of equation (10), the wages and consumption from equation (8).

def free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s):
    """Table 19.4: the North makes only computers, the South only apples, and they trade."""
    computers = L_n * z_n                      # world production of computers
    apples = L_s * x_s                         # world production of apples
    p = apples / computers                     # equation (10): half of world spending goes to each good
    w_n, w_s = z_n * p, x_s                    # wages in apples
    north = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_n, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_n / 2, "Computers per person": w_n / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 0, "Workers making computers (%)": 100,
                       "Apples produced": 0, "Computers produced": computers})
    south = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_s, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_s / 2, "Computers per person": w_s / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 100, "Workers making computers (%)": 0,
                       "Apples produced": apples, "Computers produced": 0})
    return pd.DataFrame({"North": north, "South": south})

title: 19. International Trade
text:
Some basic facts about trade
We begin with the U.S. numbers: how much the country sells abroad and buys from abroad, and how the gap between the two has grown since the 1970s. Then we put the United States next to the rest of the world.

Fig. 1: U.S. import and export shares of GDP
Goal. See how much more the United States trades today than 75 years ago.
The file us_trade.csv holds the U.S. national accounts we need, in billions of current dollars: GDP, exports, imports, net exports, private investment and the net international investment position (Fig. 6), plus the same position as it was published in July 2023.

Python note. set_index("year") makes the years the row labels, so that us.loc[2006] is the row of 2006 and us.exports is one column, a Series with years as labels. NaN (“not a number”) marks a missing value: the investment position starts only in 1976.

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), National Income and Product Accounts, via FRED: Exports of goods and services (EXPGSA), Imports of goods and services (IMPGSA) and Gross domestic product (GDPA). Prepared file: data/ch19/us_trade.csv, checked against data/ch19/fig19-1.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

In the 1950s exports and imports were each only about 4 to 5 percent of GDP. Since then exports have more than doubled and imports more than tripled.
The two lines move together until the early 1970s, and then they separate: imports have been above exports every year since 1976. The gap between them is the trade deficit of Fig. 2.
Trade falls sharply in world recessions (2009, 2020) and in the strong-dollar years of the mid-1980s, when U.S. exports dropped to 7 percent of GDP.


Key numbers: how much does the United States trade?
The textbook says that exports and imports rose “from under 5 percent of GDP in the 1950s to around 12 and 15 percent of GDP, respectively, in recent years” (Jones 2024).

Python note. ~ means “not”: ~above is True in the years when imports were not above exports. .idxmax() gives the label (here the year) of the largest value.


fifties = shares.loc[1950:1959]
print(f"1950s: highest export share {fifties.Exports.max():.2f}% ({fifties.Exports.idxmax()}), "
      f"highest import share {fifties.Imports.max():.2f}%")
print(f"2022, the textbook's last year: exports {shares.Exports[2022]:.2f}%, imports {shares.Imports[2022]:.2f}%")
above = shares.Imports > shares.Exports
print(f"Imports have been above exports every year since {above[~above].index.max() + 1}")
openness = shares.Exports + shares.Imports
print(f"Exports + imports: {openness[1950]:.1f}% of GDP in 1950, {openness.max():.1f}% at the peak "
      f"({openness.idxmax()}), {openness[last]:.1f}% in {last}")

1950s: highest export share 5.07% (1957), highest import share 4.28%
2022, the textbook's last year: exports 11.65%, imports 15.18%
Imports have been above exports every year since 1976
Exports + imports: 8.0% of GDP in 1950, 30.8% at the peak (2011), 24.6% in 2025


The textbook’s “respectively” lists the two numbers the wrong way round: exports are about 12 percent of GDP (11.65 percent in 2022) and imports about 15 percent (15.18 percent). And “under 5 percent” holds only after rounding: exports reached 5.07 percent in 1957. Exports and imports together, a common measure of how open an economy is, went from 8 percent of GDP in 1950 to a peak of 30.8 percent in 2011.


Beyond the United States: how open is each economy?
The textbook shows only the United States. The World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI) publish the same two shares, exports and imports of goods and services as a percent of GDP (series NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS and NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS), for almost every economy. The file wdi_trade.csv has one row per economy and year from 1960 to 2025 (most economies start later, and 2025 is still missing for many). Its column trade_balance is exports minus imports (NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS), which we use in Fig. 2. The small file countries.csv gives each economy’s World Bank region and income group.

Python note. .nunique() counts the different values in a column. Subtracting two Series lines them up by their labels (here the years), and a year that one of them lacks gives NaN, which .max() skips. For the United States the WDI copy the BEA’s numbers, so the two sources should agree.


world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")         # World Bank WDI, percent of GDP
regions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")       # World Bank region and income group of each economy
us_wdi = world[world.country == "U.S."].set_index("year")
gap = max((us_wdi.exports - shares.Exports).abs().max(), (us_wdi.imports - shares.Imports).abs().max())
print(f"{world.country.nunique()} economies, {world.year.min()}-{world.year.max()}; the U.S. rows start in "
      f"{us_wdi.index.min()} and differ from the BEA data by at most {gap:.2f} points")

Each economy gets one fixed color, so that it keeps its color when you add or remove others. Plotly offers 44 dark enough colors, fewer than the 214 economies, so group_colors hands them out such that the economies of one menu group (the G7, a region, …) never share a color, as far as 44 colors allow.

LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]     # too pale on a white background
PALETTE = []
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:   # 24 + 26 colors, 44 of them kept
    if color not in LIGHT and color != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # Dark24's medium blue goes last: it is close to the book's navy


Python note. For each country, score gives every color a cost: 1 for each country that already uses it, 10 for each one in a large group (Europe has more countries than there are colors) and 100 for each one in a group small enough to avoid any clash. a if test else b gives a when the test is True. min(PALETTE, key=score.get) picks the color with the lowest cost (the first one on ties). When no color is free, PALETTE[::-1] (the list in reverse order) makes the search start from the end of the list, so that the leftovers take the last, rarely used colors.


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (the menu views); fixed: the textbook countries' colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue
        score = {}                                  # the cost of each color: lower is better
        for color in PALETTE:
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)            # 1 per country using it anywhere
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10      # a clash in a small group costs most
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)                              # the cheapest color
        if score[best] >= 10:                       # no free color: the least used one, searching from the end
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors


COLORS = group_colors(regions.country, country_groups(regions, ["U.S."]).values(), {"U.S.": BLUE})

The dictionary COLORS maps each economy to its color, and color_discrete_map=COLORS makes Plotly use it, in Colab and on the website. fit_range keeps the textbook’s axis range when the data fit in it; otherwise it returns None, which lets Plotly choose a range that shows every value.

def fit_range(values, book_range):
    """The textbook's axis range if every value fits in it, otherwise None (Plotly then chooses)."""
    if values.min() >= book_range[0] and values.max() <= book_range[1]:
        return book_range
    return None

The Oddtopia example says that the trade balance must average zero over a long period. The figure function shades a window of years and reports the average trade balance in it, using our period_average.

def trade_balance_chart(start=1976, end=2025):
    """Fig. 19.2: the U.S. trade balance (% of GDP), with its average from start to end."""
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)         # in case the sliders cross
    avg = period_average(us.trade_balance, start, end)
    deficits = (us.trade_balance.loc[start:end] < 0).sum()
    fig = px.line(us.reset_index(), x="year", y="trade_balance", color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"},
                  title=f"{start}–{end}: average trade balance {avg:+.2f}% of GDP, "
                        f"deficits in {deficits} of {end - start + 1} years")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=start, x1=end, y0=avg, y1=avg, line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=1990, y=1.6, text="Above zero: exports > imports", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    fig.add_annotation(x=1965, y=-4.5, text="Below zero: imports > exports", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1948, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-6.5, 2.5], tickvals=[-5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2])   # no label in the corner
    return fig

Python note. go.Scatter(x=[start, end], y=[avg, avg], mode="lines") draws one straight segment. legendgroup=name ties it to the economy’s line, so that a click on the legend hides both, and showlegend=False keeps it out of the legend.


def add_average(fig, series, name, start, end):
    """Draw the average of a yearly series from start to end as a dotted segment, and return the average."""
    avg = period_average(series, start, end)
    if avg == avg:                                         # NaN (no data in the window) is not equal to itself
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[start, end], y=[avg, avg], mode="lines", name=name + ", average",
                                 legendgroup=name, showlegend=False,
                                 line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=3, dash="dot")))
    return avg


def trade_balance_world(countries=("U.S.",), start=1976, end=2024):
    """Fig. 19.2 for any economies: the trade balance (% of GDP, WDI) and its average from start to end."""
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)          # in case the sliders cross
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    fig = px.line(rows, x="year", y="trade_balance", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    names = []
    for name in sorted(set(rows.country)):
        avg = add_average(fig, rows[rows.country == name].set_index("year").trade_balance, name, start, end)
        if avg == avg:
            names.append(f"{name} {round(avg, 1) + 0.0:+.1f}%")     # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
        else:
            names.append(f"{name}: no data")
    more = f" + {len(names) - 2} more" if len(names) > 2 else ""
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Average trade balance {start}–{end}: " + ", ".join(names[:2]) + more,
                      legend_title_text="")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(rows.trade_balance.dropna(), [-6.5, 2.5]))
    return fig

Python note. .isin(list) is True for the rows whose value is in the list. .melt(id_vars="country") turns the two measure columns into rows, one row per country and measure, the long shape that px.bar needs. With color="Measure" and barmode="group", the bars of the two measures stand side by side. A function can return two results at once, order, missing, and the caller unpacks them into two names.


FIG3 = ["U.S.", "Japan", "China", "France", "Germany"]


def book_order(countries, book, available):
    """The chosen countries with data, the textbook's first and in its order, and the chosen ones without data."""
    order, missing = [], []
    for name in list(book) + sorted(countries):
        if name in countries and name not in order and name not in missing:
            if name in available:
                order.append(name)
            else:
                missing.append(name)
    return order, missing


def world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing):
    """The title of Fig. 3: the U.S. deficit and the largest surplus in percent of U.S. GDP."""
    if missing:
        return f"{year}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])
    if len(bars) == 0:
        return "Choose at least one country"
    text = f"{year} ({vintage}): "
    if "U.S." in bars.index:
        text += f"U.S. deficit {-bars.loc['U.S.', 'Share of own GDP']:.1f}% of GDP; "
    top = bars["Share of U.S. GDP"].idxmax()
    value = round(bars.loc[top, "Share of U.S. GDP"], 2) + 0.0     # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
    if value > 0:
        return text + f"largest surplus {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"
    return text + f"smallest deficit {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"


def world_balance_chart(year=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG3):
    """Fig. 19.3: the trade balance as a share of own GDP and of U.S. GDP, in one year."""
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    year = min(year, source[source.vintage == vintage].year.max())     # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    rows = source[(source.year == year) & (source.vintage == vintage)].set_index("country")
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG3, rows.index)
    one = rows.loc[order]
    bars = pd.DataFrame({"Share of own GDP": one.trade_balance,
                         "Share of U.S. GDP": share_of_us_gdp(one.trade_balance, one.cgdpo, rows.loc["U.S.", "cgdpo"])})
    long = bars.reset_index().melt(id_vars="country", var_name="Measure", value_name="Percent")
    fig = px.bar(long, x="country", y="Percent", color="Measure", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_map={"Share of own GDP": BLUE, "Share of U.S. GDP": GREEN},
                 labels={"country": "", "Percent": "Percent"}, title=world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    book = fit_range(long.Percent, [-9, 12.5])           # the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=book, tickvals=[-8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", title=""))
    return fig
