Inflation rises from 2 to 3 percent in period 1 and climbs toward 4 percent while the shock lasts. When the shock ends in period 10, output falls below potential and inflation starts back down to 2 percent.


Drawing tools
Both model diagrams use the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

add_curve draws a curve and writes its name at its last point inside the axes, as the textbook does;
add_point marks a point with a dot, a letter and dashed guides to the axes;
add_arrow draws an arrow between two points.


Python note. (x >= 0) & (y <= 8) is true where both conditions hold, x[inside] keeps the values where inside is true, and [-1] takes the last of them. add_annotation with axref="x" and ayref="y" draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y), both in axis units. Labels such as "AS<sub>8</sub>" use HTML to write AS₈.


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, x_range, y_range, dash="solid"):
    """Draw one curve and write its label at its last point inside the axes (no label if label is "")."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    inside = (x >= x_range[0]) & (x <= x_range[1]) & (y >= y_range[0]) & (y <= y_range[1])
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        fig.add_annotation(x=x[inside][-1], y=y[inside][-1], text=label, showarrow=False,
                           xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_point(fig, x, y, label, x0, y0, guides=True):
    """Mark the point (x, y) with a dot and a label; with guides, dashed lines to the axes at x0 and y0."""
    if guides:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x0, x, x], y=[y, y, y0], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition="top right",
                             name=label, showlegend=False, textfont=dict(size=16), marker=dict(color="black", size=10)))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, color="black"):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; nothing if the two points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y", text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor=color)



Tools for comparing countries
The textbook’s data figures show a few countries. Every one of them can show many more: the data files of this chapter hold the same series for up to 200 economies, from the World Bank, the IMF, the OECD, the Federal Reserve and the Penn World Table. The file countries.csv lists the economies with their World Bank region and income group, and says which are OECD members and since when each euro member uses the euro.

Three small tools are shared by the data figures:

group_colors gives every country a fixed color, so a line keeps its color when you add or remove others. The textbook’s countries keep the textbook’s colors, and the countries of one menu group (the G7, a region, …) never share a color, as far as Plotly’s 44 dark enough colors allow;
ratio_ticks chooses round tick values for a ratio-scale axis that spans less than a factor of 10 (Plotly’s own ticks crowd there; over wider spans we let Plotly choose);
missing_note adds a note to a title when a chosen country has no data;
high_low names the countries with the highest and the lowest value, for the titles;
book_order puts the textbook’s countries first in a bar chart.


Python note. px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 and .Alphabet are lists of colors that Plotly provides; we drop the pale ones. In group_colors, for each country, score gives every color a cost: 1 for each country that already uses it, 10 for each one in a large group (Europe has more countries than there are colors) and 100 for each one in a group small enough to avoid any clash. a if test else b gives a when the test is True. min(PALETTE, key=score.get) picks the color with the lowest cost (the first one on ties). When no color is free, PALETTE[::-1] (the list in reverse order) makes the search start from the end of the list, so that the leftovers take the last, rarely used colors.


LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]     # too pale on a white background
PALETTE = []
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:   # 24 + 26 colors, 44 of them kept
    if color not in LIGHT and color != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # Dark24's medium blue goes last: it is close to the book's navy


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (the menu views); fixed: the textbook countries' colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue
        score = {}                                  # the cost of each color: lower is better
        for color in PALETTE:
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)            # 1 per country using it anywhere
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10      # a clash in a small group costs most
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)                              # the cheapest color
        if score[best] >= 10:                       # no free color: the least used one, searching from the end
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors


def ratio_ticks(low, high):
    """Round tick values between low and high for a ratio-scale axis; None (Plotly's ticks) beyond a factor of 10."""
    if high / low >= 10:
        return None
    ticks = []
    for power in range(-3, 6):
        for step in [1, 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]:
            if low <= step * 10 ** power <= high:
                ticks.append(round(step * 10 ** power, 6))
    return ticks


Python note. ", ".join(missing) glues a list of texts into one text, with ", " between them. In f"{value:{fmt}}" the format itself is a variable: fmt=".0f" shows no decimals, ".1f" one. In a Plotly title, <br> starts a new line and <sup>...</sup> writes smaller text.


def missing_note(wanted, found):
    """A second, smaller title line naming the chosen countries that have no data ('' if all have data)."""
    missing = []
    for name in wanted:
        if name not in set(found):
            missing.append(name)
    if len(missing) == 0:
        return ""
    if len(missing) > 3:
        return f"<br><sup>no data for {len(missing)} of the chosen countries</sup>"
    return "<br><sup>no data: " + ", ".join(missing) + "</sup>"


def high_low(values, fmt=".0f"):
    """'A 12, B 3': the countries with the highest and the lowest value (one name only for one country)."""
    text = f"{values.idxmax()} {values.max():{fmt}}"
    if len(values) > 1:
        text = text + f", {values.idxmin()} {values.min():{fmt}}"
    return text


def book_order(countries, book):
    """The textbook's countries in the textbook's order, then the others alphabetically (for bar charts)."""
    order = []
    for name in book:
        if name in countries:
            order.append(name)
    for name in sorted(countries):
        if name not in order:
            order.append(name)
    return order


print(ratio_ticks(67, 142), ratio_ticks(1, 50), missing_note(("Japan", "Kosovo"), ["Japan"]))
print(high_low(pd.Series({"Japan": 2.4, "Switzerland": 2.2, "United States": 4.0}), ".1f"))

Exchange rates in the long run
We start with the data: how the dollar has moved against the yen and the euro, and whether the gap in inflation between two countries explains the move, as the law of one price predicts.

Fig. 1: The U.S. exchange rate versus the yen and the euro
Goal. See how the price of a dollar has moved since the end of fixed exchange rates in 1971.
The exchange rate here is the price of a dollar in foreign currency: how many yen, or how many euros, one dollar buys. A fall is a depreciation of the dollar, a rise an appreciation. The two series have very different units (hundreds of yen, about one euro), so the textbook draws them on two vertical scales.

def dollar_index(countries=("Japan", "Euro area"), base=1999, scale="linear"):
    """Fig. 20.1 for any currency: units of the currency per dollar, index = 100 in the base year."""
    picked = fx_all[fx_all.country.isin(countries)].copy()
    level = picked[picked.year == base].groupby("country").per_usd.mean()     # average of the base year
    picked["index"] = (100 * picked.per_usd / picked.country.map(level)).round(1)
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["index"])
    latest = picked.groupby("country")["index"].last()                        # each currency's last month
    title = f"No data in {base} for these currencies"
    if len(latest) > 0:
        title = f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100), latest: " + high_low(latest)
    fig = px.line(picked, x="date", y="index", color="label", hover_name="label", color_discrete_map=FX_COLORS,
                  log_y=(scale == "ratio"), title=title + missing_note(countries, level.index),
                  labels={"date": "Year", "index": f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100)"})
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    if scale == "ratio" and len(picked) > 0:
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=ratio_ticks(picked["index"].min(), picked["index"].max()))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", xaxis_range=["1965-01-01", "2027-06-01"])   # no tick label in the corner
    return fig

def inflation_chart(countries=("United States", "Japan")):
    """Fig. 20.2 for any countries: consumer-price inflation, percent per year."""
    picked = inflation_all[inflation_all.country.isin(countries)]
    means = picked[(picked.year >= 1971) & (picked.year <= 2024)].groupby("country").inflation.mean()

    top = 25.0
    if len(picked) > 0:
        top = min(max(25.0, 1.05 * picked.inflation.max()), 100.0)
    if len(picked) > 0 and picked.inflation.max() > 100:
        title = title + "; axis cut at 100"
    fig = px.line(picked, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country",

    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    bottom = min(-3.0, picked.inflation.min() - 1) if len(picked) > 0 else -3.0
    fig.update_layout(yaxis_range=[bottom, top], xaxis_range=[1955, 2026], legend_title_text="")   # 1960 off the corner

def big_mac_table(release="2022-07-01"):
    """Table 20.1: Big Mac prices in local currency and in dollars, for one release of the index."""

We can also build the real exchange rate ourselves, from the data of Figs. 1 and 2. Inflation tells us how fast the price level grows each year, so multiplying the growth factors \(1 + \pi_t/100\) year after year gives the price level.

Python note. fx.date.dt.year takes the year out of each date, and groupby("year").yen_per_usd.mean() averages the 12 months of each year. .cumprod() is the cumulative product: it multiplies the growth factors year after year, \(P_t = P_{t-1}(1+\pi_t/100)\). Dividing two pandas series lines up their rows by year automatically.

yen = fx.groupby("year").yen_per_usd.mean()              # annual average, yen per dollar

growth_us = 1 + prices.inflation_us / 100
growth_jp = 1 + prices.inflation_jpn / 100
P_us = growth_us.cumprod() / growth_us.loc[1971]          # consumer price level, 1971 = 1
P_jp = growth_jp.cumprod() / growth_jp.loc[1971]

estimate = (P_jp / yen) / P_us                            # dollar price of Japanese goods relative to U.S. goods

Our consumer-price estimate rises more (to 286 in 1995), because it compares consumer prices rather than the prices of everything an economy produces, but it tells the same story year by year.


Key numbers: the law of one price, 1971–1995
If the law of one price had held, the yen-dollar rate would have changed each year only by the inflation gap. We apply the growth factors of 1972–1995 to the 1971 rate.

Python note. .prod() multiplies all the values of a series, here the 24 yearly factors.

print(f"1995 rate predicted by the law of one price:      {yen[1971] * ratio:.0f}")
print(f"Actual 1995 average:                              {yen[1995]:.0f}")

Yen per dollar, 1971 average:                     348
1995 rate predicted by the law of one price:      269
Actual 1995 average:                              94


The inflation gap explains a fall to about 269 yen per dollar. The dollar actually fell to 94 yen, so the real exchange rate of the yen rose a lot. That is the “apparent contradiction” of the textbook’s case study.


The Balassa-Samuelson effect in the Big Mac data
The explanation is that only traded goods obey the law of one price. Haircuts and restaurant meals cannot be shipped, and their prices follow local wages. As an economy grows, wages rise, nontraded goods become dearer, and the real exchange rate appreciates. def rer_chart(countries=("Japan",), measure="index, 1971 = 100"):

title: 20. Exchange Rates and International Finance
section: The open economy in the short-run model
text:
The open economy in the short-run model
Now prices are sticky and the exchange rate reacts to interest rates. These two model figures show how this flattens the IS curve and turns a rise in foreign interest rates into a demand shock.

Fig. 4: Increasing interest rates and the IS curve
Goal. See why the IS curve is flatter in an open economy: a higher interest rate lowers net exports as well as investment.
The central bank raises the real interest rate from \(\bar{r}\) to \(R'\). The economy moves along the IS curve from \(A\) to \(B\). Two forces lower output:
\[\uparrow R \;\Rightarrow\; \downarrow \frac{I}{\bar{Y}} \quad\text{and}\quad
\uparrow R \Rightarrow \uparrow E \Rightarrow \uparrow \frac{EP}{P^w} \Rightarrow \downarrow \frac{NX}{\bar{Y}}.\]
From the IS curve, equation (11), \(\tilde{Y}' = -(\bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx})(R' - \bar{r})\). The dashed gray line is the IS curve without the trade channel (\(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0\)), the closed economy of Chapter 11.

R_LINE = np.linspace(9, 2, 141)              # real interest rates, high to low, at which we draw the IS curves
R_UP = np.linspace(2, 9, 141)                # the same rates, low to high: the label then goes at the upper end
X_IS, R_AXIS = [-11, 5], [2, 9]              # fixed axes, so that you can see the curve turn


def tightening(R_new=6.0, b_nx=B_NX, b_i=B_I):
    """Fig. 20.4: the central bank raises R from r_bar to R_new; the economy moves along the IS curve."""
    Y_new = is_curve(R_new, b_i=b_i, b_nx=b_nx)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if b_nx > 0:
        add_curve(fig, is_curve(R_UP, b_i=b_i, b_nx=0.0), R_UP, "IS without trade", GRAY, X_IS, R_AXIS, "dash")
    add_curve(fig, is_curve(R_LINE, b_i=b_i, b_nx=b_nx), R_LINE, "IS", BLUE, X_IS, R_AXIS)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", X_IS[0], R_AXIS[0])
    if R_new != R_BAR:                                                        # B is A when the rate does not change
        add_point(fig, Y_new, R_new, "B", X_IS[0], R_AXIS[0])
    add_arrow(fig, X_IS[0] + 0.6, R_BAR, X_IS[0] + 0.6, R_new)              # the interest rate rises ...
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, R_AXIS[0] + 0.3, Y_new, R_AXIS[0] + 0.3)            # ... and output falls
    invest = -b_i * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0                                    # + 0.0 avoids printing -0.0
    trade = -b_nx * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0
    fig.update_layout(title=f"R′ = {R_new:.1f}%  →  Ỹ′ = {Y_new + 0.0:.1f}%   "
                            f"(investment {invest:.1f}, net exports {trade:.1f})",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=X_IS, tickvals=list(range(-10, 5, 2)),
                                 zeroline=False),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Real interest rate, R (percent)", range=R_AXIS, tickvals=list(range(3, 9)),
                                 zeroline=False))
    return fig

         b_i=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="investment sensitivity b̄ᵢ", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Fig. 20.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With the baseline, raising \(R\) from 5 to 6 percent lowers output by 2 percent: 1 point through investment and 1 point through net exports. Without trade, output would fall by only 1 percent.
Raise \(\bar{b}_{nx}\): the IS curve turns flatter and point \(B\) moves left. The more net exports react to the exchange rate, the more powerful monetary policy is.
Nothing else changes: the curve still passes through \(A\), because at \(R = \bar{r}\) there is no gap to react to.

Fig. 5: An increase in foreign interest rates
Goal. Follow the international transmission of monetary policy: the European Central Bank raises its interest rate, and the U.S. economy booms, then slumps.
When the foreign real interest rate rises to \(\bar{R}^w = 7\) percent, 2 points above \(\bar{r}\), investors move from dollars to euros, the dollar depreciates, U.S. goods become cheap and U.S. net exports rise. In the IS curve, equation (11), this is a positive demand shock, \(\bar{a} = \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}) = 2\), so the AD curve shifts out to AD₁. Then the familiar dynamics of Chapter 13 take over:

period 1: the economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\), with output and inflation above normal;
periods 2–9: inflation rises, the Fed raises U.S. interest rates, and the economy climbs AD₁ toward \(C\) (period 8 in the textbook), with output back at potential but inflation above target;
period 10: the foreign rate falls back to \(\bar{r}\), the shock ends, AD shifts back, and the economy drops to a recession at \(D\); it then slides down AD back to \(A\).

The function draws period t: the original AS curve, the AS curve of period t, both AD curves (the one that holds in period t in full color), the path so far with the textbook’s letters, and the path still to come in gray.

Y_LINE = np.linspace(-6, 6, 121)                # output levels at which we draw the AS curves
PI_LINE = np.linspace(12, -4, 161)              # inflation rates, high to low, at which we draw the AD curves
X_AD, PI_AXIS = [-3.5, 3.5], [-0.5, 7.5]        # fixed axes
LETTERS = {0: "A", 1: "B", 8: "C", 10: "D"}     # the textbook's letters for periods 0, 1, 8 and 10
FADED = "rgba(22,82,140,0.35)"                  # light blue for the AD curve that does not hold in period t


def add_asad_curves(fig, a, pi_e, t, m, b):
    """The AS curves (original and period t) and the AD curves (original and shifted) of Fig. 5."""
    add_curve(fig, Y_LINE, as_inflation(Y_LINE, PI_BAR), "AS", TEAL, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    if abs(pi_e - PI_BAR) > 0.05:                                   # skip the AS of period t if it is the old one
        label = f"AS<sub>{t}</sub>" if abs(pi_e - PI_BAR) > 0.6 else ""
        add_curve(fig, Y_LINE, as_inflation(Y_LINE, pi_e), label, TEAL, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    shock_on = 1 <= t <= A_LAST
    ad_label = f"AD = AD<sub>{t}</sub>" if t > A_LAST else "AD"
    add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_LINE, 0.0, m, b), PI_LINE, ad_label, FADED if shock_on else BLUE, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    if a != 0:
        label = "AD<sub>1</sub>" if abs(a) > 0.8 and abs(a / (b * m)) > 0.6 else ""  # no label on top of AD's
        add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_LINE, a, m, b), PI_LINE, label, BLUE if shock_on else FADED, X_AD, PI_AXIS)


Python note. for x, y in written: goes through a list of pairs and unpacks each pair into x and y. A letter is left out when its point lies within 0.3 points of output and 0.6 points of inflation of a point that already has one, as happens when a small shock or a strong policy response keeps \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) close to \(A\).


def add_path(fig, path, t):
    """The economy's path up to period t (dots, arrows, letters) and the rest of the path in gray."""
    future = path[path.period >= t]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=future.Y, y=future.pi, mode="lines+markers", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dot"), marker=dict(color=GRAY, size=5)))
    for s in range(1, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s])
    written = []                                        # the points that already carry a letter
    for s in range(t + 1):
        if s in LETTERS:
            letter = LETTERS[s]
            for x, y in written:
                if abs(path.Y[s] - x) < 0.3 and abs(path.pi[s] - y) < 0.6:
                    letter = ""                         # too close to a letter already written: leave it out
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], letter, X_AD[0], PI_AXIS[0], guides=False)
            if letter != "":
                written.append((path.Y[s], path.pi[s]))


def foreign_rate_shock(gap=RW_GAP, t=10, b_nx=B_NX, m=M_BAR):
    """Fig. 20.5: period t after the foreign real interest rate rises gap points above r_bar in periods 1-9."""
    a = foreign_shock(R_BAR + gap, b_nx)                 # equation (11): the demand shock from abroad
    b = B_I + b_nx
    path = simulate(shock_list(a), m, b)
    now = path.loc[t]
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_asad_curves(fig, a, now.pi_e, t, m, b)
    add_path(fig, path, t)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0:+.2f}%   "
                            f"(Rʷ − r̄ = {gap:.1f}, so ā = {a:.2f} in periods 1–{A_LAST})",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Output, Ỹ (percent)", range=X_AD, tickvals=list(range(-3, 4)), zeroline=False),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Inflation, π (percent)", range=PI_AXIS, tickvals=list(range(0, 8)), zeroline=False))
    return fig


Python note. IntSlider is a slider for whole numbers, here the period t. path.loc[t] is the row of period t, and now.pi is its value in the column pi.

         gap=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="foreign rate gap Rʷ − r̄", style=WIDE),
         t=IntSlider(value=10, min=1, max=20, step=1, description="period t", style=WIDE),
         b_nx=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="net-export sensitivity b̄ₙₓ", style=WIDE),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version

slider_figure(foreign_rate_shock, "t", [1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, 20], start=10, label="period t")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 20.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

At \(B\) (period 1) output is 1 percent above potential and inflation 3 percent: half of the shock goes into output, half into inflation, because \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\) as in Chapter 13.
At \(C\) output is back at potential, but inflation is close to \(\bar{\pi} + \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m}) = 4\) percent. The AS curves of periods 8, 9 and 10 are almost the same line, which is why the textbook draws \(C\) and \(D\) on one curve, AS₈.
When the shock ends, the economy pays for the boom with a recession at \(D\): output 1 percent below potential.
The U.S. did nothing, yet its economy boomed and slumped: a change in interest rates abroad is a demand shock at home.

Exchange-rate regimes and the policy trilemma
Countries have chosen very different ways to manage their currencies, from the gold standard to free floating. This section follows that history and the trade-off behind every choice, including what happens when a fixed rate breaks.

Fig. 6: The U.K.-U.S. exchange rate
Goal. Read two centuries of exchange-rate history in one line: the gold standard, Bretton Woods and floating rates.
Under the gold standard each country fixed the price of an ounce of gold in its currency. From 1834 the United States paid about 20.67 dollars an ounce and the United Kingdom 4.25 pounds, so a dollar was worth \(4.25/20.67 \approx 0.206\) pounds. Under Bretton Woods (1944 to the early 1970s) other currencies were pegged to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at 35 dollars an ounce. Since 1973 the major currencies float.

Fig. 7: The policy trilemma in open economies
Goal. See why an open economy can have at most two of three good things: a stable exchange rate, its own monetary policy, and free flows of international finance.
The textbook draws the policy trilemma as a triangle: the three goals are its corners, and each side is a regime that achieves the two goals at its ends and gives up the one opposite. Here the triangle is live. A small model from the chapter computes what happens when the foreign central bank (say, the Fed) raises its interest rate by \(\Delta i^w\), while your economy needs its own interest rate to change by \(\Delta i^{need}\):

with free financial flows, the exchange rate moves with the interest gap (uncovered interest parity, equation 8: \(\uparrow i \Rightarrow \uparrow E\)), \(\%\Delta E = \eta\,(\Delta i - \Delta i^w)\), with an illustrative \(\eta = 5\) percent per point;
floating exchange rate: the central bank sets \(\Delta i = \Delta i^{need}\), and the exchange rate moves;
currency board (or monetary union): to keep \(E\) fixed, the interest rate must follow abroad, \(\Delta i = \Delta i^w\);
capital controls: the central bank sets \(\Delta i = \Delta i^{need}\) and keeps \(E\) fixed, because it rations the trade in its currency, so money cannot flow freely.


ETA = 5.0                                       # percent change of E per point of interest gap (illustrative)
LOST = {"floating exchange rate": "stable exchange rate", "currency board": "monetary autonomy",
        "capital controls": "free financial flows"}     # the goal each regime gives up: the opposite corner


def trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need):
    """Fig. 20.7 as a model: the change in the domestic interest rate and the percent change in E."""
    if regime == "currency board":
        di = di_world                           # the peg forces the domestic rate to follow the foreign rate
    else:
        di = di_need                            # floating or capital controls: the central bank chooses
    if regime == "floating exchange rate":
        dE = ETA * (di - di_world)              # free capital flows move the exchange rate
    else:
        dE = 0.0                                # fixed by the peg, or by rationing the currency
    return di, dE + 0.0, LOST[regime]

The four dictionaries above hold the geometry: the corners of the triangle, where each label goes, and which two corners each side joins (with its label position and angle). draw_triangle uses them.

def draw_triangle(fig, regime):
    """The trilemma triangle: the chosen side thick and green, the goal it gives up marked with a gray cross."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 2, 1, 0], y=[0, 0, 1.732, 0], fill="toself", fillcolor="#e6f5f1", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2), showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"))
    for side in SIDES:
        start, end, x, y, angle = SIDES[side]
        chosen = side == regime
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[CORNERS[start][0], CORNERS[end][0]], y=[CORNERS[start][1], CORNERS[end][1]],
                                 mode="lines", line=dict(color=GREEN if chosen else GRAY, width=9 if chosen else 2),
                                 name=SIDE_TEXT[side], showlegend=False))
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=SIDE_TEXT[side], textangle=angle, showarrow=False,
                           font=dict(size=13, color=TEAL if chosen else GRAY))
    for goal in CORNERS:
        kept = goal != LOST[regime]
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[CORNERS[goal][0]], y=[CORNERS[goal][1]], mode="markers", name=goal,
                                 showlegend=False, marker=dict(size=20, color=GREEN if kept else GRAY,
                                                               symbol="circle" if kept else "x")))
        x, y, xanchor, yanchor, text = CORNER_TEXT[goal]
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, xanchor=xanchor, yanchor=yanchor, showarrow=False,
                           font=dict(size=14, color="black" if kept else GRAY))


Python note. fill="toself" fills the shape that the points of the trace enclose, here the triangle. textangle=51 turns a text by 51 degrees, so that it runs along a side, and xanchor="right" makes a text end at its point instead of being centered on it. visible=False hides the axes, and the small margin lets the triangle fill the figure. The box at the top right, an annotation with a border, holds the readout.


def trilemma(regime="floating exchange rate", di_world=1.0, di_need=0.0):
    """Fig. 20.7: the policy trilemma; the foreign rate rises by di_world, the economy needs di_need."""
    di, dE, lost = trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need)
    flows = "blocked" if regime == "capital controls" else "free"
    fig = go.Figure()
    draw_triangle(fig, regime)
    fig.add_annotation(x=2.72, y=1.97, xanchor="right", yanchor="top", showarrow=False, align="left",
                       font=dict(size=13, color=BLUE), bordercolor=BLUE, borderpad=6, bgcolor="white",
                       text=f"Interest rate: {di:+.1f} pt<br>Exchange rate: {dE:+.1f}%<br>Capital flows: {flows}")
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[-0.75, 2.75])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[-0.38, 2.0])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{regime.capitalize()}: Δi = {di:+.1f}, %ΔE = {dE:+.1f}; lost: {lost}",
                      margin=dict(l=30, r=30, t=60, b=30))
    return fig

What to notice.

The Fed raises its rate by 1 point and your economy needs no change. With a floating rate you keep your interest rate, and your currency depreciates by 5 percent: the United States today.

def yield_chart(countries=("Germany", "Spain", "Italy")):
    """Fig. 20.9 for any countries: 10-year government bond yields, monthly, percent."""
    picked = yields_all[yields_all.country.isin(countries) & (yields_all.date >= "1995-01")]
    peak = picked[picked.date >= "2008-01"].sort_values("yield").tail(1)       # the highest yield since 2008
    title = "No bond yields for these countries"
    if len(peak) > 0:
        title = (f"10-year bond yields: highest since 2008 {peak.country.iloc[0]}, "
                 f"{peak['yield'].iloc[0]:.1f}% in {peak.date.iloc[0]}")
    top = max(14.5, picked["yield"].max() + 1.5) if len(picked) > 0 else 14.5
    bottom = min(-2.0, picked["yield"].min() - 0.5) if len(picked) > 0 else -2.0
    fig = px.line(picked, x="date", y="yield", color="country", hover_name="country", color_discrete_map=YIELD_COLORS,
                  title=title + missing_note(countries, picked.country.unique()), range_y=[bottom, top],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "yield": "10-year government bond yield (percent)"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    for date, text in [("1999-01", "euro"), ("2012-07", "Draghi")]:
        fig.add_vline(x=date, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
        fig.add_annotation(x=date, y=0.97, yref="paper", text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                           font=dict(color=GRAY))
    ticks = list(range(0, int(top), 2)) if top <= 20 else None
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", yaxis_tickvals=ticks, xaxis_range=["1992-07", "2027-01"])
    return fig

What to notice.

In 1995 Italy and Spain paid 4 to 6 points more than Germany. By the end of 1998 all three yields were close to 4 percent, and they moved together until 2008.
In 2011–2012 the Italian yield rose above 7 percent and the Spanish one to 6.8 percent, while Germany’s fell. After Mario Draghi promised in July 2012 that the ECB would do “whatever it takes”, the gaps closed again.
German yields were negative in mid-2016 and from April 2019 to January 2022: investors paid the German government to hold their money.
Add Greece, Portugal and Ireland, the three euro countries that needed rescue loans: Greece’s yield reached 29.2 percent in February 2012, Portugal’s 13.9 percent in January 2012 and Ireland’s 12.4 percent in July 2011.
Look at your data: the lines start and stop at different dates. Greece’s starts in mid-1997, Estonia’s only in 2020 (its government has almost no long-term debt), and Russia’s ends in 2018.


Key numbers: the spreads over Germany
The spread is the gap between a country’s yield and Germany’s. It measures how much more investors want to be paid to lend to that government.

Python note. credit_all.year.isin(LENDING_YEARS) keeps the four years (the keys of the dictionary). picked.loc[latest, "credit"] = ... replaces the values in the 2023 rows only. barmode="group" puts the bars of the four years side by side, and category_orders fixes the order of the countries and of the years.


BOOK_LENDING = ("Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Italy", "Germany")
LENDING_YEARS = {1998: "1998", 2002: "2002", 2007: "2007", 2023: "2023 (latest)"}


def lending_chart(countries=BOOK_LENDING):
    """Fig. 20.10 for any countries: bank lending to the private sector, percent of GDP, in four years."""
    picked = credit_all[credit_all.country.isin(countries) & credit_all.year.isin(LENDING_YEARS)].copy()
    picked["credit"] = picked.bank_credit                                   # the textbook's series, to 2021
    latest = picked.year == 2023
    picked.loc[latest, "credit"] = picked.loc[latest, "private_credit"]     # all private credit in 2023
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["credit"])
    wide = picked.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="credit")
    title = "Bank lending in percent of GDP"
    if 1998 in wide.columns and 2007 in wide.columns and (wide[2007] - wide[1998]).notna().any():
        rise = (wide[2007] - wide[1998]).dropna()
        title = f"Bank lending, 1998–2007: largest rise {rise.idxmax()}, {round(rise.max()):+d} points of GDP"
    picked["year"] = picked.year.map(LENDING_YEARS)
    fig = px.bar(picked, x="country", y="credit", color="year", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8"],
                 title=title + missing_note(countries, wide.index),
                 category_orders={"country": book_order(countries, BOOK_LENDING), "year": list(LENDING_YEARS.values())},
                 labels={"country": "", "credit": "Domestic bank lending (percent of GDP)"})
    top = max(200, 1.05 * picked.credit.max()) if len(picked) > 0 else 200
    fig.update_layout(yaxis_range=[0, top], legend_title_text="")
    return fig

The IMF publishes the current account of almost every economy, year by year since 1980 (current_account_imf.csv). period_means turns the yearly numbers into the textbook’s period averages, for any countries.

Python note. groupby("country").ca_gdp.mean() averages the years of each country. rows.append({...}) collects one dictionary per country and period, and pd.DataFrame(rows) turns the list into a table.


ca_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "current_account_imf.csv")
CA_PERIODS = {"1993–1997": (1993, 1997), "2003–2007": (2003, 2007), "2008–2011": (2008, 2011),
              "2021–2025 (latest)": (2021, 2025)}


def period_means(countries):
    """The current account of each country averaged over each textbook period (one row per country and period)."""
    rows = []
    for label in CA_PERIODS:
        first, last = CA_PERIODS[label]
        span = ca_all[ca_all.country.isin(countries) & (ca_all.year >= first) & (ca_all.year <= last)]
        means = span.groupby("country").ca_gdp.mean()
        for country in means.index:
            rows.append({"country": country, "period": label, "balance": means[country]})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["country", "period", "balance"])

What to notice.

Greece borrowed 2 percent of its GDP a year from abroad in 1993–97 and 9 percent in 2003–07; Spain went from about 1 to 7 percent. Germany turned from a small deficit into a surplus of about 5 percent of GDP.
Since 2021 Portugal, Spain and Italy have small surpluses; Greece still borrows 7.5 percent of GDP.
A data warning: Ireland’s surplus of 10.8 percent in 2021–25 does not mean the Irish lend a lot abroad. The profits of large multinational firms registered in Ireland pass through its accounts and inflate both GDP and the current account.
The south was not alone. Add Latvia, Estonia and Bulgaria, which tied their currencies to the euro before they adopted it: in 2003–2007 they borrowed 15.4, 12.7 and 11.3 percent of GDP a year, more than Greece. On the lending side, the Netherlands ran a surplus of 6.5 percent, more than Germany.

title: 20. Exchange Rates and International Finance
text:
Concluding remarks

The nominal exchange rate is the price of a currency; the real exchange rate \(EP/P^w\) is the price of goods. In the long run the law of one price, equation (1), sets the real exchange rate to 1, equation (3), and ties the nominal rate to relative price levels, equation (2). In growth rates, equation (4), more inflation means a weaker currency.
The law of one price holds only loosely. Japan’s real exchange rate rose 2.5-fold until 1995, and Big Macs cost more in rich countries: nontraded goods get dearer as wages rise (the Balassa-Samuelson effect, equation 6).
In the short run, prices are sticky and the exchange rate moves with interest rates (uncovered interest parity, equations 7 and 8). Net exports then react to the interest rate like investment, equation (10), which makes the IS curve flatter, equation (11), and a rise in foreign interest rates is a positive demand shock at home that ends in a recession when it is reversed (the AS/AD solution, equations 12 and 13).
The policy trilemma: an open economy can have at most two of a stable exchange rate, monetary autonomy and free capital flows; a credible peg with free flows forces \(i = i^w\), equation (9). Gold, Bretton Woods, currency boards, capital controls and the euro are different choices of two, and the crises in Mexico, Asia, Argentina and the euro area show what happens when a choice breaks down: default risk opens bond spreads, equation (14), and a currency union can regain competitiveness only through unit labor costs, equation (15).
The next chapter, Parting Thoughts, looks back at the whole book and at the open questions of macroeconomics.

text:
Practice problems
These problems use the chapter’s tools in three ways: conceptual problems apply its equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to its data files, and modeling problems answer policy questions with its interactive models. Each one is marked Basic, Intermediate or Challenge; try it on your own first, and open the Hint and the Solution only after that. The sliders in the answer cells run in Colab (open this notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): Croatia swaps the kuna for the euro. On 1 January 2023 Croatia replaced its currency, the kuna, with the euro, at a conversion rate fixed by the Council of the European Union: 7.53450 kuna per euro. In the IMF data of Fig. 8 (fx_crises.csv), one dollar bought 7.06403 kuna and 0.937559 euros at the end of 2022.

Suppose a cup of coffee cost 11.30 kuna in December 2022 (an illustrative price). What did it cost in euros on 1 January 2023?
Write the price of a dollar in Croatia in euros instead of kuna. How does it compare with the euro area’s rate?
Use the definition of the real exchange rate, \(EP/P^w\) (step 3 of the first block of the Model overview), to show that the switch changed neither the real exchange rate between the United States and Croatia nor any other real variable.
If nothing real changed on 1 January 2023, what did Croatia give up by adopting the euro? Use equation (9).



Hint

The switch divides every amount written in kuna by the same number, 7.53450: prices, wages, and the price of a dollar. What happens to a ratio when its top and its bottom are divided by the same number? For (d), ask who sets Croatia’s interest rate after the switch.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) \(11.30 / 7.53450 = 1.4998\), so the coffee costs 1.50 euros.
(b) A dollar bought 7.06403 kuna, so it buys \(7.06403 / 7.53450 = 0.93756\) euros: exactly the euro area’s rate of 0.937559 euros per dollar, up to rounding. From that day Croatia simply shares the euro area’s exchange rate.
(c) Take the United States as home, so \(E\) is Croatian money per dollar, \(P\) the U.S. price level in dollars and \(P^w\) the Croatian price level in Croatian money. Call the conversion rate \(c = 7.53450\). The switch divides both \(E\) and \(P^w\) by \(c\), and leaves \(P\) alone:
\[RER_{\text{after}} = \frac{(E/c)\,P}{P^w/c} = \frac{EP}{P^w} = RER_{\text{before}}.\]
A cup of coffee in Zagreb costs as many U.S. goods as it did the day before. The same holds for every other real variable, because each one is a ratio of two amounts in the same money (a real wage \(W/P\), the real value of savings, real GDP): the \(c\) cancels. This is the classical dichotomy of the Model overview: the level of the nominal exchange rate has no meaning of its own.
(d) Inside the euro area Croatia’s exchange rate with the other members is fixed for good and money flows freely, so by equation (9) its interest rate is the ECB’s, \(i = i^w\). Croatia gave up its own monetary policy, and with it the option to devalue against its main trading partners: the tool that Greece, Spain and Portugal lacked after 2010 (equation (15) and Fig. 13). In practice the kuna was already tied closely to the euro: in our data it stayed between 7.41 and 7.65 kuna per euro at the end of every year from 2011 to 2022. The big change in policy had happened before the switch.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Hong Kong’s peg meets the Fed. Hong Kong runs a currency board: its Monetary Authority promises to trade Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars at 7.75 and at 7.85 Hong Kong dollars per U.S. dollar, the two edges of a narrow band. In our data (fx_monthly.csv, from the Federal Reserve’s H.10 release), the monthly average has stayed between 7.7497 and 7.8498 since June 2005. Between March 2022 and July 2023 the Federal Reserve raised its target range for the federal funds rate from 0–0.25 percent to 5.25–5.50 percent, and on 27 July 2023 the Hong Kong Monetary Authority set its Base Rate at 5.75 percent, by a formula that puts it at least 0.5 point above the lower end of the Fed’s range. Yet in 2022 Hong Kong’s real GDP fell by 3.7 percent, while U.S. real GDP grew by 2.4 percent.

Which equation of the Model overview explains why Hong Kong’s interest rates rose with the Fed’s, even though its economy shrank? Which goal of the policy trilemma did Hong Kong give up?
Suppose investors suddenly expect the Hong Kong dollar to be devalued by 5 percent within a year, while the one-year U.S. rate is 5.25 percent. What one-year Hong Kong rate keeps them willing to hold Hong Kong dollars? What if they expect a devaluation of 20 percent? Compare both answers with the rough rule \(i \approx i^w +\) expected depreciation.
A critic says Hong Kong should let its currency float, so that it can cut interest rates in a recession. Name one gain and one cost of that change. Then explain when the third option of the trilemma, capital controls, would be costly.



Hint

For (a), a credible peg means \(E_t = E^e_{t+1}\); put that into equation (7). For (b), solve equation (7) for \(i_t\) with \(E_{fix}/E^e_{t+1} = 1/(1 - 0.05)\), or use the function defend_peg_rate of Check 5. For (c), look at the table of regimes at the end of the policy-trilemma block.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Equation (9), \(i_t = i^w\). When investors believe the peg, they expect no change in the exchange rate, so the ratio \(E_t/E^e_{t+1}\) in equation (7) is one, and Hong Kong’s interest rate must equal the U.S. rate. If it stayed lower, money would flow out of Hong Kong dollars into U.S. dollars until the peg broke. That is why the Base Rate follows the Fed by formula, whatever Hong Kong’s own economy needs. Hong Kong gave up monetary autonomy; it keeps a stable exchange rate and free financial flows, the currency-board side of the triangle in Fig. 7.
(b) Solve equation (7) for the interest rate, with \(E_{fix}/E^e_{t+1} = 1/(1 - d)\) for an expected devaluation \(d\):
\[1 + i = \frac{1 + i^w}{1 - d} = \frac{1.0525}{0.95} = 1.1079, \qquad\text{so}\qquad i = 10.79 \text{ percent},\]
against \(5.25 + 5 = 10.25\) percent by the rough rule. With \(d = 0.20\), \(1 + i = 1.0525/0.80 = 1.3156\), so \(i = 31.56\) percent, against 25.25 percent by the rough rule. The bigger the fear, the more the rough rule understates the rate needed, because the approximation of Appendix C.6 only works for small changes. A rate above 30 percent in a recession is the kind of cost that makes governments abandon a peg (Fig. 8).
for fall in [5.0, 20.0]:
    exact = defend_peg_rate(5.25, fall)                    # equation (7) solved for i
    print(f"Expected devaluation {fall:.0f}%: i = {exact:.2f}% (rough rule: {5.25 + fall:.2f}%)")
(c) Gain: with a floating rate Hong Kong could have kept its rates low in 2022, when its GDP fell. By equation (8) its currency would then have depreciated against the U.S. dollar, which also makes its exports cheaper. Cost: the exchange rate would move every day. Among the floating currencies of Fig. 6, the typical yearly change is 8 to 13 percent, a new risk for every firm and bank that trades or borrows in U.S. dollars, and a peg that has held near 7.8 since 17 October 1983 (HKMA, Linked Exchange Rate System; in our data, between 7.7245 and 7.852 from November 1983, its first full month) would be gone. Capital controls would let Hong Kong keep both its own interest rate and the peg, but only by rationing who may exchange currency. That is costly for any economy that lives from lending, borrowing and trading assets with the rest of the world, because the controls block exactly those flows.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Catching up inside the euro. A hypothetical country, Home, joins the euro area. Output per worker in Home’s traded sector grows 5 percent a year and in its nontraded sector 1 percent; in the rest of the euro area the two grow 2 and 1 percent. Hint

Inside a currency union the nominal exchange rate never moves, \(g_E = 0\), so equation (5) turns into a statement about the inflation gap. For the prices of the two goods: traded goods obey the law of one price, and \(P_N = P_T A_T/A_N\) (step 1 of the Balassa-Samuelson block) gives the growth of \(P_N\). For (b), keep \(\pi = \pi^w = 2\) and solve equation (5) for \(g_E\).

Solution

(a) Equation (5) says \(g_{RER} \approx g_E + \pi - \pi^w\). In the union \(g_E = 0\), so \(g_{RER} = \pi - \pi^w\). The growth-rate form of equation (6) says \(g_{RER} = (1 - \theta)\left[(g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}) - (g_{A^w_T} - g_{A^w_N})\right]\). The two expressions are the same \(g_{RER}\), so
\[\pi - \pi^w = (1 - \theta)\left[(g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}) - (g_{A^w_T} - g_{A^w_N})\right]
= \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(5 - 1) - (2 - 1)\right] = 1.5 \text{ points},\]
and Home’s inflation is \(2 + 1.5 = 3.5\) percent. To find the two prices, use \(P_N = P_T A_T/A_N\) in growth rates: \(\pi_N = \pi_T + g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}\). Abroad, \(\pi^w = \theta\pi_T + (1 - \theta)(\pi_T + 1) = \pi_T + 0.5 = 2\), so traded goods get 1.5 percent dearer a year, in Home as everywhere else (the law of one price). In Home nontraded prices then grow by \(1.5 + 4 = 5.5\) percent, and \(\pi = \tfrac{1}{2}\times 1.5 + \tfrac{1}{2}\times 5.5 = 3.5\) percent. Home’s higher inflation is all in haircuts and restaurant meals: its fast factories raise wages everywhere.
(b) With \(\pi = \pi^w = 2\), equation (5) gives \(g_E = g_{RER} - \pi + \pi^w = 1.5 - 2 + 2 = 1.5\) percent a year. Home’s currency must appreciate by 1.5 percent a year in nominal terms. The real appreciation of Home that its catching up requires comes through the exchange rate instead of through inflation.
(c) The reference value is \(1 + 1.5 = 2.5\) percent. With a fixed exchange rate, Home’s inflation is 3.5 percent and it fails by a point, although nothing is wrong with its central bank: rising service prices are the normal sign of an economy that catches up. Its way out is the route of (b): keep inflation at 2 percent and let its currency appreciate. The criterion on exchange-rate stability forbids devaluations, not appreciations. But once Home is inside, \(g_E = 0\) again and inflation returns to 3.5 percent; the criterion only postpones it. With one nominal rate \(i\) for the whole union, Home’s real rate \(R = i - \pi\) is then 1.5 points lower than in the rest of the union, which encourages borrowing. This is one road to the credit booms of Fig. 10.
(d) The numbers fit the direction of the model. All four economies had inflation 0.95 to 2.41 points a year above the euro area after they adopted the euro, and all four price levels rose relative to Germany’s, Estonia’s from 0.72 to 0.90. Inside a union the two columns should match, since \(g_{RER} = \pi - \pi^w\): the price level relative to Germany grew by 1.01 percent a year in Slovakia, 1.80 in Estonia, 0.56 in Latvia and 1.94 in Lithuania. That is close to the inflation gaps for Slovakia and Estonia, but not for Latvia and Lithuania; the two columns also use different price indexes, consumer prices for inflation and GDP prices for the price levels. Another reason: a demand boom. By (c), the same nominal rate means a lower real rate where inflation is higher, so households borrow and spend more, and the prices of nontraded goods rise without any gain in productivity. Southern Europe saw such booms before 2008 (Figs. 10 and 11).

for m in [0.5, 0.75]:
    path = simulate(shock_list(shock), m=m)
    peak = path.pi.idxmax()
    print(f"m = {m}: peak inflation {path.pi.max():.2f}% in period {path.period[peak]}, "
          f"Y~ {path.Y[1]:+.2f}% in period 1 and {path.Y[10]:+.2f}% in period 10")
(c) In period 1, equation (13) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = \bar{a}/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\): a larger \(\bar{m}\) raises the denominator, because the Fed raises U.S. rates as soon as inflation moves, which offsets part of the boom in net exports. While the shock lasts, inflation heads for \(\bar{\pi} + \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\), which is lower when \(\bar{m}\) is larger, so there is less inflation to unwind when the shock ends. In period 10, with \(\bar{a} = 0\) and inflation close to that resting point, equation (13) gives \(\tilde{Y}_{10} \approx -\bar{b}\bar{m}\,\big(\bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\big)/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) = -\bar{a}/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\), again smaller for a larger \(\bar{m}\): \(-2/2 = -1\) at \(\bar{m} = 0.5\) and \(-2/2.5 = -0.8\) at \(\bar{m} = 0.75\). A demand shock pushes output and inflation in the same direction, so fighting inflation also steadies output: there is no trade-off. A shock to the Phillips curve pushes inflation up while output falls; then a firmer response brings inflation down faster, but only with a deeper recession.

Problem 10 (Challenge): The euro in 2022, on the trilemma. In 2022 the Fed raised its target range by 4.25 points, from 0–0.25 to 4.25–4.50 percent, while the ECB raised its deposit facility rate by 2.5 points, from −0.50 to 2.00 percent. Treat the euro area as “your economy” in the trilemma model of Fig. 7, and the United States as the foreign country. (The cell below wraps trilemma in a small function that shows its readout with two decimals, since the sliders move in quarter points.)

Choose the floating regime, and set the foreign rate rise to 4.25 points and the euro area’s own change to 2.5 points. What does the model predict for the euro’s value in dollars?
From fig20-1.csv (the Federal Reserve’s H.10 data of Fig. 1), compute the dollars per euro, 1 / eur_per_usd, in December 2021 and in December 2022, and the percent change. What value of \(\eta\), the model’s percent change in \(E\) per point of interest gap, would match the data? By step 2 of the UIP block, what does that \(\eta\) say about how long investors expected the gap to last?
Find the euro’s lowest month in 2022. On the same two pages, look at how each central bank moved its rate in 2023, and suggest why the euro recovered at the end of 2022.
Policy: suppose the euro area had pegged its currency to the dollar. Switch to the currency board. What rate change would the ECB have needed? Name a gain and a cost, knowing that in 2023 real GDP grew by 0.4 percent in the euro area and 2.9 percent in the United States.



Hint

In the floating regime the model sets \(\%\Delta E = \eta\,(\Delta i - \Delta i^w)\) with \(\eta = 5\). For (b), solve the same equation for \(\eta\) with the actual change. For (c), equation (8) depends on the interest gap investors expect over the next years, not only on today’s gap.


def trilemma_two_decimals(regime="floating exchange rate", di_world=1.0, di_need=0.0):
    """Fig. 7 with its readout to two decimals, for sliders that move in quarter points."""
    fig = trilemma(regime, di_world, di_need)
    di, dE, lost = trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need)
    flows = "blocked" if regime == "capital controls" else "free"
    fig.layout.annotations[-1].text = (f"Interest rate: {di:+.2f} pt<br>Exchange rate: {dE:+.2f}%<br>"
                                       f"Capital flows: {flows}")                  # the readout box
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{regime.capitalize()}: Δi = {di:+.2f}, %ΔE = {dE:+.2f}; lost: {lost}")
    return fig


interact(trilemma_two_decimals,
         regime=ToggleButtons(options=["floating exchange rate", "currency board", "capital controls"],
                              value="floating exchange rate", description="regime", style=WIDE),
         di_world=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.0, max=5.0, step=0.25, description="Fed's rate rise Δiʷ (points)", style=WIDE),
         di_need=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=5.0, step=0.25, description="euro area's own change (points)", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 7 above, adapted from Fig. 20.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The readout box shows an interest-rate change of +2.50 points and an exchange-rate change of −8.75 percent. The model predicts that the euro’s dollar value changes by \(5 \times (2.5 - 4.25) = -8.75\) percent, because U.S. rates rose 1.75 points more than euro rates. The goal given up is a stable exchange rate.
rates = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-1.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")
dollars_per_euro = 1 / rates.eur_per_usd
before, after = dollars_per_euro["2021-12-01"], dollars_per_euro["2022-12-01"]
change = 100 * (after / before - 1)
print(f"Dollars per euro: {before:.4f} in Dec 2021, {after:.4f} in Dec 2022, a change of {change:+.2f}%")
model = trilemma_outcome("floating exchange rate", 4.25, 2.5)[1]
print(f"Model: {model:+.2f}%; the eta that matches the data: {-change / (4.25 - 2.5):.2f}")
low = dollars_per_euro.loc["2022-01-01":"2022-12-01"]
print(f"Lowest month of 2022: {low.idxmin().strftime('%Y-%m')}, {low.min():.4f} dollars per euro, "
      f"{100 * (low.min() / before - 1):+.1f}% since Dec 2021")
(b) A euro bought 1.1301 dollars in December 2021 and 1.0591 in December 2022, a fall of 6.28 percent. The model, with \(\eta = 5\), predicted −8.75 percent; the data match \(\eta = 6.28/1.75 = 3.59\). By step 2 of the UIP block, \(\eta\) is the number of years \(n\) that the gap is expected to last, so investors acted as if the extra 1.75 points of U.S. interest would last about three and a half years.
(c) The euro’s lowest month was October 2022, at 0.9853 dollars, 12.8 percent below December 2021. In 2023 the ECB raised its deposit rate by another 2 points, to 4.00 percent, while the Fed added only 1 point, to 5.25–5.50 percent. One explanation: if investors came to expect this narrowing at the end of 2022, the gap they expected over the next years fell, and by equation (8) the euro rose again before most of those increases actually happened.
(d) With a currency board the ECB would have had to match the Fed: \(\Delta i = +4.25\) points, 1.75 more than it chose, with no change in the exchange rate. Gain: no depreciation, so no extra rise in the euro prices of imports paid in dollars at a time of high inflation. Cost: a tighter policy than the ECB judged right for the euro area, which grew by only 0.4 percent in 2023, against 2.9 percent in the United States. A floating rate let each central bank choose for its own economy; that is the trilemma’s lesson for large economies.

Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website version of Lesson 2 (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def group_menu(fig, groups, start, title):
    """Show one group of countries at a time: a menu of buttons sets which traces (one per country) are visible."""
    buttons = []
    for name, members in groups.items():
        visible = [t.legendgroup in members for t in fig.data]
        ys = np.concatenate([np.asarray(t.y, dtype=float) for t, v in zip(fig.data, visible) if v] or [np.zeros(1)])
        top = np.nanmax(ys) if np.isfinite(ys).any() else 1.0
        buttons.append(dict(label=name, method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": visible}, {"yaxis.range": [0, max(1.05, 1.05 * top)]}]))
    first = list(groups).index(start)
    for t, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[first]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        t.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(title=title, yaxis_range=buttons[first]["args"][1]["yaxis.range"], margin=dict(t=115),
                      updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=first, direction="down", x=0, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])
    return fig

title: 21. Parting Thoughts
text:
Model overview
This notebook builds no new model. Instead, it puts the models of the whole book side by side, so that you can see how they fit together before we look back at the five big lessons. The book works with two horizons. The long run is about decades: the production model and the Solow and Romer models explain why some countries are rich and others poor, and why income per person keeps rising; the labor market and the quantity theory of money add unemployment and inflation. The short run is about the next year or two: the IS curve, the MP curve and the Phillips curve, joined in the AS/AD framework, explain booms and recessions and what a central bank can do about them. The last chapters open up the building blocks: how households choose consumption, how firms choose investment, how the government finances itself, and how trade and exchange rates connect a country to the rest of the world.
Each block below recaps one model or one group of related models. Building blocks lists the equations the model starts from. Key results derives the main conclusions step by step, fills in the algebra, says in plain words why each result holds, and lists the comparative statics: which parameter moves which result, in which direction and by how much. A link at the top of each block takes you back to the chapter where you built the model and played with its interactive figures. Only the results that this notebook uses again carry a number, (1) to (20). At the end, ### The model in code checks each headline result with a few lines of Python, and the five lessons that follow test the big ideas with data.
Notation, as in the rest of the book: a bar marks a parameter, a number taken as given, such as \(\bar{s}\) or \(\bar{A}\). A star marks a long-run value, such as the steady state \(y^*\). A tilde marks short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\), the percent gap between actual and potential output. \(g_x\) is the growth rate of a variable \(x\), and \(\Delta x_{t+1} \equiv x_{t+1} - x_t\) is its change from one year to the next.
The five lessons below follow the same split. Lessons 1 and 2 come from the growth models, Lesson 3 joins money to the long run, and Lessons 4 and 5 come from the short-run model. Each lesson restates one big idea in plain words, links back to the notebook and figure where you built it, and recomputes one or two of its key numbers from a small data file you have already met. Lessons 2 and 4 each draw one recap chart, and Lesson 2’s chart has a country picker in Colab (on the website, a menu of country groups). The last section turns to the questions that macroeconomics has not answered yet.

Long run: the production model
Back to Chapter 4.

Building blocks
The economy makes one good with capital \(K\) and labor \(L\). Total factor productivity \(\bar{A}\) is a parameter:
\[Y = F(K, L) = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}.\]
Firms rent capital at the rental price \(r\) and hire workers at the wage \(w\), and they pick \(K\) and \(L\) to make profit \(\Pi = F(K,L) - rK - wL\) as large as possible. The supplies of the two inputs are given, \(K = \bar{K}\) and \(L = \bar{L}\), and the two prices adjust until firms want exactly those amounts.


Key results
Factor prices. Profit is highest where one more unit of an input adds as much to output as it costs (Appendix C.8). The extra output is the marginal product, the derivative of \(F\) with respect to that input. The power rule (Appendix C.7) brings the exponent down and lowers it by one:
\[MPK = \tfrac{1}{3}\bar{A}K^{1/3-1}L^{2/3} = \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{\bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}}{K} = \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{K},
\qquad MPL = \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{L}.\]
So \(r^* = \frac{1}{3}Y^*/\bar{K}\) and \(w^* = \frac{2}{3}Y^*/\bar{L}\). Multiplying each price by its input gives the factor shares: capital earns \(r^*\bar{K}/Y^* = 1/3\) of output and labor earns \(w^*\bar{L}/Y^* = 2/3\). The two shares add up to one, so payments to the inputs use up all of output and profit is zero. This is what constant returns to scale implies.
Output per person. Divide the production function by \(\bar{L}\), use \(\bar{L}^{2/3}/\bar{L} = \bar{L}^{-1/3}\) (Appendix C.3), and write \(\bar{k} \equiv \bar{K}/\bar{L}\):
\[y^* = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}. \tag{1}\]
Comparing two countries. Write equation (1) for country 1 and for country 2 and divide the first by the second:
\[\frac{y_1^*}{y_2^*} = \frac{\bar{A}_1}{\bar{A}_2}\times\left(\frac{\bar{k}_1}{\bar{k}_2}\right)^{1/3}. \tag{2}\]
Take country 2 to be the United States. The second factor is the income that capital alone predicts; the first is relative TFP. Since we can measure \(y^*\) and \(\bar{k}\) but not \(\bar{A}\), TFP is found as the part that capital does not explain, \(\bar{A} = y^*/\bar{k}^{1/3}\). This is development accounting, and Lesson 1 applies it to the world.
Intuition. The exponent \(1/3\) means strongly diminishing returns to capital: to be ten times richer through capital alone, a country would need \(10^3 = 1{,}000\) times as much capital per person. Large income gaps therefore point to large TFP gaps.
Comparative statics. In logs (Appendix C.4), \(\ln y^* = \ln\bar{A} + \frac{1}{3}\ln\bar{k}\). A 1 percent rise in TFP raises output per person by 1 percent; a 1 percent rise in capital per person raises it by only 1/3 of a percent. The wage \(w^* = \frac{2}{3}y^*\) moves in proportion to output per person.



Long run: the Solow model
Back to Chapter 5.

Building blocks
The Solow model makes capital endogenous. Five equations hold in every year \(t\):







Equation
Meaning




\(Y_t = \bar{A}K_t^{1/3}L_t^{2/3}\)
production


\(C_t + I_t = Y_t\)
output is consumed or invested


\(\Delta K_{t+1} = I_t - \bar{d}K_t\)
capital grows by investment minus depreciation


\(L_t = \bar{L}\)
a constant labor force


\(I_t = \bar{s}Y_t\)
a constant share \(\bar{s}\) of output is invested





Key results
One equation for capital. Put \(I_t = \bar{s}Y_t\) into the accumulation equation and divide every term by \(\bar{L}\). With \(k_t \equiv K_t/\bar{L}\) and \(y_t = \bar{A}k_t^{1/3}\), as in equation (1):
\[\Delta k_{t+1} = \bar{s}\bar{A}k_t^{1/3} - \bar{d}k_t.\]
The first term is new investment per person, the second is the capital per person that wears out.
The steady state. Capital stops changing when the two terms are equal. Divide \(\bar{s}\bar{A}(k^*)^{1/3} = \bar{d}k^*\) by \(\bar{d}(k^*)^{1/3}\) to get \((k^*)^{2/3} = \bar{s}\bar{A}/\bar{d}\), then raise both sides to the power \(3/2\): \(k^* = (\bar{s}\bar{A}/\bar{d})^{3/2}\). Putting \(k^*\) into the production function multiplies the exponents, \(\frac{3}{2}\times\frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\), so \(y^* = \bar{A}(\bar{s}\bar{A}/\bar{d})^{1/2}\), and collecting the powers of \(\bar{A}\):
\[y^* = \left(\frac{\bar{s}}{\bar{d}}\right)^{1/2}\bar{A}^{3/2}. \tag{3}\]
Comparative statics. In logs, \(\ln y^* = \frac{1}{2}\ln\bar{s} - \frac{1}{2}\ln\bar{d} + \frac{3}{2}\ln\bar{A}\):








A 1% rise in …
changes \(y^*\) by
why




investment rate \(\bar{s}\)
\(+0.5\%\)
more capital, but with diminishing returns


depreciation rate \(\bar{d}\)
\(-0.5\%\)
more of each year’s investment only replaces worn-out capital


TFP \(\bar{A}\)
\(+1.5\%\)
a direct effect of 1, plus 1/2 through the extra capital it pays for



Transition dynamics. Divide the capital equation by \(k_t\) to get the growth rate of capital per person, \(g_{k,t} = \bar{s}\bar{A}k_t^{-2/3} - \bar{d}\). The steady state says \(\bar{s}\bar{A} = \bar{d}(k^*)^{2/3}\); substituting it leaves a formula that depends only on how far the economy is from its steady state:
\[g_{k,t} = \bar{d}\left[\left(\frac{k^*}{k_t}\right)^{2/3} - 1\right]. \tag{4}\]
By the power rule for growth rates (Appendix C.5), output per person grows about a third as fast, \(g_{y,t} \approx \frac{1}{3}g_{k,t}\). An economy below its steady state grows, and it grows faster the larger the gap; an economy above it shrinks. This is the simplest form of the principle of transition dynamics behind Lesson 2.
No growth in the long run. In the steady state \(k^*\) and \(y^*\) are constant. Each extra machine adds less output than the one before but wears out just as fast, so capital accumulation alone cannot keep income per person rising. With population growth at rate \(\bar{n}\), the same steps hold with \(\bar{n} + \bar{d}\) in place of \(\bar{d}\).



Long run: ideas, the Romer model and the combined model
Back to Chapter 6.

Building blocks
The Romer model explains where TFP comes from. The population \(N_t\) is split between making goods (\(L_{yt}\)) and doing research (\(L_{at}\)), and \(A_t\) is the stock of ideas:







Equation
Meaning




\(Y_t = A_t^{\gamma}L_{yt}\)
goods are made with ideas and workers


\(\Delta A_{t+1} = \bar{z}L_{at}\)
each researcher adds \(\bar{z}\) new ideas a year


\(L_{yt} + L_{at} = N_t\)
everyone works in one of the two sectors


\(\Delta N_{t+1}/N_t = \bar{n}\)
the population grows at rate \(\bar{n}\)


\(L_{at} = \bar{\ell}N_t\)
a constant share \(\bar{\ell}\) of people do research



The parameter \(\gamma > 0\) measures how much ideas raise output. Ideas are nonrival: every worker can use the whole stock \(A_t\) at the same time. That is why doubling both ideas and workers more than doubles output, by the factor \(2^{1+\gamma}\): there are increasing returns.


Key results
Income per person depends on the total stock of ideas. With \(L_{yt} = (1-\bar{\ell})N_t\), divide output by \(N_t\):
\[y_t \equiv \frac{Y_t}{N_t} = A_t^{\gamma}(1-\bar{\ell}). \tag{5}\]
A new idea raises the income of every person at once, because nobody has to give it up for someone else to use it.
Ideas grow as fast as the population. Divide the idea equation by \(A_t\): \(g_{At} = \bar{z}L_{at}/A_t\). This growth rate stays constant only if the numerator and the denominator grow at the same rate (the ratio rule of Appendix C.5). Researchers \(L_{at} = \bar{\ell}N_t\) grow at \(\bar{n}\), so in the long run \(g_A^* = \bar{n}\). The economy settles there: if ideas grew faster than \(\bar{n}\), the ratio \(L_{at}/A_t\) would fall and pull \(g_{At}\) back down, and the reverse if they grew more slowly. Solving \(\bar{n} = \bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t/A_t\) for the stock gives \(A_t^* = \bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t/\bar{n}\): more researchers support a larger stock of knowledge.
Long-run growth. Put \(A_t^*\) into equation (5): \(y_t^* = (\bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t/\bar{n})^{\gamma}(1-\bar{\ell})\). Only \(N_t\) changes over time, and the growth rate of a power is the power times the growth rate, so
\[g_y^* = \gamma\bar{n}. \tag{6}\]
Comparative statics. A higher research productivity \(\bar{z}\) or research share \(\bar{\ell}\) raises the level of income per person on the long-run path but not its long-run growth rate, which depends only on \(\gamma\) and \(\bar{n}\). A higher \(\bar{\ell}\) also has a cost today: fewer people make goods, the factor \(1-\bar{\ell}\). (In Romer’s original version, \(\Delta A_{t+1}/A_t = \bar{z}L_{at}\), the same changes raise the growth rate itself.)
The combined Solow–Romer model. Now let ideas and capital work together: \(Y_t = A_t^{\gamma}K_t^{1/3}L_{yt}^{2/3}\), with \(\Delta K_{t+1} = \bar{s}Y_t - \bar{d}K_t\) and ideas, people and researchers as above. Per person, \(y_t = A_t^{\gamma}k_t^{1/3}(1-\bar{\ell})^{2/3}\), and the growth rules for products and powers give
\[g_{yt} = \gamma g_{At} + \tfrac{1}{3}g_{kt}.\]
On a balanced growth path the capital-output ratio is constant, so capital and output grow at the same rate, \(g_k^* = g_y^*\). Substituting this and \(g_A^* = \bar{n}\): \(g_y^* = \gamma\bar{n} + \frac{1}{3}g_y^*\), so \(\frac{2}{3}g_y^* = \gamma\bar{n}\) and
\[g_y^* = \tfrac{3}{2}\gamma\bar{n}. \tag{7}\]
Growth is faster than in the Romer model alone: new ideas raise output, part of the extra output is saved, and the extra capital raises output again.
The level of the path. Divide the capital equation by \(K_t\): \(g_{Kt} = \bar{s}Y_t/K_t - \bar{d}\). On the balanced growth path \(g_K^* = g_Y^*\), so \(K_t^*/Y_t^* = \bar{s}/(g_Y^* + \bar{d})\), where \(g_Y^* = g_y^* + \bar{n}\) is the growth rate of total output. Write the production function as \(Y_t = A_t^{\gamma}(K_t/Y_t)^{1/3}Y_t^{1/3}L_{yt}^{2/3}\), move \(Y_t^{1/3}\) to the left to get \(Y_t^{2/3}\), and raise both sides to the power \(3/2\): \(Y_t = A_t^{3\gamma/2}(K_t/Y_t)^{1/2}L_{yt}\). Dividing by \(N_t\):
\[y_t^* = \left(\frac{\bar{s}}{g_Y^*+\bar{d}}\right)^{1/2}A_t^{*\,3\gamma/2}(1-\bar{\ell}). \tag{8}\]
Investment, depreciation and the research share set the level of the path, as in the Solow model; ideas set its slope. (With \(\gamma = 1\) the exponent on \(A_t^*\) is \(3/2\), as in equation (3).)
Transition dynamics in the combined model. Subtract the balanced-growth version of the growth equation, \(g_y^* = \gamma\bar{n} + \frac{1}{3}g_y^*\), from the general one, \(g_{yt} = \gamma\bar{n} + \frac{1}{3}g_{kt}\):
\[g_{yt} - g_y^* = \tfrac{1}{3}\left(g_{kt} - g_y^*\right), \qquad g_{kt} = \bar{s}\frac{Y_t}{K_t} - \bar{d} - \bar{n}. \tag{9}\]
If an economy has less capital per unit of output than on its balanced growth path, \(Y_t/K_t\) is high, capital per person grows faster than \(g_y^*\), and so does income per person. The gap closes, and growth slows back to \(g_y^*\). Countries below their own path grow fast; countries above it grow slowly. This is the version of the principle of transition dynamics that Lesson 2 checks with Japan’s catch-up.



Long run: unemployment, money and inflation
Back to Chapter 7 and Chapter 8.

Building blocks
Labor market flows. The labor force \(\bar{L}\) is split into employed and unemployed people, \(E_t + U_t = \bar{L}\). Each year a share \(\bar{s}\) of the employed lose their jobs and a share \(\bar{f}\) of the unemployed find one:
\[\Delta U_{t+1} = \bar{s}E_t - \bar{f}U_t.\]
The quantity theory of money. Money times its velocity, the number of times a dollar is spent in a year, equals nominal GDP: \(M_tV_t = P_tY_t\). Velocity is constant, \(V_t = \bar{V}\); real GDP \(\bar{Y}_t\) is set by the real side of the economy (the models above); and the central bank chooses the money supply \(\bar{M}_t\).
Interest rates and the government’s sources of funds. The nominal interest rate \(i\) is the real rate \(R\) plus inflation \(\pi\). The government pays for its spending \(G\) with taxes, new borrowing or new money, \(G = T + \Delta B + \Delta M\).


Key results
The natural rate of unemployment. Unemployment is steady when as many people find jobs as lose them, \(\bar{s}E^* = \bar{f}U^*\). Replace \(E^*\) with \(\bar{L} - U^*\), multiply out and collect the \(U^*\) terms: \(\bar{s}\bar{L} = (\bar{s}+\bar{f})U^*\). Dividing by \(\bar{L}\):
\[u^* \equiv \frac{U^*}{\bar{L}} = \frac{\bar{s}}{\bar{s}+\bar{f}}. \tag{10}\]
Unemployment is high where jobs end often (high \(\bar{s}\)) or are slow to find (low \(\bar{f}\)). Labor-market institutions such as hiring and firing costs and unemployment insurance work through these two rates, not through money.
The price level and inflation. Solving the quantity equation for prices gives \(P_t^* = \bar{M}_t\bar{V}/\bar{Y}_t\). The growth rate of a product is the sum of the growth rates (Appendix C.5), so \(\bar{g}_M + \bar{g}_V = g_P + \bar{g}_Y\). Velocity is constant, \(\bar{g}_V = 0\), and inflation is the growth rate of the price level, \(\pi = g_P\):
\[\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y. \tag{11}\]
One more point of money growth means one more point of inflation; one more point of real growth means one point less. Real GDP was set before money entered the story, so money changes prices but not real output: the classical dichotomy.
The Fisher equation.
\[i = R + \pi. \tag{12}\]
Lenders want to be paid for the purchasing power that inflation takes away. In the long run \(R\) is set by the marginal product of capital, so higher inflation shows up one for one in higher nominal interest rates.
Where high inflation comes from. Rearranging the government’s sources of funds, \(\Delta M = G - T - \Delta B\). A government that runs a large deficit and cannot borrow has to print money, and equation (11) turns that money growth into inflation.



Short run: the IS curve, the MP curve and the Phillips curve
Back to Chapter 9, Chapter 11 and Chapter 12.

Building blocks
Short-run output. Potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) is the long-run path of the models above, and short-run output is the percent gap \(\tilde{Y}_t \equiv (Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)/\bar{Y}_t\). Okun’s law links it to unemployment: \(u_t - \bar{u} = -\frac{1}{2}\tilde{Y}_t\).
Demand. Output is spent on \(Y_t = C_t + I_t + G_t + EX_t - IM_t\). Consumption, government purchases, exports and imports are constant shares of potential output, \(C_t = \bar{a}_c\bar{Y}_t\), \(G_t = \bar{a}_g\bar{Y}_t\), \(EX_t = \bar{a}_{ex}\bar{Y}_t\) and \(IM_t = \bar{a}_{im}\bar{Y}_t\). Investment falls when the real interest rate \(R_t\) rises above the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\): \(I_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_i - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r})\).
Monetary policy (the MP curve). The central bank sets the nominal interest rate \(i_t\). Inflation is sticky, so it barely moves in the short run, and by the Fisher equation (12) the real rate \(R_t = i_t - \pi_t\) moves with \(i_t\): in effect, the central bank chooses \(R_t\).
Price setting (the Phillips curve). Inflation equals expected inflation, plus a term for demand, plus a price shock \(\bar{o}\): \(\pi_t = \pi_t^e + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\). Expectations are adaptive: people expect last year’s inflation, \(\pi_t^e = \pi_{t-1}\).


Key results
The IS curve. Divide the spending identity by \(\bar{Y}_t\) and use the shares: \(Y_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r}) + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{ex} - \bar{a}_{im}\). Subtract 1 from both sides; the left side becomes \((Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)/\bar{Y}_t = \tilde{Y}_t\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r}), \qquad \bar{a} \equiv \bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{ex} - \bar{a}_{im} - 1. \tag{13}\]
When borrowing costs more than capital earns, firms buy fewer machines and output falls below potential. The demand shock \(\bar{a}\) collects everything else that shifts spending; it is zero in the long run, when also \(R_t = \bar{r}\), so that \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\). If consumption also rises with current output, \(C_t/\bar{Y}_t =
\bar{a}_c + \bar{x}\tilde{Y}_t\), the same steps give \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} + \bar{x}\tilde{Y}_t - \bar{b}(R_t -
\bar{r})\), and solving for \(\tilde{Y}_t\) multiplies the right side of equation (13) by the multiplier \(1/(1-\bar{x})\).
The Phillips curve. Substitute adaptive expectations into the price equation and subtract \(\pi_{t-1}\) from both sides:
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}. \tag{14}\]
In a boom firms raise prices faster than last year, so inflation rises; in a slump it falls.
The chain of monetary policy. Put the three curves in a row: a higher \(i_t\) raises \(R_t\) (MP curve), which lowers \(\tilde{Y}_t\) (IS curve), which lowers the change in inflation (Phillips curve) and raises unemployment (Okun’s law).
