Short run: stabilization and the AS/AD framework
Back to Chapter 13 and Chapter 14.

Building blocks
Instead of picking the real interest rate case by case, the central bank now follows a monetary policy rule: it raises the real rate above \(\bar{r}\) when inflation is above its target \(\bar{\pi}\),
\[R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}), \qquad \bar{m} > 0.\]
The IS curve (13) and the Phillips curve (14) stay as they are. Written as \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t
+ \bar{o}\), the Phillips curve is the aggregate supply (AS) curve. In a financial crisis firms borrow at the policy rate plus a risk premium, \(R_t = R_t^{ff} + \bar{f}\).


Key results
The AD curve. Replace \(R_t - \bar{r}\) in the IS curve by the policy rule:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \tag{15}\]
It slopes down: when inflation is high, the central bank raises the real rate, and spending falls. By the Fisher equation (12) the rule sets the nominal rate at \(i_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\), so each point of inflation raises the nominal rate by \(1 + \bar{m}\) points, more than one for one.
The steady state. With no shocks (\(\bar{a} = \bar{o} = 0\)), AD gives \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\) only at \(\pi_t = \bar{\pi}\), and AS then keeps inflation constant. Output is at potential and inflation is on target.
The path of inflation. Put the AD curve into the AS curve: \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\bar{a} - \bar{\nu}\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) + \bar{o}\). Subtract \(\bar{\pi}\) from both sides and move the \(\pi_t\) term to the left: \((1 + \bar{\nu}\bar{b}\bar{m})(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) = (\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}) + \bar{\nu}\bar{a} + \bar{o}\). Without shocks:
\[\pi_t - \bar{\pi} = \frac{\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}}{1 + \bar{\nu}\bar{b}\bar{m}}. \tag{16}\]
Each year the inflation gap shrinks by the same factor, a first-order difference equation (Appendix C.10), and output follows from AD, \(\tilde{Y}_t = -\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\). A central bank that reacts more strongly (a larger \(\bar{m}\)) closes the gap faster, with a deeper recession at the start.
The cost of a disinflation. Lowering the target \(\bar{\pi}\) leaves last year’s inflation above the new target, so equation (16) brings inflation down through a recession. Adding the AS curve up over all the years of the adjustment, the changes in inflation sum to the total fall, \(\pi_{\text{start}} - \bar{\pi} = -\bar{\nu}\sum_t
\tilde{Y}_t\). So the output lost per point of disinflation, the sacrifice ratio, is \(1/\bar{\nu}\) under adaptive expectations, however fast the central bank moves. If instead price setters believe the new target, expected inflation drops straight to it, \(\pi_t^e = \bar{\pi}\), and inflation can fall with \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\): the gain from credibility in Lesson 5.
Financial crises. Write the borrowing rate gap as \(R_t - \bar{r} = (R_t^{ff} - \bar{r}) + \bar{f}\) and let the central bank set the policy-rate gap by its rule. The AD curve becomes \(\tilde{Y}_t = (\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}) - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\): a higher risk premium works like a negative demand shock of size \(\bar{b}\bar{f}\), which the central bank can offset only while it can still cut \(R_t^{ff}\). Leverage makes banks fragile: with assets equal to leverage times equity, a fall in asset values of just one over the leverage ratio wipes out all of the equity.



Behind the curves: consumption and investment
Back to Chapter 16 and Chapter 17.

Building blocks
A household over two periods. It earns \(y_{\text{today}}\) and \(y_{\text{future}}\), can save or borrow \(f_{\text{future}}\) at the real rate \(R\), and starts with no assets. Today \(c_{\text{today}} + f_{\text{future}} = y_{\text{today}}\); in the future \(c_{\text{future}} = y_{\text{future}} + (1+R)f_{\text{future}}\). It chooses consumption to maximize \(U = u(c_{\text{today}}) + \beta u(c_{\text{future}})\), where \(\beta\) discounts the future.
A firm deciding whether to buy capital. One unit of capital costs \(p_k\). Put in the bank, the money earns \(R\,p_k\). Used as capital, it earns its marginal product, loses \(\bar{d}p_k\) to wear and tear, and gains (or loses) \(\Delta p_k\) in price. The firm buys capital until the two returns are equal: \(R\,p_k = MPK - \bar{d}p_k + \Delta p_k\).


Key results
The lifetime budget constraint. From today’s budget, \(f_{\text{future}} = y_{\text{today}} - c_{\text{today}}\). Put it into the future budget, divide by \(1+R\) and move consumption to the left: \(c_{\text{today}} + c_{\text{future}}/(1+R) = y_{\text{today}} + y_{\text{future}}/(1+R) \equiv \bar{X}\). The present value of consumption equals the present value of income, lifetime wealth (Appendix C.12).
The Euler equation. Giving up one unit today costs \(u'(c_{\text{today}})\) in utility. Saved, it becomes \(1+R\) units in the future, each worth \(\beta u'(c_{\text{future}})\) today. At the best plan the two are equal, \(u'(c_{\text{today}}) = \beta(1+R)u'(c_{\text{future}})\). With log utility, \(u'(c) = 1/c\), so
\[\frac{c_{\text{future}}}{c_{\text{today}}} = \beta(1+R). \tag{17}\]
Substitute \(c_{\text{future}} = \beta(1+R)c_{\text{today}}\) into the lifetime budget: the \((1+R)\) cancels and \(c_{\text{today}}(1+\beta) = \bar{X}\), so \(c_{\text{today}} = \bar{X}/(1+\beta)\). With \(\beta = 1\) the household consumes half of its lifetime wealth today.
Implications. Consumption depends on lifetime wealth, not on this year’s income alone (the permanent-income hypothesis), so a temporary change in income moves consumption only a little. A tax cut paid for by higher taxes later leaves \(\bar{X}\), and so consumption, unchanged: Ricardian equivalence. A higher \(R\) makes consumption grow faster over time.
The user cost of capital. Divide the firm’s condition by \(p_k\) and solve for the marginal product:
\[MPK = \underbrace{R + \bar{d} - \frac{\Delta p_k}{p_k}}_{\text{user cost } uc}. \tag{18}\]
With \(MPK = \frac{1}{3}Y/K\) from the production model, the desired capital-output ratio is \(K/Y = 1/(3\,uc)\). And from \(\Delta K_{t+1}/K_t = (I_t/Y_t)(Y_t/K_t) - \bar{d}\), the investment rate that keeps capital growing at \(g_K\) is \(I/Y = (g_K + \bar{d})/(3\,uc)\). A higher interest rate raises the user cost and lowers desired capital and investment: this is the microfoundation of the slope \(\bar{b}\) of the IS curve. A corporate tax \(\tau\) divides the user cost by \(1 - \tau\), so taxes on profits discourage investment too.



The government and the open economy
Back to Chapter 18, Chapter 19 and Chapter 20.

Building blocks
The government budget. Spending, transfers and interest on the debt are paid for with taxes, new debt or new money: \(G_t + Tr_t + iB_t = T_t + \Delta B_{t+1} + \Delta M_{t+1}\). Leaving out money and counting transfers in spending, the debt evolves as \(B_{t+1} = (1+i)B_t + G_t - T_t\).
National income. \(Y = C + I + G + NX\), where \(NX = EX - IM\) is net exports.
Exchange rates. The nominal exchange rate \(E\) is the number of units of foreign currency one dollar buys. If the same good costs \(P\) dollars at home and \(P^w\) abroad, trade makes it cost the same everywhere, \(EP = P^w\) (the law of one price). The real exchange rate is \(EP/P^w\), the price of home goods in terms of foreign goods.
Net exports in the short run. They fall when the home real rate rises above the world rate \(\bar{R}^w\): \(NX_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}(R_t - \bar{R}^w)\).


Key results
The intertemporal budget constraint. Take two periods and require that all debt is repaid at the end, \(B_3 = 0\). Then \(B_2 = (1+i)B_1 + G_1 - T_1\) and \(0 = (1+i)B_2 + G_2 - T_2\). Substitute the first equation into the second, divide by \(1+i\), and move the taxes to the right:
\[G_1 + \frac{G_2}{1+i} + (1+i)B_1 = T_1 + \frac{T_2}{1+i}. \tag{19}\]
The present value of spending plus the debt already owed must equal the present value of taxes. A tax cut today with no cut in spending means higher taxes later, which is why Ricardian households would save it.
The debt-GDP ratio. Let nominal GDP grow at rate \(g_Y\) and write \(b_t \equiv B_t/Y_t\). Divide the debt equation by \(Y_{t+1} = (1+g_Y)Y_t\): \(b_{t+1} = \frac{1+i}{1+g_Y}\,b_t + \frac{G_t - T_t}{(1+g_Y)Y_t}\). When \(g_Y > i\) and the deficit is a constant share of GDP, the ratio settles where \(b_{t+1} = b_t\), at \(b^* = \frac{(G-T)/Y}{g_Y - i}\). Economic growth keeps the debt ratio in check; if \(i > g_Y\), a deficit makes the ratio grow without limit.
Trade and saving. National saving is private saving plus government saving, \(S \equiv (Y - T - C) + (T - G) = Y - C - G\). By the national income identity \(Y - C - G = I + NX\), so
\[NX = S - I. \tag{20}\]
A country that saves more than it invests at home lends the difference abroad and runs a trade surplus; one that invests more than it saves borrows from abroad and runs a deficit. Separately, trade by comparative advantage raises incomes in both countries even when one is more productive in every good: each specializes where its relative cost is lowest.
Purchasing power parity. Solving the law of one price for the exchange rate, \(\bar{E} = \bar{P}^w/\bar{P}\), and by the ratio rule for growth rates, \(g_E = \pi^w - \pi\). A country with faster inflation than the rest of the world sees its currency lose value at the difference of the two rates.
The open-economy IS curve. Add and subtract \(\bar{r}\) in the net exports equation, \(NX_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}(R_t - \bar{r}) + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r})\), and repeat the steps of the IS curve. Net exports enter just like investment, so the IS curve keeps the form of equation (13), with slope \(\bar{b} = \bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx}\) and with \(\bar{a}_{nx} + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r})\) inside \(\bar{a}\). A higher home interest rate lowers investment and, by attracting foreign funds that make the currency appreciate, net exports too: a steeper fall in output. A change in world interest rates is a demand shock at home. And a country cannot have a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and its own monetary policy all at once: the policy trilemma.

We now check the headline results above with numbers. Each check builds a result in a second, independent way, by simulating the model year by year or by searching for the best choice, and compares it with the formula. All the parameter values are simple illustrative numbers.
Check 1: the production model. Factor shares come from marginal products, which we approximate by adding a tiny amount of one input and measuring the extra output. Then we split a made-up income gap with equation (2).

Python note. A derivative is the extra output from a tiny extra input, divided by that input. With step = 1e-6 (that is, 0.000001) the ratio (Y_more - Y) / step is very close to the exact derivative.


def production(A, K, L):
    """Output of the production model: Y = A K^(1/3) L^(2/3)."""
    return A * K ** (1 / 3) * L ** (2 / 3)

A, K, L, step = 1.0, 8.0, 1.0, 1e-6
Y = production(A, K, L)
MPK = (production(A, K + step, L) - Y) / step      # extra output from a tiny bit more capital
MPL = (production(A, K, L + step) - Y) / step      # extra output from a tiny bit more labor
print(f"Capital share r K / Y = {MPK * K / Y:.4f}   (theory: 1/3 = {1 / 3:.4f})")
print(f"Labor share   w L / Y = {MPL * L / Y:.4f}   (theory: 2/3 = {2 / 3:.4f})")

a_c, a_i, a_g, a_ex, a_im = 0.60, 0.17, 0.20, 0.12, 0.09    # the shares add up to exactly 1, so a = 0
b, r_bar, Y_bar = 2.0, 0.02, 100.0
for R in (0.01, 0.03, 0.05):
    C, G, EX, IM = a_c * Y_bar, a_g * Y_bar, a_ex * Y_bar, a_im * Y_bar
    I = (a_i - b * (R - r_bar)) * Y_bar
    Y = C + I + G + EX - IM
    a = a_c + a_i + a_g + a_ex - a_im - 1
    print(f"R = {100 * R:.0f}%: direct Y~ = {100 * (Y - Y_bar) / Y_bar:+.1f}%,  "
          f"equation (13): {100 * (a - b * (R - r_bar)):+.1f}%")

R = 1%: direct Y~ = +2.0%,  equation (13): +2.0%
R = 3%: direct Y~ = -2.0%,  equation (13): -2.0%
R = 5%: direct Y~ = -6.0%,  equation (13): -6.0%


Check 7: a disinflation in the AS/AD model. The central bank lowers its target from 6 to 2 percent. Each year we find the inflation rate at which the AS and AD curves cross by trial and error: guess inflation, compute output from AD, compute inflation from AS, and repeat. The result should follow equation (16), and the total output lost per point of disinflation should be \(1/\bar{\nu}\).

Python note. A loop inside a loop: for every year, the inner for repeats the guess 100 times, and each round brings the guess closer to the point where AS and AD cross.


nu, b, m, target = 0.5, 1.0, 0.5, 2.0              # inflation and output in percent
pi_last, lost = 6.0, 0.0                           # inflation was 6% under the old target
for year in range(1, 41):
    guess = pi_last
    for round_ in range(100):
        Y_tilde = -b * m * (guess - target)        # AD curve, equation (15), with a = 0
        guess = pi_last + nu * Y_tilde             # AS curve, with o = 0
    formula = target + (pi_last - target) / (1 + nu * b * m)    # equation (16)
    if year <= 3:
        print(f"Year {year}: inflation {guess:.4f}% (AS = AD),  {formula:.4f}% (equation 16),  Y~ = {Y_tilde:.2f}%")
    lost = lost - Y_tilde
    pi_last = guess
print(f"Output lost per point of disinflation: {lost / (6.0 - target):.3f};  1/nu = {1 / nu:.3f}")

Year 1: inflation 5.2000% (AS = AD),  5.2000% (equation 16),  Y~ = -1.60%
Year 2: inflation 4.5600% (AS = AD),  4.5600% (equation 16),  Y~ = -1.28%
Year 3: inflation 4.0480% (AS = AD),  4.0480% (equation 16),  Y~ = -1.02%
Output lost per point of disinflation: 2.000;  1/nu = 2.000


Check 8: consumption and investment. Search over many possible plans for the one with the highest utility and compare it with the Euler equation (17). Then find the capital stock at which the marginal product equals the user cost, equation (18).

Python note. np.linspace(a, b, n) makes n evenly spaced numbers from a to b. Arithmetic on an array works on every element at once, and np.argmax gives the position of the largest element.


beta, R, y_today, y_future = 0.95, 0.04, 10.0, 5.0
X = y_today + y_future / (1 + R)                    # lifetime wealth
c_today = np.linspace(0.01, X - 0.01, 100001)       # every plan the budget allows
c_future = (X - c_today) * (1 + R)
utility = np.log(c_today) + beta * np.log(c_future)
best = np.argmax(utility)
print(f"Best plan found: c_today = {c_today[best]:.3f};  formula X/(1+beta) = {X / (1 + beta):.3f}")
print(f"c_future / c_today = {c_future[best] / c_today[best]:.4f};  equation (17): beta(1+R) = {beta * (1 + R):.4f}")

R, d, gain, A, L = 0.02, 0.08, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0
uc = R + d - gain                                   # user cost, equation (18)
K = L * (A / (3 * uc)) ** (3 / 2)                   # solves (1/3) A (L/K)^(2/3) = uc
MPK = (production(A, K + 1e-6, L) - production(A, K, L)) / 1e-6
print(f"MPK at that K = {MPK:.4f} = user cost {uc:.4f};  K/Y = {K / production(A, K, L):.3f} = 1/(3 uc) = {1 / (3 * uc):.3f}")

Best plan found: c_today = 7.594;  formula X/(1+beta) = 7.594
c_future / c_today = 0.9880;  equation (17): beta(1+R) = 0.9880
MPK at that K = 0.1000 = user cost 0.1000;  K/Y = 3.333 = 1/(3 uc) = 3.333


Check 9: the government and the open economy. Simulate the debt-GDP ratio for 400 years with a constant deficit, check the intertemporal budget constraint (19) and \(NX = S - I\) (20) with made-up numbers, and follow a purchasing-power-parity exchange rate for one year.

i, g_Y, deficit = 0.03, 0.05, 0.02                  # interest rate, nominal GDP growth, deficit share of GDP
b = 0.4                                             # debt starts at 40% of GDP
for year in range(400):
    b = (1 + i) / (1 + g_Y) * b + deficit / (1 + g_Y)
print(f"Debt-GDP ratio after 400 years: {b:.3f};  b* = deficit / (g_Y - i) = {deficit / (g_Y - i):.3f}")

B1, G1, T1, G2 = 10.0, 20.0, 18.0, 20.0
T2 = (1 + i) * ((1 + i) * B1 + G1 - T1) + G2        # the taxes that repay all debt in period 2
print(f"Equation (19): left {G1 + G2 / (1 + i) + (1 + i) * B1:.3f},  right {T1 + T2 / (1 + i):.3f}")

Y, C, I, G, T = 100.0, 65.0, 20.0, 18.0, 16.0
NX = Y - C - I - G
S = (Y - T - C) + (T - G)                           # private plus government saving
print(f"Equation (20): NX = {NX:.1f},  S - I = {S - I:.1f}")

pi_home, pi_world = 0.05, 0.02
E_now = 1.0                                         # E = P^w / P, with both prices starting at 1
E_next = (1 + pi_world) / (1 + pi_home)             # one year of inflation at home and abroad
print(f"Change in E: {100 * np.log(E_next / E_now):.2f}% (log);  pi^w - pi = {100 * (pi_world - pi_home):.2f}%")

Equation (19): left 49.717,  right 49.717
Equation (20): NX = -3.0,  S - I = -3.0
Change in E: -2.90% (log);  pi^w - pi = -3.00%

section: Lesson 1: Capital, skills, hours and ideas set living standards
text:
Lesson 1: Capital, skills, hours and ideas set living standards
Goal. Recall what makes some countries rich and others poor, and measure how much of the gap capital explains.
In the long run, a country’s income per person depends on four things: how much it invests in machines and in people’s skills, how many hours people work, the stock of ideas and technology it can use, and how efficiently it combines all of these. You built this in the production model of Chapter 4, where output per person is (equation 1 in the Model overview above)
\[y = \bar{A}\,k^{1/3}.\]
Measured relative to the United States, a country’s income is its total factor productivity (TFP) \(\bar{A}\) times the part that capital alone explains, \(k^{1/3}\) (equation 2). See Chapter 4, Fig. 5 (the prediction from capital alone) and Chapter 4, Fig. 7 (the TFP that makes the model fit). The Solow model of Chapter 5, Fig. 4 then explained capital by the investment rate, and the Romer model of Chapter 6, Fig. 2 showed that sustained growth comes from new ideas. Because an idea can be used by everyone at once, income per person grows with the whole stock of knowledge (equations 5 and 6).

Python note. a.merge(b, on=[...]) joins two tables row by row, matching the columns listed in on. Here both tables have one row per country, so the result does too.

section: Lesson 2: Transition dynamics explain differences in growth rates
text:
Lesson 2: Transition dynamics explain differences in growth rates
Goal. See why countries far below their steady state grow fast, and check it with Japan’s catch-up.
A country on its balanced growth path grows at the rate set by the growth of world knowledge. A country below its steady state grows faster than that, and the gap shrinks; a country above it grows more slowly. This is the principle of transition dynamics (equations 4 and 9). You first saw it in the Solow model and then in the cross-country data of Chapter 5, Fig. 8 and Chapter 5, Fig. 9, and in the combined Solow–Romer model of Chapter 6, Fig. 8. The long series for each country are in Chapter 3, Fig. 6.

Python note. pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc") reshapes a long table (one row per country and year) into a wide one: one row per year and one column per country.

We measure growth as the average annual growth rate in percent, \(g = 100 \times \ln(y_{end}/y_{start})/(end -
start)\), as in Chapter 3.

def growth_rate(y, start, end):
    """Average annual growth rate, percent: 100 ln(y_end / y_start) / years (Chapter 3)."""
    return 100 * np.log(y.loc[end] / y.loc[start]) / (end - start)

for country in ["United States", "United Kingdom"]:
    print(f"{country}: {growth_rate(gdppc[country], 1870, 2022):.1f} percent a year, 1870–2022")
for country in ["Japan", "United States"]:
    print(f"{country}: {growth_rate(gdppc[country], 1950, 2000):.1f} percent a year, 1950–2000")

United States: 1.6 percent a year, 1870–2022
United Kingdom: 1.2 percent a year, 1870–2022
Japan: 4.8 percent a year, 1950–2000
United States: 2.2 percent a year, 1950–2000


The textbook quotes 4.8 percent for Japan and 2.2 percent for the United States in the second half of the 20th century, which these data reproduce exactly. For the long run it quotes 2.0 percent for the United States and 1.5 percent for the United Kingdom. The Maddison data give 1.6 and 1.2, lower for both but with a similar gap. (Chapter 3’s U.S. series, which links older estimates to the official national accounts from 1929 on, gives 1.9 percent.) Different data sets can disagree about the 19th century.
Now the ratio of Japan’s income to U.S. income, year by year:

ratio = (gdppc["Japan"] / gdppc["United States"]).loc[1950:].reset_index(name="ratio")
print(f"1950: {ratio.ratio.iloc[0]:.2f}   peak: {ratio.ratio.max():.2f} in {ratio.year[ratio.ratio.idxmax()]}"
      f"   2022: {ratio.ratio.iloc[-1]:.2f}")

1950: 0.20   peak: 0.85 in 1991   2022: 0.65



Fig. 1: Income relative to the United States since 1950
The same ratio exists for every economy in the Maddison data. The file maddison_world.csv (from Chapter 3) has GDP per person in 2022 dollars for 169 economies, most of them every year from 1950 to 2022, and the region of each. Dividing every column by the U.S. column gives each economy’s income relative to the United States.
Each economy keeps one color in the chart below. On the website, a menu shows one group of economies at a time (two groups from the textbook’s discussion, then one per region), so the economies of each group need colors that differ from each other. The function group_colors hands them out.

LIGHT = {"#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"}      # too pale on white
PALETTE = []                                                                   # 44 colors
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT and c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # too close to the book's U.S. blue: used last


Python note. group_colors gives the countries their colors one at a time. For each country, the list used collects the colors already given to the countries shown together with it, and the country takes the first palette color that is not in used, preferring one that no country has yet. If every color is taken, it takes the one that used counts least often (.count), searching from the end of the palette (reversed). dict(fixed or {}) starts from a copy of the fixed colors (or an empty dictionary), and continue skips to the next country.


def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color} for the book's countries."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []                                       # the colors of the countries shown with `name`
        for group in groups:
            for other in group:
                if name in group and other in colors:
                    used.append(colors[other])
        free, unused = [], []
        for c in PALETTE:
            if c not in used:
                free.append(c)
                if c not in colors.values():
                    unused.append(c)                    # no country has this color yet: the best choice
        least = PALETTE[-1]
        for c in reversed(PALETTE):                     # no free color: the one used least, from the end
            if used.count(c) < used.count(least):
                least = c
        colors[name] = (unused + free + [least])[0]
    return colors


Python note. table.div(series, axis=0) divides every column of a table by the same Series, row by row (here year by year). MENU_GROUPS is a dictionary of lists: each key is a group’s name in the website menu, and MENU_GROUPS.values() gives the lists. Japan keeps its textbook color. SelectMultiple is a list from which you choose several items: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click. In the title, a if test else b gives a when the test is True and b otherwise, so the title names two economies and counts the rest.


maddison_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
world_gdppc = maddison_world.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
relative = world_gdppc.div(world_gdppc["United States"], axis=0).loc[1950:]    # each economy / U.S.

               "Catching up": ["Japan", "Republic of Korea", "Taiwan, Province of China", "China", "Singapore", "Ireland"],
               "Falling behind": ["Argentina", "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)", "South Africa", "Jamaica", "Haiti"]}
for region in sorted(maddison_world.region.unique()):
    MENU_GROUPS[region] = list(maddison_world[maddison_world.region == region].country.unique())
COLORS = group_colors(relative.columns, MENU_GROUPS.values(), {"Japan": TEAL})   # Japan keeps the textbook's color
print(f"{relative.shape[1]} economies; Japan in 2022: {relative.loc[2022, 'Japan']:.2f}")

168 economies; Japan in 2022: 0.65



def catch_up_title(countries):
    """The readout of the Lesson 2 chart: one economy's path in detail, or the start and end of several."""
    if len(countries) == 1:
        path = relative[countries[0]].dropna()
        return (f"{countries[0]}: {path.iloc[0]:.2f} of U.S. income in {path.index[0]}, peak {path.max():.2f} "
                f"in {path.idxmax()}, {path.iloc[-1]:.2f} in {path.index[-1]}")
    names = []
    for name in countries[:2]:
        path = relative[name].dropna()
        names.append(f"{name} {path.iloc[0]:.2f} → {path.iloc[-1]:.2f}")
    more = f" + {len(countries) - 2} more" if len(countries) > 2 else ""
    return "U.S. = 1, first year → 2022: " + ", ".join(names) + more


def catch_up_chart(countries=("Japan",)):
    """Lesson 2: GDP per person relative to the United States since 1950 (Maddison), for any economies."""
    if len(countries) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Choose at least one economy"))
    long = relative[list(countries)].reset_index().melt(id_vars="year", var_name="country", value_name="ratio")
    fig = px.line(long, x="year", y="ratio", color="country", hover_name="country", color_discrete_map=COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "ratio": "GDP per person, U.S. = 1"}, title=catch_up_title(countries))
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    if "Japan" in countries:
        fig.add_hline(y=0.75, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY, annotation_position="top left",
                      annotation_text="0.75, the textbook's steady-state guess for Japan")
    if long.ratio.max() <= 1.05:                           # keep the textbook's scale when everything fits
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 1.05], tickvals=[0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1])
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig


interact(catch_up_chart, countries=SelectMultiple(options=list(relative.columns), value=["Japan"], rows=8,
                                                  description="economies", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: every economy relative to the U.S., one group at a time
fig = catch_up_chart(tuple(relative.columns))
fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=[1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020])   # no "1950" next to the "0" in the corner

Sources. Data: Groningen Growth and Development Centre, Maddison Project Database 2023 (doi:10.34894/INZBF2; Bolt and van Zanden 2024), GDP per person (gdppc), converted to 2022 dollars. Prepared file: data/ch21/maddison_world.csv, a copy of data/ch03/maddison_world.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by the discussion in Chapter 21 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
On the website, the menu above the chart shows one group of economies at a time; click a name in the legend to hide it.
What to notice.

In 1950 Japan earned only a fifth of U.S. income (0.20). Far below its steady state, it grew more than twice as fast as the United States for four decades.
The ratio peaked at 0.85 in 1991. Since then Japan has grown more slowly than the United States, and the ratio has drifted down to 0.65 in 2022, a little below the textbook’s guess of 0.75.
Fast growth that fades as the gap closes is exactly what transition dynamics predicts. The same logic suggests that China’s fast growth will slow as it nears its own steady state.
Add other economies in the picker. South Korea rose from 0.07 of U.S. income in 1950 to 0.71 in 2022, an even larger catch-up than Japan’s, and Taiwan from 0.10 to 0.91. Not every economy catches up: Argentina fell from 0.52 to 0.31 and Venezuela from 0.56 to 0.09. Transition dynamics is about the gap to a country’s own steady state, and policies and institutions can move that steady state down as well as up.

Your turn. Compute China’s average growth rate from 2000 to 2022 and its income relative to the United States in 2022. Is China still far below the United States? Then choose China and India in the picker: the two were level around 1970. How many times India’s income was China’s in 2022?

section: Lesson 3: In the long run, money drives inflation and real forces drive output
text:
Lesson 3: In the long run, money drives inflation and real forces drive output
Goal. Recall the classical dichotomy and test the quantity theory across 165 economies.
In the long run, the real side of the economy (output, employment, wages) is set by real forces: the inputs and ideas of Lesson 1. The nominal side (the price level and inflation) is set by money. With a stable velocity of money, the quantity theory says that inflation equals money growth minus real GDP growth (equation 11),
\[\pi = g_M - g_Y.\]
This split between the real and the nominal sides is the classical dichotomy. It means that, in the long run, there is no trade-off between inflation and real GDP. You tested it in Chapter 8, Fig. 3 (U.S. decades) and Chapter 8, Fig. 4 (countries). Behind fast money growth there is usually a government that cannot borrow and prints money to pay its bills. Long-run unemployment, by contrast, depends on labor-market institutions (through the job-losing and job-finding rates of equation 10) such as hiring and firing costs and unemployment insurance, as in Chapter 7, Fig. 7.

section: Lesson 4: In the short run, there is a trade-off between inflation and output
text:
Lesson 4: In the short run, there is a trade-off between inflation and output
Goal. Recall the Phillips curve and estimate its slope from U.S. data.
In the short run, inflation is sticky: firms set prices partly by looking at past inflation, so inflation changes only gradually. What moves it is the state of the economy. The Phillips curve of Chapter 12 says (equation 14 in the Model overview above)
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o},\]
where \(\tilde{Y}_t\) is short-run output, the percent gap between actual and potential GDP, and \(\bar{o}\) is a price shock. A boom raises inflation and a slump lowers it. Sticky inflation also breaks the classical dichotomy in the short run: when the central bank raises the nominal interest rate, the real interest rate rises too (equation 12, with inflation stuck), which lowers investment and output (equation 13). In an open economy the higher interest rate also raises the exchange rate, which lowers net exports, as in Chapter 20, Fig. 4. See also Chapter 9, Fig. 7, Chapter 12, Fig. 4, Chapter 12, Fig. 7 and the inflation-output loops of Chapter 13, Fig. 17.

Fig. 2: The U.S. Phillips curve

Python note. .diff() subtracts the previous row from each row, so it turns inflation into the change in inflation (the first year has no previous year and becomes empty, NaN). np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits a straight line \(y = a + bx\) by least squares and returns the slope \(b\) first.


us = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig13-17.csv")            # U.S. output gap and CPI inflation, percent
us["change"] = us.inflation.diff()                      # Δπ_t = π_t − π_(t−1)
us = us.dropna()                                        # drop 1960, which has no previous year
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(us.output_gap, us.change, 1)
print(f"Estimated slope ν = {slope:.2f}, intercept {intercept:.2f}, from {len(us)} years ({us.year.min()}–{us.year.max()})")

Estimated slope ν = 0.35, intercept 0.10, from 65 years (1961–2025)



fig = px.scatter(us, x="output_gap", y="change", hover_name="year", trendline="ols",
                 labels={"output_gap": "Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", "change": "Change in inflation, Δπ (points)"},
                 title=f"Inflation tends to rise in booms and fall in slumps (slope ν = {slope:.2f})")
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=8))
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), selector=dict(mode="lines"))
fig.show()




                                
                                            




Sources. Data: via FRED, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real gross domestic product (GDPC1); Congressional Budget Office, Real potential gross domestic product (GDPPOT); U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer price index for all urban consumers (CPIAUCSL). Prepared file: data/ch21/fig13-17.csv, a copy of data/ch13/fig13-17.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by the discussion in Chapter 21 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The fitted slope is about 0.35: each percent of output above potential goes with inflation about a third of a point higher than the year before. That is close to the “about 1/3” you measured in Chapter 9.
This chart stays U.S.-only: its output gap is the Chapter 13 file, built from the CBO’s estimate of U.S. potential output. Output gaps for other countries exist (the OECD and the IMF estimate them), but they are not in this book’s data files.
The points are widely scattered. Price shocks \(\bar{o}\), such as the oil shocks of the 1970s and the 2021–2022 surge, move inflation far off the line (hover over the outliers).
The trade-off is short-run only. Over decades, Lesson 3’s classical dichotomy takes over again.

Your turn. Has the Phillips curve become flatter? Estimate the slope separately for 1961–1999 and for 2000–2025.


Hint

Filter the rows by year, for example early = us[us.year <= 1999], and repeat the np.polyfit line with the columns of early. Do the same for the later years.

section: Lesson 5: A credible central bank stabilizes output as well as inflation
text:
Lesson 5: A credible central bank stabilizes output as well as inflation
Goal. Measure what the Volcker disinflation cost in lost output, and see why credibility lowers that cost.
The Phillips curve gives a central bank one sure way to bring inflation down: a recession (equation 16). But if firms and workers believe that the bank will do whatever it takes, they lower their expected inflation on their own, and a smaller recession, or none, does the job. That is why credibility, transparency and explicit inflation targets matter so much. See the disinflation in Chapter 12, Fig. 12, the costless disinflation of Chapter 13, Fig. 20, and the low, stable inflation of the inflation-targeting era in Chapter 13, Fig. 19.
One way to measure the cost of a disinflation is the sacrifice ratio: the output lost, added up over the years of the recession (the sum of the negative values of \(\tilde{Y}\)), divided by the fall in inflation.

Python note. .clip(upper=0) replaces every positive number by 0, so that only the years below potential count as losses. A function can return several values at once, separated by commas.


annual = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig13-17.csv").set_index("year")    # the same file, with the year as the row label

def sacrifice_ratio(start, end):
    """Output lost (sum of negative Ỹ) per point of lower inflation between two years (Chapter 13)."""
    lost = -annual.loc[start:end, "output_gap"].clip(upper=0).sum()
    fall = annual.loc[start, "inflation"] - annual.loc[end, "inflation"]
    return lost, fall, lost / fall

lost, fall, ratio_v = sacrifice_ratio(1980, 1985)
print(f"1980–1985: inflation fell by {fall:.1f} points; output lost {lost:.1f} percent of a year's potential GDP")
print(f"Sacrifice ratio: {ratio_v:.1f} percent of output per point of inflation")
print(f"Average inflation 1970–1989: {annual.loc[1970:1989, 'inflation'].mean():.1f}%;  1993–2019: {annual.loc[1993:2019, 'inflation'].mean():.1f}%")

1980–1985: inflation fell by 10.0 points; output lost 16.4 percent of a year's potential GDP
Sacrifice ratio: 1.6 percent of output per point of inflation
Average inflation 1970–1989: 6.3%;  1993–2019: 2.3%


What to notice.

Between 1980 and 1985, U.S. inflation fell from 13.5 to 3.5 percent. The price was a deep recession: over the six years, output summed to 16.4 percent of a year’s potential GDP below potential, about 1.6 percent for each point of disinflation.
A fully credible announcement could, in the model of Chapter 13, have lowered inflation with much smaller losses. The Fed paid for its lost credibility of the 1970s.
Once credibility was rebuilt, inflation stayed low: it averaged 6.3 percent in 1970–1989 and 2.3 percent in 1993–2019.

Your turn. How sensitive is the sacrifice ratio to the years we pick? Compute it for 1980–1983 and for 1981–1986.


Hint

Call the function again with other years, for example sacrifice_ratio(1980, 1983). It returns three numbers; the last one is the ratio.

title: 21. Parting Thoughts
text:
Open questions at the frontier
Goal. Name the big questions macroeconomics has not yet answered, and measure one of them.
The textbook closes with problems that are still open. In short:

Why are investment and TFP so low in poor countries? Lesson 1 showed that TFP explains most of the income gap. Weak property rights and the rule of law are part of the answer, but why are they weak?
Which institutions work best? For producing and spreading ideas (patents, prizes, research funding), for sharing the gains from trade and capital flows (see the comparative advantage example of Chapter 19), and for running monetary systems: currency boards, a single currency, capital controls. See the policy trilemma of Chapter 20, Fig. 7 and the currency crises of Chapter 20, Fig. 8.
How do we measure potential output in real time? Mistaking a slowdown in potential for a recession leads to too much stimulus, as in Chapter 12, Fig. 13.
Why do bubbles form, and what should policymakers do about them? See the housing boom of Chapter 14, Fig. 8.
How will governments pay for aging populations and rising health spending? See the long-term projections of Chapter 18, Fig. 6 and health spending in Chapter 18, Fig. 8.

The third question has a recent twist: since about 2003, U.S. productivity has grown much more slowly than around 2000. Is the slowdown temporary or permanent? You met it in Chapter 6, Fig. 6 and Chapter 14, Fig. 11. We measure it with the BLS growth-accounting indexes of Chapter 6 and our growth_rate function from Lesson 2.

bls = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "growth_accounting.csv").set_index("year")   # indexes, 2017 = 100
for start, end in [(1995, 2003), (2003, 2025)]:
    print(f"{start}–{end}: output per hour {growth_rate(bls.output_per_hour, start, end):.1f}% a year, "
          f"TFP {growth_rate(bls.tfp, start, end):.1f}% a year")

1995–2003: output per hour 3.2% a year, TFP 1.5% a year
2003–2025: output per hour 1.8% a year, TFP 0.8% a year


What to notice.

Growth of output per hour fell from 3.2 percent a year in 1995–2003 to 1.8 percent since 2003, and TFP growth roughly halved, from 1.5 to 0.8 percent.
A difference of 1.4 points a year adds up: over 22 years it is a gap of about a third in output per hour.
Nobody knows yet whether this is a long pause between big inventions or a lasting change. It is one of the questions you might help answer.

Your turn. Put the recent slowdown in perspective: compute the same two growth rates for 1948–1973 and 1973–1995. Which earlier period does 2003–2025 resemble?


Hint

Add the two periods to the list in the for line, as (1948, 1973), (1973, 1995).

title: 21. Parting Thoughts
text:
Concluding remarks

Long run, levels: income per person depends on capital, skills, hours, ideas and TFP, and TFP explains most of the gap between rich and poor countries. Long run, growth: sustained growth comes from new ideas.
Transition dynamics: countries far below their steady state grow fast, as Japan did after 1950, and slow down as they catch up.
Classical dichotomy: in the long run, money growth drives inflation and real forces drive output, so there is no long-run trade-off between them.
Short run: sticky inflation creates a Phillips curve trade-off and lets monetary policy move real output; a credible central bank can lower inflation at a smaller cost.
The models in one place: the Model overview collected the book’s key results, from development accounting, equations (1) and (2), the Solow steady state (3) and transition dynamics (4), through growth from ideas (5) to (9), the natural rate of unemployment (10), the quantity theory (11) and the Fisher equation (12), to the short-run model, the IS curve (13), the Phillips curve (14), the AD curve (15) and the path of inflation (16), and the building blocks behind them: the Euler equation (17), the user cost of capital (18), the government’s budget constraint (19) and \(NX = S - I\), equation (20).
This is the last chapter. Many big questions remain open, from low TFP in poor countries to the productivity slowdown, bubbles and aging. Go back to any notebook, change a parameter or a data window, and start asking your own questions.

title: A. Google Colab, Python Coding, and Data Science Libraries
text:
A.1 What is Google Colab?
A notebook is a document that mixes three things: text (like this paragraph), code, and the results of that code (numbers, tables and charts). You read it from top to bottom. When you change a piece of code and run it again, its result updates right below it. That makes notebooks a good way to learn, because the explanation, the computation and the evidence sit side by side.
Google Colab (short for Colaboratory) is a free service from Google that runs notebooks inside your web browser. The notebooks follow the open Jupyter format (.ipynb files), which is the standard in data science. When you run a notebook in Colab, the code does not run on your laptop. It runs on a computer in one of Google’s data centres, called the runtime, and the results come back to your browser.

Why this book uses Colab

Nothing to install. Python and all the libraries this book needs (NumPy, pandas, Plotly and ipywidgets) are already installed in Colab. You only need a web browser and a Google account.
The same setup for everyone. Every reader runs the same versions of the same tools. Code that works for the author works for you, on Windows, macOS, Linux or a Chromebook.
Live models. In Colab, the model figures of the book get sliders and buttons. Move a slider and the model is solved again on the spot.
Easy to save and share. You can save your own copy of any notebook in Google Drive, and share it with a classmate or an instructor with a link, much like a Google Doc.
Data straight from the source. Each notebook reads its data files over the internet from the book’s GitHub repository, so you never have to download or upload a data file.



What to keep in mind

The runtime is temporary. When you close the notebook, or leave it idle for a while, Colab disconnects the runtime and forgets every variable. Free sessions also have a maximum length of several hours (see the Colab FAQ). This is not a problem for this book: click Runtime → Run all again and everything is rebuilt in a few seconds.
Your edits are not saved automatically in a notebook you opened from GitHub. Save your own copy in Google Drive first (Section A.2, step 6).
Free resources are shared. The free tier limits how many notebooks can run at the same time. Close a runtime properly when you are done (Section A.2, step 7).
You need to be online, because the runtime and the data both live on the internet.

section: A.2 A guided tour of Colab
text:
A.2 A guided tour of Colab
We now walk through a whole session with the Chapter 5 notebook, The Solow Growth Model. The screenshots were taken with Colab’s light theme. If your Colab looks dark, you can change it under Tools → Settings → Theme. The menus may also look slightly different, because Google updates Colab from time to time.
Step 1: open a notebook. Every chapter page on the book website has an Open in Colab badge under its title (Screenshot A.1). Click it. Colab opens the notebook in a new tab. If you are not signed in to a Google account, Colab asks you to sign in before you can run anything.

Screenshot A.1. The Open in Colab badge (in the orange box) on a chapter page of the book website.
Step 2: find your way around. Screenshot A.2 shows the Colab window. The numbers mark its main parts:

The menus. File saves and downloads; Runtime runs the code; Tools holds the settings and the keyboard shortcuts.
The toolbar. + Code and + Text add a new cell below the selected one. Run all runs the whole notebook.
The table of contents. Click a heading to jump to it. (If you do not see it, click the list icon at the top of the narrow bar on the far left.)
A text cell. Text cells hold the explanations. Double-click one to see, and edit, the text behind it.
Connect. It shows whether a runtime is attached. After you run a cell it turns into small RAM and Disk bars.
Files. The folder icon opens the files of the runtime. We rarely need it, because the data come from GitHub.


Screenshot A.2. The parts of the Colab window.
Step 3: run the whole notebook. Choose Runtime → Run all (Screenshot A.3), or press Ctrl+F9 (⌘+F9 on a Mac). Colab connects to a runtime and runs every code cell from top to bottom.

Screenshot A.3. Runtime → Run all.
Step 4: accept the warning. Because the notebook comes from GitHub and not from Google, Colab first shows the warning in Screenshot A.4. It is a sensible reminder: only run code from a source you trust. The book’s notebooks only read public data files and draw charts, so click Run anyway.

Screenshot A.4. The warning shown before a notebook from GitHub runs for the first time.
Step 5: read the code cells and move the sliders. After a cell has run, a number in square brackets appears at its left, with a green tick and the time it took (box 1 in Screenshot A.5). The number counts the runs, so it tells you the order in which cells were run. Some cells are folded into a title with a Show code link (box 2). These are helper cells and website versions: you must run them, but you do not need to read them.

Screenshot A.5. A code cell after running (1) and two folded helper cells (2).
Model figures come with live sliders in Colab (Screenshot A.6). Each time you move a slider, Python solves the model again and redraws the chart. Here a higher investment rate raises the steady-state capital stock \(k^*\) from 8.00 to 12.90.

Screenshot A.6. Live sliders in Colab: the investment rate has been moved from 0.40 to 0.55.
The book website cannot run Python. So every interactive figure also has a website version: the same chart, computed in advance for a few values of one parameter and joined by a Plotly slider under the chart (Screenshot A.7). On the website you can move that slider, hover over points and click legend entries, but only Colab lets you move every slider freely and change the code.

Screenshot A.7. The website version of the same figure, with one precomputed slider.
Step 6: save your own copy. A notebook opened from GitHub is read-only: Colab says “Save in GitHub to keep changes” next to its name, and your edits are lost when you close it. To keep your work, choose File → Save a copy in Drive (Screenshot A.8), or click Copy to Drive in the toolbar. Colab opens your copy in a new tab, and saves it to a “Colab Notebooks” folder in your Google Drive as you work.

Screenshot A.8. File → Save a copy in Drive.
Step 7: close the runtime when you are done. Closing the browser tab does not stop the runtime right away, and the free tier allows only a few runtimes at the same time. So before you close the tab, choose Runtime → Disconnect and delete runtime (Screenshot A.9). If Colab ever refuses to start because of “too many sessions”, choose Runtime → Manage sessions and end the sessions you no longer need.

Screenshot A.9. Runtime → Disconnect and delete runtime.
You can also open a notebook without the badge: go to https://colab.research.google.com, choose File → Open notebook, pick the GitHub tab and paste the address of the notebook on GitHub.
Your turn. Open the Chapter 5 notebook in Colab with its badge, run it, and move the investment rate s slider of Fig. 1. Then save a copy in your Drive and delete the runtime.


Hint

The badge is under the chapter title on the book website. In the Drive copy the notebook name starts with “Copy of”, and Colab says the notebook is saved instead of showing “Save in GitHub to keep changes”.

text:
A.3 Working in a notebook
A notebook is a list of cells. Text cells are written in Markdown, a simple way to format text (**bold**, *italic*, # Heading), and they can hold equations such as \(y = \bar{A}k^{1/3}\). Code cells hold Python. To run a code cell, click inside it and press Shift+Enter, or click the round ▶ button at its left. Try it on the cell below.

# A code cell: Python works out the expression and shows the result of the last line
2 + 3

5


Only the result of the last line of a cell is shown automatically. To show anything else, use print.

print("Hello, Colab!")
x = 10
x * 2          # the last line: its value is shown below the cell

Hello, Colab!


20


Screenshot A.10 shows the same idea in Colab: a new code cell with its result underneath. The number 70 in brackets means it was the seventieth cell run in that session.

Screenshot A.10. A new code cell and its result.

The order of cells matters
A notebook remembers every variable you have created, in the order in which you ran the cells, not the order in which they appear on the page. The next two cells work only if you run the first one before the second. If you open a notebook and run a cell in the middle, you may see a NameError (Section A.4.8), because a cell above it has not run yet. The cure is almost always Runtime → Run all, or Runtime → Run before followed by the cell itself.

interest_rate = 0.05          # create a variable...


interest_rate * 100           # ...and use it in a later cell

5.0




Useful keyboard shortcuts



Action
Windows / Linux

Shift+Enter
Shift+Enter

Ctrl+Enter
⌘+Enter

Ctrl+F9
⌘+F9

Ctrl+F8
⌘+F8

Show all shortcuts

⌘+M H



The Runtime menu also has Restart session. It clears every variable, which is useful when a notebook gets into a confusing state; after a restart, run the cells again from the top.


Getting help
help(...) prints the documentation of any Python function. Inside a code cell you can also type the name of a function followed by ( and wait a moment: Colab shows the arguments it takes.

help(round)

Help on built-in function round in module builtins:

    Round a number to a given precision in decimal digits.

    The return value is an integer if ndigits is omitted or None.  Otherwise
    the return value has the same type as the number.  ndigits may be negative.

title: A. Google Colab, Python Coding, and Data Science Libraries
text:
A.4 Python fundamentals
Python is a programming language that reads almost like English. This section covers the handful of ideas you need for the whole book. Every example comes from the economics of the book.

A.4.1 Numbers and arithmetic
Python works like a calculator. ** raises a number to a power, which is all you need for compound growth.

print(7 + 3, 7 - 3, 7 * 3, 7 / 3)     # add, subtract, multiply, divide
print(7 // 3, 7 % 3)                 # whole-number division and its remainder
print(2 ** 10)                       # a power: 2 to the 10th

10 4 21 2.3333333333333335
2 1
1024


An economy that grows at 2 percent a year is multiplied by 1.02 every year. After 35 years it is \(1.02^{35}\) times as large:

1.02 ** 35

1.9998895526624565


It has almost exactly doubled. This is the rule of 70 of Chapter 3 at work: at 2 percent a year, a variable doubles in about 70/2 = 35 years.


A.4.2 Variables
A variable is a name for a value. The = sign means “store the value on the right under the name on the left”. Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, but not spaces, and they are case-sensitive (GDP and gdp are different names). In this book the names follow the notation of the textbook, such as s, d, A, k_star and y_star.

y_1990 = 47713      # U.S. GDP per person in 1990, 2022 dollars (Maddison data, Section A.5)
y_2022 = 75459      # the same in 2022
growth_factor = y_2022 / y_1990
growth_factor

1.5815186636765661


From the growth factor we get the average annual growth rate: the rate \(g\) that turns \(y_{1990}\) into \(y_{2022}\) in 32 years, \(y_{2022} = y_{1990}(1+g)^{32}\), so \(g = (y_{2022}/y_{1990})^{1/32} - 1\).

g = growth_factor ** (1 / 32) - 1
g

0.014427636896671148




A.4.3 Types of values and f-strings
Every value has a type. The four you will meet most are whole numbers (int), decimal numbers (float), text (str, for string, written in quotes) and truth values (bool: True or False).

country = "United States"           # a string
years = 2022 - 1990                 # an int
g = growth_factor ** (1 / years) - 1    # a float
is_rich = y_2022 > 50000            # a bool, the result of a comparison
print(type(country), type(years), type(g), type(is_rich))

<class 'str'> <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'bool'>



Python note. An f-string is a string with an f before the opening quote. Python replaces each {...} inside it with the value of the expression. After a colon you can set the format: {g:.2%} shows g as a percentage with 2 decimals, {y:,.0f} shows y with a thousands separator and no decimals.


print(f"{country}: GDP per person grew from {y_1990:,.0f} to {y_2022:,.0f} dollars,")
print(f"or {g:.2%} a year on average over {years} years.")

United States: GDP per person grew from 47,713 to 75,459 dollars,
or 1.44% a year on average over 32 years.




A.4.4 Lists and loops
A list holds several values in order, inside square brackets. Python counts positions from 0, so countries[0] is the first element and countries[-1] the last one.

countries = ["United States", "Japan", "China"]
print(countries[0], "|", countries[-1], "|", len(countries), "countries")
countries.append("India")        # add an element at the end
countries

United States | China | 3 countries


['United States', 'Japan', 'China', 'India']


A for loop repeats the indented lines below it, once for each value. range(1, 6) gives the whole numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Note the colon at the end of the for line and the four spaces of indentation: they tell Python which lines belong to the loop.

# Compound growth, year by year: income grows by 2 percent each year
y = 100.0
for year in range(1, 6):
    y = y * 1.02
    print(f"year {year}: {y:.2f}")

year 1: 102.00
year 2: 104.04
year 3: 106.12
year 4: 108.24
year 5: 110.41


Loops are how the book simulates models over time. Here is the capital accumulation equation of the Solow model (Chapter 5), \(k_{t+1} = k_t + s\,k_t^{1/3} - d\,k_t\), run for 50 years. Each year, capital per person grows by investment and shrinks by depreciation.

s, d = 0.2, 0.1        # investment rate and depreciation rate
k = 1.0                # capital per person in year 0
path = [k]             # a list that will hold the whole path
for t in range(50):
    k = k + s * k ** (1 / 3) - d * k
    path.append(k)
k_star = (s / d) ** 1.5                 # the steady state of this model, (s/d)^(3/2)
print(f"k after 10 years: {path[10]:.3f}, after 50 years: {path[50]:.3f}")
print(f"steady state k* = {k_star:.3f}")

k after 10 years: 1.828, after 50 years: 2.761
steady state k* = 2.828


Capital rises quickly at first and then slows down as it approaches the steady state: the principle of transition dynamics of Chapter 5.


A.4.5 Making decisions with if
if, elif (else if) and else run different lines depending on a condition. The comparisons are >, <, >=, <=, == (equal; note the double sign) and != (not equal).

g_percent = 1.4                  # an average growth rate, in percent a year
if g_percent >= 3:
    label = "fast"
elif g_percent >= 1:
    label = "moderate"
else:
    label = "slow or negative"
print(f"Growth of {g_percent}% a year is {label}.")

Growth of 1.4% a year is moderate.




A.4.6 Dictionaries
A dictionary stores values under names (keys), inside curly braces. The book uses dictionaries for sets of parameters and for colors.

params = {"s": 0.2, "d": 0.1, "A": 1.0}
print(params["s"])               # look up a value by its key
params["s"] = 0.3                # change it
for key in params:
    print(key, "=", params[key])

0.2
s = 0.3
d = 0.1
A = 1.0




A.4.7 Functions
A function packs a few lines of code under a name, so you can reuse them. def starts the definition, the names in parentheses are its arguments, and return sends back the result. An argument with a default value (A=1.0) can be left out when you call the function. The text in triple quotes, the docstring, says what the function does. In the chapters each model equation becomes one short function like this one, the production function of Chapter 4.

def output(k, A=1.0):
    """Output per person in the production model of Chapter 4: y = A k^(1/3)."""
    return A * k ** (1 / 3)

print(output(8))           # k = 8 and the default A = 1
print(output(8, A=2.0))    # the same capital with twice the productivity

2.0
4.0


A second function turns the rule of 70 into code and uses a loop to try several growth rates.

def years_to_double(g_percent):
    """Rule of 70 (Chapter 3): something growing at g percent a year doubles in about 70/g years."""
    return 70 / g_percent

for g_percent in [1, 2, 3.5, 7]:
    print(f"growth of {g_percent}% a year: doubles in about {years_to_double(g_percent):.0f} years")

growth of 1% a year: doubles in about 70 years
growth of 2% a year: doubles in about 35 years
growth of 3.5% a year: doubles in about 20 years
growth of 7% a year: doubles in about 10 years




A.4.8 Libraries and errors
A library (or package) is a collection of functions that someone else has written. import loads one. The built-in math library, for example, has the natural logarithm, which gives the exact doubling time \(\ln 2 / \ln(1+g)\) to compare with the rule of 70. The rule is very close at low growth rates and a little off at high ones.

import math
for g_percent in [2, 7]:
    exact = math.log(2) / math.log(1 + g_percent / 100)
    rule = years_to_double(g_percent)
    print(f"At {g_percent}% a year: exactly {exact:.1f} years; rule of 70: {rule:.1f} years")

At 2% a year: exactly 35.0 years; rule of 70: 35.0 years
At 7% a year: exactly 10.2 years; rule of 70: 10.0 years


Everyone writes code with mistakes. When Python cannot run a line, it stops and prints an error message (a traceback). Read it from the bottom: the last line names the kind of error and what went wrong, and an arrow ----> points to the line that failed. Screenshot A.11 shows a typo in a variable name, which gives a NameError. Colab may also offer an Explain error button that asks Google’s AI assistant for an explanation. It can help, but read its answer critically.

Screenshot A.11. A NameError: the variable grwoth was never created (the name is growth).
You can also catch an error yourself with try ... except. Python tries the indented lines under try; if they fail with the named error, it runs the lines under except instead of stopping. The setup cell of every chapter uses this to run one line that only works in Colab.

try:
    "GDP in " + 2025          # text plus a number: Python refuses to guess what you mean
except TypeError as error:
    print("TypeError:", error)
print("GDP in " + str(2025))    # the fix: turn the number into text first

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
GDP in 2025

A.5.1 The setup cell
Every chapter starts with a setup cell like the one below. It loads the libraries, sets one light blue/green look for all charts, switches on Colab’s support for interactive charts, and stores the web address of the chapter’s data files in DATA_URL. You only need to run it once per session, but it must run before anything else, which Run all takes care of.

Python note. import numpy as np loads NumPy and gives it the nickname np, so we can write np.log instead of numpy.log. from ipywidgets import interact loads one function from a library, so we can write just interact. Names in capital letters, such as BLUE or DATA_URL, are a convention for constants: values we set once and never change.


# Libraries used in this appendix
import numpy as np                              # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                             # data tables
import plotly.express as px                     # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go               # charts built piece by piece (model figures)
import plotly.io as pio
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots       # several panels in one figure
from ipywidgets import interact, FloatSlider, Dropdown, SelectMultiple

# One light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)   # same size in Colab and on the website
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#c4651a", "#8e5ea2", "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full widget labels

# Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# The data files of this appendix live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/appA/"

Most chapters also have one or two folded helper cells right after the setup cell. They build the website versions of the interactive figures. Run them and move on.


Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig




A.5.2 NumPy: math on whole arrays
A NumPy array is like a list of numbers, but you can do math on all its elements at once, without a loop. np.linspace(start, stop, n) makes n evenly spaced numbers. The chapters use it to make the x-values of every model curve.

k = np.linspace(0, 10, 6)        # 6 evenly spaced values from 0 to 10
print(k)
print(k ** (1 / 3))              # the cube root of every element at once
print(output(k))                 # our function from A.4.7 works on a whole array too

A.5.4 Plotly Express: charts from data tables
Plotly Express (px) draws a whole chart from a DataFrame in one call: you name the table and say which column goes on each axis and which column sets the colors. The charts are interactive. Hover over a line to read its values, drag to zoom, double-click to zoom back out, and click a legend entry to hide or show that country.

fig = px.line(panel, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", log_y=True,
              labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)",
                      "country": ""},
              title="GDP per person in seven economies, 1870-2022")
fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000])
fig.show()




                                
                                            




Sources. Data: Maddison Project Database 2023 (Bolt and van Zanden 2024), GDP per person converted to 2022 dollars. Prepared file: data/appA/maddison_panel.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by the discussion of long-run growth in Chapter 3 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Python note. log_y=True puts the y-axis on a ratio (log) scale: equal distances mean equal percentage changes, so a straight line means a constant growth rate. Chapter 3 explains why economists prefer it for long-run data. tickvals chooses which numbers label the axis.

A scatter plot with px.scatter shows how two variables relate. hover_name="country" puts the country name in the box that appears when you hover over a point, and color="region" gives each region its own color. We first drop Venezuela, whose PWT GDP per person after 2017 is not plausible: hyperinflation broke the price data (Chapter 3 discusses this).

          "region": "Region"}

                 hover_name="country", log_x=True, labels=labels,
                 title="Countries that grew faster since 1960 are richer today")
fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=[0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1])
fig.show()

Prepared files: data/appA/fig3-7.csv and data/appA/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 3.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
animation_frame turns a column into a play button and a slider: each frame of the animation shows the rows for one value of that column. range_y fixes the y-axis, so that the bars can grow from frame to frame.

             labels={"country": "", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)", "year": "Year"},

A.5.5 Plotly graph objects: charts built piece by piece
For model figures we want full control: which curves, which colors, which labels. Plotly graph objects (go) build a chart step by step. go.Figure() starts an empty chart, each add_trace adds one curve, and update_layout sets the title and the axes. Here are two production functions \(y = \bar{A}k^{1/3}\) from Chapter 4, drawn with the output function of Section A.4.7.

k = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=output(k), mode="lines", name="A = 1",
                         line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=output(k, A=1.5), mode="lines", name="A = 1.5",
                         line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dash")))
fig.update_layout(title="Higher productivity A shifts the production function up",
                  xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 10],
                             tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]),
                  yaxis=dict(title="Output per person, y", range=[0, 3.5]))
fig.show()




                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from the production model of Chapter 4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
make_subplots puts several panels side by side. The two panels below show the same data on a linear scale and on a ratio scale. On the linear scale, U.S. growth seems to speed up over time. On the ratio scale, the U.S. line is close to straight: its percentage growth has been fairly steady. China’s line bends upward after 1980.

Python note. The loop runs once for each (name, color) pair in the list. row= and col= say which panel a trace goes to, and showlegend=False keeps each country only once in the legend.


fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("Linear scale", "Ratio scale"))
for name, color in [("United States", BLUE), ("China", TEAL)]:
    one = panel[panel["country"] == name]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=one["year"], y=one["gdppc"], mode="lines", name=name,
                             line=dict(color=color)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=one["year"], y=one["gdppc"], mode="lines", name=name,
                             line=dict(color=color), showlegend=False), row=1, col=2)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="GDP per person (2022 dollars)", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(type="log", tickvals=[1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000], row=1, col=2)
fig.update_layout(title="The same two series on two scales")
fig.show()




                                
                                            




Sources. Data: Maddison Project Database 2023 (Bolt and van Zanden 2024). Prepared file: data/appA/maddison_panel.csv. Chart: inspired by the discussion of ratio scales in Chapter 3 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

A.5.6 ipywidgets: sliders and menus
ipywidgets turns the arguments of a function into controls. interact(f, ...) draws one control for each argument and calls f again every time you move one. This is how every model figure in the book becomes interactive: we write a function that returns a figure, and hand it to interact.

def production_figure(A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Production function y = A k^alpha (Chapter 4), with fixed axes so changes are visible."""
    k = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=k ** (1 / 3), mode="lines", name="Baseline: A = 1, α = 1/3",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=A * k ** alpha, mode="lines", name="Your production function",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Output per person at k = 8: y = {A * 8 ** alpha:.2f} (baseline 2.00)",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 10],
                                 tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Output per person, y", range=[0, 7]))
    return fig


Python note. FloatSlider makes a slider for decimal numbers, from min to max in steps of step, starting at value. Dropdown makes a menu; each option is a pair ("label shown", value). style=WIDE shows the whole description. The ; at the end hides an extra line of text.


A_slider = FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.1,
                       description="productivity A", style=WIDE)
alpha_menu = Dropdown(options=[("1/4", 0.25), ("1/3", 1 / 3), ("1/2", 0.5)], value=1 / 3,
                      description="capital exponent α", style=WIDE)
interact(production_figure, A=A_slider, alpha=alpha_menu);



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: the production function with a precomputed slider for A
slider_figure(production_figure, "A", [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0], start=1.0, label="productivity A")





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from the production model of Chapter 4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice. Doubling \(\bar{A}\) doubles output at every level of capital. A larger exponent \(\alpha\) makes the curve bend less, so diminishing returns to capital set in more slowly.

A.6 Putting it together: which economies grew fastest after 1990?
Our mini project uses every tool of this appendix. The question: which economies raised their GDP per person fastest between 1990 and 2023, and which fell behind? The data come from the Penn World Table, with one row per economy and year from 1950 to 2023.

What to notice.

China grew at 7.6 percent a year: at that pace income doubles about every nine years, and it rose more than tenfold in 33 years.
Guyana tops the list because of oil: production from its offshore oil fields began in 2019. Fast growth of GDP per person can come from a resource boom, not only from capital and ideas.
Twelve economies were poorer in 2023 than in 1990, among them Zimbabwe, Tajikistan and the United Arab Emirates. In the Emirates, total GDP grew about 3.7 times, but the population grew 5.6 times, from 1.9 to 10.6 million, so GDP per person fell.

Step 4: an interactive chart. Our last function draws GDP per person over time for any economies you pick, on a ratio scale. In Colab, hold Ctrl (⌘ on a Mac) and click names in the list to choose several.

def growth_figure(names=("China", "United States", "Zimbabwe")):
    """GDP per person since 1950 for the chosen economies, on a ratio scale."""
    chosen = pwt[pwt["country"].isin(names)]

                  range_x=[1950, 2023], range_y=[80, 400000],     # every value fits
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdp_pc": "GDP per person (2021 dollars, ratio scale)",
                          "country": ""},
                  title=f"GDP per person since 1950: {len(names)} economies")
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000, 300000])
    return fig

Most numbers start life at a national statistical office, such as the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) or Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). FRED, the World Bank, the IMF and the others collect these numbers, check them and put them in one place. That is why the same series often appears in several sources.

Four ways to get data into Python









Way
Example in this appendix
Good
Watch out




1. A specialized library for one source
wbgapi (World Bank), imfp (IMF), fredapi (FRED), eurostat
easy, with search functions and tidy tables
one library per source; libraries change over time


2. A general library that speaks SDMX, a data standard shared by many agencies
sdmx1 for the ECB, IMF, OECD and Eurostat
the same code for many agencies
you must learn each dataset’s “key” (its dimensions)


3. A collection of many sources in one place
dbnomics
one library and one search website for many providers
its copy can lag a few months behind the original


4. Read a file straight from its web address
FRED CSV, Penn World Table, Maddison, Our World in Data
works for any file on the internet, with pandas alone
you must find the address, and it can change





Three ideas to keep in mind

Series codes. Every series has a short code. UNRATE is the U.S. unemployment rate in FRED, and NY.GDP.PCAP.KD is GDP per person in constant dollars at the World Bank. Codes are precise; names are not. The first step is always to find the right code, using the source’s website or a search function.
Units. Read the units before you compute anything: percent or fraction, dollars or thousands of dollars, current or constant prices, monthly or annual, seasonally adjusted or not.
Vintages. Statistical offices revise their numbers as better information arrives. The GDP growth rate you download today for 2024 may differ from the one published in 2025. Each release is a vintage. Always write down when you downloaded your data.

B.3 FRED
FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data) is the first place to look for U.S. macroeconomic data, and it has many international series too. Every series has a page on the FRED website. For example, the U.S. unemployment rate lives at fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNRATE: the code UNRATE is the last part of the address. To find a code, type what you want in the search box of the FRED website.
FRED gives you three routes into Python. We try all three.

B.3.1 Way 4: read the CSV file of a series
Every FRED series can be downloaded as a CSV file (a plain text table with values separated by commas) from an address that ends with its code. pd.read_csv reads a CSV file, and it accepts a web address as easily as a file on your computer. This route needs no extra library and no registration.

Python note. parse_dates=["observation_date"] tells pandas that this column holds dates, so that charts put them on a time axis. .tail() shows the last five rows of a table, .head() the first five.


# The address of a FRED series: a fixed beginning plus the series code
url = "https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=UNRATE"
unrate = pd.read_csv(url, parse_dates=["observation_date"])
unrate.tail()

We will download several series, so we wrap these lines in a small function. Give it a code, and it returns the table, with the date column renamed to the shorter date.

def read_fred(code):
    """Download one FRED series as a table with the columns date and <code>."""
    url = "https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=" + code
    table = pd.read_csv(url, parse_dates=["observation_date"])
    return table.rename(columns={"observation_date": "date"})

The consumer price index (CPI) is a price level. Inflation is its growth rate. With monthly data, the inflation rate over the past 12 months is
\[\text{inflation}_t = \left(\frac{\text{CPI}_t}{\text{CPI}_{t-12}} - 1\right) \times 100 .\]
In pandas, .shift(12) moves a column down by 12 rows, so each row can see the value from 12 months earlier.

cpi["inflation"] = (cpi["CPIAUCSL"] / cpi["CPIAUCSL"].shift(12) - 1) * 100

The World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI) are the standard source for comparing countries over time. The library wbgapi, written by the World Bank, reads them. We import it with the nickname wb.
The first job is to find the code of an indicator. wb.series.info(q=...) searches the indicator names.

import wbgapi as wb

wb.series.info(q="GDP per capita")

B.5 IMF: imfp
The International Monetary Fund publishes the World Economic Outlook (WEO) twice a year, in April and October. Its database has GDP growth, inflation, unemployment and government debt for about 190 countries, and, unlike most sources, forecasts for the next five years. The library imfp reads it, and every other dataset on the IMF’s data portal, in four steps:

imf_get_dataflows(): which datasets exist?
imf_get_datastructure(dataset): which dimensions does a dataset have (country, indicator, frequency)?
imf_get_codelists(dimension, dataset): which codes can each dimension take?
imf_get(dataset, {dimension: codes}): download the data.


import imfp

# Step 1: the IMF's datasets; .str.contains keeps the rows whose name contains a word
datasets = imfp.imf_get_dataflows()
print(len(datasets), "datasets")
datasets[datasets["name"].str.contains("World Economic Outlook")][["id", "name"]]
