text:
C.13 Describing macro data: averages, volatility, trends and cycles
Goal. Summarize a series with a few numbers, measure how two series move together, and separate a long-run trend from short-run fluctuations.

Averages and volatility
The mean is the average, the median the middle value, and the standard deviation measures how much a series moves around its mean, its volatility. pandas computes them all with .describe().

growth_stats = nipa[nipa["year"] >= 1930][["year", "g_real"]]
print(growth_stats["g_real"].describe().round(2))
early = growth_stats[growth_stats["year"].between(1950, 1984)]["g_real"]
late = growth_stats[growth_stats["year"].between(1985, 2025)]["g_real"]
print(f"Standard deviation of real GDP growth: {early.std():.2f} points in 1950-1984, {late.std():.2f} in 1985-2025")

count    96.00
mean      3.28
std       4.74
min     -12.90
25%       1.87
50%       3.04
75%       4.97
max      18.89
Name: g_real, dtype: float64
Standard deviation of real GDP growth: 2.78 points in 1950-1984, 1.66 in 1985-2025


Real GDP growth became much less volatile after the mid-1980s, a change economists call the Great Moderation (Chapter 13 discusses one explanation, better monetary policy), though the 2008–2009 and 2020 recessions interrupted it.


Correlation: the Phillips curve in the data
The correlation coefficient measures how closely two series move together, from \(-1\) (exactly opposite) to \(+1\) (exactly together). The Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi_t=\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\) (12.6) predicts that inflation rises when output is above potential. A least-squares line fitted through the points estimates the slope \(\bar{\nu}\).

gap_inflation = potential[["year", "gap_percent"]].merge(cpi[["year", "inflation"]], on="year")
gap_inflation["change_in_inflation"] = gap_inflation["inflation"].diff()
gap_inflation = gap_inflation[gap_inflation["year"] >= 1950]
correlation = gap_inflation["gap_percent"].corr(gap_inflation["change_in_inflation"])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(gap_inflation["gap_percent"], gap_inflation["change_in_inflation"], 1)
print(f"Correlation: {correlation:.2f};  fitted slope ν = {slope:.2f}")

Correlation: 0.37;  fitted slope ν = 0.34



Python note. .merge(other, on="year") joins two tables row by row on the year. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits a straight line \(y=\text{slope}\cdot x+\text{intercept}\) by least squares and returns the two numbers.


phillips_fig = px.scatter(gap_inflation, x="gap_percent", y="change_in_inflation", hover_name="year",
                          trendline="ols", trendline_color_override=TEAL,
                          labels={"gap_percent": "short-run output, Ỹ (percent)",
                                  "change_in_inflation": "change in CPI inflation (points)"},
                          title=f"U.S. 1950–2025: inflation tends to rise when output is above potential "
                                f"(corr. {correlation:.2f})")
phillips_fig




                                
                                            




Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPCA), via FRED; Congressional Budget Office, Real Potential Gross Domestic Product (GDPPOT), via FRED; MeasuringWorth, The Annual Consumer Price Index for the United States. Prepared files: data/appC/fig9-2.csv and data/appC/us_cpi.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 9.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.; our own chart, built from updated data.


Trend and cycle
Chapter 9 splits GDP into a long-run trend (potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\)) and short-run fluctuations (\(\tilde{Y}_t\)). Potential output cannot be observed, so it has to be estimated. Two simple statistical methods:

A straight line through the logs. Fit \(\ln y_t=\alpha+\beta t\). The slope \(\beta\) is the trend growth rate (in log points), and the distance to the line is the cycle.
The Hodrick–Prescott (HP) filter. It draws a smooth curve through the data, trading off closeness to the data against smoothness. The parameter \(\lambda\) sets the smoothness; 100 is a common choice for annual data. It lives in statsmodels, a statistics library that comes with Colab.


trend_slope, trend_intercept = np.polyfit(gdp_pc["year"], np.log(gdp_pc["gdppc"]), 1)
print(f"Trend growth of U.S. GDP per person, 1870-2025: {100 * trend_slope:.2f} log points a year")

from statsmodels.tsa.filters.hp_filter import hpfilter      # imported here, where we first use it
postwar = potential[potential["year"] >= 1950].copy()
cycle, trend = hpfilter(np.log(postwar["gdp_actual"]), lamb=100)
postwar["gap_hp"] = 100 * cycle                              # percent deviation from the HP trend
print(f"Correlation of the HP gap with the CBO gap: {postwar['gap_hp'].corr(postwar['gap_log']):.2f}")

Trend growth of U.S. GDP per person, 1870-2025: 1.95 log points a year
Correlation of the HP gap with the CBO gap: 0.80



gaps_long = postwar.melt(id_vars="year", value_vars=["gap_log", "gap_hp"], var_name="method", value_name="gap")
gaps_long["method"] = gaps_long["method"].map({"gap_log": "CBO potential output", "gap_hp": "HP filter (λ = 100)"})
gaps_fig = px.line(gaps_long, x="year", y="gap", color="method",
                   labels={"year": "", "gap": "output gap (percent of trend)"},
                   title="Two estimates of the U.S. output gap move together, but differ in size")
gaps_fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
gaps_fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", legend=dict(x=0.99, xanchor="right", y=0.02, yanchor="bottom"))
gaps_fig




                                
                                            




Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPCA), via FRED; Congressional Budget Office, Real Potential Gross Domestic Product (GDPPOT), via FRED. Prepared file: data/appC/fig9-2.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 9.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The fitted trend, about 2 log points a year, is close to the average growth rate of Section C.4.
The points of the Phillips-curve scatter are widely spread, so the correlation is positive but far from 1: other forces, such as oil prices and expectations, also move inflation (Chapters 12 and 13).
The HP gap and the CBO gap rise and fall together, but the HP trend follows the data more closely, so its gaps are smaller and it sees less of a slump after 2008. Every estimate of potential output is a model, not a fact.

Your turn. Recompute the HP gap with a much smoother trend, \(\lambda=6{,}400\), and with a very flexible one, \(\lambda=10\). How does the volatility of the gap (its standard deviation) change?


Hint

Call hpfilter(np.log(postwar["gdp_actual"]), lamb=6400) and compute (100 * cycle).std() for each value of \(\lambda\). A smoother trend (larger \(\lambda\)) leaves more of the movement to the cycle.

24  C. Math Review for Macroeconomics

title: C. Math Review for Macroeconomics
text:
Concluding remarks

Most of the math in macroeconomics is about growth and change: percent changes, compound growth, logs, growth rates and the growth rules, and the approximations that make them simple. They work well for the small rates of normal times and break down in high inflation.
Derivatives give marginal products, elasticities and the first-order conditions of firms and households. Systems of equations give equilibria, and difference equations describe how capital, unemployment, inflation and public debt move from one year to the next; their stability depends on whether \(|a|<1\).
Present value turns streams of future payments into one number today: the value of a working life, a bond, a stock or an investment project.
Python offers three complementary ways to do this math: NumPy computes, SymPy does the algebra and calculus with letters, and SciPy solves, optimizes and simulates when there is no formula.
Every chapter of this book uses these tools. When an equation in a chapter looks hard, come back to the section of this appendix that covers it, and try it in code.
